title: Japanese N4
description: The second step in Japanese, from N5 to JLPT N4. Grammar lessons cover explaining with んです, the potential and volitional forms, plans and decisions, giving and receiving and doing favours, transitive and intransitive verbs, the conditionals と, ば, たら and なら, must and need not, seeming and hearsay, the passive, causative and causative-passive, and respectful and humble keigo. About 700 new words build on the 860 from the kana and N5 courses for about 1,500 in all, learned through typed vocabulary reviews with pitch accent, conjugation drills and sentence building; about 180 new kanji (about 280 in all) are learned through notecards, tracing and inside words, with furigana you can turn off. Requires Japanese N5.
author: Erudior

modules.title: Giving, receiving and getting things done
Polite Japanese and the N4 exam

lessons.title: Explaining and joining: 〜んです and て forms
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Welcome to N4. You finished N5 able to say what you do, what things are like and what you
want, in polite and casual Japanese. This course takes you to the level of the JLPT N4: about
700 new words, about 180 new kanji, and the grammar that lets you explain, plan, give and
receive, set conditions, guess and be polite.

This first lesson is about two small things you'll hear in almost every conversation. The
first is 〜んです, the way Japanese speakers explain: "it's that…", "you see…", "what's
happened?". The second is the て form of adjectives and nouns, which joins descriptions and
gives reasons: しずかで, {近|ちか}くて. Along the way you'll meet the casual 〜てる and the
pattern {町|まち}はみどりが{多|おお}い. The theme is your town and the people next door.

## How this course is written

A few things change from N5. None of them needs learning; they just look different.

- No spaces. Japanese is written without spaces between words, and so is this whole
  course, as N5 was from module 3.
- More kanji. A word is written with **[[kanji]]** whenever all its kanji are on the course
  list (N5's 102 plus the 177 you learn here). So words you knew in kana now appear in kanji:
  まち becomes {町|まち}, しゃしん becomes {写真|しゃしん}. Every kanji has **[[furigana]]**, and you can
  switch them off. Grammar words stay in kana (こと, ところ, つもり, 〜ている…).
- Pitch marks. Japanese words have a **[[pitch accent]]**: each beat is high or low, and
  some words differ only in pitch. Vocabulary cards now show it after you answer, and lessons
  mark it where it matters, as a line over the high beats with a tick where the pitch falls:
  {町|まち:2}, {森|もり:0}. Lesson 05h1 explains how to read the marks; until then you can
  ignore them, or turn them off next to the furigana switch.
- New drills. The Vocabulary tab has conjugation drills: the app picks one of your verbs
  or adjectives and asks for a form ("polite past negative", "て form"). Each new form joins
  the drills in the lesson that teaches it. Some questions are sentence builders, where you put
  word tiles in order. And each lesson's kanji can be traced stroke by stroke.

## Explaining: 〜んです

Compare these two answers to "Why aren't you eating?":

おなかがいっぱいです。 — I'm full.
おなかがいっぱいなんです。 — I'm full, you see. / It's that I'm full.

Both are correct. The second presents the fact as an explanation of something the listener
has noticed or asked about. That ん is a short form of の, the **[[explanatory の]]**, and the
pattern is the **[[plain form]]** + んです (in writing, のです).

| | Plain form | + んです |
|---|---|---|
| verb | {行|い}く / {行|い}かない / {行|い}った | {行|い}くんです / {行|い}かないんです / {行|い}ったんです |
| い-adjective | {高|たか}い / {高|たか}かった | {高|たか}いんです / {高|たか}かったんです |
| な-adjective | しずかだ | しずかなんです |
| noun | {休|やす}みだ | {休|やす}みなんです |

The one surprise is in the last two rows: だ turns into な before ん ({休|やす}みなんです, not
×{休|やす}みだんです). In the past, だった stays: {休|やす}みだったんです.

### Giving reasons and background

Use 〜んです when you explain why something is the way it is, especially when the other
person is waiting for a reason.

すみません、{明日|あした}は{行|い}けないんです。{用事|ようじ}があるんです。 — Sorry, I can't go tomorrow. I have something to do.
（{行|い}けない is "can't go"; you'll learn this form in lesson 2.）
{道|みち}にまよったんです。{駅|えき}はどこですか。 — I've got lost, you see. Where's the station?
じつは、{来月|らいげつ}{国|くに}に{帰|かえ}るんです。 — Actually, I'm going back to my country next month.

### Asking for an explanation

A question with 〜んですか asks about something you've noticed: you see a friend looking
pale, a bag of shopping, a suitcase in the hall.

どうしたんですか。 — What's the matter? / What happened?
ぐあいが{悪|わる}いんですか。 — Are you feeling unwell?
どこに{行|い}くんですか。 — Where are you off to? (You can see they're going somewhere.)

"Why" questions nearly always take it: どうして{日本語|にほんご}を{勉強|べんきょう}しているんですか (Why
are you studying Japanese?). どうして〜ますか without ん sounds abrupt, almost like a
complaint.

### Opening a request: 〜んですが…

Start with the background, put が or けど after it, and stop. The listener understands that a
request is coming and often offers help before you ask.

この{町|まち}の{地図|ちず}がほしいんですが…… — I'd like a map of this town…
{駅|えき}に{行|い}きたいんですけど…… — I want to get to the station…
すみません、ちょっと{聞|き}きたいんですが。 — Excuse me, I'd like to ask something.

### Casual: 〜の？ and 〜んだ

In casual speech the question is just の with a rising voice, and the statement is んだ.
Nouns and な-adjectives keep the な.

どうしたの？ — What's wrong?
どこ{行|い}くの？ — Where are you going?
{明日|あした}、テストなんだ。 — I've got a test tomorrow, you see.
うん、ちょっとつかれたんだ。 — Yeah, I'm a bit tired.

A statement that
ends in plain の (テストなの) sounds soft and is heard more from women and children; んだ is
used by everyone.

### When not to use it

〜んです adds "this is the explanation". For a plain fact that explains nothing, it sounds
odd or pushy: {私|わたし}はエレナです is an introduction; {私|わたし}はエレナなんです sounds as if
someone doubted it. Use it when there's something to explain, not on every sentence.

## The て form of adjectives and nouns

In N5 you joined verbs with the **[[て form]]**. Adjectives and nouns have one too, and it does the
same two jobs: "and" (joining descriptions) and a light "so" (a reason).

| | Dictionary form | て form |
|---|---|---|
| い-adjective | {近|ちか}い, {古|ふる}い | {近|ちか}くて, {古|ふる}くて |
| いい | いい | よくて |
| な-adjective | しずか, べんり | しずかで, べんりで |
| noun | {学生|がくせい}, {雨|あめ} | {学生|がくせい}で, {雨|あめ}で |

**[[い-adjectives]]** drop い and add くて; いい uses its old stem よ, as in よくない. **[[な-adjectives]]** and
nouns take で, the て form of だ.

この{町|まち}はしずかで、きれいです。 — This town is quiet and pretty.
{駅|えき}が{近|ちか}くて、べんりです。 — The station is close, so it's convenient.
{兄|あに}は{大学生|だいがくせい}で、{妹|いもうと}は{高校生|こうこうせい}です。 — My big brother is at university and my little sister is in high school.
このアパートは{新|あたら}しくて、{広|ひろ}くて、{安|やす}いです。 — This flat is new, spacious and cheap.

Only the last word shows the tense and politeness: しずかで、きれいでした (it was quiet and
pretty). When two qualities pull in opposite directions, join them with けど or が instead:
{安|やす}いけど、{古|ふる}いです (it's cheap but old).

The adjective て form (くて, で) now joins your conjugation drills.

### Because not: なくて

The **[[ない form]]** has a て form too: ない → なくて. It means "not …, and" or "because not …".

{車|くるま}がなくて、こまっています。 — I don't have a car, so I'm stuck.
{今日|きょう}は{雨|あめ}がふらなくて、よかったです。 — It was good that it didn't rain today.
このアパートは{駅|えき}から{近|ちか}くなくて、ちょっとふべんです。 — This flat isn't close to the station, so it's a bit inconvenient.

You also know 〜ないでください (please don't). That ないで means "without doing" and goes with
actions; なくて gives a reason or a state. You'll meet ないで properly in lesson 10; for now:
a reason → なくて.

## Verb て for cause: 〜てすみません, 〜てよかった

The verb て form can also give the cause of a feeling: "I'm glad because…", "sorry for…".
The second half is a feeling or reaction, never a request or a plan.

おそくなって、すみません。 — Sorry I'm late. (literally "I became late, sorry")
{友|とも}だちから{手紙|てがみ}が{来|き}て、うれしかったです。 — A letter came from a friend, and I was so happy.
ニュースを{見|み}て、びっくりしました。 — I was surprised when I saw the news.
{母|はは}の{声|こえ}を{聞|き}いて、{安心|あんしん}しました。 — I was relieved to hear my mother's voice.
{日本|にほん}に{来|き}て、よかったです。 — I'm glad I came to Japan.

The same pattern with an adjective: {家族|かぞく}がいなくて、さびしいです (I miss my family;
literally "my family isn't here, so I'm lonely"). But not: ×{雨|あめ}がふって、{出|で}かけないで
ください. A request after a reason needs から: {雨|あめ}がふっているから、{出|で}かけないでください.

## Casual 〜てる

In casual speech the い of 〜ている almost always drops: {住|す}んでいる → {住|す}んでる,
{知|し}っている → {知|し}ってる, {読|よ}んでいる → {読|よ}んでる. It is the same form, just said
faster.

どこに{住|す}んでるの？ — Where do you live?
あの{店|みせ}、{知|し}ってる？ — Do you know that shop?

You can say it to friends; in writing and polite speech, keep 〜ている/〜ています.

## A has a lot of B: AはBが〜

Japanese often describes a place or person with two particles: は marks what you're talking
about, and が marks the part or aspect being described.

この{町|まち}はみどりが{多|おお}いです。 — This town has a lot of greenery. (literally "As for this town, greenery is plentiful.")
{村|むら}は{空気|くうき}がきれいです。 — The air in the village is clean.
{東京|とうきょう}は{人口|じんこう}が{多|おお}いです。 — Tokyo has a large population.
{兄|あに}はせが{高|たか}いです。 — My brother is tall.

English needs "has" or a possessive; Japanese doesn't. This is also why {町|まち}のみどりが
{多|おお}いです sounds less natural as a description of the town: the town is the topic.

## Kanji

Seven kanji for the place where you live. **[[On'yomi]]** (readings from Chinese) are in katakana, **[[kun'yomi]]** (native readings) in hiragana, with
the **[[okurigana]]** (the kana that follow a kanji) in brackets: ちか(い) means the kanji is read ちか in {近|ちか}い.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 町 | town | チョウ | まち | 7 | {町|まち}, 〜{町|ちょう} (in addresses) |
| 村 | village | ソン | むら | 7 | {村|むら}, {村田|むらた} (a family name) |
| 田 | rice field | デン | た, だ | 5 | {田|た}んぼ, {田中|たなか} (a family name) |
| 森 | forest | シン | もり | 12 | {森|もり} |
| 近 | near | キン | ちか(い) | 7 | {近|ちか}い, {近|ちか}く, {近所|きんじょ} |
| 遠 | far | エン | とお(い) | 13 | {遠|とお}い, {遠|とお}く |
| 地 | ground, land | チ, ジ | — | 6 | {地図|ちず}, {土地|とち} |

Memory notes:

- 町 is a rice field (田) with a road on the right, like a hook-shaped street: fields with a road become a town.
- 村 is a tree (木) beside a hand with a dot for a measure: a few trees and measured plots, a village.
- 田 is a field seen from above, divided into four plots by paths.
- 森 is three trees (木) together: a whole forest.
- 近 and 遠 both sit on the "road" shape ⻌ that runs under them from the left: both are about
  distance along a road. 近 has an axe on the road, close enough to reach; 遠 has a long
  robe, a long way to walk.
- 地 is earth (土) on the left: ground, land, and the 地 of {地図|ちず} (a picture of the land).

{田|た}んぼ is written with one kanji and kana. 田 is read だ inside some names ({山田|やまだ}).
{近所|きんじょ} is a word with 近 + 所 (place, lesson 4): "the near place", your neighbourhood.

```trace
町村田森近遠地
```

## Dialogue: the new neighbour

Elena has just moved in. She knocks on the door of her neighbour, Ms Murata.

```dialogue
# The new neighbour
エレナ: すみません、{村田|むらた}さん。ちょっといいですか。
= Excuse me, Ms Murata. Have you got a moment?
{村田|むらた}: はい。どうしたんですか。
= Of course. What's up?
エレナ: {先週|せんしゅう}ここにひっこしたんですが、ごみの{日|ひ}が{分|わ}からないんです。
= I moved in here last week, but I don't know which days the rubbish goes out.
{村田|むらた}: ああ、もえるごみは{月曜日|げつようび}と{木曜日|もくようび}ですよ。
= Ah, burnable rubbish is Mondays and Thursdays.
エレナ: よかった。{聞|き}いて{安心|あんしん}しました。それから、{近|ちか}くにスーパーはありますか。
= Oh good, that's a relief. And is there a supermarket nearby?
{村田|むらた}: {駅|えき}の{前|まえ}にしょうてんがいがあって、スーパーもありますよ。ちょっと{遠|とお}いですけど。
= There's a shopping street in front of the station, with a supermarket too. It's a bit far, though.
エレナ: {歩|ある}いて{何分|なんぷん}ぐらいですか。
= How many minutes on foot, roughly?
{村田|むらた}: {十五分|じゅうごふん}ぐらいです。じつは、{私|わたし}も{今|いま}から{行|い}くんです。いっしょに{行|い}きませんか。あんないしますよ。
= About fifteen minutes. Actually, I'm going there now myself. Why don't we go together? I'll show you the way.
エレナ: いいんですか。ありがとうございます。この{町|まち}はしずかで、みどりが{多|おお}くて、いいですね。
= Are you sure? Thank you. This town is quiet and green; it's lovely.
{村田|むらた}: そうですね。でも、{夜|よる}は{店|みせ}が{少|すく}なくて、ちょっとさびしいんですよ。
= It is. But there are few shops at night, so it's a bit lonely, you know.
```

ひっこす = to move house (lesson 4); もえるごみ = burnable rubbish (lesson 05h2). Notice how
each 〜んです answers a question in the air: why Elena is knocking, why she's asking, why
Ms Murata is happy to walk with her.

## Reading: my town

Elena writes about her new town for her Japanese class.

> {私|わたし}が{住|す}んでいる{町|まち}は、{東京|とうきょう}から{電車|でんしゃ}で{一時間|いちじかん}ぐらいの{所|ところ}にあります。{人口|じんこう}は{三万人|さんまんにん}ぐらいで、あまり{大|おお}きくありません。{町|まち}の{北|きた}には{森|もり}と{田|た}んぼがあって、{夏|なつ}はみどりがとてもきれいです。{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}はしょうてんがいで、{古|ふる}い{店|みせ}が{多|おお}いです。{店|みせ}の{人|ひと}はみんな{親切|しんせつ}です。
>
> {都会|とかい}とちがって、{夜|よる}はしずかで、{空気|くうき}もきれいです。でも、{近|ちか}くに{大|おお}きい{病院|びょういん}がなくて、ちょっとふべんです。バスも{少|すく}ないんです。
>
> {先月|せんげつ}、{母|はは}が{国|くに}から{来|き}て、「いい{町|まち}だね」と{言|い}いました。それを{聞|き}いて、うれしかったです。

The town where I live is about an hour from Tokyo by train. Its population is about thirty
thousand, so it isn't very big. To the north of the town there are forests and rice fields,
and in summer the green is beautiful. In front of the station there's a shopping street with
a lot of old shops. The people in the shops are all kind.

Unlike the city, it's quiet at night and the air is clean too. But there's no big hospital
nearby, which is a bit inconvenient. There aren't many buses either.

Last month my mother came from my country and said, "It's a nice town." I was happy to hear
that.

（{都会|とかい}とちがって = unlike the city. {親切|しんせつ} is the kanji spelling of しんせつ, kind.）

## Pronunciation: ん before で

In 〜んです the ん is a full beat: {行|い}くんです is い・く・ん・で・す, five beats, not "ikundes" said
fast as four. Before で your tongue is already in place for d, so the ん sounds like "n". In
casual speech the whole thing is often shortened further (〜んだ, 〜の), but the ん still takes
its own beat.

```speak
どうしたんですか。
= What's the matter?
{道|みち}にまよったんです。
= I've got lost.
ちょっと{聞|き}きたいんですが。
= I'd like to ask something.
おそくなって、すみません。
= Sorry I'm late.
{日本|にほん}に{来|き}て、よかったです。
= I'm glad I came to Japan.
この{町|まち}はしずかで、きれいです。
= This town is quiet and pretty.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{休|やす}みだんです, ×しずかだんです. Before ん, だ becomes な: {休|やす}みなんです, しずかなんです.
- ×{近|ちか}いくて, ×{近|ちか}いで. Drop the い: {近|ちか}くて. And いい → よくて, not ×いくて.
- ×しずかくて. な-adjectives take で: しずかで. Watch the な-adjectives that end in い:
  きれいで, {有名|ゆうめい}で (not ×きれくて).
- Using 〜てすみません with a request after the reason: the second half must be a feeling or
  reaction. For "it's raining, so please…", use から.
- 〜んです on everything. Use it when you're explaining or asking for an explanation, not for
  plain statements of fact.

## Key points

- Plain form + んです explains ("it's that…, you see"); な-adjectives and nouns take なんです.
- 〜んですか asks for an explanation; どうしたんですか, どうして〜んですか.
- 〜んですが/けど… opens a request. Casual: 〜の？ (question), 〜んだ (statement).
- Adjective て form: い → くて (いい → よくて); な-adjective and noun + で. ない → なくて (because not).
- Verb て + feeling gives the cause: 〜てすみません, 〜てよかった, 〜てうれしい.
- Casual 〜てる = 〜ている.
- AはBが〜: {町|まち}はみどりが{多|おお}い.
- New kanji: 町 村 田 森 近 遠 地.

lessons.title: Can do: the potential form
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In N5 you said what you can do with nouns: {日本語|にほんご}ができます, テニスができます. That works
for skills with a name, but not for "I can read kanji", "I can't come tomorrow" or "you can see
the sea from here". For those Japanese changes the verb itself into the **[[potential form]]**:
{読|よ}める (can read), {来|こ}られる (can come), およげる (can swim).

This lesson shows how to make it for every verb group, which particles go with it, the more
formal 〜ことができる, the difference between {見|み}える and {見|み}られる, and the shortened
forms you'll hear in speech. The theme is sports, skills and what people are able to do.

## Making the potential form

You already know the three verb groups: **[[group 1 verbs]]** (う-verbs), **[[group 2 verbs]]**
(る-verbs) and the two **[[group 3 verbs]]**, する and {来|く}る. Each makes the potential its own way.

### Group 1: change the last u-sound to e, add る

Move the last kana of the **[[dictionary form]]** from the う-row to the え-row (く → け, む → め…)
and add る.

| Dictionary form | Potential | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {書|か}く | {書|か}ける | can write |
| およぐ | およげる | can swim |
| {話|はな}す | {話|はな}せる | can speak |
| {待|ま}つ | {待|ま}てる | can wait |
| {読|よ}む | {読|よ}める | can read |
| あそぶ | あそべる | can play |
| {買|か}う | {買|か}える | can buy |
| {帰|かえ}る | {帰|かえ}れる | can go home |
| {行|い}く | {行|い}ける | can go |

{行|い}く is regular here: {行|い}ける. Note that う becomes え ({買|か}える), not わ as in the ない form.

### Group 2: drop る, add られる

| Dictionary form | Potential | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {食|た}べる | {食|た}べられる | can eat |
| {見|み}る | {見|み}られる | can see, can watch |
| {起|お}きる | {起|お}きられる | can get up |
| {教|おし}える | {教|おし}えられる | can teach |

### Group 3: できる and {来|こ}られる

| Dictionary form | Potential | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| する | できる | can do |
| {運転|うんてん}する | {運転|うんてん}できる | can drive |
| {来|く}る | {来|こ}られる | can come |

Every する verb uses できる: {運動|うんどう}できる, {勉強|べんきょう}できる. {来|く}る changes its
vowel again: {来|こ}られる, read こられる, like the ない form {来|こ}ない.

The potential form now joins your conjugation drills.

### The potential is a group 2 verb

Every potential form ends in -eる, and it conjugates like {食|た}べる. Once you've made it, you
already know all its forms:

| | Polite | Plain |
|---|---|---|
| can | {書|か}けます | {書|か}ける |
| can't | {書|か}けません | {書|か}けない |
| could | {書|か}けました | {書|か}けた |
| couldn't | {書|か}けませんでした | {書|か}けなかった |
| て form | — | {書|か}けて |

{漢字|かんじ}が{少|すこ}し{書|か}けます。 — I can write a few kanji.
{明日|あした}は{来|こ}られません。 — I can't come tomorrow.
きのうはよくねられませんでした。 — I couldn't sleep well last night.

"Can" covers ability (I can swim) and circumstances (I can't come tomorrow, I'm busy). Japanese
uses the same form for both.

## Which particle: が or を

The object of a potential verb can take が or を.

{日本語|にほんご}が{話|はな}せます。 / {日本語|にほんご}を{話|はな}せます。 — I can speak Japanese.
{漢字|かんじ}が{読|よ}めますか。 / {漢字|かんじ}を{読|よ}めますか。 — Can you read kanji?

が is the traditional choice and sounds a little more natural in short sentences; を is very
common too, especially when the object and the verb are far apart. Either is correct on the
test. Other particles stay as they are: {駅|えき}まで{歩|ある}けます, この{店|みせ}で{買|か}えます.

{私|わたし}は{英語|えいご}が{話|はな}せます。 — I can speak English.

Here は marks who has the ability and が marks what they can do, the same AはBが shape as
{町|まち}はみどりが{多|おお}い in lesson 1.

## The formal way: 〜ことができる

Dictionary form + ことができる means the same as the potential. It's longer and more formal,
and you'll see it in notices, rules and writing.

ここでは{写真|しゃしん}をとることができます。 — You may take photos here. / Photos can be taken here.
この{図書館|としょかん}では、{本|ほん}を{二週間|にしゅうかん}{借|か}りることができます。 — At this library you can borrow books for two weeks.

With a noun, it's just Nができる, which you know from N5: {空手|からて}ができます, {運転|うんてん}が
できます. In conversation, the potential form is the usual choice: およげますか sounds more
natural than およぐことができますか.

## Shortened forms you'll hear: {食|た}べれる

In speech many people drop the ら from group 2 potentials and from {来|こ}られる: {食|た}べれる,
{見|み}れる, {来|こ}れる. These "ら-less" forms are very common, especially among younger
speakers, and you'll hear them in dramas and from friends.

これ、{食|た}べれる？ — Can you eat this? (casual)

They're still treated as non-standard: they aren't used in careful writing or on the JLPT. Use
{食|た}べられる and {来|こ}られる yourself, and recognize the short forms when you hear them.

Group 1 never has this choice: {書|か}ける is already short, and ×{書|か}けれる is a mistake.

## Seeing and hearing: {見|み}える and {聞|き}こえる

Japanese has special verbs for things that come into your eyes or ears by themselves:
{見|み}える (to be visible) and {聞|き}こえる (to be audible). The thing seen or heard takes が.

ここから{海|うみ}が{見|み}えます。 — You can see the sea from here.
{電車|でんしゃ}の{音|おと}が{聞|き}こえます。 — I can hear the train.
{後|うし}ろのせきから、{字|じ}がよく{見|み}えません。 — From the back I can't see the writing well.

（{後|うし}ろ is the kanji spelling of うしろ, behind.）

The ordinary potentials {見|み}られる and {聞|き}ける mean you have the chance or the means to
watch or listen to something.

この{映画|えいが}はネットで{見|み}られます。 — You can watch this film online.
このラジオでニュースが{聞|き}けます。 — You can listen to the news on this radio.

A simple test: if it just reaches your eyes or ears (a mountain, a noise next door), use
{見|み}える/{聞|き}こえる. If you choose to watch or listen and something makes it possible (a
ticket, an app, free time), use {見|み}られる/{聞|き}ける.

## Verbs with no potential

Some verbs already mean "can" or "be able", so they have no potential form:

- ある: ×あれる. "There can be" needs other grammar; just use ある.
- {分|わ}かる (to understand) and できる (to be able): they already describe ability.
  ×{分|わ}かれる is a different verb (わかれる, to part from someone).
- {見|み}える and {聞|き}こえる themselves.

## Kanji

Seven kanji for the body in action.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 力 | power, strength | リョク, リキ | ちから | 2 | {力|ちから}, {体力|たいりょく} |
| 運 | carry; luck | ウン | はこ(ぶ) | 12 | {運動|うんどう}, {運転|うんてん}, {運|はこ}ぶ |
| 動 | move | ドウ | うご(く) | 11 | {動|うご}く, {運動|うんどう}, {動物|どうぶつ} (animal) |
| 走 | run | ソウ | はし(る) | 7 | {走|はし}る |
| 歩 | walk | ホ | ある(く) | 8 | {歩|ある}く |
| 強 | strong | キョウ | つよ(い) | 11 | {強|つよ}い, {勉強|べんきょう} |
| 弱 | weak | ジャク | よわ(い) | 10 | {弱|よわ}い |

Memory notes:

- 力 looks like a strong arm, bent at the elbow and pushing down.
- 動 is "heavy" (重, lesson 25) plus 力: it takes strength to move something heavy.
- 運 has the road shape under it, like 近 and 遠, and a vehicle (車) under a cover on top:
  carrying things by road. With 動 it makes {運動|うんどう}, exercise: "carrying and moving".
- 走 has earth (土) at the top and a running foot underneath, kicking up the ground.
- 歩 is "stop" (止, lesson 8) on top of a foot that keeps going: step, stop, step, walking.
- 弱 is two bent bows side by side, with two small marks each: bows too weak to shoot.
- 強 has one bow (on the left) pulled tight: strong.

{勉強|べんきょう} (study) means something like "making yourself work hard", which is why it has
強. {運|はこ}ぶ, to carry, is a lesson 4 word for moving house.

```trace
力運動走歩強弱
```

## Dialogue: joining the club

Taku is asking Yui, a new student, which sport she'd like to try in the university sports club.

```dialogue
# Joining the club
たく: ユイさんは{何|なに}かスポーツができますか。
= Yui, can you play any sports?
ユイ: テニスが{少|すこ}しできます。それから、{空手|からて}を{三年|さんねん}{習|なら}っていました。
= I can play a bit of tennis. And I learned karate for three years.
たく: すごいですね。じゃあ、{力|ちから}が{強|つよ}いんですか。
= Wow. So you must be strong?
ユイ: いいえ、そんなに{強|つよ}くないです。でも、{走|はし}るのはとくいです。{十|じゅっ}キロぐらい{走|はし}れます。
= No, not that strong. But I'm good at running. I can run about ten kilometres.
たく: へえ。{今度|こんど}、{町|まち}のマラソン{大会|たいかい}があるんですが……
= Really? There's a town marathon coming up…
ユイ: マラソンはちょっと……。まだ{二十|にじゅっ}キロは{走|はし}れません。
= A marathon's a bit… I can't run twenty kilometres yet.
たく: そうですか。すいえいはどうですか。
= I see. What about swimming?
ユイ: すいえいはだめなんです。{小|ちい}さいころからおよげないんです。
= Swimming's no good, I'm afraid. I've never been able to swim, since I was little.
たく: じゃあ、テニスにしましょう。{土曜日|どようび}の{朝|あさ}、{来|こ}られますか。
= Then let's go with tennis. Can you come on Saturday morning?
ユイ: はい、{行|い}けます。
= Yes, I can.
```

{今度|こんど} = coming up, next; {大会|たいかい} = a competition or meet; 〜にしましょう = let's choose
(lesson 4); {小|ちい}さいころ = as a small child. Notice ユイ's answer: たく asks {来|こ}られますか
(can you come) and she answers {行|い}けます (I can go), because she'll be going there.

## Reading: the sports centre

A notice at the town sports centre.

> {町|まち}のスポーツセンター
>
> スポーツセンターでは、{子|こ}どもから{大人|おとな}まで、いろいろなスポーツをすることができます。
>
> ・プール：{毎日|まいにち}{朝|あさ}{九時|くじ}から{夜|よる}{九時|くじ}までおよげます。{月曜日|げつようび}は{休|やす}みです。
> ・{空手|からて}・じゅうどう：{火曜日|かようび}と{金曜日|きんようび}の{夜|よる}です。はじめての{人|ひと}も{習|なら}うことができます。
> ・テニス：コートは{一時間|いちじかん}{五百円|ごひゃくえん}です。ボールとラケットはセンターで{借|か}りられます。
>
> {車|くるま}は{二十台|にじゅうだい}{止|と}められます。{駅|えき}から{歩|ある}いて{十分|じゅっぷん}ですから、なるべく{電車|でんしゃ}で{来|き}てください。

At the sports centre, everyone from children to adults can do all kinds of sports.
- Pool: you can swim every day from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Closed on Mondays.
- Karate and judo: Tuesday and Friday evenings. Beginners can learn too.
- Tennis: courts are 500 yen an hour. You can borrow balls and rackets at the centre.

There's parking for twenty cars. It's a ten-minute walk from the station, so please come by
train if you can.

（{大人|おとな} = adult; {借|か}りる = to borrow; 〜{台|だい} counts cars and machines; なるべく = as
much as possible.）

## Pronunciation: one extra beat

The potential of a group 2 verb is two beats longer than the dictionary form: たべる (3) →
たべられる (5). Say every beat: た・べ・ら・れ・る. Learners often swallow the ら, which turns it
into the casual たべれる. The group 1 potential is the same length as the dictionary form:
かく → かける, よむ → よめる.

```speak
{日本語|にほんご}が{少|すこ}し{話|はな}せます。
= I can speak a little Japanese.
{漢字|かんじ}が{読|よ}めますか。
= Can you read kanji?
{明日|あした}は{来|こ}られません。
= I can't come tomorrow.
ここから{海|うみ}が{見|み}えます。
= You can see the sea from here.
{運転|うんてん}できますか。
= Can you drive?
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{書|か}けれる, ×{行|い}けれる. Group 1 adds only る: {書|か}ける, {行|い}ける.
- ×{食|た}べれる in writing. In speech you'll hear it; write and say {食|た}べられる.
- ×するできる, ×{運転|うんてん}するできる. する becomes できる: {運転|うんてん}できる, or
  {運転|うんてん}ができる with the noun.
- ×{来|く}られる. The potential of {来|く}る is {来|こ}られる (こられる).
- ×{分|わ}かれる for "can understand". {分|わ}かる already means that.
- Using {見|み}られる for something that's simply in view. Standing at the window, say
  ここから{海|うみ}が{見|み}えます; ここから{海|うみ}が{見|み}られます sounds like a brochure ("you get the
  chance to see the sea here").

## Key points

- Group 1: u-sound → e-sound + る ({書|か}く → {書|か}ける). Group 2: る → られる ({食|た}べる → {食|た}べられる).
  する → できる, {来|く}る → {来|こ}られる.
- The potential conjugates like a group 2 verb: {書|か}けます, {書|か}けない, {書|か}けた.
- The object takes が or を; other particles don't change.
- Dictionary form + ことができる is the formal version; Nができる for skills.
- ら-less {食|た}べれる, {来|こ}れる are common in speech but not standard.
- {見|み}える/{聞|き}こえる: comes into view or earshot. {見|み}られる/{聞|き}ける: have the chance.
- ある, {分|わ}かる, できる have no potential.
- New kanji: 力 運 動 走 歩 強 弱.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Let's and I think I'll: the volitional form
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You know 〜ましょう: {行|い}きましょう (let's go), てつだいましょうか (shall I help?). It has
a plain partner, the **[[volitional form]]**: {行|い}こう, {食|た}べよう, しよう. On its own it's the
casual "let's"; with と{思|おも}う it says what you're planning to do: {海外|かいがい}に{行|い}こうと
{思|おも}っています (I'm thinking of going abroad).

This lesson shows how to make it, how friends use it, how it builds plans with 〜と{思|おも}う
and 〜と{思|おも}っている, and the briefer 〜ようとする (try to, be about to). The theme is
holidays, trips, hobbies and plans for the new year.

## Making the volitional form

Look at the ます form you know well: 〜ましょう already has the volitional inside it. The plain
form follows the same groups as always.

### Group 1: u-sound → o-sound + う

Move the last kana of the dictionary form to the お-row and add う.

| Dictionary form | Volitional | 〜ましょう |
|---|---|---|
| {書|か}く | {書|か}こう | {書|か}きましょう |
| およぐ | およごう | およぎましょう |
| {話|はな}す | {話|はな}そう | {話|はな}しましょう |
| {待|ま}つ | {待|ま}とう | {待|ま}ちましょう |
| {読|よ}む | {読|よ}もう | {読|よ}みましょう |
| あそぶ | あそぼう | あそびましょう |
| {買|か}う | {買|か}おう | {買|か}いましょう |
| {帰|かえ}る | {帰|かえ}ろう | {帰|かえ}りましょう |
| {行|い}く | {行|い}こう | {行|い}きましょう |

The お + う at the end is a long vowel: {書|か}こう is said "kakō", three beats, か・こ・う.

### Group 2: る → よう

| Dictionary form | Volitional |
|---|---|
| {食|た}べる | {食|た}べよう |
| {見|み}る | {見|み}よう |
| {起|お}きる | {起|お}きよう |
| {始|はじ}める | {始|はじ}めよう |

### Group 3: しよう and {来|こ}よう

| Dictionary form | Volitional |
|---|---|
| する | しよう |
| {旅行|りょこう}する | {旅行|りょこう}しよう |
| {来|く}る | {来|こ}よう (こよう) |

{来|く}る takes the こ vowel again, as in {来|こ}ない and {来|こ}られる.

The volitional form now joins your conjugation drills.

## Let's: the casual 〜ましょう

Between friends and family, the volitional is "let's".

{明日|あした}、{海|うみ}に{行|い}こう！ — Let's go to the beach tomorrow!
もうおそいから、{帰|かえ}ろう。 — It's late, let's go home.

{写真|しゃしん}をとろう。 — Let's take a photo.

Add か for "shall we…?" or, when it's something you'd do, "shall I…?":

しゅうまつ、どこか{行|い}こうか。 — Shall we go somewhere this weekend?
{重|おも}そうだね。{持|も}とうか。 — That looks heavy. Shall I carry it?

（{重|おも}そう = looks heavy, lesson 16.） The polite versions are the ones you know:
{行|い}きましょう, {行|い}きましょうか, {持|も}ちましょうか.

| Polite | Casual | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {行|い}きましょう。 | {行|い}こう。 | Let's go. |
| {行|い}きましょうか。 | {行|い}こうか。 | Shall we go? |
| {持|も}ちましょうか。 | {持|も}とうか。 | Shall I carry it? |

## I think I'll: 〜(よ)うと{思|おも}う

Volitional + と{思|おも}う says what you've decided or are thinking of doing. It's softer than a
flat statement of a plan, and very common in polite speech.

{夏休|なつやす}みに{旅|たび}をしようと{思|おも}います。 — I think I'll go travelling in the summer holidays.
{今年|ことし}は{毎日|まいにち}{運動|うんどう}しようと{思|おも}います。 — This year I'm going to exercise every day.
{来年|らいねん}、{海外|かいがい}に{行|い}こうと{思|おも}っています。 — I'm thinking of going abroad next year.

### と{思|おも}います or と{思|おも}っています?

- 〜と{思|おも}います: the idea is yours, and you're saying it now. It can be a decision you've
  just made: じゃあ、これを{買|か}おうと{思|おも}います (Right, I think I'll buy this one).
- 〜と{思|おも}っています: you've had the plan for a while and still have it. It's also the only
  way to talk about someone else's intention, because you can't say from inside their head
  that they "think":

{兄|あに}は{車|くるま}を{買|か}おうと{思|おも}っています。 — My brother is thinking of buying a car.
×{兄|あに}は{車|くるま}を{買|か}おうと{思|おも}います。

### Don't mix it up with plain + と{思|おも}う

The form before と{思|おも}う changes the meaning completely:

| Sentence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {行|い}こうと{思|おも}います。 | I think I'll go. (my intention) |
| {行|い}くと{思|おも}います。 | I think (he/she/it) will go. (a guess) |
| {行|い}きたいと{思|おも}います。 | I'd like to go. (a wish) |

{行|い}きたいと{思|おも}う says you want to; {行|い}こうと{思|おも}う says you mean to. In lesson 4 you'll
add つもり, a firmer "I intend to".

## Try to, be about to: 〜(よ)うとする

Volitional + とする means "try to" (and fail, or not yet succeed) or "be just about to".

ドアを{開|あ}けようとしましたが、{開|あ}きませんでした。 — I tried to open the door, but it wouldn't open.
{出|で}かけようとしたとき、{電話|でんわ}がなりました。 — Just as I was about to go out, the phone rang.

（{開|あ}く = to open by itself, lesson 8; なる = to ring.） This is an attempt at something that
doesn't happen easily. For "try it and see what it's like" (try the cake, try the shoes on),
Japanese uses a different pattern, 〜てみる, in lesson 5.

## Kanji

Seven kanji for holidays and hobbies.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 旅 | journey | リョ | たび | 10 | {旅|たび}, {旅行|りょこう}, {旅館|りょかん} |
| 楽 | fun; music; easy | ガク, ラク | たの(しい) | 13 | {楽|たの}しい, {楽|たの}しみ, {音楽|おんがく}, {楽|らく} |
| 歌 | song | カ | うた, うた(う) | 14 | {歌|うた}, {歌|うた}う, {歌手|かしゅ} |
| 音 | sound | オン | おと | 9 | {音|おと}, {音楽|おんがく} |
| 写 | copy | シャ | うつ(す) | 5 | {写真|しゃしん}, {写|うつ}す |
| 真 | true | シン | ま | 10 | {写真|しゃしん}, {真|ま}ん{中|なか} (the middle) |
| 海 | sea | カイ | うみ | 9 | {海|うみ}, {海外|かいがい} |

Memory notes:

- 旅 has a flag on the left and people walking under it on the right: a group on a journey,
  following the flag of the tour guide.
- 楽 is white (白) in the middle of a wooden frame (木): a drum on a stand, music, and the fun it
  brings.
- 歌 has the same shape twice on the left, like a song's chorus repeated, and on the right a
  person with a wide-open mouth: singing.

- 音 is "stand" (立) on top of "sun" (日): someone standing and speaking; a sound.
- 写 is a roof over a shape like a small bird: copying, "getting the picture under a cover".
- 真 has "ten" (十) on top and "eye" (目) in the middle: looking closely, the truth.
- 海 has water (three drops on the left) and "every" (毎): the water that's everywhere.

The N5 words {写真|しゃしん}, {旅行|りょこう}, {音楽|おんがく}, {楽|たの}しい, {歌|うた} and {海|うみ} are now written
with their kanji. {真|ま}ん{中|なか} is an N5 word too (まんなか). 楽 has three readings:
たの in {楽|たの}しい, ガク in {音楽|おんがく}, and らく in the な-adjective {楽|らく} (easy,
comfortable).

```trace
旅楽歌音写真海
```

## Dialogue: plans for the long weekend

Two friends, Haruto and Mio, are planning the long weekend. They speak casually.

```dialogue
# The long weekend
はると: ねえ、{今度|こんど}のれんきゅう、どこか{行|い}こうよ。
= Hey, let's go somewhere this long weekend.
みお: いいね！{海|うみ}はどう？
= Good idea! How about the sea?
はると: {海|うみ}もいいけど、{去年|きょねん}も{行|い}ったから、{今年|ことし}は{山|やま}にしよう。
= The sea's nice too, but we went last year, so let's go to the mountains this year.
みお: じゃあ、ハイキングしよう。{森|もり}の{中|なか}を{歩|ある}くの、{好|す}きなんだ。
= Then let's go hiking. I love walking in the woods.
はると: うん。{夜|よる}は{旅館|りょかん}にとまって、おんせんに{入|はい}ろう。
= Yeah. And at night let's stay at a ryokan and get in a hot spring.
みお: {楽|たの}しみ！{写真|しゃしん}もたくさんとろうね。
= I can't wait! Let's take lots of photos too.
はると: {旅館|りょかん}は{早|はや}くよやくしないと…… ぼくがしらべようか。
= We'll have to book the ryokan soon… Shall I look one up?
みお: ありがとう。{電車|でんしゃ}の{時間|じかん}は{私|わたし}が{見|み}ておくね。
= Thanks. I'll check the train times.
はると: よし。じゃあ、{今夜|こんや}{電話|でんわ}しよう。
= Right. Let's talk on the phone tonight, then.
```

〜にしよう = let's choose (lesson 4); よやくしないと = we've got to book (short for "if we don't
book…", lesson 11); {見|み}ておく = check in advance (lesson 5). ぼく is a casual "I" used
mostly by men and boys.

## Reading: my plans for the new year

Ken writes on his blog in the first week of January. Blogs and diaries use plain forms.

> あけましておめでとうございます。{新年|しんねん}だから、{今年|ことし}の{計画|けいかく}を{書|か}こうと{思|おも}う。
>
> まず、{十二月|じゅうにがつ}にN4の{試験|しけん}をうけようと{思|おも}っている。だから、{毎朝|まいあさ}{三十分|さんじゅっぷん}{漢字|かんじ}を{勉強|べんきょう}する。それから、{体|からだ}のために{走|はし}ろうと{思|おも}う。{去年|きょねん}は{何回|なんかい}も{始|はじ}めようとしたけど、{寒|さむ}くてやめてしまった。{今年|ことし}こそ！
>
> {夏|なつ}には、{一人|ひとり}で{北海道|ほっかいどう}を{旅|たび}しようと{思|おも}っている。{自転車|じてんしゃ}で{海|うみ}の{近|ちか}くの{道|みち}を{走|はし}りたい。
>
> {母|はは}は「{計画|けいかく}はいいけど、ぜんぶできる？」と{言|い}っている。たしかに、{去年|きょねん}のもくひょうも{半分|はんぶん}しかできなかった。でも、{今年|ことし}はがんばろう。

Happy New Year. Since it's the new year, I thought I'd write my plans for this year.

First, I'm planning to take the N4 exam in December. So every morning I'll study kanji for
thirty minutes. And I think I'll take up running, for my health. Last year I tried to start
lots of times, but it was cold and I gave up. This year for sure!

In summer I'm thinking of travelling around Hokkaido on my own. I want to ride my bike along
the roads by the sea.

My mother says, "The plans are fine, but can you do them all?" It's true: last year I only
managed half of my goals. But this year, I'll do my best.

（うける = to take (an exam); たしかに = it's true; {体|からだ}のために = for my health; やめてしまった = gave up, sadly
(lesson 9); 〜こそ = this time for sure; しか…ない = only (lesson 14).）

## Say it

```speak
{海|うみ}に{行|い}こう！
= Let's go to the sea!
どこか{行|い}こうか。
= Shall we go somewhere?
{持|も}とうか。
= Shall I carry it?
{夏休|なつやす}みに{旅|たび}をしようと{思|おも}います。
= I think I'll go travelling in the summer holidays.
{来年|らいねん}、{海外|かいがい}に{行|い}こうと{思|おも}っています。
= I'm thinking of going abroad next year.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{行|い}きよう. Group 1 goes to the お-row: {行|い}こう. Only group 2 adds よう.
- ×{来|き}よう. {来|く}る → {来|こ}よう.
- ×するよう, ×しよう for {来|く}る. Group 3 is しよう and {来|こ}よう.
- ×{行|い}くと{思|おも}います for "I think I'll go". That's a guess about someone else. Your own
  plan needs the volitional: {行|い}こうと{思|おも}います.
- ×{兄|あに}は{行|い}こうと{思|おも}います. For someone else's plan use 〜と{思|おも}っています.
- Using the volitional to a teacher or a customer: {行|い}こう is casual. Use {行|い}きましょう.
- Saying {書|か}こう with a short こ. It's a long vowel: か・こ・う.

## Key points

- Group 1: u-sound → o-sound + う ({行|い}く → {行|い}こう). Group 2: る → よう ({食|た}べる → {食|た}べよう).
  する → しよう, {来|く}る → {来|こ}よう.
- On its own: casual "let's"; with か: "shall we / shall I". Polite: 〜ましょう(か).
- 〜(よ)うと{思|おも}う: I think I'll (an intention). 〜と{思|おも}っている: a plan you've had for a
  while; also for other people's plans.
- Compare {行|い}こうと{思|おも}う (I mean to), {行|い}きたいと{思|おも}う (I'd like to),
  {行|い}くと{思|おも}う (I think it will).
- 〜(よ)うとする: try to; be about to.
- New kanji: 旅 楽 歌 音 写 真 海.

lessons.title: Plans and decisions: つもり, よてい, ことにする, ことになる
topics: つもり and よてい
ことにする and ことになる
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 3 gave you 〜(よ)うと{思|おも}う, "I think I'll". Japanese has several more ways to talk
about plans, and they aren't interchangeable: one is your own intention, one is a fixed
arrangement, one is a decision you made, one is a decision made for you. This lesson sorts
them out:

- 〜つもりだ: I intend to
- 〜よていだ: it's scheduled, the plan is
- 〜ことにする: I've decided to (and 〜ことにしている: I make a point of)
- 〜ことになる: it's been decided (and 〜ことになっている: the rule is)

It also adds Nにする (choosing: コーヒーにします) and 〜ことがある (sometimes). All of them
follow the **[[dictionary form]]** or the ない form, so you need no new verb forms. The theme is
study and work plans, schedules and moving house.

## Intention: 〜つもりだ

You met つもり lightly in N5. In full: dictionary form + つもりです is a plan you've made in your
own head; ない form + つもりです is a plan not to do something.

{来年|らいねん}、{日本|にほん}の{大学|だいがく}にりゅうがくするつもりです。 — I intend to study at a Japanese university next year.
しょうらいは{先生|せんせい}になるつもりです。 — I mean to become a teacher one day.
{今年|ことし}はお{金|かね}をあまり{使|つか}わないつもりです。 — This year I'm planning not to spend much money.

### ないつもり or つもりはない?

Both are negative, but they feel very different.

| Sentence | Feels like |
|---|---|
| {車|くるま}を{買|か}わないつもりです。 | My plan is not to buy a car. (calm) |
| {車|くるま}を{買|か}うつもりはありません。 | I have no intention whatsoever of buying a car. (firm) |

つもりはない denies the intention itself. It's what you say when someone assumes you'll do
something:

「{会社|かいしゃ}をやめるんですか。」「いいえ、やめるつもりはありません。」 — "Are you leaving the company?" "No, I have no intention of quitting."

### つもりでした: what you meant to do

In the past, つもりだった / つもりでした is what you meant to do, often something that didn't
happen.

{今日|きょう}は{早|はや}く{帰|かえ}るつもりでしたが、{仕事|しごと}が{終|お}わりませんでした。 — I meant to go home early today, but my work didn't get finished.

### Careful with superiors

つもりですか asks about someone's intention directly. To a teacher or a boss it can sound
blunt, as if you're checking up on them. Ask about the schedule instead
({明日|あした}もいらっしゃるよていですか is very polite; you'll learn いらっしゃる in lesson 27), or
simply ask {明日|あした}も{来|き}ますか.

## Schedule: 〜よていだ

よてい is a plan that has been arranged: a timetable, a booking, an entry in a diary, often
with other people. It follows the dictionary form, or a noun with の. Its kanji aren't
on the N4 list, so it's written in kana here.

{来週|らいしゅう}の{月曜日|げつようび}にひっこすよていです。 — I'm due to move house next Monday.
{電車|でんしゃ}は{十時|じゅうじ}に{着|つ}くよていです。 — The train is scheduled to arrive at ten.
{明日|あした}は{友|とも}だちと{食事|しょくじ}のよていです。 — I'm having a meal with a friend tomorrow (that's the plan).

| | つもり | よてい |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | an intention in your head | an arrangement, a schedule |
| Whose | yours (or someone you report on) | anyone's, even a train's |
| Sounds | personal | factual, polite |

So a train can be due to arrive ({着|つ}くよてい), but it can't "intend" to (×{着|つ}くつもり).

## Deciding: 〜ことにする

Dictionary form (or ない form) + ことにする means "decide to". Usually you'll hear it in the
past, ことにした / ことにしました: the decision is made, and it was yours.

{大学|だいがく}のりょうに{住|す}むことにしました。 — I've decided to live in the university dorm.
たばこをやめることにしました。 — I've decided to give up smoking.
{今年|ことし}は{海外|かいがい}に{行|い}かないことにしました。 — I've decided not to go abroad this year.

### A habit: 〜ことにしている

With 〜ている it becomes a rule you've set yourself and keep to: "I make a point of…".

まいばん、{日本語|にほんご}でにっきを{書|か}くことにしています。 — Every night I make a point of writing my diary in Japanese.
エレベーターは{使|つか}わないで、{歩|ある}くことにしています。 — I make a point of walking instead of taking the lift.

（〜ないで = without doing, instead of; lesson 10.）

## Decided for you: 〜ことになる

Dictionary form + ことになる says a decision has been reached, but not by you alone: your
company, your school, your family or circumstances decided. In the past, ことになりました, it's
how people announce transfers, moves and events.

{来月|らいげつ}から{京都|きょうと}の{店|みせ}で{働|はたら}くことになりました。 — It's been decided that I'll work at the Kyoto shop from next month.
{今度|こんど}の{土曜日|どようび}に{試合|しあい}をすることになりました。 — We're going to have a match this Saturday (it's been arranged).

People also use ことになりました for their own big decisions, such as a marriage or a move. It
sounds modest, as if the matter settled itself: けっこんすることになりました (I'm getting
married).

### The rule is: 〜ことになっている

With 〜ている it describes a rule, custom or arrangement that stands.

このりょうでは、{夜|よる}{十一時|じゅういちじ}までに{帰|かえ}ることになっています。 — In this dorm you're supposed to be back by 11 p.m.
{日本|にほん}では、{家|いえ}に{入|はい}る{前|まえ}にくつをぬぐことになっています。 — In Japan the custom is to take your shoes off before going into a house.

（〜までに = by (a deadline); lesson 19.）

### ことにする or ことになる?

| | Who decided | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ことにした | I did | ひっこすことにしました。 (I decided to move.) |
| ことになった | it was decided: work, family, circumstances | ひっこすことになりました。 (I'm going to be moving.) |
| ことにしている | my own habit | {毎朝|まいあさ}{走|はし}ることにしています。 (I make a point of running every morning.) |
| ことになっている | a rule or arrangement | {八時|はちじ}に{集|あつ}まることになっています。 (We're supposed to meet at eight.) |

## Choosing: Nにする

Noun + にする means "decide on, choose, go with". You'll hear it constantly in shops and
restaurants.

「{何|なに}にしますか。」「コーヒーにします。」 — "What will you have?" "I'll have coffee."
{旅行|りょこう}は{来月|らいげつ}にしましょう。 — Let's make the trip next month.
プレゼントは{本|ほん}にしました。 — I went with a book for the present.

Compare: コーヒーをください asks for it; コーヒーにします announces your choice from the options.

## Sometimes: 〜ことがある

You know 〜たことがある (have ever done). With the dictionary form, ことがある means "it sometimes
happens that…".

{仕事|しごと}が{終|お}わらなくて、{十時|じゅうじ}まで{会社|かいしゃ}にいることがあります。 — Sometimes work doesn't get finished and I'm at the office until ten.
{朝|あさ}は{電車|でんしゃ}がおくれることがあります。 — The trains are sometimes late in the morning.
{日曜日|にちようび}は{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べないことがあります。 — On Sundays I sometimes skip breakfast.

| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {行|い}ったことがある | have been (at least once) |
| {行|い}くことがある | sometimes go |
| {行|い}かないことがある | sometimes don't go |

## Kanji

Seven kanji for where you live and the work you do.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 住 | live | ジュウ | す(む) | 7 | {住|す}む, {住所|じゅうしょ} |
| 所 | place | ショ, ジョ | ところ | 8 | {所|ところ}, {住所|じゅうしょ}, {近所|きんじょ}, {台所|だいどころ} |
| 引 | pull | イン | ひ(く) | 4 | {引|ひ}く |
| 始 | begin | シ | はじ(める), はじ(まる) | 8 | {始|はじ}める, {始|はじ}まる |
| 終 | end | シュウ | お(わる) | 11 | {終|お}わる, {終|お}わり |
| 仕 | serve | シ | — | 5 | {仕事|しごと} |
| 事 | thing, matter | ジ | こと | 8 | {仕事|しごと}, {用事|ようじ}, {食事|しょくじ}, {火事|かじ} (a fire) |

Memory notes:

- 住 is a person (the narrow イ on the left) beside "master" (主, lesson 22): the place where a
  person is master, their home.
- 所 has a door on the left: a spot with a door, a place.
- 引 is a bow (the left part) with its string, the line on the right, pulled back.
- 始 has "woman" (女) on the left: life begins with a mother.
- 終 has "thread" on the left and "winter" (冬, lesson 17) on the right: the end of the thread,
  the end of the year.
- 仕 is a person (イ) beside a man of learning: someone serving, doing a job.
- 事 is a hand holding a writing brush upright: business, a matter to write down.

N5 words now written with kanji: {住|す}む, {住所|じゅうしょ}, {始|はじ}める, {始|はじ}まる, {終|お}わる,
{仕事|しごと}, {用事|ようじ}. The grammar word こと, as in ことにする, stays in kana. 引 is also the first
kanji of ひっこす (to move house), but the second kanji of that word isn't an N4 kanji, so this
course writes ひっこす in kana.

```trace
住所引始終仕事
```

## Dialogue: news at work

Sato tells his colleague Kaori some news over lunch.

```dialogue
# News at work
さとう: じつは、{来月|らいげつ}から{京都|きょうと}の{店|みせ}で{働|はたら}くことになったんです。
= Actually, it's been decided that I'll work at the Kyoto shop from next month.
かおり: えっ、そうなんですか。ひっこすんですか。
= Oh, really? Are you moving?
さとう: ええ。{店|みせ}の{近|ちか}くに{住|す}むことにしました。{毎日|まいにち}{電車|でんしゃ}で{通|かよ}うのはたいへんですから。
= Yes. I've decided to live near the shop. Commuting by train every day would be hard.
かおり: いつひっこすよていですか。
= When are you due to move?
さとう: {二十日|はつか}のよていです。それまでに、{今|いま}の{仕事|しごと}を{終|お}わらせないと……
= On the twentieth. Before then I've got to get my current work finished…
かおり: てつだいましょうか。
= Shall I help?
さとう: ありがとうございます。でも、{一人|ひとり}でやるつもりです。かおりさんもいそがしいでしょう。
= Thank you. But I intend to do it myself. You're busy too, aren't you?
かおり: {京都|きょうと}かあ。いいですね。{休|やす}みの{日|ひ}にあそびに{行|い}ってもいいですか。
= Kyoto, huh. Lovely. Could I come and visit on a day off?
さとう: もちろん。{京都|きょうと}をあんないしますよ。
= Of course. I'll show you around Kyoto.
```

{二十日|はつか} = the twentieth; {終|お}わらせないと = I've got to get it finished ({終|お}わらせる is the
causative, lesson 22, and 〜ないと "I've got to" comes in lesson 11). Notice the plan words:
the company decided (ことになった), Sato decided where to live (ことにした), the date is fixed
(よてい), and how he'll do the work is his own intention (つもり).

## Reading: an email about moving

Sato writes to an old friend.

> {田中|たなか}さん
>
> ごぶさたしています。お{元気|げんき}ですか。
>
> じつは、{仕事|しごと}で{京都|きょうと}に{住|す}むことになりました。{二十日|はつか}にひっこすよていです。
>
> アパートは{店|みせ}の{近|ちか}くにしました。{古|ふる}いですが、{広|ひろ}くて、{近所|きんじょ}にしょうてんがいもあって、べんりです。{毎朝|まいあさ}、{店|みせ}まで{歩|ある}いて{通|かよ}うつもりです。
>
> {京都|きょうと}では、{毎週|まいしゅう}{一|ひと}つおてらを{見|み}に{行|い}こうと{思|おも}っています。{田中|たなか}さんも、{時間|じかん}があるときに、ぜひあそびに{来|き}てください。{京都|きょうと}をあんないします。
>
> {新|あたら}しい{住所|じゅうしょ}は{下|した}に{書|か}きます。
>
> さとう

Dear Tanaka,

It's been a long time. How are you?

Actually, I'm going to be living in Kyoto for work. I'm due to move on the twentieth.

I chose a flat near the shop. It's old, but it's spacious, and there's a shopping street in
the neighbourhood, so it's convenient. I intend to walk to the shop every morning.

In Kyoto I'm thinking of going to see one temple every week. Please do come and visit when
you have time. I'll show you around Kyoto.

I'll write my new address below.

Sato

（ごぶさたしています = it's been a long time (polite, in letters and when you meet again).）

## Say it

```speak
{来年|らいねん}、りゅうがくするつもりです。
= I intend to study abroad next year.
{来週|らいしゅう}ひっこすよていです。
= I'm due to move next week.
たばこをやめることにしました。
= I've decided to give up smoking.
{京都|きょうと}で{働|はたら}くことになりました。
= I'm going to be working in Kyoto.
コーヒーにします。
= I'll have coffee.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{行|い}ったつもりです for "I meant to go". The intention is past, not the going:
  {行|い}くつもりでした. ({行|い}ったつもり means "I was sure I'd gone", a different idea.)
- つもり for timetables: ×{電車|でんしゃ}は{十時|じゅうじ}に{着|つ}くつもりです. Trains have よてい.
- Mixing up ことにした and ことになった. If you chose, it's ことにした; if your company or
  circumstances chose, ことになった.
- ×コーヒーをします for ordering. Choosing is にする: コーヒーにします.
- {行|い}くことがある vs {行|い}ったことがある: the dictionary form is "sometimes"; the た form is
  "have ever".
- つもりですか to a teacher or a boss. Ask about the plan (よてい) or just ask.

## Key points

- Dictionary form + つもりだ: my intention; ないつもり: plan not to; つもりはない: no intention
  at all; つもりだった: meant to.
- Dictionary form / Nの + よていだ: it's scheduled (kana: よてい).
- 〜ことにする: decide to (my choice); 〜ことにしている: make a point of.
- 〜ことになる: it's been decided (not by me alone); 〜ことになっている: the rule is.
- Nにする: choose, go with.
- Dictionary form + ことがある: sometimes; ない + ことがある: sometimes not.
- New kanji: 住 所 引 始 終 仕 事.

lessons.title: Trying and preparing: 〜てみる, 〜ておく
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In N5 the て form joined verbs to helpers like いる (〜ている) and ください (〜てください). N4 has
a whole family of these helpers. This lesson adds two that you'll need for any trip:

- 〜てみる: do something to see what it's like ("try it and see")
- 〜ておく: do something in advance, or leave something as it is

You'll also learn the casual 〜とく, which you'll hear far more often than 〜ておく. The theme
is getting ready for a trip: packing, booking and checking.

Both helpers are written in kana, even though みる and おく are ordinary verbs on their own: the
course writes auxiliary verbs after て in kana.

## Try and see: 〜てみる

て form + みる means "do it and see": you do the action to find out what it's like, whether
it works, whether you like it. みる conjugates like {見|み}る, a group 2 verb.

このくつ、はいてみてもいいですか。 — May I try these shoes on?
{日本|にほん}のおかしを{食|た}べてみました。おいしかったです。 — I tried some Japanese sweets. They were good.
{分|わ}からないことばは、じしょでしらべてみてください。 — Look up any words you don't know in a dictionary and see.
{一度|いちど}、{一人|ひとり}で{旅行|りょこう}してみたいです。 — I'd like to try travelling on my own some time.

〜てみたい (I'd like to try) is one of the most useful forms in the language, and so is the
request 〜てみてください (give it a try). With the volitional you get "let's try":
{行|い}ってみよう (let's go and see).

### てみる or ようとする?

Lesson 3's 〜(よ)うとする is an attempt that may not succeed; 〜てみる is doing the action
itself, as an experiment.

{漢字|かんじ}で{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}いてみました。 — I tried writing my name in kanji. (I did write it.)
{漢字|かんじ}で{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}こうとしましたが、{書|か}けませんでした。 — I tried to write my name in kanji, but I couldn't.

"Try" in English covers both; in Japanese, ask yourself whether the action happened.

## Do it in advance: 〜ておく

て form + おく (to put, to place) means doing something now, in preparation for later.
おく is a group 1 verb, so the forms are 〜ておきます, 〜ておいた, 〜ておこう, 〜ておいてください.

ホテルをよやくしておきました。 — I've booked the hotel (in advance).
{出|で}かける{前|まえ}に、{電車|でんしゃ}の{時間|じかん}をしらべておきます。 — Before I go out, I'll look up the train times.
{明日|あした}の{服|ふく}を{用意|ようい}しておこう。 — I'll get tomorrow's clothes ready.

It's also the standard way to offer or ask for a bit of preparation:

{地図|ちず}をコピーしておきましょうか。 — Shall I make a copy of the map (for later)?
{来週|らいしゅう}までに、この{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んでおいてください。 — Please read this book before next week.

（〜までに = by, lesson 19.）

### Leave it as it is

The same pattern also means "leave something in a state", deliberately:

まどは{開|あ}けておいてください。 — Please leave the window open.
そのままにしておいてください。 — Please leave it as it is.

（{開|あ}ける = to open, lesson 8; そのまま = as it is.） In lesson 8 you'll contrast this with
〜てある, which describes the state someone has left.

### てみる and ておく side by side

| Pattern | Question it answers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜てみる | What's it like? Does it work? | {着|き}てみる (try it on) |
| 〜ておく | Will I be ready? | {洗|あら}っておく (wash it beforehand) |

## Casual: 〜とく and 〜どく

In speech, 〜ておく shrinks to 〜とく, and 〜でおく (after verbs whose て form ends in で) to
〜どく. These are everywhere in casual conversation and messages.

| 〜ておく | Casual | |
|---|---|---|
| {買|か}っておく | {買|か}っとく | buy in advance |
| {書|か}いておく | {書|か}いとく | write down (for later) |
| しておく | しとく | do in advance |
| {読|よ}んでおく | {読|よ}んどく | read beforehand |

The short form conjugates as a group 1 verb in く, like {書|か}く: しとく, しといて (please do it
beforehand), しといた, しとこう (I'll do it now, then).

きっぷ、{買|か}っといたよ。 — I bought the tickets already.
{明日|あした}までにやっといて。 — Get it done by tomorrow, will you?
じゃあ、ぼくがよやくしとくね。 — OK, I'll make the booking, then.

Use とく with friends and family. To a teacher or a customer, say 〜ておきます.

## Kanji

Six kanji for getting ready and getting going.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 持 | hold | ジ | も(つ) | 9 | {持|も}つ, {気持|きも}ち |
| 用 | use, business | ヨウ | — | 5 | {用意|ようい}, {用事|ようじ} |
| 意 | mind, meaning | イ | — | 13 | {意味|いみ}, {用意|ようい}, {意見|いけん} |
| 急 | hurry | キュウ | いそ(ぐ) | 9 | {急|いそ}ぐ, {急|きゅう}に, {急行|きゅうこう} |
| 乗 | ride | ジョウ | の(る) | 9 | {乗|の}る, {乗|の}り{物|もの}, {乗|の}り{場|ば} |
| 早 | early | ソウ | はや(い) | 6 | {早|はや}い, {早|はや}く |

Memory notes:

- 持 is a hand (the left part, as in many action kanji) next to a temple: holding something
  safe.
- 用 looks like a wooden frame or fence: something built to be used.
- 意 is "sound" (音, lesson 3) above "heart" (心, lesson 9): the sound of your heart, what you
  mean.
- 急 has a hand reaching out above a heart (心): your heart racing to catch up, hurrying.
- 乗 is a person standing on top of a tree (木): climbing up and riding.
- 早 is the sun (日) just above the horizon line, with a sprout under it: early morning.

{早|はや}い means early. はやい meaning fast is written with a different kanji that isn't on the
N4 list, so for speed this course writes はやい in kana: {早|はや}く{起|お}きる (get up early), but
はやく{走|はし}る (run fast). N5's もつ, いそぐ, のる, いみ and ようじ are now written with kanji.
{気持|きも}ち (feeling) is a new word from this lesson.

```trace
持用意急乗早
```

## Dialogue: the night before the trip

Natsumi and Daniel are leaving for Hokkaido tomorrow. They speak casually.

```dialogue
# The night before
なつみ: {明日|あした}の{旅行|りょこう}のじゅんび、できた？
= Are you ready for tomorrow's trip?
ダニエル: うん、だいたい。きっぷはきのう{買|か}っといたよ。
= Yeah, more or less. I bought the tickets yesterday.
なつみ: よかった。ホテルの{住所|じゅうしょ}も、メモしといて。
= Great. Make a note of the hotel's address too.
ダニエル: もうしといたよ。{電話|でんわ}にも{入|い}れといた。
= Already done. I put it in my phone as well.
なつみ: さすが。あ、カメラの{電池|でんち}は？
= Brilliant. Oh, what about the camera battery?
ダニエル: あ、まだだ。{明日|あした}、{駅|えき}で{買|か}っとくよ。
= Oh, not yet. I'll buy one at the station tomorrow.
なつみ: それから、{北海道|ほっかいどう}は{寒|さむ}いから、セーターもかばんに{入|い}れといてね。
= And it's cold in Hokkaido, so put a sweater in your bag too.
ダニエル: うん。ねえ、むこうで{何|なに}を{食|た}べてみたい？
= OK. Hey, what do you want to try eating there?
なつみ: ラーメン！それから、{海|うみ}のものもいろいろ{食|た}べてみたい。
= Ramen! And I want to try all sorts of seafood.
ダニエル: じゃあ、{今夜|こんや}いい{店|みせ}をしらべとこう。
= Then let's look up some good places tonight.
```

さすが = that's you all over, as expected (praise); むこう = over there, at the other end;
{海|うみ}のもの = things from the sea, seafood.

## Reading: things to do before I go

Natsumi's list, with a note at the end. Lists and notes to yourself use plain forms.

> {旅行|りょこう}の{前|まえ}にしておくこと
>
> ・パスポートをたしかめておく。
> ・{電車|でんしゃ}のせきをよやくしておく。（{急行|きゅうこう}、{朝|あさ}{七時|しちじ}{発|はつ}）
> ・くうこうで{少|すこ}しりょうがえしておく。
> ・ホテルの{住所|じゅうしょ}と{電話|でんわ}ばんごうをメモしておく。
> ・{新|あたら}しいくつを{一度|いちど}はいてみる。たくさん{歩|ある}くから。
> ・{新聞|しんぶん}を{止|と}めておく。
> ・{近所|きんじょ}の{人|ひと}に、{一週間|いっしゅうかん}るすにすると{言|い}っておく。
> ・{出|で}かける{前|まえ}に、まどをしめて、{電気|でんき}をけしておく。
>
> {去年|きょねん}は{何|なに}もしらべておかなかったから、{旅行|りょこう}の{間|あいだ}、ずっとこまった。{今年|ことし}はちゃんとじゅんびしておこう。

Things to do before the trip:
- Check my passport.
- Book seats on the train. (Express, 7 a.m. departure)
- Change a little money at the airport.
- Write down the hotel's address and phone number.
- Try on the new shoes once, since I'll be walking a lot.
- Stop the newspaper.
- Tell the neighbours I'll be away for a week.
- Before leaving, shut the windows and turn off the lights.

Last year I didn't look anything up beforehand, so I had trouble the whole trip. This year
I'll prepare properly.

（〜{発|はつ} = departing at; るすにする = to be away from home; {旅行|りょこう}の{間|あいだ} = during the
trip, lesson 19.）

## Pronunciation: とく and どく

The casual forms keep the small っ or ん of the て form: {買|か}っとく is か・っ・と・く, four
beats, with the pause of っ; {読|よ}んどく is よ・ん・ど・く. Don't drop the っ: かとく is not a
word. And 〜てみる is said as one unit, with no pause between て and み.

```speak
このくつ、はいてみてもいいですか。
= May I try these shoes on?
{一度|いちど}{行|い}ってみたいです。
= I'd like to go there once.
ホテルをよやくしておきました。
= I've booked the hotel.
{地図|ちず}をコピーしておきましょうか。
= Shall I make a copy of the map?
きっぷ、{買|か}っといたよ。
= I've bought the tickets.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{食|た}べてを{見|み}る, ×{食|た}べて{見|み}る written with kanji. The helper is みる, in kana,
  straight after the て form: {食|た}べてみる.
- 〜てみる for an action that never happened: {書|か}いてみましたが、{書|か}けませんでした sounds
  contradictory. If you couldn't do it at all, use 〜(よ)うとしました.
- ×{読|よ}んとく. After a で, the short form is どく: {読|よ}んどく.
- Forgetting that おく is group 1: 〜ておいて (not ×〜ておきて), 〜ておこう (not ×〜ておきよう).
- 〜とく to a customer or teacher. Keep 〜ておきます in polite speech.
- はやい for speed written as {早|はや}い. {早|はや}い is early; fast stays in kana here.

## Key points

- て form + みる: try it and see; 〜てみたい (I'd like to try), 〜てみてください (give it a try).
- て form + おく: do in advance; also leave as it is. 〜ておきましょうか offers to prepare.
- Casual: 〜ておく → 〜とく, 〜でおく → 〜どく (しとく, {読|よ}んどく).
- 〜てみる is doing it; 〜(よ)うとする is trying, maybe failing.
- みる and おく are written in kana after て.
- New kanji: 持 用 意 急 乗 早.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Pitch accent
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Since lesson 1 your vocabulary cards have shown a line over each new word's reading after you
answer. This honors lesson explains what that line means: the word's **[[pitch accent]]**, the
pattern of high and low that every Japanese word carries. You'll learn how the Tokyo system
works, how to read the marks, which words it tells apart, how it behaves in verbs and
adjectives, and how much it matters for being understood. It isn't needed for the rest of the
course, but it will make your Japanese sound much more natural.

## High and low, not loud and soft

English marks one syllable in a word as strong: PHO-to-graph, pho-TO-gra-pher. The stressed
syllable is louder and longer, and the others are weakened.

Japanese works differently. Every beat keeps its full length and loudness, and what changes is
the pitch of the voice: each beat is either high or low. The beat is the **[[mora]]**, the unit you
already count when you clap out words: が・っ・こ・う is four morae, に・ほ・ん three,
コ・ー・ヒ・ー four. Small ゃ, ゅ, ょ belong to the kana before them (きょ is one mora), while
っ, ん and the second half of a long vowel count on their own.

## Two rules of Tokyo Japanese

Standard Japanese (ひょうじゅんご, the Japanese of news broadcasts and textbooks) is based on Tokyo speech, and its pitch follows two rules:

1. The first and second morae are different. If the first is high, the second is low; if the
   first is low, the second is high.
2. Once the pitch falls inside a word, it doesn't rise again in that word.

So all that matters is where the pitch falls, if it falls at all. That point is the **accent
nucleus**: the last high mora before the drop (the drop itself is called the **downstep**).
Dictionaries and this course give it as a number: the mora after which the pitch falls, with
0 for words where it never falls.

## The four patterns

| Pattern | Number | Example | Pitch of the word + が |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[[flat (heiban)]]** | 0 | {名前|なまえ:0} (name) | な low, ま え high, が high |
| **[[atamadaka]]** (head-high) | 1 | {雨|あめ:1} (rain) | あ high, め low, が low |
| **[[nakadaka]]** (middle-high) | 2, 3… | {先生|せんせい:3} (teacher) | せ low, ん せ high, い low, が low |
| **[[odaka]]** (tail-high) | = number of morae | {山|やま:2} (mountain) | や low, ま high, が low |

Look at the last column. A flat word and an odaka word sound the same on their own: low, then
high. The difference only shows on the particle that follows. After a flat word the particle
stays high ({名前|なまえ:0}が); after an odaka word it drops ({山|やま:2}が). That's why it pays to
learn words with a particle attached.

More examples you know:

- Flat (0): {学生|がくせい:0}, {水|みず:0}, {電話|でんわ:0}… no fall anywhere.
- Atamadaka (1): {本|ほん:1}, {木|き:1}, {今|いま:1}.
- Nakadaka: {日本|にほん:2} (に low, ほ high, ん low), {先生|せんせい:3}.
- Odaka: {花|はな:2}, {川|かわ:2}, {犬|いぬ:2}, {男|おとこ:3}, {女|おんな:3}.

## Reading this course's marks

Wherever pitch is marked, a line runs over the high morae, and a short tick hangs down where
the pitch falls. An odaka word has its tick after the last mora, warning you that the particle
will be low. A flat word has a line and no tick. Here are the same four patterns, marked:

[なまえ:0] · [あめ:1] · [せんせい:3] · [やま:2]

You can switch the marks off next to the furigana switch. On vocabulary cards the accent
appears after you've answered; answers are never marked wrong for pitch.

## One sound, three words: はし

The classic example is はし, which can mean three things. Their kanji aren't on the N4 list,
so they're in kana here.

| Word | Accent | Alone | With が |
|---|---|---|---|
| chopsticks | [はし:1] | high-low | は high, し low, が low |
| bridge | [はし:2] | low-high | は low, し high, が low |
| edge | [はし:0] | low-high | は low, し high, が high |

On their own, "bridge" and "edge" sound the same. Add a particle and all three differ:
[はし:1]で{食|た}べる (eat with chopsticks), [はし:2]をわたる (cross a bridge),
{道|みち}の[はし:0]を{歩|ある}く (walk at the edge of the road).

## Minimal pairs

Some everyday pairs differ only in pitch:

| Word | Accent | Word | Accent |
|---|---|---|---|
| {雨|あめ:1} rain | high-low | あめ candy | [あめ:0] low-high |
| かき oyster | [かき:1] high-low | かき persimmon | [かき:0] low-high |
| {木|き:1} tree | き high, が low | {気|き:0} mind, mood | き low, が high |
| {今|いま:1} now | high-low | いま living room | [いま:2] low-high, then が low |
| {花|はな:2} flower | low-high, が low | はな nose | [はな:0] low-high, が high |

In real conversation, context almost always makes the meaning clear: nobody eats a bridge.
Pitch is mostly about sounding natural, and only occasionally about being understood.

```speak
# Listen and compare
{雨|あめ}がふっています。
= It's raining. (あめ: high-low)
あめを{一|ひと}つください。
= One sweet, please. (あめ: low-high)
はしで{食|た}べます。
= I eat with chopsticks.
はしをわたります。
= I cross the bridge.
{道|みち}のはしを{歩|ある}きます。
= I walk at the edge of the road.
{花|はな}がきれいです。
= The flowers are pretty. (が is low)
```

These phrases are read by your device's voice, which usually, but not always, chooses the
right pitch from the context. Native recordings, from a teacher, a podcast or a dictionary
with audio, are the best models.

## Verbs and adjectives

Verbs and い-adjectives come in two kinds: flat, and accented (falling on one particular mora).

| Flat (0) | Accented |
|---|---|
| [いく:0] go, [いう:0] say, [あそぶ:0] play, [する:0] do | {食|た}べる [たべる:2], {見|み}る [みる:1], {書|か}く [かく:1], {話|はな}す [はなす:2], {帰|かえ}る [かえる:1] |
| {赤|あか}い [あかい:0], {明|あか}るい [あかるい:0] | {高|たか}い [たかい:2], {白|しろ}い [しろい:2] |

The accent moves as a word is conjugated, but in regular ways. Two you can use right away:

- Every ます form falls after ま, whatever the verb: [たべます:3], [いきます:3], [します:2].
- The て form of an accented verb falls early; a flat verb stays flat: [たべて:1], [かいて:1], but
  [いって:0] (go), [あそんで:0].

You don't need to learn rules for every form. Listen to whole phrases and copy them.

## Other regions

The Tokyo pattern is the standard, but it isn't the only one. The Kansai region (かんさい: Osaka,
Kyoto, Kobe) has its own accent system, and many everyday words have a different pitch there,
so Kansai speakers sound quite different even when they use the same words. Some areas, in
parts of northern Kantō, southern Tōhoku and Kyūshū, hardly distinguish words by pitch at all.
Japanese people understand each other across all of these, which tells you how much context
carries.

## How much does it matter?

- For being understood: a little. Wrong pitch rarely causes a real misunderstanding.
- For sounding natural: a lot. Pitch is one of the main things that makes a learner's
  pronunciation ({発音|はつおん}) sound foreign, even when every sound is right.
- For the JLPT: not at all directly; the test has no pitch questions. Good pitch does make
  listening easier, because you hear where one word ends and the next begins.

A practical approach: notice the mark when you learn a new word, say it with a particle
({山|やま}が, {名前|なまえ}が), and copy native speakers phrase by phrase rather than word by word.
Don't let pitch stop you speaking.

## Key points

- Japanese pitch accent is high and low on each mora, not loud and soft.
- Tokyo rules: the first two morae differ; once the pitch falls, it stays low.
- The number is where it falls: 0 flat (particle high), 1 atamadaka, middle nakadaka, last
  mora odaka (particle low).
- Flat and odaka words differ only on the following particle: learn words with が.
- Pairs like [はし:1]/[はし:2]/[はし:0], {雨|あめ:1}/[あめ:0], {花|はな:2}/[はな:0] differ only in pitch.
- ます forms fall after ま; regions like Kansai have different patterns.
