lessons.title: Moving in: renting and the neighbours
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 4 talked about plans to move. This honors lesson is about what happens next, if you
rent a flat in Japan: the estate agent, the money you pay at the start, the contract, meeting
the neighbours, and the famous rubbish rules. Customs differ from region to region and from
building to building, so take the details as typical, not fixed.

## Finding a flat

Most people find a flat through a ふどうさんや, an estate agent, or the websites they run.
Listings are packed with short words and numbers. The ones you'll see most:

| On the listing | Meaning |
|---|---|
| やちん | the monthly rent |
| かんりひ | a monthly fee for the building's upkeep, paid with the rent |
| しききん | a deposit |
| れいきん | "key money", a one-off payment to the landlord |
| 1K, 2LDK… | the layout: number of rooms, plus L (living), D (dining), K (kitchen) |
| {駅|えき}からとほ{5分|ごふん} | five minutes' walk from the station |

とほ means "on foot". It's written with two kanji, and the second is 歩 (lesson 2), read ほ;
the first isn't an N4 kanji.

## Money at the start

Moving in can cost several months' rent before you've spent a night there. As background:

- しききん, the deposit, is often one or two months' rent. When you leave, the {大家|おおや}
  (landlord) takes out the cost of cleaning and repairs and returns the rest.
- れいきん, key money, is a thank-you payment to the landlord that you don't get back. It used
  to be one or two months' rent almost everywhere; today many flats ask for none.
- The agent usually charges a fee, often around one month's rent.
- Many landlords want a guarantor, ほしょうにん, someone who promises to pay if you can't.
  Newcomers often use a guarantee company instead, for a fee.

Ask what each listing includes. A flat with no しききん or れいきん may have other fees.

## The contract and the hanko

The contract, けいやく, is often for two years. It was traditionally stamped with your personal
seal, a はんこ, and some agents still ask for one. Many now accept a signature, and contracts
signed online are becoming common. Read the rules in the contract: whether pets or musical
instruments are allowed, and how much notice to give before you leave.

## Greeting the neighbours

The traditional custom is to visit your neighbours soon after moving in, introduce yourself
and give a small gift: a towel, a packet of washing powder or some sweets, worth about 500 to
1,000 yen. In a house, that's the neighbours on each side and across the road; in a block of
flats, the doors on each side and the flats above and below.

はじめまして。となりにひっこしてきたリサです。よろしくおねがいします。 — Hello, I'm Lisa. I've just moved in next door. Pleased to meet you.

（ひっこしてきた = have moved here; 〜てくる is in lesson 24.） Many people who live alone in
big blocks of flats no longer do this, and some, especially women living alone, skip it for
safety. In a small building or a family neighbourhood, a short あいさつ still makes life
easier, not least when you have a question about the rubbish.

## Rubbish days

Every town has its own rules for sorting rubbish, ごみの{分|わ}け{方|かた}, and its own calendar of
collection days. You get a chart from the city office or the landlord, often in several
languages. The usual groups:

| Group | Typically |
|---|---|
| もえるごみ (burnable) | kitchen waste, paper scraps, small plastic items in some towns |
| もえないごみ (non-burnable) | glass, ceramics, metal objects, old umbrellas |
| しげんごみ (recyclable) | cans, bottles, plastic drink bottles, newspapers and cardboard |
| そだいごみ (large items) | furniture, bicycles: book a collection and pay a fee |

The details vary: one town burns plastic, the next recycles it. Common rules are to put rubbish
out on the morning of collection (often by 8 a.m.), not the night before; to use the town's
own bags where it has them; and to rinse bottles and take off their caps. Rubbish that isn't
sorted may be left behind with a sticker on it, which every neighbour can see.

## Registering your address

After moving, you must register your new address at the city or ward office, within 14 days
of moving in. That includes foreign residents, who also have their residence card updated. You
can read more about the city office in honors lesson 15h2.

## Dialogue: at the estate agent

Lisa is looking for a flat. Mr Morita works at the agent's.

```dialogue
# At the estate agent
リサ: すみません、{駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くでへやをさがしているんですが。
= Excuse me, I'm looking for a flat near the station.
{森田|もりた}: はい。やちんはいくらぐらいがいいですか。
= Certainly. About how much rent were you thinking of?
リサ: {七万円|ななまんえん}までです。{一人|ひとり}で{住|す}むんです。{小|ちい}さいへやでいいです。
= Up to seventy thousand yen. I'll be living alone, so a small flat is fine.
{森田|もりた}: では、こちらはどうですか。{駅|えき}から{歩|ある}いて{五分|ごふん}で、やちんは{六万八千円|ろくまんはっせんえん}です。
= Then how about this one? It's five minutes' walk from the station, and the rent is 68,000 yen.
リサ: しききんとれいきんはありますか。
= Is there a deposit, and key money?
{森田|もりた}: しききんは{一|いっ}か{月|げつ}{分|ぶん}です。れいきんはありません。
= The deposit is one month's rent. There's no key money.
リサ: よかった。へやを{見|み}てみたいんですが。
= Good. I'd like to see the flat.
{森田|もりた}: はい、{今|いま}からごあんないしましょうか。
= Of course. Shall I take you there now?
リサ: おねがいします。けいやくのときは、はんこがいりますか。
= Yes, please. Do I need a hanko for the contract?
{森田|もりた}: はんこでも、サインでもだいじょうぶですよ。
= Either a hanko or a signature is fine.
```

{一|いっ}か{月|げつ}{分|ぶん} = one month's worth; ごあんないする = a polite (humble) way of saying
あんないする, which you'll learn about in lesson 28; AでもBでも = either A or B; はんこがいる = to need a hanko (いる "to need"
is a different verb from いる "to be": group 1, いります).

## Reading: a notice from the landlord

> {大家|おおや}からのおねがい：ごみの{出|だ}し{方|かた}
>
> ごみは、{下|した}の{日|ひ}の{朝|あさ}{八時|はちじ}までに、アパートの{前|まえ}のごみおきばに{出|だ}してください。{前|まえ}の{日|ひ}の{夜|よる}には{出|だ}さないでください。
>
> ・もえるごみ（{台所|だいどころ}のごみ、{紙|かみ}くずなど）：{月曜日|げつようび}と{木曜日|もくようび}
> ・もえないごみ（ガラス、{古|ふる}いかさなど）：{毎月|まいつき}、{二|に}ばん{目|め}の{水曜日|すいようび}
> ・しげんごみ（かん、びん、ペットボトル）：{金曜日|きんようび}。ペットボトルはキャップをとって、{水|みず}で{洗|あら}ってから{出|だ}してください。
> ・そだいごみ（つくえ、{自転車|じてんしゃ}など）：{市|し}に{電話|でんわ}して、よやくしてください。お{金|かね}がかかります。
>
> ごみはちゃんと{分|わ}けてください。{分|わ}けていないごみは、{市|し}が{持|も}っていきません。
>
> {大家|おおや} {田村|たむら}

A request from the landlord: how to put out rubbish.

Please put rubbish out at the collection point in front of the building by 8 a.m. on the days
below. Please don't put it out the night before.
- Burnable rubbish (kitchen waste, paper scraps and so on): Mondays and Thursdays
- Non-burnable rubbish (glass, old umbrellas and so on): the second Wednesday of every month
- Recyclables (cans, bottles, plastic bottles): Fridays. Take the caps off plastic bottles and
  rinse them with water before putting them out.
- Large items (desks, bicycles and so on): phone the city and book a collection. There's a fee.

Please sort your rubbish properly. The city won't take rubbish that isn't sorted.

The landlord, Tamura

（ごみおきば = the rubbish collection point; {紙|かみ}くず = scraps of paper; {持|も}っていく = to take
away, lesson 24.）

## Key points

- やちん (rent), しききん (deposit, mostly returned), れいきん (key money, not returned; often
  none today), an agent's fee and a guarantor or guarantee company.
- Contracts (けいやく) are often two years; a はんこ or, increasingly, a signature.
- A small gift and an あいさつ for the neighbours is traditional, though less common in big
  blocks of flats.
- Sort rubbish by your town's chart and put it out on the right morning.
- Register your new address at the city office within 14 days.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Giving and receiving: あげる, くれる, もらう
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

English gets by with two verbs for handing things over: give and receive. Japanese has three
everyday ones, あげる, くれる and もらう, and which one you choose depends on something English
doesn't mark at all: whose side the giver and the receiver are on. "My sister gave me a tie" and
"I gave my sister a tie" don't just swap the names; they use different verbs.

This module is about giving, receiving and getting things done. This lesson sets up the three
verbs with things (presents, cards, money); lesson 7 puts the same three verbs after a て form
for favours ("she helped me", "I'll carry it for you"). If the choice between あげる and くれる
feels automatic by the end of this lesson, lesson 7 will be easy. The theme is gifts in the
family: birthdays, weddings, and the return gift, おかえし.

## Whose side are you on?

Japanese divides people into your own side and everyone else. You met this in N5 with family
words: {父|ちち} for your own father, お{父|とう}さん for someone else's. The idea is
**[[in-group and out-group]]** (uchi and soto): you, your family, and in many situations your own company or
team are "inside"; other people are "outside".

The giving verbs follow the same line. Picture the gift moving:

- **outward**, from you (or your side) to someone else: あげる;
- **inward**, from someone else to you (or your side): くれる;
- and from the receiver's point of view, whichever way it moves: もらう ("receive, get").

Together these are the **[[giving and receiving verbs]]**. Their polite forms come later in this
lesson.

## あげる: giving outward

The giver is the topic or subject, the receiver takes に, the gift takes を.

**giver は receiver に thing を あげる**

{私|わたし}は{姉|あね}にネクタイをあげました。 — I gave my older sister a tie.
{父|ちち}のたんじょうびに{時計|とけい}をあげるつもりです。 — I'm going to give my father a watch for his birthday.

あげる is also the neutral verb for giving between two other people, when neither is on your
side, as in a story or a report:

けんじさんはさきさんに{花|はな}をあげました。 — Kenji gave Saki some flowers.

What あげる can never do is point at you. "My friend gave me a book" is not
×{友|とも}だちは{私|わたし}に{本|ほん}をあげました. When the gift comes to you, you need くれる.

## くれる: giving inward

くれる is "give" when the receiver is you, or someone on your side. The giver is the subject
(usually with が in a new statement, は when it's already the topic), the receiver takes に, and
you usually leave out {私|わたし}に because it's obvious.

{友|とも}だちが{本|ほん}をくれました。 — A friend gave me a book.
{姉|あね}がこのネクタイをくれたんです。 — My older sister gave me this tie, you see.
となりの{人|ひと}が{妹|いもうと}におかしをくれました。 — The neighbour gave my little sister some sweets.

The last sentence is the important one. Your little sister isn't you, but she's in your family,
so from where you stand the sweets came inward: くれる. If you said あげました there, it would
sound as if your sister were an outsider.

Two things くれる can't do: the giver can't be you (×{私|わたし}は{友|とも}だちに{本|ほん}をくれました),
and it can't describe giving between two outsiders.

## もらう: receiving

もらう looks at the same event from the receiver's side. The receiver is the topic, the giver
takes に or から.

**receiver は giver に/から thing を もらう**

{私|わたし}は{兄|あに}にカードをもらいました。 — I got a card from my older brother.
りょうしんからお{金|かね}をもらいました。 — I got some money from my parents.

に and から both work with a person. With a company, school or other organization, use から:
{会社|かいしゃ}からカードをもらいました (I got a card from the company). に after a person
looks like the に of "to", but with もらう it marks where the thing came from, so read it as
"from".

The receiver is usually you or your side, but it can be anyone: さきさんはけんじさんに{花|はな}を
もらいました (Saki got flowers from Kenji). What sounds odd is you as the giver:
{友|とも}だちは{私|わたし}に{本|ほん}をもらいました is grammatical, but Japanese speakers tell their own
giving with あげる: {私|わたし}は{友|とも}だちに{本|ほん}をあげました.

## One event, two sentences

Most gifts can be told two ways: with the giver as subject (あげる or くれる) or with the
receiver as subject (もらう).

| What happened | Giver's view | Receiver's view |
|---|---|---|
| I → my sister | {私|わたし}は{姉|あね}にあげました | {姉|あね}は{私|わたし}にもらいました (possible, but you'd normally tell your own giving with あげる) |
| my sister → me | {姉|あね}がくれました | {私|わたし}は{姉|あね}にもらいました |
| a friend → my brother | {友|とも}だちが{弟|おとうと}にくれました | {弟|おとうと}は{友|とも}だちにもらいました |
| Kenji → Saki (both outsiders) | けんじさんはさきさんにあげました | さきさんはけんじさんにもらいました |

The full chart is on the reference sheet for this module.

A quick way to choose: find the receiver. If it's you or your side and the giver is the
subject, くれる. If it's someone else and the giver is the subject, あげる. If the receiver is the
subject, もらう.

## Polite giving: さしあげる, くださる, いただく

Each verb has a polite partner for when someone above you is involved: a teacher, a boss, a
customer, someone much older.

| Plain | Polite | Who's being respected |
|---|---|---|
| あげる | さしあげる | the receiver (you lower yourself as giver) |
| くれる | くださる | the giver (you raise them) |
| もらう | いただく | the giver (you lower yourself as receiver) |

{先生|せんせい}に{手紙|てがみ}をさしあげました。 — I gave the teacher a letter.
{先生|せんせい}が{本|ほん}をくださいました。 — The teacher gave me a book.
{先生|せんせい}に{本|ほん}をいただきました。 — I received a book from the teacher.

さしあげる and いただく are humble words (you make your own action smaller), and くださる is a
respectful word (you raise the other person); module 6 teaches this kind of polite language
properly. For now, learn them as set words. A few points:

- くださる has a slightly odd ます form: くださいます, くださいました, not ×くださります.
  ください, which you've used since N5, comes from this verb.
- いただく is the いただきます you say before eating: "I humbly receive".
- さしあげる is fine when you talk *about* a gift to a superior, but saying さしあげます straight
  to that person can sound stiff or even showy, so people often just say どうぞ as they hand
  something over.

## やる: to plants and animals

A fourth verb, やる, is a plain, casual "give" for animals and plants, and in some families for
younger relatives.

{毎朝|まいあさ}、{花|はな}に{水|みず}をやります。 — I water the flowers every morning.
{犬|いぬ}にえさをやりました。 — I fed the dog. (えさ = animal food)

Many speakers now say あげる here too ({花|はな}に{水|みず}をあげる), and you'll hear both. Don't use
やる to or about people outside the family: it sounds rough.

## 〜ずつ: each, at a time

ずつ after a number or amount means "each" or "so many at a time". It follows the number
directly, with no particle.

{子|こ}どもたちにおかしを{二|ふた}つずつあげました。 — I gave the children two sweets each.
{一人|ひとり}{千円|せんえん}ずつ{出|だ}しましょう。 — Let's each put in a thousand yen.
{漢字|かんじ}を{少|すこ}しずつおぼえています。 — I'm learning kanji little by little.

Notice {一人|ひとり}{千円|せんえん}ずつ: a common way to split a group present.

## Gifts in the family

Gifts in Japan follow a calendar: birthdays and Christmas, as in many countries, but also a
present for a child starting school ({入学|にゅうがく}), finishing school (そつぎょう), a wedding,
a new baby. For the big occasions people give おいわい, a celebration gift, which is often money
in a special envelope.

An おかえし is a return gift. After a wedding or a new baby, a family usually sends something
back to the people who gave おいわい, often worth a third to a half of what they received; the
habit and the amount vary by family and region. For birthday presents between friends, people
don't usually send おかえし: a thank-you, おれい, is enough. Honors lesson 10h1 has more about
gift customs.

{手作|てづく}り (handmade) presents are popular in families, especially from children:
{妹|いもうと}が{手作|てづく}りのカードをくれました (My little sister gave me a handmade card).

## Kanji

Seven kanji for your family and the people in it. You've written all of these words in kana
since N5 ({私|わたし}, かぞく, あに…); from now on write them with kanji.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 私 | I; private | シ | わたし, わたくし | 7 | {私|わたし}, {私|わたくし} (formal) |
| 家 | house; family | カ, ケ | いえ, うち, や | 10 | {家|いえ}, {家|うち}, {家族|かぞく}, {家事|かじ} (lesson 10) |
| 族 | family, tribe | ゾク | — | 11 | {家族|かぞく} |
| 兄 | older brother | キョウ, ケイ | あに | 5 | {兄|あに}, お{兄|にい}さん, {兄弟|きょうだい} |
| 姉 | older sister | シ | あね | 8 | {姉|あね}, お{姉|ねえ}さん, {姉妹|しまい} (sisters) |
| 弟 | younger brother | ダイ, テイ | おとうと | 7 | {弟|おとうと}, {弟|おとうと}さん, {兄弟|きょうだい} |
| 妹 | younger sister | マイ | いもうと | 8 | {妹|いもうと}, {妹|いもうと}さん, {姉妹|しまい} |

Special readings to learn as words: お{兄|にい}さん and お{姉|ねえ}さん (the kanji is read にい and
ねえ only here), and {一人|ひとり}っ{子|こ} (an only child: {一人|ひとり} + っ + {子|こ}).

**家: いえ or うち?** Both are written 家. {家|いえ:2} is the house as a building: {大|おお}きい{家|いえ}, {新|あたら}しい{家|いえ}.
うち is home and the household, and it's the word you met in N5: うちに{帰|かえ}る (go home), うちの{犬|いぬ}
(our dog). うち is often written in kana, especially in うちの (our). When you see 家 alone, the
context decides; furigana in this course will tell you which.

Memory notes:

- 家 is a roof on top with a pig underneath: in old China the family pig lived under the house roof.
- 私 has a grain plant on the left: what's "mine" started with my own share of the harvest.
- 兄 is a big mouth (口) on two legs: the older brother, who does the talking.
- 姉 and 妹 both have 女 (woman) on the left. The right side of 妹 is a character meaning "not yet": the sister who isn't grown
  up yet. 姉 has what looks like 市 (market, lesson 15): the older sister, old enough to go to market.
- 弟 looks like a cord wound round a stick, in steps: the brother who comes after.
- 族: the left side (like 方 with a hat) is a flag, and under the cover on the right is an arrow: a clan gathered under one flag.

```trace
私家族兄姉弟妹
```

## Dialogue: a birthday tie

```dialogue
# A birthday tie
はるか: ルーカスさん、そのネクタイ、すてきですね。
= Lucas, that's a nice tie.
ルーカス: ありがとうございます。きのうたんじょうびだったんです。{姉|あね}がくれました。
= Thanks. Yesterday was my birthday. My older sister gave it to me.
はるか: おめでとうございます！ほかに{何|なに}かもらいましたか。
= Happy birthday! Did you get anything else?
ルーカス: りょうしんからカードと{本|ほん}をもらいました。それから、{会社|かいしゃ}のみんながケーキをくれました。
= I got a card and a book from my parents. And everyone at work gave me a cake.
はるか: いいですね。{私|わたし}は{来週|らいしゅう}、{父|ちち}に{時計|とけい}をあげるつもりです。{父|ちち}もたんじょうびなんです。
= Nice. Next week I'm going to give my father a watch. It's his birthday too.
ルーカス: お{父|とう}さん、よろこびますね。{日本|にほん}では、プレゼントのおかえしをしますか。
= Your father will be pleased. In Japan, do people give something back for a present?
はるか: けっこんしきのおいわいには、たいていおかえしをします。でも、たんじょうびはあまりしません。
= For wedding gifts, they usually do. But not much for birthdays.
ルーカス: じゃあ、{姉|あね}のたんじょうびに、{私|わたし}が{何|なに}かあげます。
= Then I'll give my sister something for her birthday.
はるか: それがいちばんのおかえしですね。
= That's the best return gift.
```

すてき = nice, lovely; ケーキ = cake; たいてい = usually; よろこぶ = to be pleased. Notice
that Lucas uses くれました for his sister and his colleagues (inward, to him) and もらいました
when he is the subject; Haruka uses あげる for her own gift to her father, because she is the
giver.

## Reading: Grandma turns eighty

> {先月|せんげつ}、そぼが{八十|はちじゅう}さいになりました。{日曜日|にちようび}に、{家族|かぞく}といとこたちがそぼの{家|いえ}に{来|き}て、みんなでおいわいをしました。
>
> {私|わたし}はそぼに{花|はな}をあげました。{兄|あに}は{家族|かぞく}の{写真|しゃしん}で{本|ほん}を{作|つく}って、あげました。{一人|ひとり}っ{子|こ}のいとこのゆいは、{手作|てづく}りのカードをあげました。
>
> そぼはとてもよろこんで、「ありがとう。みんなのプレゼント、{大切|たいせつ}にするね」と{言|い}いました。そぼの{手|て}には、むかしそふにもらったゆびわがありました。
>
> それから、そぼはまごたちにおかしを{三|みっ}つずつくれました。{私|わたし}たちはもう{大人|おとな}ですが、そぼはいつもおかしをくれます。{来年|らいねん}も、みんなでおいわいをしたいです。

Last month my grandmother turned eighty. On Sunday the family and my cousins came to her house
and we all celebrated together. I gave her flowers. My older brother made a book of family
photos and gave her that. My cousin Yui, who's an only child, gave her a handmade card. Grandma
was very pleased and said, "Thank you. I'll treasure everyone's presents." On her hand was the
ring she got from my grandfather long ago. Then she gave each of us grandchildren three sweets.
We're grown up now, but Grandma always gives us sweets. Next year I want us all to celebrate
together again.

Notice the direction words. Inside the family the line is drawn closer, at you: the writer,
the writer's brother and cousin give to Grandma with あげる, and when Grandma gives to the
grandchildren, the writer among them, it's くれました. むかし = long ago; {大人|おとな} = adult.

A word you'll meet in this module: {親|おや} is a plain word for a parent or parents. Children
talk about their {親|おや}, and {親|おや}にもらったお{金|かね} is money you got from your parents.
For "my parents" in polite conversation, りょうしん is still the usual word.

## Pronunciation

あげる, くれる and もらう are all flat: [あげる:0], [くれる:0], [もらう:0]. The pitch stays up to the
end and onto the next word, so あげました and もらいました don't fall until ま. くださる falls after
さ: [くださる:3].

## Say it

```speak
たんじょうびおめでとうございます。
= Happy birthday.
これ、どうぞ。
= Here, this is for you.
ありがとうございます。{大切|たいせつ}にします。
= Thank you. I'll take good care of it.
{姉|あね}がくれました。
= My older sister gave it to me.
りょうしんにもらいました。
= I got it from my parents.
{先生|せんせい}にいただきました。
= I received it from my teacher.
```

{大切|たいせつ}にします ("I'll treasure it") is a warm thing to say when you get a present.

## Common mistakes

- あげる for something given to you: ×{友|とも}だちは{私|わたし}にくつしたをあげました. Inward is
  くれる: {友|とも}だちがくつしたをくれました.
- くれる with yourself as the giver: ×{私|わたし}は{妹|いもうと}にペンをくれました. Outward is あげる.
- Mixing up the particle with もらう: in {兄|あに}にもらいました, {兄|あに} is the giver, not the
  receiver. The receiver is the topic.
- Forgetting your family is on your side: a neighbour gives your brother something → くれる,
  not あげる.
- ×くださります. The ます form is くださいます.
- やる to or about people outside the family. It sounds rough; use あげる.

## Key points

- あげる: giving outward (from you or your side to others, or between outsiders).
- くれる: giving inward (to you or your side). The giver is never you.
- もらう: receiving; the giver takes に or から (から for organizations).
- Polite: さしあげる (for あげる), くださる (for くれる; くださいます), いただく (for もらう).
- やる: giving to plants and animals (casual). 〜ずつ: each, at a time.
- New kanji: 私 家 族 兄 姉 弟 妹. Special readings: お{兄|にい}さん, お{姉|ねえ}さん, {一人|ひとり}っ{子|こ}, {家|いえ}/{家|うち}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Doing favours: 〜てあげる, 〜てくれる, 〜てもらう
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 6 things moved between people: presents, cards, money. Actions move between people
too. When a friend drives you to the station, Japanese doesn't just say "my friend drove me";
it says the friend drove you *and gave you that* as a favour. The three giving verbs go after a
て form and do exactly this:

- {友|とも}だちが{駅|えき}まで{送|おく}ってくれました。 — My friend kindly took me to the station.
- {友|とも}だちに{駅|えき}まで{送|おく}ってもらいました。 — I had my friend take me to the station.
- {友|とも}だちを{駅|えき}まで{送|おく}ってあげました。 — I took my friend to the station (for them).

Here あげる, くれる and もらう are **[[auxiliary verbs]]**: they follow another verb's て form and
add a meaning (here, who benefits) instead of their own literal meaning. They're written in
kana, like the 〜てみる and 〜ておく you met in lesson 5. This lesson also shows how to ask for
help politely, which is where these forms are used most: 〜てくれませんか, 〜てもらえませんか,
〜ていただけませんか, and how to say you want someone to do something, 〜てほしい.

## The same directions as lesson 6

The rules for who can be the giver are exactly the rules from lesson 6. Only now the "gift" is
an action.

| Pattern | Who does the action | Who benefits | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜てあげる | you (or your side), or anyone | someone else | {妹|いもうと}に{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んであげました。 |
| 〜てくれる | someone else | you or your side | {兄|あに}が{写真|しゃしん}をとってくれました。 |
| 〜てもらう | the person with に | the topic (usually you) | {兄|あに}に{写真|しゃしん}をとってもらいました。 |

## 〜てくれる: someone did something for me

〜てくれる is the one you'll use most, because it carries thanks. Compare:

{兄|あに}が{教|おし}えました。 — My brother taught (me). (just a fact)
{兄|あに}が{教|おし}えてくれました。 — My brother taught me (and I'm grateful).

When someone does something that helps you, a Japanese speaker nearly always adds くれる. Leaving
it out can sound cold, or even as if you didn't want the help.

{森|もり}さんが{町|まち}をあんないしてくれました。 — Mrs Mori kindly showed me around the town.
となりの{人|ひと}が{妹|いもうと}の{自転車|じてんしゃ}をなおしてくれました。 — The neighbour fixed my little sister's bicycle.

As in lesson 6, "my side" includes your family: the neighbour helped your sister, so it's
くれる. The person who benefits usually isn't said at all.

The polite form is 〜てくださる, for a teacher, boss or customer:

{先生|せんせい}がていねいに{説明|せつめい}してくださいました。 — The teacher kindly explained it carefully.
(ていねいに = carefully, politely)

## 〜てもらう: I had someone do it

〜てもらう tells the same event from the receiver's side. The receiver is the topic, and the
person who does the action takes に. (から is heard with a few verbs such as {教|おし}える, but
に always works.)

{友|とも}だちにひっこしをてつだってもらいました。 — I got friends to help me move house.
{駅員|えきいん}さんに{道|みち}を{教|おし}えてもらいました。 — I had the station staff tell me the way.

〜てもらう often hints that you asked for the favour, or at least that you're the one who got
something out of it. 〜てくれる puts the other person's kindness first. Both are fine for
thanking; which one you pick is mostly a matter of who you want as the subject.

The polite form is 〜ていただく:

{先生|せんせい}に{作文|さくぶん}を{見|み}ていただきました。 — I had the teacher look at my essay.

## 〜てあげる: doing something for someone

〜てあげる is the outward one: you do something for someone else.

{友|とも}だちに{日本語|にほんご}を{教|おし}えてあげました。 — I taught my friend some Japanese.
おばあさんにせきをゆずってあげました。 — I gave up my seat to an elderly woman.

**Particles stay with the verb.** The person you help keeps whatever particle the main verb
gives them. {教|おし}える and ゆずる have a slot for a person with に, so に works. Most verbs don't:
{持|も}つ, {見|み}る, なおす have no "to someone" slot. Then show whose thing it is with の:

{友|とも}だちのかばんを{持|も}ってあげました。 — I carried my friend's bag for them.
{弟|おとうと}のしゅくだいを{見|み}てあげました。 — I looked over my little brother's homework.

×{友|とも}だちにかばんを{持|も}ってあげました is a common learner's mistake. The same goes for
〜てくれる: {兄|あに}が{私|わたし}のパソコンをなおしてくれました, not ×{私|わたし}にパソコンをなおしてくれました.

### When 〜てあげる sounds pushy

Talking *about* what you did (as above) is fine. Saying it *to* the person you're helping is
different: てつだってあげます sounds like "I'll do you the favour of helping", which puts
you above them. To a superior it's rude; even to a friend it can sound patronizing. To offer
help, use 〜ましょうか (N5) instead:

にもつを{運|はこ}びましょうか。 — Shall I carry your luggage?
まどを{開|あ}けましょうか。 — Shall I open the window?

The same goes for 〜てさしあげる, the humble form: it exists, but people avoid saying it to the
person concerned.

〜てあげる is natural with your own children, younger people and pets: {子|こ}どもに{本|ほん}を
{読|よ}んであげました (I read a book to my child).

## Asking for help: a politeness scale

Lesson 2 taught you the potential form, so you can now turn もらう and いただく into "can I
receive…?": もらえる, いただける. With くれる and くださる, these make a set of requests, from
casual to very polite. Most are negative questions ("won't you…?"), which are softer than a
straight question.

| Request | Feels like | Use with |
|---|---|---|
| 〜てくれる？ / 〜てくれない？ | can you…? | friends, family (casual) |
| 〜てください | please do | instructions; fine, but direct |
| 〜てくれませんか | would you…? | people you know, politely |
| 〜てもらえませんか | could I ask you to…? | a little softer: colleagues, shop staff |
| 〜てくださいませんか | would you kindly…? | strangers, people above you |
| 〜ていただけませんか | might I ask you to…? | the most polite here: bosses, customers |

The order of the middle rows is a rough guide; tone of voice and すみません count as much as the
form. Starting with すみません、ちょっといいですか or a reason with 〜んですが (lesson 1) makes any
of them kinder:

すみません、ちょっとペンを{貸|か}してもらえませんか。 — Excuse me, could I borrow your pen for a moment?
{日本語|にほんご}のメールなんですが、ちょっと{見|み}ていただけませんか。 — It's an email in Japanese; might I ask you to look at it?
ねえ、それ、とってくれない？ — Hey, can you pass me that?

Notice ペンを{貸|か}してもらえませんか: you ask the other person to lend ({貸|か}す), not to
borrow. If you want to say "may I borrow", that's {借|か}りてもいいですか (N5's 〜てもいい).

**Answering.** Yes: いいですよ, はい、どうぞ, ええ、よろこんで (gladly). No:
すみません、ちょっと… (from N5). Thanks afterwards: ありがとうございました、たすかりました
(thank you, that was a big help).

## 〜てほしい: I want you to…

N5's ほしい means "want (a thing)": {新|あたら}しいかばんがほしい. After a て form, 〜てほしい means
"I want someone to do something". The person you want to do it takes に.

{母|はは}に{早|はや}く{元気|げんき}になってほしいです。 — I want my mother to get well soon.
{友|とも}だちにけっこんしきに{来|き}てほしいです。 — I want my friends to come to my wedding.
ここでたばこをすわないでほしいです。 — I'd like people not to smoke here.

The negative is 〜ないでほしい ("I want you not to"). Like 〜たい and ほしい, 〜てほしい is about
your own wishes and sounds direct. Saying {先生|せんせい}、{来|き}てほしいです to a teacher sounds
like a demand. To a superior, ask instead: {来|き}ていただけませんか. Adding んですが softens it
with people you know: ちょっとてつだってほしいんですが… (I'd like you to give me a hand…).

## Words for help and favours

- たのむ: to ask (someone) for something: {友|とも}だちに{仕事|しごと}をたのみました (I asked a
  friend to do the job).
- たすける: to help, save someone (often from danger): たすけて！ (Help!). たすかる: to be
  helped, saved: たすかります (that's a great help) is how you thank someone for a favour.
- {世話|せわ}をする / めんどうを{見|み}る: to look after: {犬|いぬ}の{世話|せわ}をしてもらいました.
  お{世話|せわ}になりました is a set phrase: thank you for all you've done for me.
- じゃま: in the way, a nuisance. おじゃまします (literally "I'll be a nuisance") is what you say
  when you go into someone's home.
- えんりょする: to hold back out of politeness: えんりょしないでください (please don't hold back,
  go ahead).
- おごる: to treat someone, pay for them (casual): {今日|きょう}は{私|わたし}がおごります. (The polite
  word is ごちそうする.)
- おかげさまで: thanks to you (and everyone): the polite reply when someone asks how you are or
  how something went. {試験|しけん}はどうでしたか。— おかげさまで、よくできました (it went well, thanks).

## Kanji

Six kanji for kindness, lending and waiting. Four of them write verbs you know from N5 in kana:
かす, かりる, おしえる, まつ. Write them with kanji from now on, and しんせつ (kind) becomes
{親切|しんせつ}.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 親 | parent; close, intimate | シン | おや | 16 | {親|おや}, {親切|しんせつ}, {親子|おやこ} (parent and child) |
| 切 | cut; important | セツ | き(る), き(れる) | 4 | {切|き}る, {大切|たいせつ}, {親切|しんせつ}, {切手|きって} |
| 貸 | lend | タイ | か(す) | 12 | {貸|か}す |
| 借 | borrow | シャク | か(りる) | 10 | {借|か}りる |
| 教 | teach | キョウ | おし(える) | 11 | {教|おし}える, {教室|きょうしつ} |
| 待 | wait | タイ | ま(つ) | 9 | {待|ま}つ, お{待|ま}ちください |

Memory notes:

- 親: stand (立) on a tree (木) and look (見): a parent watching for the children to come home.
- 切: seven (七) and a sword: cut it into pieces. In {大切|たいせつ} and {親切|しんせつ} it's read
  セツ and has nothing to do with cutting.
- 貸 and 借 are a pair, and they're easy to mix up. 貸 (lend) has a shell at the bottom, which
  was once used as money: you hand over the money. 借 (borrow) has a person on the left: you
  get something from a person.
- 教: a child (子) on the left, under crossed lines (things to learn), and a hand with a stick
  on the right. Old-fashioned teaching.
- 待: the left side means "going", the right side is the character for a temple: going to the
  temple and waiting.

```trace
親切貸借教待
```

## Dialogue: a favour from the neighbour

```dialogue
# A favour from the neighbour
ルーカス: {森|もり}さん、こんにちは。ちょっとおねがいがあるんですが……。
= Hello, Mrs Mori. There's something I'd like to ask you…
{森|もり}: はい、{何|なん}でしょう。
= Yes, what is it?
ルーカス: {来週|らいしゅう}、{一週間|いっしゅうかん}{国|くに}に{帰|かえ}るんです。るすのとき、ベランダの{花|はな}に{水|みず}をやってもらえませんか。
= Next week I'm going home to my country for a week. While I'm away, could you water the flowers on my balcony?
{森|もり}: ええ、いいですよ。{毎日|まいにち}やりましょうか。
= Yes, of course. Shall I do it every day?
ルーカス: {二日|ふつか}に{一回|いっかい}でだいじょうぶです。これ、スペアのかぎです。{持|も}っていてもらえますか。
= Every other day is fine. This is the spare key. Could you keep hold of it?
{森|もり}: はい、あずかります。ポストの{手紙|てがみ}も{見|み}ておきましょうか。
= Sure, I'll look after it. Shall I check your postbox for letters too?
ルーカス: それはたすかります。ほんとうにすみません。
= That would be a great help. I'm really sorry to trouble you.
{森|もり}: えんりょしないでください。{前|まえ}に{私|わたし}のパソコンをなおしてくれたでしょう？
= Don't mention it. You fixed my computer for me before, didn't you?
ルーカス: じゃあ、{国|くに}のおかしを{買|か}ってきますね。
= Then I'll bring you back some sweets from home.
{森|もり}: まあ、{楽|たの}しみにしています。
= Oh, I'll look forward to it.
```

ベランダ = balcony; スペア = spare; あずかる = to look after (something for someone), the
partner of あずける (to leave something in someone's care: かぎを{森|もり}さんにあずける);
{楽|たの}しみにする = to look forward to; まあ = oh, my (a soft exclamation). {二日|ふつか}に{一回|いっかい}
= once every two days. {買|か}ってくる = go and buy (and come back), a pattern you'll meet
properly in lesson 24.

Look at how the favours run. Lucas asks with 〜てもらえませんか, not 〜てください: he's asking a
neighbour, not giving instructions. Mrs Mori offers with 〜ましょうか, not 〜てあげます. And she
remembers his favour with 〜てくれた, the inward direction from her point of view.

## Reading: a note on the desk

> ルーカスさんへ
>
> {明日|あした}の{朝|あさ}、アメリカからおきゃくさんが{来|き}ます。じょうしの{村田|むらた}さんがくうこうまでむかえに{行|い}きますが、{私|わたし}は{行|い}けません。すみませんが、{村田|むらた}さんといっしょに{行|い}ってもらえませんか。おきゃくさんは{日本語|にほんご}があまり{分|わ}からないから、ルーカスさんにほんやくしてほしいんです。
>
> それから、ミーティングで{使|つか}う{紙|かみ}を{十|じゅう}まいコピーしておいてくれませんか。
>
> いつもたすけてもらって、ありがとうございます。{今度|こんど}、ランチをおごりますね。
>
> どうりょうのさき

Dear Lucas, a client is coming from America tomorrow morning. Our boss, Mr Murata, is going to
the airport to meet them, but I can't go. Sorry, but could you go with Mr Murata? The client
doesn't understand much Japanese, so I'd like you to translate. Also, would you make ten copies
of the sheet we're using in the meeting? Thank you for always helping me. I'll treat you to
lunch next time. — Saki, your colleague

おきゃくさん = customer, client; ミーティング = meeting; ランチ = lunch. Notice
コピーしておいてくれませんか: 〜ておく (do in advance, lesson 5) + 〜てくれませんか (would you…).
Two auxiliary verbs can follow one another like this. And {行|い}けません is the potential of
{行|い}く (lesson 2).

## Pronunciation

Two verbs you know are both read きる, and the pitch tells them apart: [きる:1] ({切|き}る, to cut)
falls after き, while [きる:0] ({着|き}る, to wear) is flat. So {切|き}ってください (high-low-low…)
and {着|き}てください (low-high-high…) sound different even before you notice the っ.

## Say it

```speak
すみません、ちょっとてつだってもらえませんか。
= Excuse me, could you give me a hand?
にもつを{運|はこ}びましょうか。
= Shall I carry your bags?
{写真|しゃしん}をとっていただけませんか。
= Would you mind taking a photo for us?
ありがとうございました。たすかりました。
= Thank you. That was a big help.
いろいろお{世話|せわ}になりました。
= Thank you for everything you've done for me.
えんりょしないでください。
= Please don't hold back.
```

## Common mistakes

- Leaving くれる out when someone helped you: {友|とも}だちがてつだいました sounds like a report.
  {友|とも}だちがてつだってくれました says thank you.
- The wrong particle with 〜てもらう. The person who does the favour takes に (not で or が): {友|とも}だちに{教|おし}えてもらいました.
- ×{友|とも}だちにかばんを{持|も}ってあげました. Use の: {友|とも}だちのかばんを{持|も}ってあげました.
- Offering with 〜てあげます to the person's face. Say 〜ましょうか.
- {貸|か}して and {借|か}りて mixed up. "Could you lend me…" is {貸|か}してもらえませんか or
  {貸|か}してください; "May I borrow…" is {借|か}りてもいいですか.
- 〜てほしいです to a superior. Ask with 〜ていただけませんか.

## Key points

- 〜てあげる (outward), 〜てくれる (inward, with thanks), 〜てもらう (I had someone do it; the doer
  takes に). Polite: 〜てくださる, 〜ていただく. These auxiliary verbs are written in kana.
- The person helped keeps the main verb's particle; if there's no slot, use の.
- Don't offer with 〜てあげます; use 〜ましょうか.
- Requests from casual to polite: 〜てくれる？ → 〜てくれませんか → 〜てもらえませんか →
  〜てくださいませんか → 〜ていただけませんか.
- 〜てほしい: want someone to do; 〜ないでほしい: want them not to.
- New kanji: 親 切 貸 借 教 待.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Transitive and intransitive pairs; 〜ている and 〜てある
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In English, "open" works two ways: "I opened the door" and "the door opened". Japanese uses two
different verbs: ドアを{開|あ}けました (I opened the door) and ドアが{開|あ}きました (the door
opened). You've already met several of these pairs in N5 without seeing them side by side:
あける and あく, {入|い}れる and {入|はい}る, {出|だ}す and {出|で}る (and つける, whose partner つく is new here).

This lesson puts the pairs together, shows the patterns that help you guess which is which, and
then uses them for two kinds of state: 〜ている after an intransitive verb (the window is open)
and 〜てある after a transitive verb (the window has been left open, by someone, on purpose).
The theme is around the house: doors and windows, lights, machines, and things that break.

## Transitive and intransitive

A **[[transitive verb]]** has an object: someone does something *to* something. The object takes
を. An **[[intransitive verb]]** has no object: something happens, or something changes by itself.
The thing that changes is the subject, with が.

| Transitive (someone does it, を) | Intransitive (it happens, が) |
|---|---|
| ドアを{開|あ}ける (open the door) | ドアが{開|あ}く (the door opens) |
| {電気|でんき}をつける (turn on the light) | {電気|でんき}がつく (the light comes on) |
| {車|くるま}を{止|と}める (stop the car) | {車|くるま}が{止|と}まる (the car stops) |
| じゅぎょうを{始|はじ}める (start the class) | じゅぎょうが{始|はじ}まる (the class starts) |

The particle is the quickest clue. を + verb: a transitive verb, and somebody did it. が + verb
from the same pair: an intransitive one, and the sentence is about what happened.

{弟|おとうと}がまどを{開|あ}けました。 — My little brother opened the window.
{風|かぜ}でまどが{開|あ}きました。 — The window blew open in the wind. (lit. opened because of the wind)

## The main pairs

| Transitive | Intransitive | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {開|あ}ける | {開|あ}く | open |
| しめる | しまる | close, shut |
| つける | つく | turn on / come on (lights, machines) |
| けす | きえる | turn off / go off (lights); put out / go out (fire) |
| {始|はじ}める | {始|はじ}まる | start, begin |
| {止|と}める | {止|と}まる | stop |
| {入|い}れる | {入|はい}る | put in / go in, enter |
| {出|だ}す | {出|で}る | take out / come out, leave |
| {起|お}こす | {起|お}きる | wake (someone) / wake up, get up |
| おとす | おちる | drop / fall |
| こわす | こわれる | break (something) / break, get broken |
| なおす | なおる | fix, repair / get fixed, get better |
| かける | かかる | hang, lock, put on / be hung, be locked |
| {下|さ}げる | {下|さ}がる | lower / go down |
| {動|うご}かす | {動|うご}く | move (something) / move |

Some pairs differ only in the last part (しめる/しまる), and some look very different
(けす/きえる). The whole table, with more pairs, is on the reference sheet.

### Patterns that help

You can't predict every pair, but three tendencies cover most of them:

1. **〜aる is intransitive**, and its partner ends in 〜eる: しまる/しめる, {始|はじ}まる/{始|はじ}める,
   {止|と}まる/{止|と}める, かかる/かける, {下|さ}がる/{下|さ}げる, {見|み}つかる/{見|み}つける (N5).
2. **〜す is transitive**: {出|だ}す, おとす, こわす, {起|お}こす, なおす, {動|うご}かす, けす. If
   a verb ends in す, it almost always takes を.
3. **〜れる is often intransitive**: こわれる, and in lesson 9 われる (crack, break) and ぬれる (get
   wet). But not always: {入|い}れる is transitive.

When there's no 〜aる or 〜す to guide you (つける/つく, {開|あ}ける/{開|あ}く, {入|い}れる/{入|はい}る),
the 〜eる verb is the transitive one. Learn these few as pairs.

### Which one sounds natural?

Japanese often prefers the intransitive verb when what matters is the result, not who did it.
Shop staff and announcements use it a lot: ドアがしまります (the doors are closing), {電車|でんしゃ}が
{止|と}まります. And when something goes wrong, the intransitive verb keeps the blame vague:
パソコンがこわれました (the computer broke) sounds like an accident; パソコンをこわしました (I broke the
computer) says you did it. Lesson 9 comes back to this.

## 〜ている after an intransitive verb: the state now

In N5 you learned that 〜ている can mean a state that results from an earlier change
(けっこんしています: is married). With intransitive verbs of change, this is the meaning you
get: the change happened, and the result is still there.

まどが{開|あ}いています。 — The window is open.
{電気|でんき}がついています。 — The light is on.
このパソコンはこわれています。 — This computer is broken.
{店|みせ}がしまっています。 — The shop is closed.

Compare the transitive verb + ている, which is an action in progress:

{父|ちち}がまどを{開|あ}けています。 — My father is opening the window.

## 〜てある after a transitive verb: left like that on purpose

〜てある describes a state too, but one that **someone created deliberately**, usually as
preparation, and left for a reason. It goes after a transitive verb, and the thing (which was
the object) now takes が:

まどが{開|あ}けてあります。 — The window has been opened (someone opened it, to air the room).
テーブルに{花|はな}がかざってあります。 — Flowers have been put out on the table (as decoration). (かざる = to decorate)
{名前|なまえ}が{書|か}いてあります。 — A name has been written (on it).

Who did it isn't said, and usually doesn't matter. What 〜てある adds is the purpose: somebody
did this for a reason, and the result is ready. You'll sometimes hear を instead of が here
(まどを{開|あ}けてあります); learn が first.

| Sentence | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| まどが{開|あ}いています。 | The window is open. (Just the state; maybe the wind did it.) |
| まどが{開|あ}けてあります。 | The window has been opened and left open on purpose. |
| まどを{開|あ}けています。 | Someone is opening the window right now. |

A good test: if you could add "on purpose" or "ready for…", 〜てある fits.

{明日|あした}のパーティーの{飲|の}み{物|もの}は、もう{買|か}ってあります。 — The drinks for tomorrow's party have already been bought.

〜てある always goes on a transitive verb. ×まどが{開|あ}いてあります is wrong: {開|あ}く is
intransitive.

## 〜ておく and 〜てある

Lesson 5's 〜ておく ("do in advance, leave as is") is the action; 〜てある is the state that
the action leaves behind.

まどを{開|あ}けておきます。 — I'll open the window (now, so the room airs out).
まどが{開|あ}けてあります。 — The window has been opened (it's done; it's open, ready).

{友|とも}だちが{来|く}るから、ジュースを{買|か}っておきました。 — My friends are coming, so I bought juice in advance.
→ ジュースが{買|か}ってあります。 — The juice has been bought (it's there, ready).

## Kanji

Seven kanji for the house and the street.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 開 | open | カイ | あ(ける), あ(く), ひら(く) | 12 | {開|あ}ける, {開|あ}く |
| 止 | stop | シ | と(まる), と(める) | 4 | {止|と}まる, {止|と}める, {中止|ちゅうし} (cancellation) |
| 屋 | shop; roof | オク | や | 9 | {本屋|ほんや}, {八百屋|やおや}, パン{屋|や}, {屋上|おくじょう} (rooftop) |
| 室 | room | シツ | — | 9 | {教室|きょうしつ}, {待合室|まちあいしつ} (waiting room) |
| 台 | stand, platform; counter for machines | ダイ, タイ | — | 5 | {台所|だいどころ}, {一台|いちだい}, {台風|たいふう} |
| 門 | gate | モン | — | 8 | {門|もん} |
| 広 | wide, spacious | コウ | ひろ(い) | 5 | {広|ひろ}い |

Notes on the words:

- 〜{屋|や} after a noun is a shop, or the person who runs it: {本屋|ほんや} (bookshop), パン{屋|や}
  (bakery). People often add さん: パン{屋|や}さん, {八百屋|やおや}さん. {八百屋|やおや} (greengrocer) is a
  special reading: {八百|やお} literally means "eight hundred", "all kinds" of vegetables.
- 〜{台|だい} counts machines and vehicles: {車|くるま}が{二台|にだい}, パソコンが{三台|さんだい}.
  The N5 word たいふう (typhoon) can now be written {台風|たいふう}, and {台所|だいどころ} (kitchen) is a new
  word in this lesson.
- {開|あ}く has another reading, {開|ひら}く (to open, as a book or a meeting); in this course
  furigana will tell you which.

Memory notes:

- 開 and 門: 開 is a gate (門) with two hands lifting the bar: open the gate.
- 止 is a footprint: the foot stops here. Lesson 2's 歩 (walk) has 止 on top: one foot after
  the other.
- 屋 and 室 share a bottom part that means "reach, arrive". In 屋 it sits under a bent,
  roof-like stroke; in 室 it sits under the roof from the top of 家. Both are places you arrive
  at and stay under cover: a shop, a room.
- 台: a small triangle over a mouth (口): a raised stand, like a platform to speak from.
- 広 is a roof with one wall on the left, over a small triangle: a wide hall with one side open.

```trace
開止屋室台門広
```

## Dialogue: the air conditioner

```dialogue
# The air conditioner
ゆい: ただいま。あれ、{電気|でんき}がついてる。ルーカス、いるの？
= I'm home. Huh, the light's on. Lucas, are you here?
ルーカス: おかえり。うん、いるよ。ねえ、エアコンがつかないんだけど。
= Welcome back. Yes, I'm here. Listen, the air conditioner won't come on.
ゆい: え、ほんとう？スイッチは{入|い}れた？
= What, really? Did you switch it on?
ルーカス: {入|い}れたよ。でも、ぜんぜん{動|うご}かない。こわれたと{思|おも}う。
= Yes. But it won't run at all. I think it's broken.
ゆい: こまったね。あ、まどが{開|あ}いてるよ。
= That's a nuisance. Oh, the window's open.
ルーカス: うん、{暑|あつ}いから、{開|あ}けておいたんだ。
= Yeah, it was hot, so I opened it.
ゆい: {大家|おおや}さんに{電話|でんわ}しようか。
= Shall we call the landlord?
ルーカス: もうしたよ。{明日|あした}の{朝|あさ}、しゅうりの{人|ひと}に{来|き}てもらうことにした。
= I already have. We've arranged for a repair person to come tomorrow morning.
ゆい: よかった。あ、げんかんのかぎは？かけてある？
= Good. Oh, what about the front door? Is it locked?
ルーカス: うん、さっきかけたよ。それから、{台所|だいどころ}の{電気|でんき}、けしてくれる？
= Yes, I locked it a moment ago. And could you turn off the kitchen light?
ゆい: はいはい。
= OK, OK.
```

{大家|おおや}さん = landlord; さっき = a moment ago; かぎをかける = to lock (lit. put the key
on). {電気|でんき}がついてる and まどが{開|あ}いてる are intransitive + ている (casual 〜てる):
just the state. かぎ、かけてある？ asks whether someone has locked it, so it's ready: 〜てある.

## Reading: notes for the house-sitter

> ルーカスさん、{一週間|いっしゅうかん}、{家|いえ}をおねがいします。
>
> ・かぎは、げんかんの{引|ひ}き{出|だ}しに{入|い}れてあります。
>
> ・れいぞうこにジュースが{入|い}れてあります。どうぞ{飲|の}んでください。
>
> ・エアコンはこしょうしていましたが、もうなおっています。スイッチは{台所|だいどころ}のかべにあります。
>
> ・{二|に}かいのまどはしめてあります。ねこが{出|で}ますから、{開|あ}けないでください。
>
> ・{八百屋|やおや}さんは、{門|もん}を{出|で}て{右|みぎ}です。{本屋|ほんや}は{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}にあります。
>
> {森|もり}

Lucas, please look after the house for a week. The key has been put in the drawer in the
entrance. There's juice in the fridge (I put it there for you); please drink it. The air
conditioner was out of order, but it's fixed now. The switch is on the kitchen wall. The
upstairs windows have been shut; please don't open them, because the cat gets out. The
greengrocer is to the right when you go out of the gate. The bookshop is in front of the
station. — Mori

かべ = wall; {二|に}かい = upstairs, the first floor (British) / second floor (American).
Notice the mix: 〜てあります for what Mrs Mori did on purpose, なおっています (intransitive +
ている) for the state of the air conditioner.

## Pronunciation

Most pairs share an accent type, so pitch won't tell you which verb you heard: [あける:0] and
[あく:0] are both flat, [しめる:2] and [しまる:2] both fall after the second mora, and so do
[おこす:2] and [おきる:2]. One pair that differs is [いれる:0] (flat) and [はいる:1] (falls after
は). Mostly, listen for the particle (を or が) and the shape of the verb (〜aる, 〜す).

## Say it

```speak
まどを{開|あ}けてもいいですか。
= May I open the window?
{電気|でんき}がついていますよ。
= The light's on, you know.
エアコンがこわれています。
= The air conditioner is broken.
{名前|なまえ}が{書|か}いてあります。
= Someone's written a name on it.
ドアがしまります。ご{注意|ちゅうい}ください。
= The doors are closing. Please be careful.
```

ご{注意|ちゅうい}ください (please take care) is the polite announcement form of {注意|ちゅうい}.

## Common mistakes

- Using the wrong particle: ×ドアを{開|あ}きました. {開|あ}く has no object: ドアが{開|あ}きました, or
  with the transitive verb, ドアを{開|あ}けました.
- 〜てある on an intransitive verb: ×{電気|でんき}がついてあります. Use ついています, or
  つけてあります (someone turned it on and left it on).
- Reading 〜ている on a transitive verb as a state: まどを{開|あ}けています means "is opening",
  not "is open".
- Thinking 〜てある tells you who did it. It doesn't; it tells you it was deliberate.
- Using the transitive verb for an accident: コップをこわしました admits you broke it. If it
  just broke, こわれました.

## Key points

- Transitive verbs take を (someone does it); intransitive verbs take が (it happens).
- Patterns: 〜aる is intransitive; 〜す is transitive; 〜れる is often intransitive.
- Intransitive + ている: the resulting state (まどが{開|あ}いている).
- Transitive + てある: a state someone left on purpose (まどが{開|あ}けてある).
- 〜ておく is the action done in advance; 〜てある is the state it leaves.
- New kanji: 開 止 屋 室 台 門 広. Special reading: {八百屋|やおや}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Done and regretted: 〜てしまう; starting, finishing and continuing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Things go wrong. You oversleep, drop your phone, spill coffee on someone's papers. Japanese has
one small pattern that turns "I did X" into "I went and did X (and I wish I hadn't)": 〜てしまう.
The same pattern also means "do it completely, get it done", and in casual speech it shrinks
to 〜ちゃう: {食|た}べちゃった, なくしちゃった. You'll hear 〜ちゃった constantly.

The second half of this lesson is about **[[compound verbs]]**: two verbs joined into one, such
as {読|よ}み{始|はじ}める (start reading), {食|た}べ{終|お}わる (finish eating) and {歩|ある}きつづける
(keep walking). The theme is mishaps: accidents, losing things, and saying sorry.

## 〜てしまう: completely, and too bad

Put しまう after a て form. しまう is a group 1 verb on its own (to put away, finish), so it
conjugates the usual way: しまいます, しまいました, しまった, しまって. Like the other auxiliary
verbs in this module, it's written in kana.

| Verb | て form | 〜てしまう | Past |
|---|---|---|---|
| {食|た}べる | {食|た}べて | {食|た}べてしまう | {食|た}べてしまいました / {食|た}べてしまった |
| {読|よ}む | {読|よ}んで | {読|よ}んでしまう | {読|よ}んでしまいました / {読|よ}んでしまった |
| わすれる | わすれて | わすれてしまう | わすれてしまいました / わすれてしまった |
| する | して | してしまう | してしまいました / してしまった |

It has two meanings. Context, and the verb, decide which.

### 1. Done completely

With an action you meant to do, 〜てしまう means "finish it off, get it done":

しゅくだいはもうぜんぶやってしまいました。 — I've already finished all my homework.
この{本|ほん}は{一日|いちにち}で{読|よ}んでしまいました。 — I read this whole book in one day.
{先|さき}に{仕事|しごと}をしてしまいます。 — I'll get the work done first.

With the volitional form (lesson 3), it's "let's get it done": {早|はや}く{食|た}べてしまおう (let's
hurry up and finish eating).

### 2. Something you regret, or an accident

Much more often, 〜てしまう says that something happened that you didn't want, or that you did
by mistake. It adds a sigh.

さいふをなくしてしまいました。 — I've lost my wallet (and it's a disaster).
{電車|でんしゃ}にかさをわすれてしまいました。 — I left my umbrella on the train.
{金魚|きんぎょ}が{死|し}んでしまいました。 — My goldfish died. ({金魚|きんぎょ} = goldfish)
ケーキを{三|みっ}つも{食|た}べてしまいました。 — I ended up eating three pieces of cake. (〜も: as many as)

Compare: さいふをなくしました is a plain report. さいふをなくしてしまいました tells the listener
how you feel about it. That's why 〜てしまう is so common in apologies:

すみません、ちこくしてしまいました。 — I'm sorry, I'm late.
コーヒーをこぼしてしまって、すみません。 — I'm sorry I spilled the coffee.

The second pattern is lesson 1's て form for a cause before an apology: 〜てしまって、すみません
(I'm sorry for having…).

### With intransitive verbs

Lesson 8 showed that the intransitive verb makes an accident sound like no one's fault.
Combined with 〜てしまう, it's the natural way to report something that just happened:

コップがわれてしまいました。 — The glass broke. (われる = to crack, break)
くつがぬれてしまいました。 — My shoes got wet. (ぬれる = to get wet)
パソコンがこわれてしまいました。 — The computer has broken.

If you broke it, say so with the transitive verb, and apologize: すみません、コップをわってしまいました
(わる, to smash or crack, is the transitive partner of われる).

## Casual: 〜ちゃう and 〜じゃう

In speech between friends and family, 〜てしまう shortens:

| Full form | Casual | Past (casual) |
|---|---|---|
| 〜てしまう | 〜ちゃう | 〜ちゃった |
| 〜でしまう | 〜じゃう | 〜じゃった |

{食|た}べてしまった → {食|た}べちゃった
{読|よ}んでしまった → {読|よ}んじゃった
{行|い}ってしまった → {行|い}っちゃった
{来|き}てしまった → {来|き}ちゃった
してしまった → しちゃった
なくしてしまった → なくしちゃった

The rule: て + しま → ちゃ; で + しま → じゃ. So verbs whose て form ends in で ({読|よ}んで,
{死|し}んで, およいで) get じゃう. 〜ちゃう conjugates like a group 1 verb: ちゃいます, ちゃった,
ちゃって, and the volitional ちゃおう (ぜんぶ{食|た}べちゃおう, let's eat it all up).

〜ちゃう is casual. Use it with friends, and in casual polite speech (〜ちゃいました) with people
you know well, but not in writing, at work with a superior, or in an apology that matters.
There, say 〜てしまいました.

## Compound verbs: start, finish, keep on

Japanese can join two verbs into one: the first verb's ます stem plus a second verb. The
second verb does the work of an English helper word ("start", "finish", "keep"). These are
compound verbs; the four below are the most useful at N4.

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| stem + {始|はじ}める | start doing | {雨|あめ}がふり{始|はじ}めました。 — It started to rain. |
| stem + {出|だ}す | suddenly start doing | {赤|あか}ちゃんがなき{出|だ}しました。 — The baby suddenly burst out crying. |
| stem + {終|お}わる | finish doing | この{本|ほん}を{読|よ}み{終|お}わりました。 — I've finished reading this book. |
| stem + つづける | keep on doing | {三時間|さんじかん}{歩|ある}きつづけました。 — I kept walking for three hours. |

(なく = to cry.) All four conjugate as their second verb does: {始|はじ}める and つづける are group
2, {出|だ}す, {終|お}わる are group 1. A few points:

- 〜{始|はじ}める is neutral and works with anything. 〜{出|だ}す is for something sudden or
  uncontrolled (rain, crying, laughing, running off). Don't use 〜{出|だ}す in a request or a plan:
  {読|よ}み{始|はじ}めてください, not ×{読|よ}み{出|だ}してください.
- 〜{終|お}わる goes with actions that have an end: {食|た}べ{終|お}わる, {書|か}き{終|お}わる,
  {読|よ}み{終|お}わる.
- つづける and つづく are a transitive/intransitive pair like those in lesson 8: {雨|あめ}が
  {三日|みっか}つづいています (the rain has gone on for three days). For compounds, use つづける.

Compare 〜てしまう and 〜{終|お}わる: {読|よ}み{終|お}わった is "finished reading", a fact about the
book; {読|よ}んでしまった is "read it all (already)", with a feeling attached: satisfaction, or
"oops, there's nothing left to read".

## Words for mishaps

- ねぼうする: to oversleep. ちこくする: to be late (for school, work, a meeting).
- {転|ころ}ぶ: to fall over. すべる: to slip. ぶつかる: to bump into (intransitive);
  ぶつける: to bump, hit something against something (transitive): ドアに{頭|あたま}を
  ぶつけてしまいました (I banged my head on the door).
- じこ: an accident (traffic, at work). けが: an injury. けがをする: to get hurt.
- こぼす / こぼれる: to spill (something) / to spill (by itself). われる: to crack, break (glass,
  china). ぬれる: to get wet.
- {運転|うんてん}する: to drive. {運転|うんてん}していて、じこを{起|お}こしてしまいました (I had an
  accident while driving; じこを{起|お}こす = to cause an accident).
- びっくりする: to be surprised, startled. うっかり: carelessly, without thinking.
- あやまる: to apologize. {安心|あんしん}する: to feel relieved. しまった！: Oh no! (said when you
  realize your mistake; it's the past of しまう).

## Kanji

Five kanji. Two of them write words you know from N5 in kana: おきる and じてんしゃ.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 起 | rise, wake | キ | お(きる), お(こす) | 10 | {起|お}きる, {起|お}こす |
| 転 | turn, roll | テン | ころ(ぶ) | 11 | {自転車|じてんしゃ}, {運転|うんてん}する, {転|ころ}ぶ |
| 死 | death | シ | し(ぬ) | 6 | {死|し}ぬ |
| 通 | pass through; commute | ツウ | とお(る), かよ(う) | 10 | {通|とお}る, {通|かよ}う |
| 心 | heart, mind | シン | こころ | 4 | {心|こころ}, {安心|あんしん}する |

{通|とお}る and {通|かよ}う share a kanji but are different verbs: {通|とお}る is to pass along or
through (この{道|みち}は{車|くるま}がたくさん{通|とお}ります: lots of cars go along this road);
{通|かよ}う is to go somewhere regularly (バスで{学校|がっこう}に{通|かよ}っています: I go to school by
bus). しんぱい (worry) stays in kana, because its second kanji isn't on the course list.

Memory notes:

- 起 has 走 (run, lesson 2) on the left: you get up and run.
- 転 has 車 (vehicle) on the left: wheels turning and rolling.
- 死: the left part is a piece of bone, the right part a person bent over it.
- 通 has the "moving along a road" part that you know from 道, 近 and 遠: passing through.
- 心 is a picture of a heart. As a part of other kanji it often turns into a short form on the
  left, but at N4 you'll mostly see it whole: {安心|あんしん}, and 思 (think, lesson 20).

```trace
起転死通心
```

## Dialogue: a bad day

```dialogue
# A bad day
さき: ルーカス、どうしたの？{元気|げんき}ないね。
= Lucas, what's wrong? You look down.
ルーカス: {今日|きょう}はついてないんだ。{朝|あさ}、ねぼうしちゃって、いつもの{電車|でんしゃ}に{乗|の}れなかった。
= I'm out of luck today. I overslept this morning and couldn't catch my usual train.
さき: えっ、ちこくしたの？
= What? Were you late?
ルーカス: うん、{十分|じゅっぷん}。それに、{駅|えき}で{転|ころ}んじゃった。
= Yeah, ten minutes. And I fell over at the station.
さき: だいじょうぶ？けがは？
= Are you OK? Did you hurt yourself?
ルーカス: {足|あし}はだいじょうぶ。でも、スマホをおとしちゃって、こわれちゃった。
= My leg's fine. But I dropped my phone, and it broke.
さき: うわあ、たいへんだったね。
= Oh no, what a day.
ルーカス: それから、{会社|かいしゃ}でコーヒーをこぼしちゃって、{村田|むらた}さんのしりょうがぬれちゃったんだ。
= Then at work I spilled coffee, and Mr Murata's documents got wet.
さき: あらら。ちゃんとあやまった？
= Oh dear. Did you apologize properly?
ルーカス: うん、すぐあやまったよ。{村田|むらた}さんは「だいじょうぶですよ」と{言|い}ってくれた。
= Yes, straight away. Mr Murata told me, "It's fine."
さき: よかったね。じゃあ、{今日|きょう}は{早|はや}く{帰|かえ}って、ゆっくり{休|やす}んでね。
= That's good. Well, go home early today and have a good rest.
ルーカス: うん。あ、しまった！さきに{借|か}りたかさ、{電車|でんしゃ}にわすれちゃった……。
= Yeah. Oh no! I left the umbrella I borrowed from you on the train…
```

ついてない = unlucky, out of luck (casual); しりょう = documents, papers; あらら = oh dear;
ちゃんと = properly. Notice how Lucas uses the intransitive verbs for what just happened to
things (こわれちゃった, ぬれちゃった) and the transitive ones for what he did (おとしちゃって,
こぼしちゃって).

## Reading: an apology to the boss

> {村田|むらた}さん
>
> {今朝|けさ}はちこくしてしまって、もうしわけありませんでした。ねぼうしてしまいました。これからは{気|き}をつけます。
>
> それから、しりょうにコーヒーをこぼしてしまって、すみませんでした。{新|あたら}しいしりょうを{十|じゅう}まいコピーしておきました。{村田|むらた}さんのつくえの{上|うえ}においてあります。
>
> ルーカス

Mr Murata, I'm very sorry I was late this morning. I overslept. I'll be careful from now on.
Also, I'm sorry I spilled coffee on the documents. I've made ten new copies; they're on your
desk. — Lucas

In writing to his boss, Lucas uses the full 〜てしまいました and 〜てしまって, never 〜ちゃった.
And he tells Mr Murata what he's done to fix things: コピーしておきました (lesson 5) and
おいてあります (lesson 8). {今朝|けさ} (this morning) is a special reading; you've used けさ
since N5, and lesson 10 teaches its kanji.

## Pronunciation

〜ちゃう and 〜じゃう are one mora each for ちゃ and じゃ: {食|た}べちゃった is た・べ・ちゃ・っ・た,
five morae, with a full beat on the small っ. Don't drop the っ: {食|た}べちゃた is wrong.
しまった！ has its accent on the second mora: [しまった:2].

## Say it

```speak
すみません、ちこくしてしまいました。
= I'm sorry, I'm late.
さいふをなくしてしまいました。
= I've lost my wallet.
あ、しまった！
= Oh no!
{食|た}べちゃった。
= I (went and) ate it.
{雨|あめ}がふり{始|はじ}めましたね。
= It's started to rain, hasn't it.
けががなくて、{安心|あんしん}しました。
= I'm relieved nobody was hurt.
```

## Common mistakes

- Thinking 〜てしまう is always bad news. With a planned action it just means "finish it":
  しゅくだいをやってしまいました can be good news.
- ちゃう after a で form: {読|よ}んちゃった is wrong. で + しま → じゃ: {読|よ}んじゃった.
- 〜ちゃいました to your boss or in an email. Write 〜てしまいました.
- The transitive verb for an accident that wasn't you: ×{風|かぜ}でまどをこわしてしまいました.
  Say まどがこわれてしまいました.
- 〜{出|だ}す for a plan: ×{明日|あした}から{勉強|べんきょう}し{出|だ}します. Use 〜{始|はじ}めます.
- Putting the compound on the dictionary form: ×{読|よ}む{始|はじ}める. It's the ます stem: {読|よ}み{始|はじ}める.

## Key points

- 〜てしまう: (1) do completely; (2) something regrettable or accidental happened.
- Casual: 〜ちゃう / 〜じゃう, past 〜ちゃった / 〜じゃった. Not for formal speech or writing.
- 〜てしまって、すみません: apologizing for what you did.
- Compound verbs: stem + {始|はじ}める (start), {出|だ}す (suddenly start), {終|お}わる (finish),
  つづける (keep on).
- New kanji: 起 転 死 通 心.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: While, just and still: 〜ながら, 〜ところ, 〜たばかり, 〜まま, 〜ないで
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A day is full of things done at the same time, just done, about to be done, or left undone.
This lesson gives you five small patterns for describing them:

- 〜ながら: doing two things at once ({音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}きながら{料理|りょうり}する);
- 〜ところ: where you are in an action: about to, in the middle of, just finished;
- 〜たばかり: something happened only a short time ago;
- 〜まま: a state left unchanged (くつをはいたまま);
- 〜ないで: without doing something.

The theme is daily routine and housework: cooking, washing up, cleaning, laundry. Most of the
verbs are ones you already know, so the lesson is about the patterns. It closes the module, and
the honors lessons after it look at gift customs and at deliveries.

## 〜ながら: while doing

Take the ます stem and add ながら: {聞|き}きます → {聞|き}きながら, {食|た}べます → {食|た}べながら,
します → しながら. The sentence means "do B while doing A":

{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}きながら、そうじをします。 — I clean while listening to music.
テレビを{見|み}ながら{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べました。 — I ate breakfast watching TV.
{歩|ある}きながら{電話|でんわ}をしないでください。 — Please don't talk on the phone while walking.

Two rules:

1. **One person does both actions.** 〜ながら can't join two people: "I cooked while my sister
   cleaned" needs a different pattern (〜あいだ, lesson 19).
2. **The main action goes last.** The ながら action is the background one. {音楽|おんがく}を
   {聞|き}きながら{勉強|べんきょう}する is studying (with music on), not listening to music (with
   a book open). Tense and politeness are shown only on the last verb.

〜ながら also works for things done regularly together: アルバイトをしながら{大学|だいがく}に
{通|かよ}っています (I go to university while working part-time).

## 〜ところ: about to, in the middle of, just done

ところ is the N5 word for "place", but after a verb it means a point in time: where you are in
an action. Which point depends on the verb form in front of it. Like other grammar words, it's
written in kana.

| Form | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| dictionary form + ところだ | about to do | {今|いま}から{出|で}かけるところです。 — I'm just about to go out. |
| 〜ている + ところだ | in the middle of doing | {今|いま}、ご{飯|はん}を{作|つく}っているところです。 — I'm in the middle of cooking. |
| た form + ところだ | have just done | {今|いま}、{帰|かえ}ったところです。 — I've just got home. |

These are answers to "what are you doing now?" or reasons why now is or isn't a good time, so
they often come with {今|いま}, ちょうど (just) or これから (from now):

ちょうどおふろに{入|はい}るところです。 — I'm just about to have a bath.
すみません、{今|いま}、{電話|でんわ}で{話|はな}しているところです。 — I'm on the phone right now.
{駅|えき}に{着|つ}いたところです。 — I've just arrived at the station.

The difference between 〜ている and 〜ているところ: {料理|りょうり}をしています is a plain
description; {料理|りょうり}をしているところです stresses "at this very moment", usually because it
matters to the listener (I can't come to the phone).

## 〜たばかり: only just

〜たばかり also means "have just done", but it measures time the way the speaker *feels* it, not
by the clock. It can be minutes, days or months, as long as it feels recent:

{先月|せんげつ}、{日本|にほん}に{来|き}たばかりです。 — I only came to Japan last month.
この{本|ほん}は{買|か}ったばかりです。 — I've only just bought this book.
{昼|ひる}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べたばかりだから、おなかがいっぱいです。 — I've only just had lunch, so I'm full.

ばかり works like a noun: 〜たばかりです, 〜たばかりだから, and before another noun 〜たばかりの:
{買|か}ったばかりのかさ (an umbrella I've only just bought).

### 〜たところ or 〜たばかり?

| | 〜たところ | 〜たばかり |
|---|---|---|
| How recent | the moment just after the action, really just now | feels recent to the speaker; can be weeks ago |
| With {先月|せんげつ}, {去年|きょねん} | ×{先月|せんげつ}{来|き}たところです | ○{先月|せんげつ}{来|き}たばかりです |
| Typical feeling | "so I'm free now / so I'm not ready yet" | "it's still new / no wonder" |

{今|いま}、{起|お}きたところです (I've just this minute got up) fits a phone call at 7:05.
{起|お}きたばかりです says the same, with a hint of "so I'm still half asleep".

## 〜まま: left as it is

〜まま means a state continues unchanged while something else happens, often when it
shouldn't. It follows a た form, or a noun + の:

くつをはいたまま、{家|いえ}に{入|はい}らないでください。 — Please don't come into the house with your shoes on.
{電気|でんき}をつけたまま、ねてしまいました。 — I fell asleep with the light on.
まどを{開|あ}けたまま{出|で}かけました。 — I went out leaving the window open.
そのままでいいですよ。 — It's fine as it is. / Leave it as it is.

Notice the past form: the action (putting shoes on, turning the light on) is finished, and its
result stays. 〜まま is the natural partner of lesson 8's states and lesson 9's mishaps:
{電気|でんき}をつけたままねてしまった is a small accident.

Compare lesson 8: {電気|でんき}がついています just says the light is on. {電気|でんき}をつけたまま
{出|で}かけました says you went out and didn't turn it off.

## 〜ないで: without doing

The ない form + で means "without doing" or "instead of doing":

{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べないで、{学校|がっこう}に{行|い}きました。 — I went to school without eating breakfast.
かさを{持|も}たないで{出|で}かけて、ぬれてしまいました。 — I went out without an umbrella and got wet.
エレベーターに{乗|の}らないで、{歩|ある}いて{上|あ}がりました。 — I walked up instead of taking the lift.

You've used 〜ないでください (please don't) since N5. This is the same ないで, used to join two
actions.

### ないで or なくて?

Lesson 1 taught なくて, "because not": {時間|じかん}がなくて、{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べられません
でした (I didn't have time, so I couldn't eat breakfast). Both come from the ない form, but they
do different jobs:

| | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜ないで | without, instead of (how you did the main action) | {朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べないで{出|で}かけた。 — I went out without breakfast. |
| 〜なくて | because not (the cause of what follows) | {朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べなくて、おなかがすいた。 — I hadn't eaten breakfast, so I got hungry. |

A test: if the second half is something you did on purpose (went out, walked, studied), it's
ないで. If it's a feeling or a result you didn't choose (got hungry, was worried, was glad),
it's なくて. ないで also works only after verbs; after adjectives and nouns, "not … so" is
always 〜くなくて / 〜じゃなくて.

## Words for housework

- そうじする: to clean (a room). せんたくする: to do the laundry. せんたくもの: the laundry
  (clothes to wash or that have been washed).
- ほす: to hang out to dry. たたむ: to fold. しまう: to put away (lesson 9).
- かたづける: to tidy up. ちらかる: to be messy, in a mess: へやがちらかっている (the room is a mess).
- ふく: to wipe: テーブルをふく, ゆかをふく (wipe the floor; ゆか = floor). (Not the same
  word as ふく, clothes.) アイロン: an iron;
  アイロンをかける: to iron.
- さら (often おさら): a plate, dish. {家事|かじ}: housework. {食事|しょくじ}: a meal (a little more
  formal than ご{飯|はん}). はみがき: brushing your teeth: ご{飯|はん}の{後|あと}で、
  はみがきをします.

## Kanji

Six kanji for the times of day and the meals. You've written あさ, ひる, よる and ごはん in kana
since N5.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 朝 | morning | チョウ | あさ | 12 | {朝|あさ}, {毎朝|まいあさ}, {朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}, {今朝|けさ} |
| 昼 | daytime, noon | チュウ | ひる | 9 | {昼|ひる}, {昼|ひる}ご{飯|はん}, {昼休|ひるやす}み |
| 夜 | night | ヤ | よる, よ | 8 | {夜|よる}, {今夜|こんや}, {夜中|よなか} |
| 夕 | evening | セキ | ゆう | 3 | {夕方|ゆうがた}, {夕飯|ゆうはん}, {七夕|たなばた} |
| 飯 | meal; cooked rice | ハン | めし | 12 | ご{飯|はん}, {夕飯|ゆうはん}, {朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん} |
| 洗 | wash | セン | あら(う) | 9 | {洗|あら}う |

Special readings to learn as words: {今朝|けさ} (this morning: you know けさ from N5) and
{七夕|たなばた} (the Star Festival on 7 July, when people write wishes on strips of paper and hang
them on bamboo).

A few notes:

- ご{飯|はん} is written with ご in kana (its kanji isn't on the course list), so: {朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん},
  {昼|ひる}ご{飯|はん}, and ばんご{飯|はん} with ばん in kana. {夕飯|ゆうはん} is another word for dinner.
  めし (飯 alone) is a rough, mostly male word for a meal.
- せんたく (laundry) is written in kana in this course: its second kanji isn't on the list. You
  may see 洗たく on washing machines.
- {夜|よ} appears in {夜中|よなか} (the middle of the night); {夜|よる} alone is night.

Memory notes:

- 朝: the left side is the sun (日) rising between plants, with the moon (月) still in the sky
  on the right. Early morning.
- 昼: the top is the same bent, roof-like shape as in 屋, and under it is the sun (日)
  standing on a line: the sun high over the rooftops at noon.
- 夜: a person (the top two strokes and the line on the left) with the moon (夕) under their arm:
  night.
- 夕 is a crescent moon, only half up: evening.
- 飯: 食 (eat) on the left, in its narrow form, and on the right a part that gives the kanji its reading, ハン.
- 洗 has the three drops of water on the left (as in 海, lesson 3) and 先 on the right: wash
  with water first.

```trace
朝昼夜夕飯洗
```

## Dialogue: washing up on the phone

```dialogue
# Washing up on the phone
さき: もしもし、ルーカス？{今|いま}、だいじょうぶ？
= Hello, Lucas? Is now OK?
ルーカス: うん。ちょうど{夕飯|ゆうはん}を{食|た}べ{終|お}わったところ。
= Yeah. I've just finished dinner.
さき: よかった。{土曜日|どようび}のこと、{話|はな}したいんだけど。
= Good. I want to talk about Saturday.
ルーカス: いいよ。あ、{今|いま}、おさらを{洗|あら}っているところだから、{洗|あら}いながら{話|はな}してもいい？
= Sure. Oh, I'm in the middle of washing up, so is it OK if I talk while I wash?
さき: もちろん。{土曜日|どようび}は{十時|じゅうじ}に{駅|えき}でいい？
= Of course. Is ten at the station OK for Saturday?
ルーカス: {分|わ}かった。どこに{行|い}くの？
= Got it. Where are we going?
さき: {駅|えき}の{前|まえ}のパン{屋|や}。{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べないで{来|き}てね。
= The bakery in front of the station. Come without eating breakfast.
ルーカス: あ、{先月|せんげつ}できたばかりの{店|みせ}？
= Oh, the shop that only opened last month?
さき: そうそう。{昼|ひる}はいつもならぶから、{朝|あさ}{行|い}こう。
= That's the one. There's always a queue at lunchtime, so let's go in the morning.
ルーカス: いいね。……あっ、しまった！{水|みず}を{出|だ}したまま{話|はな}してた！
= Sounds good. …Ah, oh no! I've been talking with the tap running!
さき: もう、ルーカス！
= Honestly, Lucas!
```

できる = to open (of a new shop) as well as "can"; ならぶ = to queue, line up; {水|みず}を
{出|だ}す = to run water (turn on the tap). {話|はな}してた is the casual 〜てた (= 〜ていた) from
lesson 1.

## Reading: my Saturday

> {土曜日|どようび}の{朝|あさ}は、めざまし{時計|どけい}をかけないで、ゆっくりねます。{九時|くじ}ごろ{起|お}きて、ラジオを{聞|き}きながら{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べます。
>
> それから、{家事|かじ}をします。まず、せんたくをして、せんたくものをベランダにほします。それから、へやをそうじします。{私|わたし}のへやはいつもちらかっていますから、かたづけるのはたいへんです。
>
> {昼|ひる}ご{飯|はん}は、{近所|きんじょ}のおべんとう{屋|や}さんで{買|か}います。{夕方|ゆうがた}、ほしたせんたくものをたたんで、しまいます。{夜|よる}は、テレビを{見|み}ながらアイロンをかけます。
>
> {先週|せんしゅう}は、アイロンのスイッチを{入|い}れたまま、ソファでねむってしまいました。あぶなかったです。{日曜日|にちようび}は、{何|なに}もしないで、{一日中|いちにちじゅう}{家|いえ}にいます。

On Saturday mornings I sleep in without setting the alarm clock. I get up about nine and have
breakfast listening to the radio. Then I do the housework. First I do the laundry and hang it
out on the balcony. Then I clean my room. My room is always a mess, so tidying it is hard work.
For lunch I buy something at the bento shop in my neighbourhood. In the early evening I fold the
dry laundry and put it away. In the evening I do the ironing while watching TV. Last week I fell
asleep on the sofa with the iron still switched on. That was dangerous. On Sundays I do nothing
and stay at home all day.

めざまし{時計|どけい} = alarm clock ({時計|とけい} becomes どけい inside the word); めざまし{時計|どけい}を
かける = to set the alarm; ソファ = sofa; {一日中|いちにちじゅう} = all day; {近所|きんじょ} =
neighbourhood. Find the five patterns: かけないで and しないで (without), {聞|き}きながら and
{見|み}ながら (while), {入|い}れたまま (left on).

## Pronunciation

{夕方|ゆうがた} and {夕飯|ゆうはん} begin with a long vowel: ゆ・う, two morae (typing: yuugata,
yuuhan). {今夜|こんや} has ん before や, so type it kon'ya: konya would give こにゃ. {今朝|けさ}
falls after the first mora: [けさ:1].

## Say it

```speak
{今|いま}、{出|で}かけるところです。
= I'm just about to go out.
{今|いま}、ご{飯|はん}を{作|つく}っているところです。
= I'm in the middle of cooking.
{今|いま}、{帰|かえ}ったところです。
= I've just got home.
{日本|にほん}に{来|き}たばかりです。
= I've only just come to Japan.
そのままでいいですよ。
= It's fine as it is.
{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}きながら{勉強|べんきょう}します。
= I study while listening to music.
```

## Common mistakes

- Two people with 〜ながら: ×{私|わたし}が{料理|りょうり}をしながら、{姉|あね}がそうじをしました. One
  person does both.
- The main action first: {料理|りょうり}をしながら{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}く means you're mainly
  listening. Put the main action last.
- 〜たところ for something long ago: ×{去年|きょねん}けっこんしたところです.
  Use 〜たばかり: {去年|きょねん}けっこんしたばかりです.
- The dictionary form with まま: ×くつをはくまま. It's the た form: はいたまま.
- なくて for "without": ×{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べなくて{学校|がっこう}に{行|い}きました. Use ないで.

## Key points

- Stem + ながら: while (one person; main action last).
- Dictionary form + ところ (about to); 〜ているところ (in the middle of); 〜たところ (just did).
- 〜たばかり: only just (feels recent; can be weeks ago). 〜たばかりの + noun.
- た form / noun の + まま: in an unchanged state.
- 〜ないで: without, instead of. 〜なくて: because not.
- New kanji: 朝 昼 夜 夕 飯 洗. Special readings: {今朝|けさ}, {七夕|たなばた}.

lessons.title: Gifts in Japan
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 6 gave you the verbs for giving. This honors lesson is about the customs around them:
the two seasonal gifts, souvenirs for colleagues, return gifts, wrapping, and the polite words
people say as they hand something over. Customs vary between families, regions and generations,
and many are changing, so read this as a guide to what you'll see, not a set of rules you must
follow. Nobody expects a visitor to get everything right; a little care is noticed and
appreciated.

## The seasonal gifts: お{中元|ちゅうげん} and おせいぼ

Twice a year, many people send a gift to those who have helped them: a boss, a teacher, a
landlord, relatives, business clients.

| | When | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| お{中元|ちゅうげん} | summer: roughly early to mid July around Tokyo, later (into August) in some regions | thanks for the first half of the year |
| おせいぼ | the end of the year: usually the first weeks of December | thanks for the whole year |

おせいぼ is written お{歳暮|せいぼ} (its two kanji are beyond N4; learn to recognize the word on
shop signs). The gifts are usually useful things that get used up: coffee, beer, juice, fruit,
ham, cooking oil, good soap or towels, sweets. Many people order them from a department store,
which wraps them and sends them by delivery (see lesson 10h2), often at a price of a few
thousand yen.

The custom is weaker than it was. Many companies have stopped exchanging them, and many younger
people never send them. You don't need to start; but if someone sends you one, a thank-you is
expected, by phone, letter or message.

{村田|むらた}さんにお{中元|ちゅうげん}をいただきました。{明日|あした}、おれいの{電話|でんわ}をしようと{思|おも}います。
— I received a summer gift from Mr Murata. I think I'll phone tomorrow to thank him.

## おみやげ: souvenirs to share

When people come back from a trip, they often bring おみやげ for their family, friends and
colleagues. At work, the usual おみやげ is a box of local sweets, each one wrapped separately,
left in the staff room or handed round: one each for everyone. Stations and airports sell
these boxes by the thousand, and almost every town has its specialty.

{北海道|ほっかいどう}のおかしです。{一人|ひとり}{一|ひと}つずつどうぞ。
— They're sweets from Hokkaido. Please take one each.

A useful habit: when you take a few days off, bring something back for the people who covered
for you. It says thank you without words.

## おかえし: giving back

Lesson 6 introduced the return gift. A few occasions where it's expected:

- **After a wedding or a birth**, people who gave おいわい usually receive a return gift, often
  worth about a third to a half of what they gave. A family may also give guests at a wedding
  a gift to take home.
- **White Day.** In Japan, chocolate is traditionally given by women on Valentine's Day (14
  February), and the おかえし comes on White Day, 14 March. Habits are changing here too: many
  people now give chocolate to friends, or buy it for themselves.
- **After a visit to someone in hospital**, the patient's family may send something small once
  the patient is well.

For everyday presents (a birthday, a dinner invitation), a sincere thank-you, おれい, is usually
enough, and a quick return gift can feel too formal, as if you wanted to settle a debt.

## Wrapping and のし

Wrapping matters. Department stores wrap carefully, and for a formal gift they add のしがみ, a
sheet of paper on the box printed with two things:

- のし, a small folded decoration in the top right corner, a sign that this is a celebration
  gift;
- cords (みずひき, {水引|みずひき}) tied across the middle.

Above the cords goes the purpose (お{中元|ちゅうげん}, おいわい…), and below them the giver's
name. Shop staff will ask what it's for and write it for you: just say the occasion. The way the
cords are tied also carries meaning: a bow that can be untied for things that may happen again
(a birth, starting school), a tight knot for things that should happen only once (a wedding).

There's no のし on gifts for sad occasions: a funeral or condolence gift has black and white or
silver cords and no decoration.

The traditional cloth for carrying and wrapping a gift is a ふろしき, a square of cloth that
folds round almost any shape. People use them less now, but they're having a comeback as a
reusable alternative to paper bags.

## Numbers and things to avoid

Some numbers and items carry unlucky associations. Not everyone cares, but older people may, so
it's easy to avoid them:

- **4 and 9.** {四|し} sounds like {死|し} (death) and {九|く} like くるしい (painful). Avoid sets of
  four (four cups, four plates).
- **Even amounts of money at a wedding.** An even number can be "divided", like a couple
  splitting up, so wedding gifts of money are usually an odd number of 10,000-yen notes.
- **Potted plants for someone in hospital**: a plant "takes root", which sounds like staying in
  bed for a long time. Cut flowers are fine, though some hospitals don't allow flowers at all.
- **White chrysanthemums** are funeral flowers.
- **Knives and scissors** as wedding presents can suggest cutting ties; some people mind.

## Giving and receiving

How you hand a gift over says as much as the gift.

- Use **both hands** (りょうて), and turn the gift so that its front faces the receiver. Receive
  with both hands too.
- If you carried it in a shop's paper bag, it's traditional to take it out and hand over the
  gift alone, keeping the bag. Many people now hand it over in the bag, especially when it's
  raining or the receiver has far to carry it.
- Traditionally, people don't open a gift in front of the giver; they thank you, and open it
  later. With friends, and with people used to Western customs, opening it at once is common
  now. If you're not sure, ask: {開|あ}けてもいいですか.

## What to say

| Phrase | Meaning | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| これ、どうぞ。 | Here, this is for you. | Simple and always fine. |
| ほんの{気持|きも}ちですが… | It's just a small token… | Modest and current. ほんの = just, merely; {気持|きも}ち = feeling. |
| つまらないものですが… | It's nothing much, but… | The classic humble phrase. |
| よかったら、どうぞ。 | Please, if you'd like. | Friendly, for small things like sweets. |
| ありがとうございます。{大切|たいせつ}にします。 | Thank you. I'll treasure it. | Receiving a gift. |
| わざわざありがとうございます。 | Thank you for going to so much trouble. | わざわざ = specially, taking the trouble. |

つまらないものですが literally says "this is a boring thing". It's humble language, lowering
your own gift in the way lesson 6's さしあげる lowers your own action. It still appears in
formal settings and among older people, but many speakers now find it old-fashioned or even
odd, since why would you give someone something boring? Etiquette guides often suggest ほんの
{気持|きも}ちですが or simply naming the gift: {国|くに}のおかしです。よかったらどうぞ.

## Dialogue: a summer gift

```dialogue
# A summer gift
ルーカス: {森|もり}さん、いつもお{世話|せわ}になっています。これ、ほんの{気持|きも}ちですが……。
= Mrs Mori, thank you for all your help. This is just a small token…
{森|もり}: まあ、わざわざすみません。ありがとうございます。
= Oh, you shouldn't have. Thank you.
ルーカス: {国|くに}のコーヒーです。{森|もり}さんはコーヒーが{好|す}きだと{聞|き}きましたから。
= It's coffee from my country. I heard you like coffee.
{森|もり}: うれしい！{大切|たいせつ}にいただきます。
= How lovely! I'll enjoy it.
ルーカス: いえいえ。{花|はな}に{水|みず}をやってくださって、ほんとうにたすかりました。
= Not at all. You watered my flowers for me, and it was a real help.
{森|もり}: そんなこと、いいんですよ。
= Oh, that was nothing.
```

いつもお{世話|せわ}になっています is the everyday version of lesson 7's お{世話|せわ}になりました:
"thank you for always looking after me". {大切|たいせつ}にいただきます is a warm way to accept
food or drink. Notice Mrs Mori says すみません as well as ありがとう: in Japanese, thanks often
come with an apology for the trouble the giver went to.

## Key points

- お{中元|ちゅうげん} (summer) and おせいぼ (year-end) thank people who helped you; the custom is
  declining.
- おみやげ for colleagues: local sweets, one each.
- おかえし is expected after weddings and births, and on White Day; not usually for birthdays.
- のし and cords on formal celebration gifts; none on condolence gifts.
- Avoid sets of four; give and receive with both hands.
- ほんの{気持|きも}ちですが is a modern alternative to つまらないものですが.
