lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japan runs on deliveries. Shopping arrives at your door, often the next day; suitcases go ahead
of you to the airport; the summer and year-end gifts in lesson 10h1 travel by delivery van. And
much of the paperwork of daily life, from paying bills to picking up parcels, happens at the
convenience store on the corner. This honors lesson shows how these services work and gives you
some original notices to read, using this module's grammar: 〜てもらう, 〜ておく, 〜てある and
〜ところ.

## たくはいびん: parcel delivery

たくはいびん are door-to-door parcel services run by private delivery companies. (One company's
brand name, たっきゅうびん, is often used for all of them, the way some brand names are in
English.) The post office has its own parcel service too.

**Sending a parcel.** You can take it to the company's office, to many コンビニ, or ask for a
pick-up at home. You fill in a waybill, でんぴょう, with:

- the address, name and phone number of the person it's going to (おくりさき, {送|おく}り{先|さき}) and your own;
- what's inside (しなもの, written {品物|しなもの});
- the date and time slot you'd like it delivered: {午前中|ごぜんちゅう} (in the morning), or a
  two-hour window in the afternoon or evening. The slots vary by company.

Many companies now let you fill this in on a phone app and show a code at the counter instead.
The price depends on the size (the three sides added together, in centimetres: 60, 80,
100…), the weight and the distance. Usually the sender pays (もとばらい); the receiver can pay
instead (ちゃくばらい).

{明日|あした}の{午前中|ごぜんちゅう}にとどけてもらえますか。 — Could you deliver it tomorrow morning?

**Receiving.** The driver rings the bell, and you may be asked for a はんこ (your seal, from N5)
or a signature, サイン, though many deliveries now need neither. Some services can leave a parcel
outside your door or in a delivery locker in the building if you ask in advance.

## When you're out: the missed-delivery slip

If no one is home, the driver leaves a ふざいれんらくひょう in your postbox: a "notice of your
absence". In kanji it's {不在連絡票|ふざいれんらくひょう} (most of these kanji are outside N4); learn to
recognize the first two, {不在|ふざい} (absence). The slip tells you:

- who tried to deliver what, and when;
- a tracking number;
- how to ask for redelivery, さいはいたつ ({再配達|さいはいたつ}, kanji outside N4): by an automatic
  phone line, a website, a QR code, or by calling the driver;
- how long the parcel will be kept before it goes back to the sender, often about a week.

Redelivery is normally free. You pick a day and a time slot, as when sending.

## Reading: a missed-delivery slip

> **ごふざいれんらくひょう**
>
> ルーカス　さま
>
> {十一月|じゅういちがつ}{九日|ここのか}　{十四時|じゅうよじ}{二十分|にじゅっぷん}に、おにもつをとどけに{来|き}ましたが、おるすでした。
>
> おにもつは、えいぎょうしょで{一週間|いっしゅうかん}おあずかりします。
>
> さいはいたつは、{下|した}のQRコードか、{自動|じどう}{電話|でんわ}でおもうしこみください。{今日|きょう}の{十八時|じゅうはちじ}までにおもうしこみいただくと、{今日|きょう}の{夜|よる}にもう{一度|いちど}とどけられます。
>
> お{問|と}い{合|あ}わせばんごう：4402-1735-0968
>
> ことり{運送|うんそう}　ドライバー：{森|もり}

Notice of absence. To Lucas. We came to deliver a parcel at 14:20 on 9 November, but you were
out. We will keep the parcel at the depot for one week. Please request redelivery with the QR
code below or by the automatic phone line. If you apply by 18:00 today, we can deliver it again
this evening. Tracking number: … Kotori Transport, driver: Mori.

The slip uses polite business language you'll learn in module 6: おあずかりします (we will keep
it, humble), おもうしこみください (please apply), おもうしこみいただくと (if you apply: the と
conditional of lesson 11). {十八時|じゅうはちじ}までに means "by 18:00" (lesson 19). For now, pick
out the facts. Other words: えいぎょうしょ = office, depot; {自動|じどう}{電話|でんわ} = automatic phone
line; お{問|と}い{合|あ}わせばんごう = enquiry (tracking) number; {運送|うんそう} = transport, delivery;
{一度|いちど} = once.

## The コンビニ counter

A Japanese convenience store is open all day, every day, and does much more than sell snacks.
At the counter you can:

- **pay bills**: electricity, gas, water, phone, some local taxes. You bring the payment
  slip with a barcode and pay in cash (and at some stores by other methods); the clerk stamps
  and returns the receipt part. Utility bills like these are called こうきょう{料金|りょうきん}.
- **pay for online shopping**: choose "pay at a convenience store" when you order, and you get
  a number or barcode to show at the counter.
- **pick up parcels**: have your online order sent to a コンビニ near you, and pick it up with
  the number in your email.
- **send parcels** with the delivery companies that the store works with.

And at the machines in the store: an ATM, a copy machine that also prints from your phone,
and a ticket machine for concerts and events.

## Dialogue: at the convenience store

```dialogue
# At the convenience store
{店員|てんいん}: いらっしゃいませ。
= Hello.
ルーカス: すみません、これ、おねがいします。
= Excuse me, this, please.
{店員|てんいん}: はい、{電気|でんき}の{料金|りょうきん}ですね。{三千二百円|さんぜんにひゃくえん}です。
= Certainly, your electricity bill. That's 3,200 yen.
ルーカス: はい。それから、このにもつを{送|おく}りたいんですが。
= Here you are. Also, I'd like to send this parcel.
{店員|てんいん}: たくはいびんですね。こちらのでんぴょうに、{送|おく}り{先|さき}の{住所|じゅうしょ}とお{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}いていただけますか。
= By parcel delivery, then. Could you write the address and name of the person it's going to on this waybill?
ルーカス: はい。……{書|か}きました。とどけるのは、{明後日|あさって}の{午前中|ごぜんちゅう}でもいいですか。
= OK. …Done. Can it be delivered the day after tomorrow, in the morning?
{店員|てんいん}: はい、だいじょうぶです。サイズをはかりますね。……{八十|はちじゅう}サイズで、{千五百円|せんごひゃくえん}です。
= Yes, that's fine. I'll measure it. …It's size 80, so that's 1,500 yen.
ルーカス: カードではらえますか。
= Can I pay by card?
{店員|てんいん}: はい、どうぞ。……{今|いま}、レシートを{出|だ}しているところです。しょうしょうお{待|ま}ちください。
= Yes, of course. …The receipt is printing now. Please wait a moment.
```

はかる = to measure; はらう = to pay (しはらう in writing and formal speech); レシート = receipt;
{送|おく}り{先|さき} = the person and address something is sent to. The clerk uses 〜ていただけますか, the
politest request from lesson 7, and the set phrase しょうしょうお{待|ま}ちください from N5.

## Reading: a notice in a convenience store

> **おにもつのうけとりについて**
>
> インターネットで{買|か}った{品物|しなもの}を、この{店|みせ}でうけとることができます。
>
> ・{品物|しなもの}が{店|みせ}にとどいた{日|ひ}に、メールでお{知|し}らせします。
>
> ・メールにあるばんごうを、レジの{店員|てんいん}に{見|み}せてください。
>
> ・{品物|しなもの}は、とどいた{日|ひ}から{七日間|なのかかん}おあずかりします。その{後|あと}は、{送|おく}った{店|みせ}にもどります。
>
> ・{夜中|よなか}も、うけとることができます。
>
> ・{大|おお}きい{品物|しなもの}は、うけとれないことがあります。

Picking up parcels. You can pick up things you bought online at this shop. We'll let you know
by email on the day the item arrives at the shop. Show the number in the email to the staff at
the till. We keep items for seven days from the day they arrive. After that, they go back to
the shop that sent them. You can pick them up in the middle of the night too. Large items
sometimes can't be received.

〜について = about, concerning (a heading word); うけとる = to receive, pick up; お{知|し}らせする =
to inform (humble; the N5 word お{知|し}らせ is a notice); レジ = till, checkout; もどる = to go back;
{七日間|なのかかん} = for seven days. うけとれないことがあります combines the potential (lesson 2)
with 〜ことがある, "sometimes" (lesson 4).

## Words for deliveries and bills

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| とどける / とどく | to deliver, send (something) / to arrive, be delivered |
| はいたつ | delivery (also はいたつする) |
| うけとる | to receive, pick up |
| しはらう | to pay (formal; everyday はらう) |
| {料金|りょうきん} | charge, fee: {電気|でんき}{料金|りょうきん}, {送|おく}る{料金|りょうきん} |
| ふざい | being out, absence (written {不在|ふざい}) |

とどける and とどく are another transitive/intransitive pair from lesson 8: {友|とも}だちに
{本|ほん}をとどけました (I delivered the book to my friend), {本|ほん}がとどきました (the book has
arrived). When you're waiting for something, ask もうとどきましたか.

## Key points

- たくはいびん: door-to-door parcel delivery. Fill in a でんぴょう, choose a date and time slot.
- If you're out, a ふざいれんらくひょう tells you how to ask for さいはいたつ (redelivery).
- At a コンビニ you can pay bills (こうきょう{料金|りょうきん}), pay for and pick up online orders,
  and send parcels.
- Useful requests: {午前中|ごぜんちゅう}にとどけてもらえますか, カードではらえますか.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: When A, B happens: the と conditional
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

English has one little word, "if", and it does a lot of work: "if you press this, it opens",
"if it rains, we'll stay in", "if I were you…". Japanese splits that work between several
patterns, each with its own job. This module teaches four of them, the **[[conditional]]** forms
と, ば, たら and なら, then uses one of them for "must" in lesson 15.

We start with the easiest and the most limited: the **[[と conditional]]**. A と B means "when A
happens, B happens (every time)". It's the "if" of machines, nature, habits and directions:
the second thing follows the first automatically, and nobody chooses it.

このボタンをおすと、ドアが{開|あ}きます。 — When you press this button, the door opens.
{春|はる}になると、さくらがさきます。 — When spring comes, the cherry trees bloom.
この{道|みち}をまっすぐ{行|い}くと、{駅|えき}があります。 — If you go straight along this road, you come to the station.

That last kind of sentence is everywhere in Japan: ask anyone the way and you'll hear と in
every second sentence. Ticket machines, ATMs and the instructions on a vending machine are
full of it too, so that's this lesson's theme.

## Making it

Put と after the **[[plain non-past]]** form: the dictionary form or the ない form. That's all.
と itself never changes.

| Word | Plain non-past | + と | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| verb | おす | おすと | when you press |
| verb, negative | {入|い}れない | {入|い}れないと | if you don't put (it) in |
| い-adjective | {高|たか}い | {高|たか}いと | when it's expensive |
| い-adjective, negative | {高|たか}くない | {高|たか}くないと | when it isn't expensive |
| な-adjective | しずかだ | しずかだと | when it's quiet |
| noun | {雨|あめ}だ | {雨|あめ}だと | when it's rain(y) |

Two things to notice:

- Nouns and な-adjectives keep their だ: {雨|あめ}だと, しずかだと. {雨|あめ}と on its own means
  "rain and…" or "with rain", the と you learned in N5.
- The と clause stays non-past, even when the whole sentence is about the past. The tense goes
  on the last verb only: ボタンをおすと、ドアが{開|あ}きました (when I pressed the button, the
  door opened). Never おしたと.

Even in a polite sentence, the と clause is normally plain: おすと, not おしますと. Only the last
verb shows politeness. (おしますと exists in very formal announcements, but you don't need it.)

The subject inside the と clause takes が, not は, because は would mark the topic of the whole
sentence: {雨|あめ}がふると、バスがおくれます (when it rains, the bus is late). おくれる = to be
late.

## Use 1: it always happens (nature, machines, habits)

The core meaning of と is "whenever A, B". The result is natural and automatic: no one decides
it.

{冬|ふゆ}になると、{寒|さむ}くなります。 — When winter comes, it gets cold.
お{金|かね}を{入|い}れないと、きかいは{動|うご}きません。 — If you don't put money in, the machine won't work.
この{赤|あか}いボタンをおすと、おゆが{出|で}ます。 — If you press this red button, hot water comes out.
{右|みぎ}に{回|まわ}すと、{音|おと}が{大|おお}きくなります。 — When you turn it to the right, the sound gets louder.

A person's habit works the same way, as long as it really happens every time:

{父|ちち}は{家|うち}に{帰|かえ}ると、すぐテレビをつけます。 — Whenever my father gets home, he turns on the TV straight away.
{私|わたし}はコーヒーを{飲|の}むと、ねむれません。 — Whenever I drink coffee, I can't sleep.

## Use 2: directions

In directions, と links one step to the next thing you'll see: "go along here and you'll come
to…".

この{道|みち}をまっすぐ{行|い}くと、つきあたりに{銀行|ぎんこう}があります。 — Go straight along this road and there's a bank at the end.
{二|ふた}つ{目|め}のかどを{右|みぎ}にまがると、{左|ひだり}に{病院|びょういん}が{見|み}えます。 — Turn right at the second corner and you'll see a hospital on the left.
ふみきりをわたると、すぐです。 — It's just after the level crossing.

The instructions themselves (turn here, cross there) are often in the て form or 〜てください,
and と adds what you'll find: {駅|えき}を{出|で}て、{右|みぎ}に{行|い}くと、コンビニがあります.

## Use 3: what happened next (〜と、〜た)

With a past verb at the end, A と B た tells a story: A happened, and then B happened, often
something you found or didn't expect. The と clause is still non-past.

まどを{開|あ}けると、{外|そと}はゆきでした。 — When I opened the window, it was snowing outside.
ボタンをおすと、{大|おお}きい{音|おと}がしました。 — When I pressed the button, there was a loud noise.
{家|うち}に{帰|かえ}ると、{友|とも}だちから{手紙|てがみ}が{来|き}ていました。 — When I got home, there was a letter from a friend waiting.

The B part is something outside your control: what you saw, what you found, what another
person or a machine did. ({音|おと}がする, there is a sound, comes back in lesson 18.)

A sentence can also begin with すると (and then, at that moment), the same と after する:
ボタンをおしました。すると、ドアが{開|あ}きました. It's common in stories and written
instructions.

## What と can't do

Because B follows A automatically, B can't be something someone chooses to do. After と you
can't put:

| After と you can't put… | Wrong | Use instead (lessons 12–13) |
|---|---|---|
| a request (〜てください) | ×{駅|えき}に{着|つ}くと、{電話|でんわ}してください。 | {着|つ}いたら、{電話|でんわ}してください。 |
| an invitation (〜ましょう) | ×{春|はる}になると、{旅行|りょこう}しましょう。 | {春|はる}になったら、{旅行|りょこう}しましょう。 |
| a wish (〜たい) | ×お{金|かね}があると、{車|くるま}を{買|か}いたいです。 | お{金|かね}があれば / あったら、{買|か}いたいです。 |
| your own plan (〜つもり, 〜(よ)う) | ×{帰|かえ}ると、{勉強|べんきょう}するつもりです。 | {帰|かえ}ったら、{勉強|べんきょう}するつもりです。 |
| permission (〜てもいい) | ×{終|お}わると、{帰|かえ}ってもいいです。 | {終|お}わったら、{帰|かえ}ってもいいです。 |

The fix is almost always たら, which you'll meet in lesson 13. For now, a test that works:
if you could say "every time A, B" or "A, and as a result B", と is fine. If B is someone's
decision, a request or a hope, it isn't.

One set phrase looks like an exception: 〜といいですね (I hope…, it would be nice if…), as
in {明日|あした}はれるといいですね (I hope it's sunny tomorrow). Learn it as a phrase: the wish
is in いいですね, not after と.

## Kanji

Six kanji for ways, steps and machines.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 方 | direction; way; person (polite) | ホウ | かた | 4 | {駅|えき}の{方|ほう} (towards the station), この{方|かた} (this person), {読|よ}み{方|かた} (way of reading), {夕方|ゆうがた} (evening) |
| 計 | measure, count | ケイ | — | 9 | {時計|とけい} (clock, watch), {合計|ごうけい} (total) |
| 回 | turn; times | カイ | まわ(す), まわ(る) | 6 | {回|まわ}す, {回|まわ}る, {何回|なんかい}, {今回|こんかい} |
| 発 | depart, start; emit | ハツ (ハッ, パツ) | — | 9 | {出発|しゅっぱつ} (departure), {発音|はつおん} (pronunciation) |
| 進 | advance | シン | すす(む) | 11 | {進|すす}む (to go forward), {進|すす}める (to move something forward) |
| 自 | self | ジ | — | 6 | {自分|じぶん} (oneself), {自動|じどう} (automatic), {自転車|じてんしゃ} (bicycle) |

Notes:

- 方 has two readings that you already know as words: ほう in comparisons (N5's
  こっちのほうが…) and directions ({駅|えき}の{方|ほう}へ{行|い}く, go towards the station),
  and かた for a person (polite) and for "way of doing" after a ます stem: {読|よ}み{方|かた},
  {使|つか}い{方|かた} (how to use). Lesson 25 does "way of doing" properly.
- {時計|とけい} is a special reading: neither kanji is read like that anywhere else. N5 wrote it
  とけい; from now on it's {時計|とけい}.
- 〜{回|かい} counts times: {一回|いっかい}, {二回|にかい}, {三回|さんかい}, {四回|よんかい},
  {六回|ろっかい}, {八回|はっかい} (or はちかい), {十回|じゅっかい}. It overlaps with N5's なんど.
- 発 is read はつ, but before k, s, t and p sounds it shortens to はっ and can become ぱつ:
  {出発|しゅっぱつ}. Typing: shuppatsu.
- N5's じてんしゃ can now be written {自転車|じてんしゃ} (転 is in lesson 9).

Memory notes:

- 回 is a small box inside a big box, like something going round and round.
- 計 is 言 (say) and 十 (ten): saying the numbers out loud to count and measure.
- 進 has the "road" part that runs along the left and bottom of many movement kanji, with a
  bird sitting on it. A bird hops forward, never backward: to advance.
- 自 was first a picture of a nose. In Japan you point at your nose to say "me": self.
- 発 has two feet at the top, pushing off: setting out.

```trace
方計回発進自
```

## Dialogue: the ticket machine

Hannah wants a ticket and asks a member of the station staff for help.

```dialogue
# At the ticket machine
ハンナ: すみません、このきかいの{使|つか}い{方|かた}を{教|おし}えてくださいませんか。
= Excuse me, could you show me how to use this machine?
{駅員|えきいん}: はい。まず、がめんのここをタッチすると、{行|い}き{先|さき}が{出|で}ます。
= Sure. First, if you touch here on the screen, the destinations come up.
ハンナ: {山川|やまかわ}{駅|えき}までです。あ、{料金|りょうきん}が{出|で}ました。
= I'm going to Yamakawa station. Oh, the fare's come up.
{駅員|えきいん}: {三百二十円|さんびゃくにじゅうえん}ですね。そこにお{金|かね}を{入|い}れると、きっぷが{出|で}てきます。
= 320 yen. If you put the money in there, the ticket comes out.
ハンナ: ICカードも{持|も}っているんですが、お{金|かね}が{少|すく}ないんです。
= I've got an IC card too, but there isn't much money on it.
{駅員|えきいん}: じゃあ、カードをここに{入|い}れて、「チャージ」をおすと、お{金|かね}が{入|い}れられますよ。
= Then put the card in here and press "Top up", and you can add money.
ハンナ: {千円|せんえん}{入|い}れました。…あれ？カードが{出|で}てきません。
= I've put in 1,000 yen... Huh? The card isn't coming out.
{駅員|えきいん}: ちょっとまってください。…ああ、このきかいはこしょうしていますね。
= Just a moment... Ah, this machine is out of order.
{駅員|えきいん}: {今|いま}、カードを{出|だ}しますから、となりのきかいを{使|つか}ってください。
= I'll get your card out now, so please use the machine next to it.
ハンナ: ありがとうございます。{自分|じぶん}でやってみます。
= Thank you. I'll try it myself.
```

{使|つか}い{方|かた} = how to use (lesson 25); {行|い}き{先|さき} = destination; {入|い}れられます is the
potential of {入|い}れる. Notice that every と is followed by what the machine does, never by
what Hannah should do. When the station staff ask her to do something, they use 〜て and
〜てください.

## Reading: how to get to my flat

A message from Kaito to a friend who's visiting for the first time.

> {駅|えき}の{北口|きたぐち}を{出|で}ると、{前|まえ}に{大|おお}きい{道|みち}があります。その{道|みち}を{右|みぎ}にまっすぐ{行|い}くと、ふみきりがあります。ふみきりをわたって、{二|ふた}つ{目|め}のかどを{左|ひだり}にまがってください。{少|すこ}し{歩|ある}くと、{右|みぎ}にコンビニが{見|み}えます。コンビニの{前|まえ}を{通|とお}って、つきあたりまで{行|い}くと、{白|しろ}いアパートがあります。{私|わたし}の{家|うち}はその{二|に}かいです。かいだんを{上|あ}がると、{右|みぎ}がわのドアです。{駅|えき}から{歩|ある}いて{十分|じゅっぷん}ぐらいです。{分|わ}からないときは、{電話|でんわ}してください。

From the north exit of the station there's a big road in front of you. Go straight along
that road to the right and you'll come to a level crossing. Cross it and turn left at the
second corner. After a short walk you'll see a convenience store on the right. Go past the
convenience store to the end of the road and there's a white apartment building. My place
is on the second floor. At the top of the stairs it's the door on the right. It's about ten
minutes on foot from the station. If you can't find it, call me.

{北口|きたぐち} = north exit; {通|とお}る = to pass, go past (lesson 9's kanji); かいだん = stairs.
The requests (まがってください, {電話|でんわ}してください) stand in their own sentences, not
after と.

## Say it

```speak
このボタンをおすと、ドアが{開|あ}きます。
= When you press this button, the door opens.
まっすぐ{行|い}くと、{右|みぎ}に{銀行|ぎんこう}があります。
= Go straight on and there's a bank on the right.
お{金|かね}を{入|い}れないと、{動|うご}きません。
= It won't work if you don't put money in.
このきかいの{使|つか}い{方|かた}を{教|おし}えてください。
= Please show me how to use this machine.
{春|はる}になると、あたたかくなりますね。
= When spring comes, it gets warm, doesn't it?
```

## Pronunciation

- {出発|しゅっぱつ} has two small-っ beats: shu-p-pa-tsu. Hold the pause before ぱ.
- {何回|なんかい} has ん before a k sound; say it as one smooth word, nan-kai, with the pitch
  falling after the first beat: {何回|なんかい:1}.
- まず (first) starts high and falls: [まず:1]. Don't confuse it with まずい (tastes bad).

## Common mistakes

- A request or plan after と: ×{着|つ}くと、れんらくしてください. Use たら (lesson 13):
  {着|つ}いたら、れんらくしてください.
- A past verb before と: ×おしたと、{出|で}ました. Keep it non-past: おすと、{出|で}ました.
- Dropping だ: ×{雨|あめ}と、{行|い}きません means nothing; {雨|あめ}だと、{行|い}きません (if it
  rains, I don't go).
- は in the と clause: ×{雨|あめ}はふると…. Use が: {雨|あめ}がふると….
- Using と for one-time hopes: ×{明日|あした}{雨|あめ}がふると、{家|うち}にいたいです. Use ば or
  たら (lessons 12–13).

## Key points

- A と B: when A, B happens (automatically, every time). Plain non-past + と; nouns and
  な-adjectives + だと.
- Uses: nature, machines, habits, directions, and 〜と、〜た for what happened next or what you
  found.
- The tense and politeness go on the last verb only.
- After と: no requests, invitations, wishes, plans or permission. Use たら for those.
- 〜といいですね (I hope) is a set phrase.
- New kanji: 方 計 回 発 進 自. {時計|とけい}, {自転車|じてんしゃ} and {合計|ごうけい} can now be written
  with kanji.

lessons.title: If: the ば form
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 11, と linked two things that always go together: press the button and the door
opens. This lesson's conditional is about the condition itself: "if (and only if) A, then B".
It's the "if" of advice and of what it takes to get a result: if you sleep more, you'll feel
better; what should I do?; I should have gone to bed earlier.

{早|はや}くねれば、{朝|あさ}{早|はや}く{起|お}きられます。 — If you go to bed early, you can get up early.
どうすればいいですか。 — What should I do?
もっと{早|はや}くねればよかった。 — I should have gone to bed earlier.

The form is called the **[[ば conditional]]** (the ば form), and it's the first new verb form in
this module. From this lesson it joins your conjugation drills as "conditional".

## Making the ば form

Every verb ends in -eba. Find the vowel change the same way you did for the potential form
in lesson 2: the last kana moves to the え row, then add ば.

### Group 1: u → e + ば

| Dictionary form | ば form | | Dictionary form | ば form |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| {書|か}く | {書|か}けば | | {待|ま}つ | {待|ま}てば |
| {行|い}く | {行|い}けば | | {読|よ}む | {読|よ}めば |
| およぐ | およげば | | あそぶ | あそべば |
| {話|はな}す | {話|はな}せば | | {帰|かえ}る | {帰|かえ}れば |
| {買|か}う | {買|か}えば | | {死|し}ぬ | {死|し}ねば |

う becomes え: {買|か}う → {買|か}えば (not かわば). {行|い}く is regular here: {行|い}けば.

### Group 2: る → れば

{食|た}べる → {食|た}べれば, {見|み}る → {見|み}れば, {起|お}きる → {起|お}きれば, やめる → やめれば.

### Group 3 and ある

する → すれば ({勉強|べんきょう}すれば), {来|く}る → {来|く}れば (くれば). ある → あれば.

### Negatives: ない → なければ

Any ない form drops い and adds ければ, exactly like an い-adjective:

{行|い}かない → {行|い}かなければ (if you don't go) · {食|た}べない → {食|た}べなければ ·
しない → しなければ · ない → なければ (if there isn't).

### Adjectives and nouns

| Word | ば form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {高|たか}い | {高|たか}ければ | if it's expensive |
| いい | よければ | if it's good (いい uses よ-, as always) |
| {高|たか}くない | {高|たか}くなければ | if it isn't expensive |
| しずか (な-adj.) | しずかなら(ば) | if it's quiet |
| {学生|がくせい} (noun) | {学生|がくせい}なら(ば) | if you're a student |

い-adjectives replace い with ければ. な-adjectives and nouns use なら, and the ば after it is
usually dropped in speech. (You'll also see であれば in formal writing: {学生|がくせい}であれば.)
なら has a second, separate job that lesson 14 teaches.

A quick check for any word: the ば form always has れ, け, せ, て, め, べ, げ, ね or え before ば,
or ends in なら.

## Use 1: if A, then B (the condition)

ば puts the weight on the condition: B happens provided that A is true. It's common for
general truths and for "what it takes".

{時間|じかん}があれば、{行|い}きます。 — If I have time, I'll go.
{安|やす}ければ、{買|か}いたいです。 — If it's cheap, I'd like to buy it.
{毎日|まいにち}{歩|ある}けば、{体|からだ}が{強|つよ}くなります。 — If you walk every day, your body gets stronger.
{薬|くすり}を{飲|の}めば、ねつが{下|さ}がりますよ。 — If you take the medicine, the fever will go down.
{雨|あめ}がふらなければ、{明日|あした}はジムに{行|い}きます。 — If it doesn't rain, I'll go to the gym tomorrow.

The second part can be what you want or plan (〜たい, 〜ます as "I will"), and after a state
(ある, いる, an adjective, a potential, ない) it can even be a request:

{時間|じかん}があれば、{来|き}てください。 — If you have time, please come.
{暑|あつ}ければ、まどを{開|あ}けてもいいですよ。 — If you're hot, you can open the window.

But when the ば part is an action, the second part usually isn't a request or an invitation:
×{駅|えき}に{着|つ}けば、{電話|でんわ}してください sounds wrong; use たら (lesson 13):
{駅|えき}に{着|つ}いたら、{電話|でんわ}してください.

ば also isn't the word for "when (this event) happens" in time order. "When I get home, I'll
eat" is {家|うち}に{帰|かえ}ったら、{食|た}べます (lesson 13), not {帰|かえ}れば.

## Use 2: advice with 〜ばいい

〜ばいい literally means "it's good if you…", and it's the everyday way to say what someone
should do. The question どうすればいいですか (what should I do?) is one of the most useful
sentences in this course.

「よくねむれないんです。どうすればいいですか。」「ねる{前|まえ}に、おふろに{入|はい}ればいいですよ。」 — "I can't sleep well. What should I do?" "You should take a bath before bed."
{首|くび}がいたいときは、{少|すこ}し{休|やす}めばいいです。 — When your neck hurts, you just need a little rest.
{何|なに}を{持|も}って{行|い}けばいいですか。 — What should I bring?
{何時|なんじ}に{来|く}ればいいですか。 — What time should I come?

〜なければいい is "you just shouldn't…": コーヒーを{飲|の}まなければいいんです (you just need to
not drink coffee). Lesson 13 adds 〜たらいいですか, which means the same in most questions.

## Use 3: regret with 〜ばよかった

〜ばよかった (it would have been good if…) is "I should have…" or "I wish I had…". The
negative 〜なければよかった is "I shouldn't have…".

もっと{早|はや}くねればよかったです。 — I should have gone to bed earlier.
あんなにたくさん{食|た}べなければよかった。 — I wish I hadn't eaten so much.
かさを{持|も}って{来|く}ればよかった。 — I should have brought an umbrella.

It's usually about yourself. Said to someone about what they did ({行|い}けばよかったですね, you
should have gone), it can sound like a criticism, so use it with care.

## ば and と

Both can describe general results, and often either works:
{春|はる}になると / なれば、あたたかくなります. The difference is the focus:

| | と | ば |
|---|---|---|
| Feels like | whenever A, B follows | if (and only if) A, B |
| Typical use | machines, nature, habits, directions | conditions, advice, regret |
| Request after it | never | after a state (ある, adjective…), yes |
| Set phrases | 〜といい (I hope) | 〜ばいい (should), 〜ばよかった (should have) |

The reference sheet "The conditionals" has all four conditionals side by side.

One line for later: 〜ば〜ほど (the more…, the more…: {読|よ}めば{読|よ}むほど) is an N3 pattern
built on this form. You'll meet it after N4.

## Kanji

Six kanji for the body, all with words you know in kana from N5.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 体 | body | タイ | からだ | 7 | {体|からだ}, {体重|たいじゅう} (body weight) |
| 頭 | head | トウ, ズ | あたま | 16 | {頭|あたま}, {先頭|せんとう} (the front of a line) |
| 顔 | face | ガン | かお | 18 | {顔|かお}, {顔色|かおいろ} (complexion), {洗顔|せんがん} (washing your face) |
| 首 | neck; head, chief | シュ | くび | 9 | {首|くび}, {首都|しゅと} (capital city) |
| 声 | voice | セイ | こえ (ごえ) | 7 | {声|こえ}, {大声|おおごえ} (a loud voice) |
| 太 | fat, thick | タイ | ふと(い), ふと(る) | 4 | {太|ふと}い, {太|ふと}る (to put on weight) |

Notes:

- {体|からだ}, {頭|あたま}, {顔|かお}, {声|こえ} and {太|ふと}い were kana words in N5; write them with
  kanji from now on.
- こえ becomes ごえ after another word: {大声|おおごえ}. Words often change like this when they're
  the second half of a compound (くすり → {目薬|めぐすり} in lesson 13).
- 太 is read タイ in たいよう (the sun), which you'll meet later. ふとい is "thick" (a line, a
  stick); ふとる is "to put on weight". Its partner やせる (to lose weight) has no kanji at this
  level.

Memory notes:

- 体 is a person (the thin form of 人, on the left) and 本 (origin, main part): the main part of a person, the body.
- 太 is 大 (big) with one extra dot: even bigger, fat.
- 首 has two little marks like hair on top of 自 (a nose, a face): a head sitting on its neck.
- 頭 and 顔 have the same right-hand part, which pictures a head. Look at the left to tell them
  apart: 頭 has a short, round shape like a bowl on a stand; 顔 has a longer, slanted one.
- 声 starts with a cross over a line, like a soldier standing on a box and calling out: a voice.

```trace
体頭顔首声太
```

## Dialogue: I can't sleep

Alex has been tired at work. His colleague Miho asks what's wrong. (Casual speech: they're
colleagues and friends.)

```dialogue
# At lunch
ミホ: アレックスさん、{顔色|かおいろ}がわるいね。だいじょうぶ？
= Alex, you look pale. Are you OK?
アレックス: うん、さいきんよくねむれないんだ。どうすればいいかな。
= Yeah, I haven't been sleeping well lately. What should I do, I wonder.
ミホ: ねる{前|まえ}に{何|なに}をしてる？
= What do you do before bed?
アレックス: ベッドでスマホを{見|み}たり、ゲームをしたりしてる。{一時|いちじ}ごろまで。
= I look at my phone in bed, play games, that kind of thing. Until about one.
ミホ: それだよ。ねる{前|まえ}にスマホを{見|み}なければ、すぐねむれると{思|おも}う。
= That's it. If you don't look at your phone before bed, I think you'll fall asleep quickly.
アレックス: でも、ゲームをしないと、つまらないんだ。
= But if I don't play games, I get bored.
ミホ: じゃあ、{夕方|ゆうがた}にすればいいよ。それから、コーヒーは{一日|いちにち}に{何|なん}ばい{飲|の}んでる？
= Then play in the evening. And how many cups of coffee do you drink a day?
アレックス: ごはいぐらい。{午後|ごご}も{飲|の}むよ。
= About five. In the afternoon too.
ミホ: {午後|ごご}に{飲|の}まなければ、もっとよくねむれるよ。
= If you don't drink it in the afternoon, you'll sleep better.
アレックス: そうか。もっと{早|はや}くミホさんに{聞|き}けばよかった。{今夜|こんや}からやってみる。
= I see. I should have asked you sooner. I'll try it from tonight.
```

さいきん = recently (N5); 〜はい / 〜ばい counts cups and glasses (ごはい, five cups; なんばい, how
many cups); {今夜|こんや} = tonight. どうすればいいかな is the casual, thinking-aloud version of
どうすればいいですか.

## Reading: an advice column

From a health magazine's page of readers' questions.

> 「{仕事|しごと}がいそがしくて、{毎日|まいにち}つかれています。どうすればいいですか。」（{会社員|かいしゃいん}、{三十二|さんじゅうに}さい）
>
> まず、ねる{時間|じかん}を{見|み}てください。{夜|よる}おそくまで{起|お}きていれば、{体|からだ}は{休|やす}めません。まいばん{同|おな}じ{時間|じかん}にねれば、{朝|あさ}も{楽|らく}に{起|お}きられます。つぎに、{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}です。{朝|あさ}{何|なに}も{食|た}べなければ、{頭|あたま}がよく{働|はたら}きません。パンやぎゅうにゅうなど、{何|なに}か{食|た}べてください。それから、{体|からだ}を{動|うご}かすことです。{会社|かいしゃ}まで{歩|ある}けば、それがいい{運動|うんどう}になります。{首|くび}やせなかがいたいときは、{一時間|いちじかん}に{一回|いっかい}{立|た}って、うでを{回|まわ}せばいいです。むりをしないで、できることから{始|はじ}めてください。

"I'm so busy at work that I'm tired every day. What should I do?" (office worker, 32)

First, look at the time you go to bed. If you stay up late at night, your body can't rest. If
you go to bed at the same time every night, it's easier to get up in the morning too. Next,
breakfast. If you eat nothing in the morning, your brain doesn't work well. Eat something, such as bread or
milk. Then there's moving your body. If you walk to work, that
becomes good exercise. When your neck or back hurts, you just need to stand up once an hour
and swing your arms round. Don't overdo it: start with what you can do.

{動|うご}かす = to move (something), the transitive partner of {動|うご}く; {運動|うんどう} =
exercise; {楽|らく}に = easily. Count the ば forms: there are six, and each one is a condition
for a good (or bad) result.

## Say it

```speak
どうすればいいですか。
= What should I do?
{何時|なんじ}に{来|く}ればいいですか。
= What time should I come?
{時間|じかん}があれば、{行|い}きます。
= If I have time, I'll go.
もっと{早|はや}くねればよかった。
= I should have gone to bed earlier.
むりをしなければ、すぐよくなりますよ。
= If you don't overdo it, you'll soon get better.
```

## Common mistakes

- {買|か}う → ×かわば. The ば form of an う verb is 〜えば: {買|か}えば, {会|あ}えば, つかえば.
- {来|く}る → ×{来|き}れば or ×これば. It's くれば.
- い-adjectives: ×{高|たか}いれば, ×{高|たか}いなら(ば) for the plain condition. Use {高|たか}ければ.
  (いい → よければ, never いければ.)
- Nouns and な-adjectives: ×{学生|がくせい}ば, ×しずかければ. Use {学生|がくせい}なら, しずかなら.
- A request after an action in the ば part: ×{着|つ}けば、{電話|でんわ}してください. Use たら.
- ×{十時|じゅうじ}になれば、{出|で}かけましょう for a plan in time order. Use たら:
  {十時|じゅうじ}になったら、{出|で}かけましょう.

## Key points

- ば form: group 1 u → e + ば ({書|か}けば, {買|か}えば); group 2 る → れば; すれば, くれば, あれば;
  い-adj. 〜ければ (よければ); ない → なければ; な-adj./noun + なら(ば).
- ば focuses on the condition: "if (and only if)". After a state it can take a request.
- 〜ばいい: should; どうすればいいですか: what should I do?
- 〜ばよかった: I should have…; 〜なければよかった: I shouldn't have….
- The ば form ("conditional") now joins your conjugation drills.
- 〜ば〜ほど (the more…the more) is N3.
- New kanji: 体 頭 顔 首 声 太.

lessons.title: If and after: 〜たら
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

と (lesson 11) can't take a request after it, and ば (lesson 12) is awkward with one. Real life
is full of sentences like "if you get lost, call me", "when you get to the hotel, let me
know" and "if it hurts, why don't you see a doctor?". For all of them Japanese uses the
**[[たら conditional]]**. It's the most flexible of the four and the one you'll use most in
conversation: when in doubt, たら is usually right.

もし{道|みち}にまよったら、{電話|でんわ}してください。 — If you get lost, call me.
ホテルに{着|つ}いたら、れんらくします。 — When I get to the hotel, I'll let you know.
いたかったら、{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}ったらどうですか。 — If it hurts, why don't you go to the hospital?

This lesson's theme is what can go wrong on a trip: getting ill, getting hurt, losing your
passport, and what to say at the hospital and the pharmacy.

## Making it: the た form + ら

If you can make the plain past (the た form from N5), you can make たら: add ら.

| Word | Plain past | たら form |
|---|---|---|
| {行|い}く | {行|い}った | {行|い}ったら |
| {飲|の}む | {飲|の}んだ | {飲|の}んだら |
| {食|た}べる | {食|た}べた | {食|た}べたら |
| する | した | したら |
| {来|く}る | {来|き}た | {来|き}たら (きたら) |
| {行|い}かない | {行|い}かなかった | {行|い}かなかったら |
| いたい | いたかった | いたかったら |
| いい | よかった | よかったら |
| しずか (な-adj.) | しずかだった | しずかだったら |
| {雨|あめ} (noun) | {雨|あめ}だった | {雨|あめ}だったら |

Don't be misled by the past shape: たら isn't past. {着|つ}いたら is "when I arrive", in the
future. The tense of the sentence is in the last verb, as with と.

The polite 〜ましたら exists ({着|つ}きましたら) and you'll hear it from hotel and shop staff, but
in your own sentences the plain たら is normal even in polite speech.

## Use 1: "if" (a **[[hypothetical]]**)

When A may or may not happen, A たら B is "if A, B". The second part can be anything: a
request, an invitation, a wish, a plan, a fact.

パスポートをなくしたら、すぐ{大使館|たいしかん}にれんらくしてください。 — If you lose your passport, contact your embassy at once.
ねつが{出|で}たら、この{薬|くすり}を{飲|の}んでください。 — If you get a fever, take this medicine.
{雨|あめ}だったら、{家|うち}で{映画|えいが}を{見|み}ましょう。 — If it rains, let's watch a film at home.
お{金|かね}がたくさんあったら、{世界|せかい}{旅行|りょこう}がしたいです。 — If I had lots of money, I'd like to travel round the world.

### もし: announcing an "if"

もし at the start of a sentence warns the listener that a condition is coming. It adds "if by
any chance, supposing" and makes the "if" reading certain:

もしぐあいがわるくなったら、{言|い}ってください。 — If (by any chance) you start to feel unwell, tell me.

もし goes with "if" only, never with something that's sure to happen (×もし{十時|じゅうじ}になったら).
It works with ば and なら too, but たら is its most common partner.

## Use 2: "when" (something that will surely happen)

When A is sure to happen, A たら B is "when A (has happened), B", "once A, B". English says
"when", not "if", but Japanese uses the same たら.

{日本|にほん}に{着|つ}いたら、{電話|でんわ}します。 — When I arrive in Japan, I'll call.
{薬|くすり}を{飲|の}んだら、すぐねてください。 — Once you've taken the medicine, go straight to bed.
{十時|じゅうじ}になったら、{出|で}かけましょう。 — Let's go out when it gets to ten.
{仕事|しごと}が{終|お}わったら、{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}きます。 — When I finish work, I'll go to the hospital.

The order matters: B happens after A is complete. {帰|かえ}ったら{電話|でんわ}します is "I'll call
after I get home", never "while I'm on my way".

This is where と and ば can't follow: after them, B can't be a request or your plan. たら can.

## Use 3: what happened, what you found (〜たら、〜た)

With a past verb at the end, たら tells what happened after A, or what you found. It's the
same as lesson 11's 〜と、〜た, a little more conversational.

{外|そと}に{出|で}たら、{雨|あめ}がふっていました。 — When I went outside, it was raining.
{薬|くすり}を{飲|の}んだら、すぐよくなりました。 — After I took the medicine, I soon got better.
{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}ったら、{今日|きょう}は{休|やす}みでした。 — I went to the hospital and found it was closed today.

B is something you noticed or that happened by itself, not a second thing you chose to do.
For "I did A, then I did B", use the て form: {薬|くすり}を{飲|の}んで、ねました.

## Suggestions: 〜たらどうですか

〜たらどうですか (how about doing…?) suggests something to someone. It's friendly advice; the
more polite version is 〜たらいかがですか, and between friends it shortens to 〜たらどう？ or just
〜たら？ with a rising voice.

ねつがあるときは、{早|はや}く{帰|かえ}ったらどうですか。 — When you have a fever, why don't you go home early?
おなかがいたいの？{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}ったら？ — Your stomach hurts? Why not go to the hospital?
{一度|いちど}、{大|おお}きい{病院|びょういん}でけんさをうけたらいかがですか。 — Why don't you have a test at a big hospital?

Use it with people at your level or below, or soften it. Suggesting something to a teacher or
a boss with 〜たらどうですか can sound like you're telling them what to do.

## Asking for advice: 〜たらいいですか

どうしたらいいですか means exactly the same as lesson 12's どうすればいいですか (what should I
do?), and both are common. So do {何|なに}を{持|も}って{行|い}ったらいいですか and
{何|なに}を{持|も}って{行|い}けばいいですか (what should I take?).

パスポートをなくしたんですが、どうしたらいいですか。 — I've lost my passport. What should I do?
{薬|くすり}は{何|なん}{回|かい}{飲|の}んだらいいですか。 — How many times should I take the medicine?

## よかったら: if you like

よかったら (from いい, "if it's good for you") is a polite way to offer or invite: "if you
like", "if it's no trouble". It's one of the most useful words in this lesson.

よかったら、この{目薬|めぐすり}を{使|つか}ってください。 — Use these eye drops if you like.
よかったら、いっしょに{行|い}きましょうか。 — Shall I come with you, if that's OK?

## と, ば or たら?

| | と | ば | たら |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core idea | whenever A, B | if (only if) A, B | if A / when A has happened, B |
| Request or plan after it | no | after a state only | yes |
| "When" for a sure event | (only for automatic results) | no | yes |
| 〜、〜た (what happened) | yes | rare | yes |
| Advice | — | 〜ばいい | 〜たらいい, 〜たらどうですか |

If you're not sure, たら is the safe choice in conversation. と is best for machines and
directions, ば for conditions and 〜ばよかった, and lesson 14 adds なら.

## Kanji

Six kanji for illness, doctors and going home. Most of their words are N5 words you've been
writing in kana.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 病 | illness | ビョウ | — | 10 | {病気|びょうき}, {病院|びょういん} |
| 医 | medicine, healing | イ | — | 7 | {医者|いしゃ}, {医学|いがく} (medicine, as a science) |
| 者 | person | シャ | もの | 8 | {医者|いしゃ}, {学者|がくしゃ} (scholar) |
| 院 | institution | イン | — | 10 | {病院|びょういん}, {入院|にゅういん}, {大学院|だいがくいん} (graduate school) |
| 薬 | medicine (drug) | ヤク | くすり (ぐすり) | 16 | {薬|くすり}, {目薬|めぐすり} (eye drops) |
| 帰 | return | キ | かえ(る) | 10 | {帰|かえ}る, {帰国|きこく}, {日帰|ひがえ}り (a day trip) |

Notes:

- From now on write {病気|びょうき}, {病院|びょういん}, {医者|いしゃ}, {薬|くすり} and {帰|かえ}る with
  kanji. {帰|かえ}る is still group 1: {帰|かえ}ります, {帰|かえ}って.
- 者 is the "person" in job and role words: {医者|いしゃ} (a medicine person), {学者|がくしゃ} (a
  learning person). Its kun'yomi もの means "person" in formal and written Japanese; you'll meet
  it later.
- くすり becomes ぐすり in {目薬|めぐすり}, and かえる becomes がえる in {日帰|ひがえ}り: the same
  voicing you saw in {大声|おおごえ} (lesson 12).
- {病院|びょういん} has a small ょ: びょ・う・い・ん. びよういん, with a full-size よ, is a hair
  salon.

Memory notes:

- 病 has a frame like a bed under a roof, with someone lying in it. Many kanji for illnesses
  use this frame.
- 薬 is grass (the plant top) over 楽 (comfortable, lesson 3): plants that make you feel
  better.
- 帰: the right-hand part pictures a broom. Home is where your broom is.
- 院: the left-hand part, like a tall letter B, is a hill or a wall. A big place behind walls:
  an institution.
- 医 is an arrow in a box. Taking the arrow out is the doctor's job.

```trace
病医者院薬帰
```

## Dialogue: at a clinic

Oliver caught a cold on holiday and goes to a small clinic near his hotel.

```dialogue
# At the clinic
{医者|いしゃ}: どうしましたか。
= What seems to be the problem?
オリバー: きのうから、ねつがあって、のどがいたいんです。
= I've had a fever since yesterday, and my throat hurts.
{医者|いしゃ}: そうですか。{口|くち}を{開|あ}けてください。…ああ、かぜですね。
= I see. Open your mouth, please... Ah, it's a cold.
{医者|いしゃ}: {薬|くすり}を{出|だ}しますから、{一日|いちにち}{三回|さんかい}、{食後|しょくご}に{飲|の}んでください。
= I'll give you some medicine. Take it three times a day after meals.
オリバー: {明後日|あさって}{帰国|きこく}するんですが、ひこうきに{乗|の}ってもだいじょうぶですか。
= I'm going home the day after tomorrow. Is it all right to fly?
{医者|いしゃ}: ねつが{下|さ}がったら、だいじょうぶですよ。
= Once the fever has gone down, you'll be fine.
{医者|いしゃ}: もし{明日|あした}の{朝|あさ}もねつが{高|たか}かったら、また{来|き}てください。
= If you still have a high temperature tomorrow morning, come back.
オリバー: わかりました。{旅行|りょこう}のほけんは{使|つか}えますか。
= OK. Can I use my travel insurance?
{医者|いしゃ}: うけつけで{聞|き}いてください。{薬|くすり}はとなりのやっきょくでもらえますよ。
= Please ask at reception. You can get the medicine at the pharmacy next door.
オリバー: ありがとうございました。
= Thank you very much.
```

どうしましたか is the doctor's "what's wrong?"; かぜ = a cold; {下|さ}がる = to go down (lesson
8). Notice the two たら: one for a sure event (the fever will go down) and one, with もし, for
something that may or may not happen.

## Reading: if you lose your passport

From a travel guide's page of advice for visitors.

> {旅行|りょこう}{中|ちゅう}にパスポートをなくしたら、まず{近|ちか}くのこうばんかけいさつに{行|い}って、なくしたことを{話|はな}してください。けいさつでもらった{紙|かみ}は{後|あと}で{使|つか}いますから、なくさないでください。つぎに、{自分|じぶん}の{国|くに}の{大使館|たいしかん}にれんらくします。{大使館|たいしかん}に{行|い}ったら、{新|あたら}しいパスポートか、{帰国|きこく}するときに{使|つか}うしょるいを{作|つく}ってもらいます。{写真|しゃしん}も{持|も}って{行|い}ってください。パスポートのコピーがあったら、てつづきが{早|はや}くなります。{旅行|りょこう}の{前|まえ}に、コピーをかばんに{入|い}れておけば{安心|あんしん}です。

If you lose your passport during your trip, first go to a nearby police box or police
station and tell them you've lost it. You'll need the paper the police give you later, so
don't lose it. Next, contact your country's embassy. When you go to the embassy, they'll make
you a new passport or a document for going home. Take photos with you too. If you have a copy
of your passport, the procedure is quicker. If you put a copy in your bag before the trip,
you can feel at ease.

{旅行|りょこう}{中|ちゅう} = during the trip; しょるい = documents; てつづき = the procedure (both lesson
15); {安心|あんしん} = peace of mind. Find the three たら: two are "if" and one ({行|い}ったら) is
"when". The last sentence uses ば (〜ておけば, if you do it in advance).

## Say it

```speak
{日本|にほん}に{着|つ}いたら、{電話|でんわ}します。
= When I get to Japan, I'll call.
パスポートをなくしたんですが、どうしたらいいですか。
= I've lost my passport. What should I do?
{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}ったらどうですか。
= Why don't you go to the hospital?
よかったら、どうぞ。
= Please, if you like.
もしねつが{出|で}たら、{休|やす}んでください。
= If you get a fever, please rest.
```

## Pronunciation

{帰|かえ:1}る (to go home) starts high and falls after the first beat: KA-e-ru. Another
common verb, [かえる:0] (to change), is flat: ka-E-RU, staying high. Most of the time the
context tells them apart, but say {帰|かえ}る with its falling start and you'll sound natural.

## Common mistakes

- Reading たら as past. {着|つ}いたら is "when I arrive", not "when I arrived".
- ×{来|く}たら. The た form of {来|く}る is {来|き}た, so it's {来|き}たら.
- もし with a sure event: ×もし{明日|あした}になったら. Just {明日|あした}になったら.
- Using と or ば for a request after an action: ×{着|つ}くと / {着|つ}けば、{電話|でんわ}してください.
  たら: {着|つ}いたら、{電話|でんわ}してください.
- 〜たらどうですか to your boss or teacher. It can sound like an instruction; with them, just
  give the information or ask a question.

## Key points

- たら = plain past + ら: {行|い}ったら, {来|き}たら, {高|たか}かったら, {雨|あめ}だったら,
  {行|い}かなかったら. It isn't past.
- "If" (hypothetical, often with もし) and "when/once" (a sure future event).
- Anything can follow たら: requests, invitations, wishes, plans.
- 〜たら、〜た: what happened next or what you found.
- 〜たらどうですか: suggestions; どうしたらいいですか = どうすればいいですか.
- よかったら: if you like.
- New kanji: 病 医 者 院 薬 帰.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: なら, 〜ても, and only: しか, だけ, ばかり
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Someone says "I want to buy a camera" and you answer "if it's a camera you want, the shop by
the station is cheap". That "if it's…" picks up the other person's words and gives advice
about them. It's the job of the last conditional, the **[[なら conditional]]**, and it's how
Japanese people recommend places and things.

The lesson then turns "if" round into "even if" (〜ても), adds "anything, anyone, anywhere"
({何|なん}でも, だれでも, どこでも), and finishes with three words for "only": しか, だけ and
ばかり. The theme is recommending and choosing: shops, sights, banks and cinemas.

## なら: "if it's…", taking up a topic

Put なら after a noun, and you're saying "as for X, since you mention it…", then giving a
tip or an opinion about X.

「カメラを{買|か}いたいんです。」「カメラなら、{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}の{店|みせ}が{安|やす}いですよ。」 — "I want to buy a camera." "If it's a camera, the shop in front of the station is cheap."
「しゅうまつ、{映画|えいが}を{見|み}ませんか。」「{映画|えいが}なら、{日曜日|にちようび}がいいです。」 — "Shall we see a film at the weekend?" "For a film, Sunday's good for me."
「{日本|にほん}の{古|ふる}い{物|もの}が{見|み}たいです。」「それなら、はくぶつかんに{行|い}ったらどうですか。」 — "I'd like to see old Japanese things." "In that case, why not go to the museum?"

それなら (in that case, if that's so) is なら after それ, and you'll hear it constantly. In casual
speech it's often just なら at the start: なら、いっしょに{行|い}こう (then let's go together).

### なら after a verb or an adjective

なら can follow the plain form of a verb or an い-adjective too. A: "I'm going to Kyoto", B:
"if you're going to Kyoto, (here's my advice)…":

{京都|きょうと}に{行|い}くなら、{秋|あき}がいいですよ。 — If you're going to Kyoto, autumn is a good time.
カメラを{買|か}うなら、この{店|みせ}がいちばん{安|やす}いです。 — If you're buying a camera, this shop is the cheapest.
{高|たか}いなら、{買|か}いません。 — If it's expensive, I won't buy it.

Nouns and な-adjectives take なら directly, with no だ: {学生|がくせい}なら, しずかなら (not
×{学生|がくせい}だなら). That's the same なら as the ば form of nouns in lesson 12; here it's
used to take up a topic. In casual speech you'll also hear 〜んなら / 〜のなら
({行|い}くんなら); they mean the same.

### Before or after? 〜なら vs 〜たら

With verbs, なら and たら put the two events in opposite orders:

| | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| A なら B | if you're going to do A, (first) do B | {日本|にほん}に{行|い}くなら、{日本語|にほんご}を{勉強|べんきょう}してください。 — If you're going to Japan, study Japanese (before you go). |
| A たら B | when A has happened, B | {日本|にほん}に{行|い}ったら、おんせんに{入|はい}ってください。 — When you get to Japan, try a hot spring. |

なら looks ahead: the advice in B comes before A happens. たら looks back from after A.

## Which conditional? と, ば, たら, なら

You now have all four. They overlap a lot, and native speakers often have a choice, but each
has a home:

| Conditional | Home ground | Can B be a request or plan? | Typical sentence |
|---|---|---|---|
| と | automatic results: machines, nature, habits, directions | no | ボタンをおすと、{出|で}ます。 |
| ば | the condition: "if only…", advice, regret | after states, yes; after actions, rarely | どうすればいいですか。 |
| たら | one-off ifs, "when/once", what happened | yes | {着|つ}いたら、{電話|でんわ}してください。 |
| なら | taking up a topic; advice before A happens | yes | {京都|きょうと}なら、{秋|あき}がいいです。 |

When you're not sure, たら is the safe choice for "if/when", and なら is the one for answering
what someone has just said. The reference sheet "The conditionals" has the full table.

## Even if: 〜ても

The て form + も is "even if", "even though": B happens (or is true) whatever A is.

{雨|あめ}がふっても、{行|い}きます。 — I'll go even if it rains.
{高|たか}くても、{買|か}いたいです。 — I want to buy it even if it's expensive.
しずかでも、ねむれません。 — Even when it's quiet, I can't sleep.
{子|こ}どもでも、{分|わ}かります。 — Even a child can understand it.

| Word | て form | 〜ても |
|---|---|---|
| ふる | ふって | ふっても |
| {高|たか}い | {高|たか}くて | {高|たか}くても (いい → よくても) |
| しずか | しずかで | しずかでも |
| {子|こ}ども | {子|こ}どもで | {子|こ}どもでも |
| {行|い}かない | {行|い}かなくて | {行|い}かなくても (even if you don't go) |

The negative 〜なくても comes back in lesson 15 as 〜なくてもいい (you don't have to).

### いくら〜ても: no matter how much

いくら (how much, from N5) + 〜ても is "no matter how much…", "however much…":

いくら{食|た}べても、{太|ふと}りません。 — However much I eat, I don't put on weight.
いくらさがしても、ねだんが{書|か}いてありません。 — However hard I look, there's no price on it.

### Question word + 〜ても: whatever, whoever, wherever

{何|なに}を{食|た}べても、おいしいです。 — Whatever you eat, it's delicious.
だれに{聞|き}いても、{分|わ}かりませんでした。 — Whoever I asked, nobody knew.
どこへ{行|い}っても、{人|ひと}が{多|おお}いです。 — Wherever you go, there are lots of people.

## Anything, anyone, anywhere: 〜でも

A question word + でも means "any… at all", with a positive verb. Compare N5's
{何|なに}も / だれも / どこにも, which go with a negative.

| + でも (positive) | Meaning | + も (negative), from N5 | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {何|なん}でも | anything, everything | {何|なに}も〜ない | nothing |
| だれでも | anyone, everyone | だれも〜ない | no one |
| どこでも | anywhere, everywhere | どこにも〜ない | nowhere |
| いつでも | any time, always | — | — |

この{店|みせ}には{何|なん}でもあります。 — This shop has everything.
この{図書館|としょかん}は、だれでも{使|つか}えます。 — Anyone can use this library.
「いつがいいですか。」「いつでもいいですよ。」 — "When suits you?" "Any time is fine."

Note the reading: {何|なん}でも, but {何|なに}も.

## Only: しか, だけ and ばかり

### しか〜ない: only (and not enough)

しか always comes with a negative verb, even though it means "only". It stresses that the
amount is small, often too small:

{千円|せんえん}しかありません。 — I've only got 1,000 yen.
この{店|みせ}は、げんきんしか{使|つか}えません。 — This shop only takes cash.
{日本語|にほんご}は{少|すこ}ししか{話|はな}せません。 — I can only speak a little Japanese.

げんきん = cash.

### だけ: only, just (neutral)

だけ is "only, just" without any feeling of shortage, and it goes with positive or negative
verbs:

{千円|せんえん}だけあります。 — I have just 1,000 yen.
「{何|なに}かおさがしですか。」「いいえ、{見|み}るだけです。」 — "Can I help you find something?" "No, I'm just looking."
{今週|こんしゅう}だけ、わりびきがあります。 — There's a discount this week only.

{千円|せんえん}しかありません and {千円|せんえん}だけあります are both true of the same wallet; the
first one complains.

Where they go: しか replaces が and を ({水|みず}しか{飲|の}みません, not ×{水|みず}をしか). だけ usually replaces
them too ({水|みず}だけ{飲|の}みます), though {水|みず}だけを and {水|みず}だけが are also correct.
With other particles, しか goes after the particle: {駅|えき}でしか{買|か}えません (you can only
buy it at the station), {日曜日|にちようび}にしか{来|き}ません. だけ usually goes after the noun:
{駅|えき}だけで{買|か}えます.

### ばかり: nothing but

Noun + ばかり is "nothing but…", "all…", and it usually sounds like a complaint or a worry:

{弟|おとうと}はゲームばかりしています。 — My brother does nothing but play games.
{夜|よる}おそくまでスマホばかり{見|み}ています。 — I'm always on my phone until late at night.
この{店|みせ}は{高|たか}い{物|もの}ばかりです。 — Everything in this shop is expensive.

With a verb, 〜てばかりいる is "does nothing but…":

{休|やす}みの{日|ひ}は、ねてばかりいます。 — On my days off I do nothing but sleep.
{食|た}べてばかりいないで、{少|すこ}し{歩|ある}きましょう。 — Let's stop eating all the time and go for a walk.

Don't confuse it with lesson 10's 〜たばかり (have just done): {食|た}べたばかりです is "I've
just eaten"; {食|た}べてばかりいます is "I do nothing but eat".

| Word | Goes with | Feeling | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| しか | a negative verb | only, not enough | {一人|ひとり}しか{来|き}ませんでした。 |
| だけ | any verb | only, just (neutral) | {一人|ひとり}だけ{来|き}ました。 |
| ばかり | a noun, or 〜てばかりいる | nothing but (often a complaint) | {友|とも}だちとあそんでばかりいます。 |

## Kanji

Seven kanji for the places in this lesson. Most of their words are N5 words: from now on
write them with kanji.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 映 | reflect, project | エイ | — | 9 | {映画|えいが}, {上映|じょうえい} (screening) |
| 画 | picture; plan | ガ, カク | — | 8 | {映画|えいが}, {計画|けいかく} (plan) |
| 館 | large building, hall | カン | — | 16 | {映画館|えいがかん}, {図書館|としょかん}, {大使館|たいしかん}, {旅館|りょかん} |
| 図 | drawing, plan | ズ, ト | — | 7 | {地図|ちず} (map), {図書館|としょかん} (library) |
| 銀 | silver | ギン | — | 14 | {銀行|ぎんこう} (bank), {銀色|ぎんいろ} (silver colour) |
| 売 | sell | バイ | う(る), う(れる) | 7 | {売|う}る, {売|う}れる, {売|う}り{場|ば}, {売店|ばいてん} (kiosk) |
| 特 | special | トク | — | 10 | {特|とく}に, {特別|とくべつ}, {特急|とっきゅう} (limited express) |

Notes:

- 画 has two readings: ガ in {映画|えいが}, カク in {計画|けいかく} (plan, with lesson 11's 計).
- 図 is ズ in {地図|ちず} and ト in {図書館|としょかん}.
- 特 + 急 is read とっきゅう: トク shortens to トッ before a k sound, like 発 in
  {出発|しゅっぱつ}.
- The museum words びじゅつかん and はくぶつかん end in 館 too, but their first kanji aren't on
  the list, so this course writes them in kana.

Memory notes:

- 映 has 日 (the sun) on the left: light thrown on a screen.
- 画 is a field (田) inside a frame: a picture you could hang on a wall.
- 館 has 食 (eat) on the left: a big building where travellers once ate and stayed.
- 図 is a drawing inside a square frame: a plan or a map.
- 銀 has 金 (gold, metal) on the left: the metal next to gold, silver.
- 売 is the right-hand part of 読 (read): a seller calls out what's for sale.
- 特 has 牛 (cow, lesson 16) on the left: a bull kept for a special day.

```trace
映画館図銀売特
```

## Dialogue: where should I go?

Sophia, who is visiting Japan, asks her friend Kenji for advice.

```dialogue
# Recommendations
ソフィア: しゅうまつ、{京都|きょうと}に{行|い}きたいんですが、どこがいいですか。
= I want to go to Kyoto at the weekend. Where's good?
けんじ: {京都|きょうと}なら、{古|ふる}いおてらがたくさんありますよ。{何|なに}を{見|み}ても、きれいです。
= If it's Kyoto, there are lots of old temples. Whatever you see, it's beautiful.
ソフィア: {東京|とうきょう}から{行|い}くなら、{何|なに}で{行|い}けばいいですか。
= If I'm going from Tokyo, how should I get there?
けんじ: しんかんせんが{早|はや}いですよ。でも、{安|やす}いのがよければ、{夜|よる}のバスもあります。
= The Shinkansen is quick. But if you want something cheap, there's a night bus too.
ソフィア: バスは{安|やす}くても、ちょっと…。{長|なが}い{時間|じかん}すわっているのがにがてなんです。
= Even if the bus is cheap, hmm... I'm not good at sitting for a long time.
けんじ: じゃあ、しんかんせんですね。きっぷは{駅|えき}の{売|う}り{場|ば}でも、ネットでも{買|か}えますよ。
= Then it's the Shinkansen. You can buy tickets at the station ticket office or online.
ソフィア: {京都|きょうと}では、{何|なに}を{食|た}べたらいいですか。
= What should I eat in Kyoto?
けんじ: {何|なん}でもおいしいですよ。{特|とく}に、とうふの{料理|りょうり}が{有名|ゆうめい}です。
= Everything's delicious. Tofu dishes are especially famous.
ソフィア: でも、{今|いま}お{金|かね}が{二万円|にまんえん}しかないんです。
= But I've only got 20,000 yen at the moment.
けんじ: {二万円|にまんえん}あれば、だいじょうぶですよ。{学生|がくせい}なら、おてらのわりびきもありますから。
= If you've got 20,000 yen, you'll be fine. If you're a student, there are discounts at the temples too.
```

とうふ = tofu; ネット = the internet; {有名|ゆうめい} = famous (N5). Most of Kenji's answers
start from Sophia's words and use a conditional (なら, ば) to give advice.

## Reading: a cinema notice

> みどり{映画館|えいがかん}　{今月|こんげつ}の{特別|とくべつ}{上映|じょうえい}
>
> 「{夏|なつ}の{海|うみ}」（{英語|えいご}じまく）
>
> {上映|じょうえい}{時間|じかん}：{毎日|まいにち} 10:00 / 14:00 / 19:00（{月曜日|げつようび}は19:00だけ）
>
> {料金|りょうきん}：{大人|おとな} 1,800{円|えん}、{学生|がくせい} 1,500{円|えん}。{水曜日|すいようび}は、だれでも1,200{円|えん}です。
>
> ※{特別|とくべつ}{上映|じょうえい}のチケットは、{上映|じょうえい}の{日|ひ}に{映画館|えいがかん}でしか{買|か}えません。
>
> ※{上映|じょうえい}{中|ちゅう}は、{写真|しゃしん}をとらないでください。{飲|の}み{物|もの}は{売店|ばいてん}で{買|か}えます。

Midori Cinema: this month's special screening. "Summer Sea" (English subtitles). Showings:
every day at 10:00, 14:00 and 19:00 (Mondays 19:00 only). Prices: adults 1,800 yen,
students 1,500 yen. On Wednesdays it's 1,200 yen for everyone. ※ Tickets for the special
screening can only be bought at the cinema on the day of the showing. ※ Please don't take
photos during the film. Drinks are on sale at the kiosk.

{大人|おとな} = adult; {上映中|じょうえいちゅう} = during the showing.

## Say it

```speak
{京都|きょうと}なら、{秋|あき}がいいですよ。
= If it's Kyoto, autumn is good.
それなら、いっしょに{行|い}きましょう。
= In that case, let's go together.
{雨|あめ}がふっても、{行|い}きます。
= I'll go even if it rains.
{見|み}るだけです。
= I'm just looking.
{千円|せんえん}しかありません。
= I've only got 1,000 yen.
いつでもいいですよ。
= Any time is fine.
```

## Common mistakes

- なら after だ: ×{学生|がくせい}だなら. Nouns and な-adjectives take なら directly:
  {学生|がくせい}なら.
- なら out of nowhere. なら answers or picks up something already mentioned; to start a fresh
  "if", use たら.
- なら and たら mixed up with verbs: {日本|にほん}に{行|い}くなら (advice for before you go) vs
  {日本|にほん}に{行|い}ったら (once you're there).
- しか with a positive verb: ×{千円|せんえん}しかあります. It must be negative:
  {千円|せんえん}しかありません.
- ×{水|みず}をしか: しか replaces を and が.
- {何|なに}でも for "anything". It's read {何|なん}でも.
- Mixing up 〜てばかりいる (does nothing but) and 〜たばかり (has just done).

## Key points

- なら: "if it's…", taking up what someone said, often with advice. Noun/な-adj. + なら (no
  だ); plain verb/い-adj. + なら. それなら = in that case.
- 〜なら looks ahead (advice before A); 〜たら looks back (after A).
- 〜ても: even if. いくら〜ても: however much. Question word + 〜ても: whatever, whoever,
  wherever.
- {何|なん}でも, だれでも, どこでも, いつでも: any… at all (positive verbs).
- しか + negative: only (not enough). だけ: only, just (neutral). ばかり: nothing but;
  〜てばかりいる.
- New kanji: 映 画 館 図 銀 売 特.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Must and don't have to; commands
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Living in Japan means rules and paperwork: you must register your address, you have to write
in black ink, you don't need to bring a photo. This lesson builds "must" and "don't have to"
from the conditionals you've just learned, adds advice ("you'd better") and a formal "in case
of", and then looks at
commands: 〜なさい, which parents and tests use, and the blunt **[[imperative]]** ({止|と}まれ, がんばれ),
which you'll mostly see on signs and hear in sports and manga.

The theme is the city office: forms, documents and the rules that come with them.

## Must: 〜なければならない

Japanese has no single verb for "must". It says "if you don't, it won't do": the ば form of
the ない form (lesson 12) + ならない (it won't do) or いけない (it's no good).

{行|い}かない → {行|い}かなければ → {行|い}かなければならない / {行|い}かなければいけない

| Verb | ない form | must (plain) | must (polite) |
|---|---|---|---|
| {書|か}く | {書|か}かない | {書|か}かなければならない | {書|か}かなければなりません |
| {見|み}せる | {見|み}せない | {見|み}せなければいけない | {見|み}せなければいけません |
| する | しない | しなければならない | しなければなりません |
| {来|く}る | {来|こ}ない | {来|こ}なければならない | {来|こ}なければなりません |

ひっこしたら、しやくしょに{行|い}かなければなりません。 — When you move house, you have to go to the city office.
この{用紙|ようし}は、ボールペンで{書|か}かなければいけません。 — You have to fill in this form in ballpoint pen.
{明日|あした}は{早|はや}く{起|お}きなければならない。 — I have to get up early tomorrow.

ならない and いけない are often interchangeable. Roughly, 〜なければならない sounds more formal and
general (laws, rules, writing), and 〜なければいけない is more spoken and personal (what I have
to do today). Both are correct in both places.

A third shape uses the て form of ない: 〜なくてはいけない / 〜なくてはならない ({書|か}かなくては
いけません). It means the same.

Adjectives and nouns work the same way: {写真|しゃしん}は{新|あたら}しくなければなりません (the
photo has to be recent); {名前|なまえ}は{本人|ほんにん}のサインでなければなりません (the name has
to be the person's own signature).

### Casual: 〜なきゃ, 〜なくちゃ

In speech, なければ shortens to なきゃ and なくては to なくちゃ, and the いけない at the end is
usually dropped:

もう{行|い}かなきゃ。 — I've got to go.
しょるいを{出|だ}さなくちゃ。 — I need to hand in the documents.
{明日|あした}{早|はや}く{起|お}きなきゃいけない。 — I have to get up early tomorrow.

You'll also hear 〜ないと (いけない), from lesson 11's と: もう{行|い}かないと (I must go). All of
these are casual: use them with friends and family, and the full forms in polite speech.

## Don't have to: 〜なくてもいい

"Even if you don't, it's fine": the ない form's て form なくて + も (lesson 14's "even if") +
いい. The more formal version ends in かまわない (it doesn't matter), polite かまいません.

{写真|しゃしん}は{持|も}って{来|こ}なくてもいいです。 — You don't have to bring a photo.
はんこがなければ、サインでもかまいません。 — If you don't have a seal, a signature is fine.
{本人|ほんにん}が{来|こ}なくてもかまいません。 — The person concerned doesn't have to come in person.
{今日|きょう}は{来|こ}なくてもいいよ。 — You don't have to come today. (casual)

This is the natural "no" to a "must" question:

「{写真|しゃしん}を{持|も}って{来|こ}なければなりませんか。」「いいえ、{持|も}って{来|こ}なくてもいいです。」 — "Do I have to bring a photo?" "No, you don't have to."

Keep it apart from N5's 〜てはいけない (must not). {書|か}かなくてもいい is "you don't have to
write it"; {書|か}いてはいけない is "you mustn't write it". They're opposites in English too:
"don't have to" is permission not to; "mustn't" is a ban.

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜なければならない / いけない | must | {書|か}かなければなりません。 |
| 〜なくてもいい / かまわない | don't have to | {書|か}かなくてもいいです。 |
| 〜てもいい (N5) | may | {書|か}いてもいいです。 |
| 〜てはいけない (N5) | must not | {書|か}いてはいけません。 |

## Had better: 〜たほうがいい, 〜ないほうがいい

Between "must" and "don't have to" sits advice: "you'd better…", "you should…". Japanese
uses the ほう of N5's comparisons (こっちのほうがいい, this one is better): doing it is the
better side. Write ほう in kana, as in comparisons.

- Do it: **[[た form]]** + ほうがいい. {行|い}く → {行|い}ったほうがいい.
- Don't do it: **[[ない form]]** + ほうがいい. {行|い}かない → {行|い}かないほうがいい. Not the past:
  the negative stays in the plain ない form.

{早|はや}く{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}ったほうがいいですよ。 — You'd better go to the hospital soon.
この{薬|くすり}は、{毎日|まいにち}{飲|の}んだほうがいいです。 — You should take this medicine every day.
{用紙|ようし}は、えんぴつで{書|か}かないほうがいいです。 — You'd better not fill in the form in pencil.
{夜|よる}は、あまり{食|た}べないほうがいいよ。 — Better not to eat much at night. (casual)

The た form here doesn't mean the past: {行|い}ったほうがいい is advice about now or later. It's
the natural answer to lesson 12's どうすればいいですか: 「どうすればいいですか。」「{午前中|ごぜんちゅう}に
{行|い}ったほうがいいですよ。」

### How strong it is

〜たほうがいい is stronger than lesson 13's 〜たらどうですか. 〜たらどうですか offers an idea and
leaves the choice to the listener; 〜たほうがいい says this is the better thing to do, often
with a hint that something bad will happen if you don't.

{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}ったらどうですか。 — Why don't you go to the hospital? (a suggestion)
{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}ったほうがいいですよ。 — You'd better go to the hospital. (advice, firmer)

Because it tells the listener what to do, 〜たほうがいいですよ can sound pushy to a teacher, a
boss or a customer. Soften it with と{思|おも}います (I think) or かもしれません (it might be;
taught in lesson 19):

{先生|せんせい}、{少|すこ}し{休|やす}んだほうがいいと{思|おも}います。 — (to a teacher) I think you should rest a little.
{電話|でんわ}で{聞|き}いたほうがいいかもしれません。 — It might be better to ask by phone.

### With the dictionary form

You'll also hear the dictionary form: {毎日|まいにち}{少|すこ}しずつ{勉強|べんきょう}するほうがいい.
It's less common, and sounds more like a general statement (it's better to study a little
every day) than advice to one person about one thing. For advice, use the た form.

```dialogue
# Before going to the city office
アナ: {明日|あした}しやくしょに{行|い}くんですが、{何時|なんじ}ごろ{行|い}けばいいですか。
= I'm going to the city office tomorrow. What time should I go?
{森|もり}: {朝|あさ}{早|はや}く{行|い}ったほうがいいですよ。{昼|ひる}はこみますから。
= You'd better go early in the morning. It gets crowded at midday.
アナ: パスポートも{持|も}って{行|い}ったほうがいいですか。
= Should I take my passport too?
{森|もり}: ええ、{持|も}って{行|い}ったほうがいいと{思|おも}います。それから、{用紙|ようし}はえんぴつで{書|か}かないほうがいいですよ。
= Yes, I think you should take it. And you'd better not fill in the form in pencil.
アナ: ボールペンで{書|か}くんですね。
= So I write in ballpoint pen.
{森|もり}: そうです。{分|わ}からないことがあったら、まどぐちで{聞|き}いたほうがいいですよ。
= That's right. If there's anything you don't understand, you should ask at the counter.
```

こむ = to get crowded. Notice that Mori softens one piece of advice with と{思|おも}います.

## Need to: 〜ひつようがある

ひつよう is "necessary". Noun + がひつようだ is "N is needed", and the dictionary form +
ひつようがある is "it's necessary to…". It's more formal than 〜なければならない and common on
forms, websites and notices.

てつづきには、パスポートがひつようです。 — You need your passport for the procedure.
{市|し}の{外|そと}にひっこす{場合|ばあい}は、てつづきをするひつようがあります。 — If you move out of the city, you need to do the paperwork.
{今日|きょう}は{写真|しゃしん}を{出|だ}すひつようはありません。 — There's no need to hand in a photo today.

The negative is 〜ひつようはない (no need to), with は, a little like 〜なくてもいい.

## In case of: 〜{場合|ばあい}は

{場合|ばあい} (case, situation) + は is a formal "if", "in the event that", used in instructions,
forms and announcements. It follows a plain verb (dictionary, ない or た form), an
adjective, or a noun + の.

しょるいがない{場合|ばあい}は、まどぐちで{聞|き}いてください。 — If you don't have the documents, ask at the counter.
{本人|ほんにん}が{来|こ}られない{場合|ばあい}は、{家族|かぞく}でもかまいません。 — If the person can't come, a family member is fine.
{住所|じゅうしょ}がかわった{場合|ばあい}は、しやくしょにれんらくしなければなりません。 — If your address changes, you must notify the city office.
{雨|あめ}の{場合|ばあい}は、{中止|ちゅうし}です。 — In case of rain, it's cancelled.

まどぐち = counter (at an office); かわる = to change; {中止|ちゅうし} = cancellation. 〜{場合|ばあい}は
sounds like a notice or an official: in conversation, たら does the same job.

## Commands with 〜なさい

The ます stem + なさい is a command from someone with authority over the listener: parents to
children, teachers to pupils, and the instructions on tests.

{早|はや}くねなさい。 — Go to bed now.
ちゃんと{食|た}べなさい。 — Eat properly.
{正|ただ}しいものをえらびなさい。 — Choose the correct answer.
しゅくだいをしてから、あそびなさい。 — Do your homework before you play.

〜なさい is not rude, but it's firmly from above. Never use it to anyone older than you or above
you; to an equal it sounds bossy. The polite request is still 〜てください. (おやすみなさい,
"good night", is the same なさい, softened by long use.)

## The imperative and 〜な (to recognize)

The imperative is the bare command form: "Stop!", "Run!", "Hang in there!". In everyday
conversation it's very blunt, mostly heard from men to close friends or juniors, and in anger.
But you'll meet it every day on signs, in sports, in emergencies and in manga, so learn to
recognize it. (It isn't one of your conjugation drills.)

| Group | Rule | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | u → e | {止|と}まる → {止|と}まれ (stop), がんばる → がんばれ (hang in there), {急|いそ}ぐ → {急|いそ}げ, {待|ま}つ → {待|ま}て, {行|い}く → {行|い}け |
| 2 | る → ろ | {起|お}きる → {起|お}きろ (get up), にげる → にげろ (run!), {見|み}る → {見|み}ろ |
| 3 | irregular | する → しろ (written: せよ), {来|く}る → こい (come here) |

くれる (give me) → くれ is the blunt "give me / do it for me": {水|みず}をくれ.

Where you'll see and hear it:

- Signs: {止|と}まれ, painted on the road before a crossing. Road signs and warnings are short
  and impersonal, so the imperative isn't rude there.
- Sport: がんばれ! (come on!, go for it!) shouted for a team or a runner.
- Emergencies: にげろ! (run!), {急|いそ}げ! (hurry!).
- Manga, anime and games, where tough characters speak in commands.

### Don't: dictionary form + な

The blunt "don't" (the negative imperative, or prohibitive) is the dictionary form + な:

{入|はい}るな — Keep out. · さわるな — Don't touch. · {走|はし}るな — No running. · わすれるな — Don't forget.

It's even stronger than the imperative, so it lives on warning signs and in shouted warnings.
Polite signs use 〜ないでください or 〜きんし instead: {入|はい}らないでください, {立|た}ち{入|い}りきんし.
Don't mix it up with the soft な at the end of a sentence, as in いいな (that's nice, I wish):
{行|い}くな (don't go) has a dictionary form before it and a falling, sharp voice.

| How strong | Do | Don't |
|---|---|---|
| polite request | {書|か}いてください | {書|か}かないでください |
| from above (parents, tests) | {書|か}きなさい | — |
| blunt (signs, sport, anger) | {書|か}け | {書|か}くな |
| written rules | 〜なければならない, 〜ひつようがある | 〜てはいけない, 〜きんし |

## Kanji

Six kanji for places and paperwork: cities, prefectures, capitals, paper and "correct".

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 市 | city; market | シ | いち | 5 | {市|し}, {京都市|きょうとし}, {市場|いちば} (market) |
| 県 | prefecture | ケン | — | 9 | {県|けん}, {山口県|やまぐちけん} |
| 都 | capital, metropolis | ト, ツ | — | 11 | {東京都|とうきょうと}, {京都|きょうと}, {都合|つごう} (convenience) |
| 京 | capital | キョウ | — | 8 | {東京|とうきょう}, {京都|きょうと} |
| 紙 | paper | シ | かみ (がみ) | 10 | {紙|かみ}, {手紙|てがみ} (letter), {用紙|ようし} (form) |
| 正 | correct; main | セイ, ショウ | ただ(しい) | 5 | {正|ただ}しい, お{正月|しょうがつ} (New Year), {正午|しょうご} (noon) |

Notes:

- Japan has 47 prefectures. Most are 〜{県|けん}; Tokyo is {東京都|とうきょうと} (the metropolis of
  Tokyo), and a few others have their own endings. Addresses start with the biggest unit:
  prefecture, then city, then the district.
- 都 is ツ in {都合|つごう}: {都合|つごう}がいい means "it suits me", {都合|つごう}がわるい "it doesn't
  suit me", a polite way to decline a time.
- {手紙|てがみ} and お{正月|しょうがつ} were kana words in N5 (てがみ, おしょうがつ); write them with
  kanji from now on. かみ becomes がみ in {手紙|てがみ}.
- 正 is ショウ in {正月|しょうがつ} and {正午|しょうご}; セイ comes in words you'll meet later.

Memory notes:

- 市 is a roof with a cloth hanging under it: a market stall. Towns grew around markets.
- 京 is a tall building on a hill: where the emperor lived, the capital.
- 都 has 者 (person, lesson 13) on the left and a "town" part on the right: a place full of
  people.
- 紙: the left-hand part means thread. Paper was first made from plant fibres.
- 正 is 一 (one, a line) over 止 (stop, lesson 8): stop right at the line, exactly correct.
- 県 has 目 (an eye) on a stand: the prefecture keeps an eye on its towns.

```trace
市県都京紙正
```

## Dialogue: at the city office

Ana moved to a new city last week and goes to the city office.

```dialogue
# At the city office
アナ: すみません、{先週|せんしゅう}この{市|し}にひっこして{来|き}たんですが、{何|なに}をしなければなりませんか。
= Excuse me, I moved to this city last week. What do I have to do?
しやくしょの{人|ひと}: {転入|てんにゅう}のてつづきですね。まず、この{用紙|ようし}に{住所|じゅうしょ}と{名前|なまえ}をきにゅうしてください。
= That's the moving-in procedure. First, please fill in your address and name on this form.
アナ: {名前|なまえ}はカタカナで{書|か}かなければいけませんか。
= Do I have to write my name in katakana?
しやくしょの{人|ひと}: ローマ{字|じ}でもかまいません。でも、ふりがなはカタカナで{書|か}いてください。
= The Latin alphabet is fine. But please write the reading in katakana.
アナ: はんこもひつようですか。
= Do I need a seal too?
しやくしょの{人|ひと}: いいえ、はんこはなくてもいいです。サインでだいじょうぶです。
= No, you don't need a seal. A signature is fine.
アナ: よかった。ほかに{何|なに}か{見|み}せなければなりませんか。
= Good. Do I have to show anything else?
しやくしょの{人|ひと}: ざいりゅうカードを{見|み}せてください。{写真|しゃしん}は{出|だ}すひつようはありません。
= Please show me your residence card. There's no need to hand in a photo.
アナ: はい、これです。
= Here you are.
しやくしょの{人|ひと}: ありがとうございます。また{市|し}の{外|そと}にひっこす{場合|ばあい}は、その{前|まえ}にてつづきをしなければなりませんから、{気|き}をつけてください。
= Thank you. If you move out of the city again, you'll have to do the paperwork before you
  go, so please remember that.
```

{転入|てんにゅう} = moving in (lesson 15h2); ローマ{字|じ} = the Latin alphabet (romaji); ざいりゅうカード =
residence card. Notice how the official uses 〜てください and 〜ひつようはありません, while Ana
asks with 〜なければなりませんか.

## Reading: before you come to the city office

A notice on the city's website.

> {市|し}からのおしらせ：しやくしょに{来|く}る{前|まえ}に
>
> ・てつづきには、{本人|ほんにん}が{来|こ}なければなりません。{本人|ほんにん}が{来|こ}られない{場合|ばあい}は、{家族|かぞく}でもかまいませんが、{本人|ほんにん}が{書|か}いた{紙|かみ}を{持|も}って{来|き}てください。
>
> ・{用紙|ようし}は、{黒|くろ}いボールペンで{書|か}いてください。えんぴつで{書|か}いてはいけません。
>
> ・まどぐちは、へいじつは{午前|ごぜん}{八時半|はちじはん}から{午後|ごご}{五時|ごじ}まで、{土曜日|どようび}は{正午|しょうご}までです。{日曜日|にちようび}は{休|やす}みです。
>
> ・しょるいが{足|た}りない{場合|ばあい}は、もう{一度|いちど}{来|こ}なければなりません。{来|く}る{前|まえ}に、{電話|でんわ}で{聞|き}けば{安心|あんしん}です。
>
> ・ちゅうしゃじょうは{小|ちい}さいですから、なるべくバスか{自転車|じてんしゃ}で{来|き}てください。

Notice from the city: before you come to the city office. · The person concerned must come
in person for the procedures. If they can't come, a family member is fine, but bring a paper
written by the person concerned. · Fill in forms with a black ballpoint pen. You mustn't use
pencil. · The counters are open on weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and on Saturdays until
noon. They're closed on Sundays. · If you don't have all the documents, you'll have to come
again. You'll feel more at ease if you ask by phone before you come. · The car park is
small, so please come by bus or bicycle if you can.

へいじつ = weekdays; {足|た}りる = to be enough; なるべく = as far as possible.

## Say it

```speak
{何|なに}をしなければなりませんか。
= What do I have to do?
もう{行|い}かなきゃ。
= I've got to go.
はんこはなくてもいいです。
= You don't need a seal.
{正|ただ}しいものをえらびなさい。
= Choose the correct answer.
がんばれ！
= Go for it!
```

## Pronunciation

Three common words are written かみ. {紙|かみ:2} (paper) and [かみ:2] (hair) both rise and then
fall on the particle: ka-MI-ga. [かみ:1] (god) starts high: KA-mi-ga. Listen for the start:
low is paper or hair, high is a god.

## Common mistakes

- ×{行|い}かないければなりません. Build it from the ない form: {行|い}かない → {行|い}かなければ.
- ×{行|い}かなければなります. The ending is negative: なりません / ならない ("it won't do").
- Answering a "must" question with 〜てはいけません. 「{来|こ}なければなりませんか」「いいえ、
  {来|こ}なくてもいいです」, not {来|き}てはいけません (you mustn't come).
- ×{行|い}かなかったほうがいい. Advice against uses the plain ない form, not the past:
  {行|い}かないほうがいい. Only the positive uses the た form ({行|い}ったほうがいい).
- 〜たほうがいいですよ straight to a teacher or a boss. Soften it: 〜たほうがいいと{思|おも}います.
- 〜なさい to a teacher, a boss or a customer. Use 〜てください.
- Using the imperative in conversation. {待|ま}て for "wait" sounds aggressive; say
  {待|ま}ってください or casual {待|ま}って.
- Confusing {行|い}くな (don't go) with the soft sentence-final な (いいな).

## Key points

- Must: 〜なければならない / 〜なければいけない / 〜なくてはいけない; casual 〜なきゃ, 〜なくちゃ
  (and 〜ないと).
- Don't have to: 〜なくてもいい / 〜なくてもかまわない.
- Had better: た form + ほうがいい ({行|い}ったほうがいい); better not: ない form + ほうがいい
  ({行|い}かないほうがいい, not ×{行|い}かなかった). Firmer than 〜たらどうですか; soften with
  と{思|おも}います to people above you.
- Formal need: 〜ひつようがある / Nがひつようだ; no need: 〜ひつようはない.
- 〜{場合|ばあい}は: in case of (notices, forms).
- 〜なさい: firm command from above (parents, teachers, tests).
- Imperative (recognize): group 1 u → e, group 2 る → ろ, しろ, こい; dictionary form + な = don't.
  Fine on signs and in sport, rude in conversation.
- New kanji: 市 県 都 京 紙 正.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Earthquakes and emergencies
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japan has many earthquakes, most of them small. Schools, offices and towns practise for the
big ones, and the instructions people learn are full of this module's grammar: たら and
〜{場合|ばあい}は for "if this happens", 〜てください and 〜ないでください for what to do, and the
blunt imperative for what someone might shout. This lesson gives you the words to understand
those instructions and the phrases to call for help.

It uses two kanji compounds that are outside N4, because you'll see them on every sign and
screen: {地震|じしん} (earthquake) and {避難|ひなん} (evacuation). 地 is on your list (lesson 1),
but the other kanji in these words aren't, so here they always have furigana, and your word
list writes the words in kana.

## When the ground shakes

When a strong earthquake is coming, phones and TVs may sound an alarm a few seconds before
the shaking starts: the きんきゅうじしんそくほう (earthquake early warning). A few seconds is
enough to get under a table.

The usual advice, in the words you'll hear it in:

| When | What to do | In Japanese |
|---|---|---|
| it starts shaking | protect your head; get under a strong table or desk | ゆれたら、つくえの{下|した}に{入|はい}って、{頭|あたま}をまもってください。 |
| it's shaking | don't run outside; stay away from windows and tall furniture | ゆれている{間|あいだ}は、{外|そと}に{出|で}ないでください。 |
| it stops | open the door so you can get out; put on shoes (there may be glass) | ゆれがおさまったら、ドアを{開|あ}けてください。 |
| you're near the sea | go to high ground at once: a tsunami may follow | {海|うみ}の{近|ちか}くにいる{場合|ばあい}は、すぐ{高|たか}い{所|ところ}ににげてください。 |
| there's a fire | leave the building; never use the lift | {火事|かじ}の{場合|ばあい}は、エレベーターを{使|つか}わないでください。 |

ゆれ = the shaking; おさまる = to die down; まもる = to protect (N5). Notice the grammar: たら for
"when it happens", 〜{場合|ばあい}は for "in the case of", 〜ている{間|あいだ} for "while" (lesson
19 explains {間|あいだ}).

How strong an earthquake feels in a place is given as its しんど (seismic intensity) on the
Japanese scale, from 0 to 7. Levels 5 and 6 are split into "lower" and "upper" (5{弱|じゃく},
5{強|きょう}…), so there are ten steps in all. On the news you'll hear, for example,
「しんど4の{地震|じしん}がありました」 (there was an earthquake of intensity 4).

## Signs and announcements

Look for these on streets, in stations and in buildings:

| Sign | Reading | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {避難|ひなん}{場所|ばしょ} | ひなんばしょ | evacuation area (an open space such as a park or a school ground) |
| {避難所|ひなんじょ} | ひなんじょ | evacuation shelter (a building where people can stay) |
| つなみ{避難|ひなん}ビル | つなみひなんビル | a tall building you can climb to escape a tsunami |
| ひじょうぐち | ひじょうぐち | emergency exit |

The signs for evacuation areas are often green and show a running figure. Find the ones near
your home and work before you need them.

An announcement in an office or a school might sound like this:

> ただいま、{大|おお}きい{地震|じしん}がありました。ゆれがおさまるまで、つくえの{下|した}に{入|はい}って、{頭|あたま}をまもってください。ゆれがおさまったら、{先生|せんせい}の{話|はなし}をよく{聞|き}いて、こうていに{避難|ひなん}してください。エレベーターは{使|つか}わないでください。{走|はし}らないで、{歩|ある}いて{外|そと}に{出|で}てください。

There has just been a large earthquake. Until the shaking stops, get under your desk and
protect your head. When the shaking stops, listen carefully to your teacher and evacuate to
the school ground. Don't use the lifts. Don't run: walk outside.

こうてい = school ground. Japanese schoolchildren learn a short rule for
evacuating, often taught as おかしも: おさない (don't push), かけない (don't run), しゃべらない
(don't talk), もどらない (don't go back). Some schools use はしらない (don't run) instead of
かけない, which makes おはしも. Each line is a ない form, a rule rather than a request.

## Shouted commands

In a real emergency nobody says 〜てください. You may hear the imperative from lesson 15:

| Shout | From | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| にげろ！ | にげる | Run! Get out! |
| {急|いそ}げ！ | {急|いそ}ぐ | Hurry! |
| {出|で}ろ！ | {出|で}る | Get out! |
| {止|と}まれ！ | {止|と}まる | Stop! |
| さわるな！ | さわる + な | Don't touch it! |

They're not rude here: in danger, short is kind.

## Calling for help: 119 and 110

| Number | For | What they ask first |
|---|---|---|
| 119 | fire and ambulance (きゅうきゅうしゃ) | {火事|かじ}ですか、きゅうきゅうですか。 (Fire or ambulance?) |
| 110 | police (けいさつ) | じけんですか、じこですか。 (A crime or an accident?) |

Calls are free from any phone, including public phones. Speak slowly, and give the answers
in this order: what happened, where (the address, or a big building nearby), your name and
phone number. If your Japanese runs out, say {英語|えいご}を{話|はな}せる{人|ひと}はいますか (is there
anyone who speaks English?).

```dialogue
# Calling 119
しょうぼうの{人|ひと}: はい、119ばんです。{火事|かじ}ですか、きゅうきゅうですか。
= Emergency services. Fire or ambulance?
ナオミ: きゅうきゅうです。{友|とも}だちが{急|きゅう}にたおれて、{動|うご}かないんです。
= Ambulance. My friend suddenly collapsed and she isn't moving.
しょうぼうの{人|ひと}: {住所|じゅうしょ}を{教|おし}えてください。
= Please tell me the address.
ナオミ: {山川市|やまかわし}{中町|なかまち}{三|さん}の{五|ご}の{二|に}です。{中町|なかまち}{小学校|しょうがっこう}のとなりのアパートです。
= 3-5-2 Nakamachi, Yamakawa City. It's the apartment block next to Nakamachi Elementary School.
しょうぼうの{人|ひと}: お{友|とも}だちは{話|はな}せますか。
= Can your friend speak?
ナオミ: {話|はな}せません。でも、いきはしています。
= No. But she's breathing.
しょうぼうの{人|ひと}: わかりました。すぐきゅうきゅうしゃが{行|い}きます。あなたのお{名前|なまえ}と{電話|でんわ}ばんごうは？
= Understood. An ambulance is on its way. Your name and phone number?
ナオミ: {森|もり}ナオミです。{電話|でんわ}ばんごうは、090の1234の5678です。
= Naomi Mori. My number is 090-1234-5678.
しょうぼうの{人|ひと}: きゅうきゅうしゃが{着|つ}いたら、{外|そと}に{出|で}て、{場所|ばしょ}を{教|おし}えてください。
= When the ambulance arrives, go outside and show them where to come.
ナオミ: はい、わかりました。
= Yes, OK.
```

しょうぼう = the fire service (which also runs the ambulances); たおれる = to collapse; いきをする
= to breathe. Addresses are read number by number with の between them. Notice the たら at the
end: "once the ambulance arrives, go outside", a sure event followed by a request.

## The emergency kit

Many homes keep a ready-packed bag by the door, the ひじょうもちだしぶくろ (emergency grab bag).
Town guides and websites suggest what to put in it; a typical list:

| Item | Japanese |
|---|---|
| drinking water (often about 3 litres per person per day, for at least three days) | {飲|の}み{水|みず} |
| food that keeps (tins, crackers) | {食|た}べ{物|もの} |
| torch and spare batteries | かいちゅうでんとう、でんち |
| a small radio | ラジオ |
| medicine and plasters | {薬|くすり}、ばんそうこう |
| cash, including coins (cards may not work) | お{金|かね} |
| copies of your passport and residence card | パスポートとざいりゅうカードのコピー |
| a phone charger or a battery pack | じゅうでんき |
| a whistle, to call for help if you're trapped | ふえ |

If you live in Japan, your city's website will have its own list, a map of evacuation areas
and, in many places, an English or "easy Japanese" (やさしい{日本語|にほんご}) version.

## Rules in the module's grammar

Instructions for emergencies use every pattern from lessons 11–15. Read these and say which
pattern each uses:

1. ゆれたら、まず{頭|あたま}をまもってください。 — When it shakes, first protect your head. (たら + request)
2. {海|うみ}の{近|ちか}くで{大|おお}きくゆれた{場合|ばあい}は、すぐ{高|たか}い{所|ところ}に{避難|ひなん}してください。 — If you feel strong shaking near the sea, evacuate to high ground at once. (〜{場合|ばあい}は)
3. ガスのにおいがしたら、{火|ひ}を{使|つか}ってはいけません。 — If you smell gas, you mustn't use fire. (たら + must not)
4. {避難|ひなん}するときは、{電気|でんき}のブレーカーを{切|き}らなければなりません。 — When you evacuate, you have to turn off the electricity at the breaker. (must)
5. {家|いえ}がこわれていなければ、{避難所|ひなんじょ}に{行|い}かなくてもかまいません。 — If your home isn't damaged, you don't have to go to a shelter. (ば + don't have to)
6. このボタンをおすと、ひじょうベルがなります。 — Press this button and the alarm bell rings. (と)

ガス = gas; におい = smell; ブレーカー = circuit breaker; {切|き}る = to cut off, switch off; なる =
to ring (a different なる from "become").

## Key points

- {地震|じしん} and {避難|ひなん} are outside N4: learn to recognize them; your word list has じしん
  and ひなん.
- In an earthquake: protect your head, don't rush outside, open a door when it stops; near
  the sea, go to high ground at once.
- しんど is the Japanese intensity scale, 0 to 7, ten steps in all.
- 119: fire and ambulance (きゅうきゅうしゃ); 110: police. Say what happened, where, and who you
  are.
- Signs: {避難|ひなん}{場所|ばしょ} (evacuation area), {避難所|ひなんじょ} (shelter), ひじょうぐち
  (emergency exit).
- Emergency instructions use たら, 〜{場合|ばあい}は, 〜てください, 〜なければならない, and in shouts
  the imperative (にげろ！).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: At the city office
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 05h2 followed a move into a new flat. This lesson follows the paperwork that comes
after it, at the city office (しやくしょ; in big cities, the ward office, くやくしょ). It's where
lesson 15's grammar lives: 〜なければなりません, 〜なくてもいいです, 〜{場合|ばあい}は and
〜ひつようがあります are on every form and every notice. The facts below are general: rules
change, and each city's website has the details for that city.

## Registering a move

Everyone who lives in Japan, Japanese or not, is registered at the office of the town they
