live in. When you move:

| When | What | Japanese |
|---|---|---|
| before you leave your old town | report that you're moving out | {転出|てんしゅつ}とどけ |
| within 14 days of moving in | register at your new town | {転入|てんにゅう}とどけ |
| moving within the same town | report the new address | てんきょとどけ |

とどけ = a notification, a form you hand in. Moving to another town is two steps: the old town
gives you a paper when you report the move out, and you take it to the new town.

If you're a foreign resident staying for more than a short visit, you'll have a residence
card (ざいりゅうカード) from the immigration office. When you register at the city office, they
write your new address on the back of the card, so you must bring it. Keep it with you: you
may be asked to show it.

Two other things usually happen at the same visit, one line each:

- Health insurance: if you aren't covered through your job, you join the national health
  insurance (こくみんけんこうほけん) at the city office.
- Pension: people aged 20 to 59 who live in Japan generally have to join the national pension
  (こくみん{年金|ねんきん}); the city office can tell you what applies to you.

## Numbered tickets and windows

Big offices work like a bank: you take a ticket with a number from a machine and wait. A
screen and an announcement call the numbers:

> {三十五|さんじゅうご}ばんのかた、{二|に}ばんまどぐちへどうぞ。

Number 35, please go to window 2. (かた = person, polite; まどぐち = counter, service window.)

Useful phrases at the entrance or the information desk (あんない):

| You want to… | Say |
|---|---|
| find the right window | {転入|てんにゅう}のてつづきは、どのまどぐちですか。 |
| check what to bring | {何|なに}を{持|も}って{来|こ}なければなりませんか。 |
| check if you need something | はんこはひつようですか。 |
| ask for a form | {用紙|ようし}をください。 |
| ask for help in English | {英語|えいご}ができる{人|ひと}はいますか。 |
| ask them to slow down | すみません、もう{少|すこ}しゆっくり{話|はな}してください。 |

## Filling in a form

Japanese forms follow a fixed order, and some boxes surprise first-timers.

| Box | What to write | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| しめい / {名前|なまえ} | your name | Family name first. Foreign names: as on your residence card. |
| フリガナ / ふりがな | the reading of your name | In katakana when the box says フリガナ. |
| {生年月日|せいねんがっぴ} | date of birth | Year, month, day: 1998{年|ねん}7{月|がつ}{3日|みっか}. |
| せいべつ | sex | Circle {男|おとこ} or {女|おんな}. |
| {住所|じゅうしょ} | address | 〒 postcode first, then prefecture, city, district, and block numbers. |
| {電話|でんわ}ばんごう | phone number | |
| サイン / はんこ | signature or seal | Many forms now accept a signature. |

Two date systems are in use. Many forms let you choose the Western year (せいれき) or the era
name, and some print the eras for you to circle: しょうわ (1926–1989), へいせい (1989–2019),
れいわ (from 2019). Count era years from 1: 2026 is れいわ8{年|ねん}.

Addresses go from the biggest unit to the smallest, the opposite of English:
{山口県|やまぐちけん}{山川市|やまかわし}{中町|なかまち}3-5-2. The numbers at the end are read
さんのごのに.

Most forms have a thick border round the part you fill in; the rest is for the office. A
note such as {太|ふと}いせんの{中|なか}だけきにゅうしてください (fill in only inside the thick lines)
tells you so. Write in black ballpoint, never pencil, and if you make a mistake, ask whether
to start a new form or cross the mistake out.

## Dialogue: at window 1

```dialogue
# Window 1
しやくしょの{人|ひと}: {二十八|にじゅうはち}ばんのかた、どうぞ。
= Number 28, please.
マリア: はい。{転入|てんにゅう}のてつづきをしたいんですが。
= Hello. I'd like to register that I've moved in.
しやくしょの{人|ひと}: {前|まえ}の{市|し}でもらった{転出|てんしゅつ}しょうめいしょはありますか。
= Do you have the moving-out certificate from your previous city?
マリア: はい、これです。
= Yes, here it is.
しやくしょの{人|ひと}: この{用紙|ようし}の{太|ふと}いせんの{中|なか}をきにゅうしてください。{生年月日|せいねんがっぴ}は、せいれきでもかまいません。
= Please fill in the part of this form inside the thick lines. For your date of birth, the Western year is fine.
マリア: せいべつも{書|か}かなければなりませんか。
= Do I have to fill in the sex box too?
しやくしょの{人|ひと}: はい、おねがいします。それから、ざいりゅうカードを{見|み}せてください。うらに{新|あたら}しい{住所|じゅうしょ}を{書|か}きますから。
= Yes, please. And please show me your residence card. We'll write your new address on the back.
マリア: けんこうほけんのてつづきも、ここでできますか。
= Can I do the health insurance procedure here too?
しやくしょの{人|ひと}: ほけんは{三|さん}ばんのまどぐちです。こちらが{終|お}わったら、そちらに{行|い}ってください。
= Insurance is window 3. When you've finished here, please go there.
マリア: わかりました。ありがとうございます。
= OK. Thank you.
```

しょうめいしょ = certificate; うら = the back (of a card or sheet).

## Key points

- Register a move-in within 14 days ({転入|てんにゅう}とどけ); report a move-out before you leave
  ({転出|てんしゅつ}とどけ). Bring your residence card if you have one.
- Health insurance and the national pension are often arranged at the same visit.
- Take a numbered ticket and wait for 〜ばんのかた、〜ばんまどぐちへどうぞ.
- Forms: family name first, フリガナ in katakana, {生年月日|せいねんがっぴ} as year–month–day (era
  or Western year), addresses from the biggest unit down, black ballpoint, thick-bordered
  part only.
- Useful questions: 〜はどのまどぐちですか, {何|なに}を{持|も}って{来|こ}なければなりませんか,
  〜はひつようですか.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Looks like: 〜そう
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This module is about saying how sure you are. Up to now most of your sentences have stated
facts: この{料理|りょうり}はおいしいです, {雨|あめ}がふっています. Real conversation is full of
softer statements: it *looks* tasty, *I hear* it'll rain, it *seems* someone was here, it
*should* arrive by six, it *might* be in the lost-property office. Japanese marks each of
these with its own ending. Endings like these, which show what a statement is based on, are
called **[[evidential]]** endings, and choosing the right one is a big part of sounding natural.

The module goes from what you can see to what you can only guess:

| Lesson | Pattern | Based on |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | おいしそう, ふりそう | what something looks like right now |
| 17 | ふるそうです, 〜って | what you heard or read |
| 18 | ようだ, みたい, らしい | clues you noticed, or something you read |
| 19 | はずだ, かもしれない | reasoning, and how sure you are |
| 20 | 〜か{知|し}っていますか | questions inside sentences |

This lesson starts with 〜そう, "looks (like it will)". The theme is food and cooking, where
it gets used all the time: おいしそう! is what everyone says when the dish arrives.

## Adjectives: it looks…

Take an い-adjective, drop the final い and add そう:

| Adjective | 〜そう | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| おいしい | おいしそう | looks delicious |
| からい | からそう | looks spicy |
| すっぱい | すっぱそう | looks sour |
| {高|たか}い | {高|たか}そう | looks expensive |
| やわらかい | やわらかそう | looks soft, tender |
| いい | よさそう | looks good |
| ない | なさそう | there seems to be none |

いい is irregular, as always: it becomes よ- and adds さ, so よさそう. ない does the same:
なさそう. Learn these two as words; they're very common. この{店|みせ}はよさそうですね (this
restaurant looks good), もう{時間|じかん}がなさそうです (it looks like there's no time left).

For a な-adjective, add そう to the word itself:

| Adjective | 〜そう | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {元気|げんき} | {元気|げんき}そう | looks well |
| ひま | ひまそう | looks free, not busy |
| {親切|しんせつ} | {親切|しんせつ}そう | looks kind |
| じょうぶ | じょうぶそう | looks sturdy |

{見|み}てください。このケーキ、おいしそうですね。 — Look. This cake looks delicious, doesn't it?
このカレーはちょっとからそうです。 — This curry looks a bit spicy.
おばあさんは{元気|げんき}そうでした。 — Grandma looked well.

〜そう is a guess from appearance: you haven't tasted the curry yet. Once you have, say
what you know: からいです.

## Verbs: it looks like it's going to…

With a verb, add そう to the ます stem (the form before ます):

| Verb | ます form | 〜そう | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| ふる | ふります | ふりそう | looks like it'll rain/snow |
| こげる | こげます | こげそう | looks like it's going to burn |
| {足|た}りる | {足|た}ります | {足|た}りそう | looks like there'll be enough |
| {終|お}わる | {終|お}わります | {終|お}わりそう | looks like it'll finish |
| なく | なきます | なきそう | looks about to cry |

With a verb, 〜そう means "it looks as if this is about to happen" or "from the look of it,
this will happen". It's a prediction from what you can see now:

{空|そら}が{暗|くら}いですね。{雨|あめ}がふりそうです。 — The sky is dark. It looks like rain.
フライパンがあついから、{肉|にく}がこげそう！ — The pan's very hot: the meat's going to burn!
この{仕事|しごと}は{早|はや}く{終|お}わりそうです。 — It looks like this job will be finished early.

{今|いま}にも (at any moment) makes it more urgent: {今|いま}にも{雨|あめ}がふりそうです (it could
start raining any second). {子|こ}どもは{今|いま}にもなきそうな{顔|かお}をしていました: the child looked
ready to burst into tears.

## Before nouns and verbs: そうな, そうに

〜そう behaves like a な-adjective, so it changes the same way:

- Before a noun: そうな. おいしそうなケーキ (a delicious-looking cake), {高|たか}そうなレストラン
  (an expensive-looking restaurant), {雨|あめ}がふりそうな{空|そら} (a sky that looks like rain).
- Before a verb: そうに. おいしそうに{食|た}べる (eat with obvious enjoyment, "eat
  deliciously"), {楽|たの}しそうに{話|はな}す (talk happily).
- At the end: そうだ / そうです, past そうだった / そうでした.

{弟|おとうと}はおいしそうにラーメンを{食|た}べています。 — My little brother is eating his ramen
with obvious enjoyment.
{父|ちち}はいそがしそうでした。 — Dad looked busy.

〜そう (and そうに + verb) is how you describe other people's feelings from the outside. You can't
look inside someone, so you can't say ゆきさんはうれしいです as a plain fact (lesson 20 of N5
made the same point about 〜たい). ゆきさんはうれしそうです (Yuki looks happy) is natural.

## Negatives

There are two ways to say "doesn't look…", and they mean slightly different things.

| Pattern | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| adjective + なさそう | おいしくなさそう | looks not tasty, looks bad |
| 〜そうじゃない | おいしそうじゃない | doesn't look tasty |
| verb + そうにない / そうもない | ふりそうにない | doesn't look like it will rain |

For い-adjectives, make the ない form and change ない to なさそう: おいしくない →
おいしくなさそう, からくない → からくなさそう. For な-adjectives: ひまじゃない → ひまじゃなさそう.
This is the negative you'll hear most for adjectives. おいしそうじゃない (it doesn't look
tasty) is correct too.

For verbs, the usual negative is 〜そうにない or 〜そうもない: {雨|あめ}はやみそうにありません
(the rain doesn't look like stopping). Learn to recognize these; you'll see them in writing
and hear them in forecasts. Casually you'll also hear ふらなさそう.

## What そう can't do

Two limits keep 〜そう from being used everywhere.

Not with nouns: 〜そう doesn't attach to a noun: there's no ×{学生|がくせい}そう. For "looks
like a student" you need みたい or よう (lesson 18).

Not for what you can plainly see: 〜そう is a guess, so it's odd with words that describe
how something looks at a glance. If a dress is obviously red, it isn't "red-looking": it's
{赤|あか}い. A view in front of you is きれい, not きれいそう. Compare:

- このりんごはおいしそうです。 — natural: you're guessing the taste from the look.
- このりんごは{赤|あか}そうです。 — odd: you can see that it's red.

One trap: かわいそう isn't "looks cute". It's its own word, "poor thing, pitiful":
かわいそうな{犬|いぬ} (the poor dog). For "looks cute", just say かわいい.

## Food and taste words

| Japanese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {肉|にく}, {牛肉|ぎゅうにく}, ぶたにく | meat, beef, pork |
| {魚|さかな} | fish |
| {野菜|やさい}, くだもの | vegetables, fruit |
| しお, さとう, しょうゆ, あぶら | salt, sugar, soy sauce, oil |
| {味|あじ} | taste, flavour |
| すっぱい | sour |
| うすい / こい | weak (thin) / strong (rich) in taste |
| かたい / やわらかい | hard, tough / soft, tender |
| やく, にる, まぜる | grill or bake, simmer, mix |
| こげる | burn (of food) |
| {足|た}りる | be enough |
| のこす | leave (food uneaten) |
| なべ, ざいりょう | pot, ingredients |

{味|あじ} combines with うすい and こい: この{味|あじ}はちょっとうすいですね (this is a bit bland),
{味|あじ}がこい (strongly seasoned). うすい also means thin (paper, a jacket) and こい also means
dark or strong (colour, coffee). やく covers any cooking with direct heat: grilling fish,
frying an egg in a pan, baking bread. にる is simmering in liquid, as in a stew.

## Kanji

Eight kanji for food. Several of them let you write N5 words with kanji now: {料理|りょうり}
(cooking, a dish) and {意味|いみ} (meaning; 意 is from lesson 5). ぎゅうにゅう (milk) stays in kana,
because its second kanji isn't on the list.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 料 | materials, fee | リョウ | — | 10 | {料理|りょうり}, {料金|りょうきん} (charge, fee) |
| 理 | reason, logic | リ | — | 11 | {料理|りょうり} |
| 味 | taste | ミ | あじ | 8 | {味|あじ}, {意味|いみ}, {味見|あじみ} (tasting) |
| 肉 | meat | ニク | — | 6 | {肉|にく}, {牛肉|ぎゅうにく} |
| 魚 | fish | ギョ | さかな, うお | 11 | {魚|さかな}, {金魚|きんぎょ} (goldfish), {魚屋|さかなや} (fishmonger) |
| 牛 | cow | ギュウ | うし | 4 | {牛|うし}, {牛肉|ぎゅうにく} |
| 野 | field | ヤ | の | 11 | {野菜|やさい} |
| 菜 | vegetable, greens | サイ | な | 11 | {野菜|やさい}, {菜|な}の{花|はな} (rape blossoms) |

Memory notes:

- 料 has grains of rice on the left (a cross with four dots) and a ladle on the right:
  measuring out the ingredients. 理 has a jewel on the left and a village on the right. Put
  together, {料理|りょうり} is "handling the materials well", which is what cooking is.
- 味 is a mouth (口) on the left and a tree-like shape on the right: the mouth tasting the
  fruit.
- 肉 looks like a cut of meat with the lines of the grain inside a frame.
- 魚 is a picture: the head at the top, the scaly body in the middle (田), and the four
  dots at the bottom were once the tail fins.
- 牛 is 午 (noon, from N5) with the top stroke poking through: the horn that sticks up.
- 野 is a village (the shape on the left, a field 田 above earth 土) with a shape beside it:
  the fields beyond the village. 菜 has grass on top, like 花, over a hand picking from a tree
  (木): picking greens.

{牛肉|ぎゅうにく} uses the on'yomi ギュウ, but the animal alone is {牛|うし}. The same split
happens with many animals: the animal has a native word, the meat a Sino-Japanese one.

```trace
料理味肉魚牛野菜
```

## Dialogue: cooking for friends

Haruto is cooking dinner; his friend Mio has come early to help. They're friends, so it's
casual.

```dialogue
# Cooking for friends
みお: わあ、いいにおい！それ、{何|なに}？
= Wow, that smells good! What is it?
はると: {肉|にく}じゃが。{牛肉|ぎゅうにく}と{野菜|やさい}をしょうゆとさとうでにてるんだ。
= Nikujaga. I'm simmering beef and vegetables in soy sauce and sugar.
みお: おいしそう！じゃがいもも、もうやわらかそうだね。
= Looks delicious! The potatoes look soft already.
はると: うん。ちょっと{味見|あじみ}してくれない？{味|あじ}、うすくない？
= Yeah. Can you taste it for me? Is it too bland?
みお: …うーん、ちょうどいいよ。でも、じゃがいもがこげそう！
= …Mm, it's just right. But the potatoes look like they're going to burn!
はると: あ、ほんとうだ！{火|ひ}を{小|ちい}さくしよう。
= Oh, you're right! I'll turn the heat down.
みお: {魚|さかな}もあるの？ごはん、{足|た}りそう？
= Is there fish too? Does it look like there'll be enough rice?
はると: {魚|さかな}はこれからやく。ごはんは…ちょっと{足|た}りなさそうだね。
= I'm about to grill the fish. The rice… doesn't look like it'll be enough.
みお: じゃ、わたし、コンビニでおにぎりを{買|か}ってくるよ。
= OK, I'll go and buy some rice balls at the convenience store.
はると: ありがとう。{足|た}りなかったら、こまるからね。
= Thanks. It'd be a problem if there wasn't enough.
```

{肉|にく}じゃが is a home-style stew of meat and potatoes (じゃがいも = potato). におい (smell)
is a lesson 18 word. {火|ひ} is the flame on the stove (火 from N5); {火|ひ}を{小|ちい}さくする
is "turn the heat down". {足|た}りなさそう is "doesn't look like enough" (the ない form
{足|た}りない → {足|た}りなさそう). {買|か}ってくる is "go and buy (and come back)"; 〜てくる gets its own
lesson in module 5.

## Pronunciation

- そう has a long vowel: so-o. Don't shorten it to "so"; そ alone isn't a word here.
- The いい → よさそう change catches everyone: "yo-sa-so-o". Say it a few times with
  なさそう: よさそう、なさそう、よさそう.
- Pitch: {雨|あめ:1} (rain) falls after the first mora; [あめ:0] (sweets) is flat. Both appear
  in food talk, so listen to the pitch: {雨|あめ:1}がふりそう.

```speak
おいしそう！
= Looks delicious!
{雨|あめ}がふりそうですね。
= It looks like rain, doesn't it?
このお{店|みせ}、よさそうですね。
= This place looks good.
もう{時間|じかん}がなさそうです。
= It looks like there's no time left.
{肉|にく}がこげそう！
= The meat's going to burn!
{楽|たの}しそうに{話|はな}していますね。
= They're chatting happily, aren't they?
```

## Common mistakes

- いいそう and ないそう. They're よさそう and なさそう. (いいそうです exists, but it's lesson 17's
  hearsay: "I hear it's good".)
- Keeping the い: ×おいしいそう. With "looks", the い goes: おいしそう. (おいしいそう is, again,
  hearsay.)
- Adding そう to a noun: ×{学生|がくせい}そう. Use みたい (lesson 18).
- Using そう for what you can plainly see: ×{赤|あか}そう, ×きれいそう for a view in front of you.
- Thinking かわいそう means "looks cute". It means "poor thing".
- Forgetting な before a noun: ×おいしそうケーキ. It's おいしそうなケーキ.
- Stating someone else's feelings flatly: ×{母|はは}はさびしいです. Say {母|はは}はさびしそうです
  (Mum looks lonely; さびしい = lonely).

## Key points

- い-adjective − い + そう: おいしそう. な-adjective + そう: {元気|げんき}そう. いい → よさそう,
  ない → なさそう.
- ます stem + そう: ふりそう (looks like it'll rain), こげそう (it's going to burn). {今|いま}にも
  adds "any moment".
- そう is a な-adjective: そうなケーキ, そうに{食|た}べる, そうです, そうでした.
- Negatives: おいしくなさそう / おいしそうじゃない; verbs ふりそうにない / ふりそうもない.
- Not with nouns, not for what you can plainly see. かわいそう = poor thing.
- New kanji: 料 理 味 肉 魚 牛 野 菜.

〜そう works like any な-adjective, so it doesn't get a drill of its own; the adjective and
verb drills you already have practise the stems it's built on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: I hear that: hearsay そうだ and 〜って
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 16 〜そう meant "looks": you saw the dark sky and said {雨|あめ}がふりそうです. This
lesson is about information you got from somewhere else: the forecast, the news, a friend.
"I hear it's going to rain tomorrow", "Kenta says he can't come", "a shop called…".
Passing on what you heard without claiming it as your own knowledge is called **[[hearsay]]**,
and Japanese marks it clearly: if the forecast told you, you say so.

The theme is news, weather forecasts and the seasons, the topics people pass on to each
other every day.

## I hear that: plain form + そうだ

Put そうだ (polite そうです) after a full plain-form sentence:

| Before そうだ | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| verb | {雨|あめ}がふるそうです | I hear it'll rain |
| verb, past | {雨|あめ}がふったそうです | I hear it rained |
| verb, negative | {雨|あめ}はふらないそうです | I hear it won't rain |
| い-adjective | {寒|さむ}いそうです | I hear it's cold |
| い-adjective, past | {寒|さむ}かったそうです | I hear it was cold |
| な-adjective | しずかだそうです | I hear it's quiet |
| noun | {雨|あめ}だそうです | I hear it'll be rainy |
| noun, past | {台風|たいふう}だったそうです | I hear there was a typhoon |

Everything before そうだ is in the plain form you learned in N5, with だ kept after
な-adjectives and nouns. The tense and the negative go inside, before そうだ, never on it:
"I heard it rained" is ふったそうです, not ×ふるそうでした. そうだ itself doesn't change, and it
can't be made negative: for "I haven't heard that", say そうは{聞|き}いていません.

{明日|あした}は{雨|あめ}がふるそうです。 — I hear it's going to rain tomorrow.
{山|やま}の{上|うえ}はもうゆきだそうです。 — Apparently there's already snow up in the mountains.
あの{店|みせ}のラーメンはとてもおいしいそうです。 — I hear the ramen at that place is really good.
{田中|たなか}さんは{先週|せんしゅう}{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}ったそうです。 — I hear Mr Tanaka went to hospital
last week.

## Two kinds of そう

The two そう look almost the same, so compare them side by side:

| | Lesson 16: looks like | Lesson 17: I hear |
|---|---|---|
| Based on | what you see now | what someone told you |
| い-adjective | おいしそう (drop い) | おいしいそう (keep い) |
| いい | よさそう | いいそう |
| な-adjective | しずかそう | しずかだそう |
| Verb | ふりそう (ます stem) | ふるそう (plain form) |
| Noun | — (use みたい) | {雨|あめ}だそう |
| Before a noun | おいしそうなケーキ | — (not used) |
| Past | ふりそうでした (it looked like rain) | ふったそうです (I hear it rained) |

The quick test: if a full plain form comes before そう (おいしい, ふる, しずかだ), it's
hearsay. If the word is cut short (おいし, ふり, しずか), it's "looks like".

このケーキ、おいしそうですね。 — This cake looks delicious.
このケーキ、おいしいそうですよ。 — I hear this cake is delicious.

## According to: 〜によると

To say where the information came from, start the sentence with 〜によると:

てんきよほうによると、{明日|あした}は{寒|さむ}くなるそうです。 — According to the forecast, it'll get
cold tomorrow.
ニュースによると、{台風|たいふう}が{来|く}るそうです。 — According to the news, a typhoon is coming.
{母|はは}の{話|はなし}によると、むかしこのあたりは{田|た}んぼだったそうです。 — According to my
mother, this area used to be rice fields.

〜によると goes with a hearsay ending (そうだ here, らしい in lesson 18): the start names the
source and the end marks the sentence as something you were told. You'll sometimes hear a
plain statement after 〜によると in conversation, but finishing with そうだ is the standard
pattern, and it's the one to use.

## He said: 〜と{言|い}っていた, 〜と{聞|き}いた

To pass on what a particular person said, use a **[[quotation]]** with と: 〜と{言|い}っていました
(casual 〜って{言|い}ってた).
The ている form presents it as a message you're passing on, not just a past event.

けんたさんは{明日|あした}{来|こ}られないと{言|い}っていました。 — Kenta said he can't come tomorrow.
{先生|せんせい}は{試験|しけん}はやさしいと{言|い}っていましたよ。 — The teacher said the exam would be easy.

The quoted part is in the plain form, and it's turned round to fit the speaker: Kenta said
"I can't come" ({来|こ}られません), you report {来|こ}られないと{言|い}っていました. {言|い}いました is
fine for a single moment in a story ("then he said…"), but for passing on a message,
{言|い}っていました is the natural choice.

〜と{聞|き}きました is "I heard (that)":

ゆかさんがけっこんすると{聞|き}きました。 — I heard that Yuka is getting married.

## Casual: 〜って

In casual speech, って replaces と in quotes, and often the verb {言|い}う disappears:

{明日|あした}、{雨|あめ}だって。 — They say it'll rain tomorrow.
けんた、{来|こ}られないって。 — Kenta says he can't come.
{先生|せんせい}が、{試験|しけん}はやさしいって{言|い}ってたよ。 — The teacher said the exam's easy.

って at the end of a sentence like this is casual hearsay: friends and family only. Said as a
question, with rising pitch, it asks what someone said: {何|なん}だって？ (What did he say?)

って also marks a topic you're asking about or commenting on, a casual "this thing called…":

{夕立|ゆうだち}って{何|なん}ですか。 — What's a "yuudachi"?
{日本|にほん}の{夏|なつ}って、{暑|あつ}いね。 — Japanese summers are so hot, aren't they?

## Called: 〜という + noun

To name something the listener may not know, use 〜という + noun: "a … called X".

「みどり」というレストランを{知|し}っていますか。 — Do you know a restaurant called Midori?
{夕立|ゆうだち}ということばを{聞|き}いたことがありますか。 — Have you heard the word "yuudachi"?

In casual speech という becomes っていう: 「みどり」っていう{店|みせ}, "a place called Midori".

〜ということ turns a whole sentence into a noun, "the fact that…":

{来週|らいしゅう}{台風|たいふう}が{来|く}るということを、ニュースで{知|し}りました。 — I learned from the news
that a typhoon is coming next week.

In news and announcements, 〜ということです at the end is a formal "it is reported that":
{電車|でんしゃ}は{一時間|いちじかん}ぐらいおくれるということです (trains are reported to be running
about an hour late; おくれる = be late, lesson 19).

## Weather words

| Japanese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| てんきよほう | weather forecast |
| きおん | temperature (of the air) |
| 〜{度|ど} | degrees (度 is taught in lesson 19) |
| {上|あ}がる / {下|さ}がる | go up / go down |
| {風|かぜ}, {空気|くうき} | wind, air |
| ふく | blow (of wind) |
| はれる, くもる | clear up, cloud over |
| やむ | stop (of rain or snow) |
| ひえる | get cold, chill |
| {大雨|おおあめ}, かみなり, {夕立|ゆうだち} | heavy rain, thunder, summer evening shower |
| まつり | festival |
| うわさ | rumour |
| つたえる | pass on (a message) |

きおんが{上|あ}がる and きおんが{下|さ}がる are the usual phrases for temperature. {風|かぜ}がふく is
"the wind blows". {雨|あめ}がやむ is "the rain stops"; やむ is for weather and noises, while a bus
that stops is とまる. {夕立|ゆうだち} is the sudden heavy shower of a summer afternoon or evening,
usually over in less than an hour.

## Kanji

Eight kanji for the seasons and weather. N5 wrote the seasons in kana; from now on they're
{春|はる}, {夏|なつ}, {秋|あき}, {冬|ふゆ}, and {夏休|なつやす}み gets its kanji too.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 春 | spring | シュン | はる | 9 | {春|はる}, {春休|はるやす}み |
| 夏 | summer | カ | なつ | 10 | {夏|なつ}, {夏休|なつやす}み |
| 秋 | autumn | シュウ | あき | 9 | {秋|あき} |
| 冬 | winter | トウ | ふゆ | 5 | {冬|ふゆ}, {冬休|ふゆやす}み |
| 暑 | hot (weather) | ショ | あつ(い) | 12 | {暑|あつ}い |
| 寒 | cold | カン | さむ(い) | 12 | {寒|さむ}い |
| 風 | wind, style | フウ | かぜ | 9 | {風|かぜ}, {台風|たいふう} |
| 空 | sky, empty | クウ | そら, あ(く), から | 8 | {空|そら}, {空気|くうき}, {青空|あおぞら} |

The four together make {春夏秋冬|しゅんかしゅうとう}, "the four seasons", a set phrase. {台風|たいふう}
(typhoon) is the N5 word with its kanji (台 is from lesson 8).

{暑|あつ}い is for hot weather and hot rooms: {夏|なつ}は{暑|あつ}い. Hot things you touch use a
different kanji that isn't on the list, so write them in kana: あついお{茶|ちゃ}. In the same
way {寒|さむ}い is cold air and weather, while cold things you touch are つめたい.

空 has three readings to know: {空|そら} (sky); クウ in {空気|くうき} (air) and くうこう (airport,
written in kana because its second kanji isn't on the list); and {空|あ}く, "become empty or
free": {明日|あした}の{午後|ごご}は{空|あ}いています (I'm free tomorrow afternoon).

Memory notes:

- 春 has the sun (日) at the bottom, under three lines of new growth: spring sunshine.
- 夏 has a head (the top part) above slow, dragging feet: moving
  slowly in the heat. The same dragging feet are at the top of 冬.
- 冬 is those feet with two drops of ice below.
- 秋 is a rice plant on the left and fire (火) on the right: harvest, and burning the stubble.
- 暑 has the sun (日) on top, beating down. 寒 has a roof on top and two drops of ice at the
  bottom: a cold house in winter.
- 風 is a frame with an insect inside: the wind blowing round it. 空 is a roof with a hole
  over 工 (work, lesson 28): the empty space above.

```trace
春夏秋冬暑寒風空
```

## Reading: the weather report

> {今日|きょう}の{天気|てんき}です。{台風|たいふう}{十二|じゅうに}ごうが{南|みなみ}から{近|ちか}づいています。
> てんきよほうによると、{明日|あした}の{午後|ごご}から{風|かぜ}が{強|つよ}くなって、{夜|よる}は{大雨|おおあめ}になるそうです。
> かみなりもなるということです。{電車|でんしゃ}がとまるかもしれないので、{明日|あした}の{夜|よる}は
> {早|はや}く{家|いえ}に{帰|かえ}ってください。{台風|たいふう}は{明後日|あさって}の{朝|あさ}には{東|ひがし}へ{行|い}って、
> {空|そら}ははれるそうです。でも、そのあときおんが{下|さ}がって、{急|きゅう}に{秋|あき}らしくなるそうです。
> {夏|なつ}の{服|ふく}は、そろそろしまいましょう。

{近|ちか}づく = come closer; {十二|じゅうに}ごう = number 12 (typhoons are numbered through each
year); なる = sound, rumble (of thunder); 〜かもしれない = may (lesson 19); 〜ので = because
(lesson 26); {急|きゅう}に = suddenly; {秋|あき}らしい = autumn-like (lesson 18); しまう = put away.

Today's weather. Typhoon no. 12 is approaching from the south. According to the forecast,
from tomorrow afternoon the wind will get stronger, and at night there'll be heavy rain.
Thunder is also reported. The trains may stop, so please go home early tomorrow evening.
By the morning of the day after tomorrow the typhoon will have moved east and the sky will
clear, they say. After that, though, the temperature will drop and it'll suddenly feel like
autumn. Time to start putting the summer clothes away.

Notice how the report moves between sources: てんきよほうによると…そうです for the forecast,
〜ということです for a news item, and plain 〜てください when the announcer speaks for themself.

## Dialogue: did you hear?

Two colleagues talk at lunch. あおい speaks politely to her senior, {森|もり}さん.

```dialogue
# Did you hear?
あおい: {森|もり}さん、{明日|あした}{台風|たいふう}が{来|く}るそうですね。
= Mr Mori, I hear a typhoon's coming tomorrow.
もり: ええ。ニュースによると、{夜|よる}から{風|かぜ}がかなり{強|つよ}くなるそうですよ。
= Yes. According to the news, the wind's going to get quite strong from the evening.
あおい: じゃあ、{明日|あした}のまつりはどうなるんでしょう。
= So what's going to happen with tomorrow's festival?
もり: さっき{山田|やまだ}さんが、まつりは{来週|らいしゅう}になったと{言|い}っていました。
= Just now Yamada-san said the festival has been moved to next week.
あおい: そうですか。ざんねんですね。{夏|なつ}のまつり、{楽|たの}しみにしていたんです。
= Oh, really. What a shame. I was looking forward to the summer festival.
もり: {来週|らいしゅう}はいい{天気|てんき}だそうですから、だいじょうぶですよ。
= They say the weather will be good next week, so it'll be fine.
あおい: よかった。あ、「ほたる」というお{店|みせ}、{知|し}っていますか。まつりの{日|ひ}に{行|い}きたくて。
= Good. Oh, do you know a place called Hotaru? I'd like to go there on the festival day.
もり: ああ、{駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くの。かきごおりがおいしいそうですよ。
= Ah, the one near the station. I hear their shaved ice is good.
```

かなり = quite; {楽|たの}しみにする = look forward to; かきごおり = shaved ice with syrup.

## Pronunciation

- {風|かぜ:0} (wind) and かぜ (a cold) sound the same, both flat: context decides.
  {風|かぜ}が{強|つよ}い is the wind; かぜをひく is catching a cold.
- In casual hearsay the final って often rises slightly when it's a question (…って？) and
  falls when it's a report (…って。).

```speak
{明日|あした}は{雨|あめ}がふるそうです。
= I hear it's going to rain tomorrow.
てんきよほうによると、{寒|さむ}くなるそうです。
= According to the forecast, it's going to get cold.
けんたさんは{来|こ}られないと{言|い}っていました。
= Kenta said he can't come.
{明日|あした}、{雨|あめ}だって。
= They say it'll rain tomorrow.
「みどり」というお{店|みせ}を{知|し}っていますか。
= Do you know a place called Midori?
```

## Common mistakes

- Dropping い in hearsay: ×おいしそうです for "I hear it's tasty". That's "looks tasty"; hearsay
  is おいしいそうです.
- Forgetting だ after nouns and な-adjectives: ×{雨|あめ}そうです, ×しずかそうです (that's "looks
  quiet"). Hearsay: {雨|あめ}だそうです, しずかだそうです.
- Putting the tense on そうだ: ×ふるそうでした. The past goes inside: ふったそうです.
- Using そうだ before a noun: ×ふるそうな{日|ひ}. Hearsay そうだ only ends a sentence.
- Using 〜って with your boss. It's casual; say 〜と{言|い}っていました.
- Mixing up {暑|あつ}い (weather) and あつい for hot things, and {寒|さむ}い (air) with つめたい (to the
  touch).

## Key points

- Plain form + そうだ: I hear. ふるそうだ, ふったそうだ, {寒|さむ}いそうだ, しずかだそうだ,
  {雨|あめ}だそうだ. The tense goes inside; そうだ doesn't change.
- Looks like (16) vs I hear (17): おいしそう / おいしいそう, よさそう / いいそう, ふりそう / ふるそう.
- 〜によると names the source; 〜と{言|い}っていました passes on a message; 〜と{聞|き}きました: I heard.
- Casual 〜って: quotes (…って), topics (〜って{何|なん}？) and っていう (called).
- 〜という + noun: "called"; 〜ということ: "the fact that"; 〜ということです: it is reported.
- New kanji: 春 夏 秋 冬 暑 寒 風 空.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Seems: 〜ようだ, 〜みたい, 〜らしい
topics: Seems (ようだ / みたい / らしい)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You come home and the light is on, there's a smell of curry and a pair of shoes in the
entrance. You didn't see anyone arrive, but you can work it out: someone seems to be home.
Drawing a conclusion from clues like these is **[[inference]]**, and Japanese has three common
endings for it: ようだ, its casual twin みたい, and らしい. The same words also say what
something is like ("like a dream", "like a child"), and the lesson adds the phrases for the
senses: 〜に{見|み}える (looks) and 〜がする (there's a smell, a sound, a taste).

The theme is the senses, colours, light and impressions, with a small mystery at the end.

## It seems: ようだ

ようだ (polite ようです) says "it seems, judging from what I can see, hear, smell or feel".
It joins the plain form the way a noun does, so な-adjectives keep な and nouns take の:

| Before ようだ | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| verb | だれか{来|き}たようです | someone seems to have come |
| い-adjective | {外|そと}は{寒|さむ}いようです | it seems cold outside |
| な-adjective + な | へやはしずかなようです | the room seems quiet |
| noun + の | かぜのようです | it seems to be a cold |

The tense and the negative go before ようだ: {来|こ}なかったようです (it seems they didn't
come), {寒|さむ}くないようです (it doesn't seem cold).

{電気|でんき}がついていますね。だれかいるようです。 — The light's on. Someone seems to be in.
{外|そと}は{雨|あめ}がふっているようです。かさを{持|も}っていきましょう。 — It seems to be raining
outside. Let's take umbrellas.
のどがいたいです。かぜのようです。 — My throat hurts. I think I've caught a cold.

ようだ is your own judgment from evidence you have now. It sounds careful and a little
formal: good for polite speech and for writing.

## Casual: みたい

みたい (みたいだ, polite みたいです) means the same as ようだ and is what you'll hear most in
conversation. It joins a little differently: after な-adjectives and nouns, nothing comes
between.

| Before みたい | Example |
|---|---|
| verb | だれか{来|き}たみたい |
| い-adjective | {外|そと}は{寒|さむ}いみたい |
| な-adjective | へやはしずかみたい |
| noun | かぜみたい |

だれかいるみたいだね。 — Seems like someone's in.
この{店|みせ}、{今日|きょう}は{休|やす}みみたい。 — This shop seems to be closed today.

ようだ: {休|やす}みのようです. みたい: {休|やす}みみたいです. The double み in {休|やす}みみたい is
right: {休|やす}み + みたい.

## From what I've heard: らしい

らしい also means "it seems", but its evidence is usually something you heard or read rather
than something you observed yourself. It's close to lesson 17's そうだ, with more distance:
"apparently, from what people say".

| Before らしい | Example |
|---|---|
| verb | {電車|でんしゃ}がおくれているらしい |
| い-adjective | あの{店|みせ}は{高|たか}いらしい |
| な-adjective | その{町|まち}はしずからしい |
| noun | はんにんはあの{男|おとこ}らしい |

ニュースによると、{台風|たいふう}が{来|く}るらしいです。 — According to the news, it seems a typhoon is
coming.
{山田|やまだ}さんは{会社|かいしゃ}をやめるらしいですよ。 — Apparently Mr Yamada is leaving the company.

Compare: {雨|あめ}がふっているようです (you can hear it on the window) and
{雨|あめ}がふっているらしいです (a friend messaged that it's raining where she is).

### Noun + らしい: typical of

After a noun, らしい can also mean "just like a real …, typical of …". This らしい is an
い-adjective of its own, so it goes before nouns and has a negative:

{今日|きょう}は{春|はる}らしい{天気|てんき}ですね。 — It's real spring weather today.
{子|こ}どもらしいえですね。 — That's such a childlike picture.
そんなことを{言|い}うのは、あなたらしくないですよ。 — It's not like you to say that.

Context tells the two apart: あの{人|ひと}は{先生|せんせい}らしい is "apparently he's a teacher",
while {先生|せんせい}らしい{話|はな}し{方|かた} is "a very teacher-like way of speaking".

## Like: のような, みたいな, のように

ようだ and みたい also compare one thing with another: "like".

- Before a noun: N のような / N みたいな + noun. ゆめのような{話|はなし} (a story like a dream).
- Before a verb or an adjective: N のように / N みたいに. {子|こ}どものようにわらう (laugh like a
  child).
- For examples: {東京|とうきょう}のような{大|おお}きい{町|まち} (big cities such as Tokyo).

まるで (just like, as if) often comes first to make the comparison stronger: まるでゆめのようです
(it's just like a dream). In this sense まるで goes with ようだ or みたい; it can't make a comparison on its own.

{空|そら}がまるで{海|うみ}のように{青|あお}いです。 — The sky is as blue as the sea.
{弟|おとうと}はねこみたいに{一日中|いちにちじゅう}ねています。 — My brother sleeps all day, like a cat.

## The senses: 〜に{見|み}える, 〜がする

〜に{見|み}える is "looks (to me)". After an い-adjective use く; after a な-adjective or a noun
use に:

| Pattern | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| い-adjective く + {見|み}える | わかく{見|み}える | looks young |
| な-adjective に + {見|み}える | {元気|げんき}に{見|み}える | looks well |
| noun に + {見|み}える | {学生|がくせい}に{見|み}える | looks like a student |

{父|ちち}は{六十|ろくじゅう}さいですが、わかく{見|み}えます。 — My father is sixty, but he looks young.

For the other senses, Japanese says "there is a smell, a sound, a taste": 〜がする.

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| いいにおいがする | there's a nice smell |
| {音|おと}がする | there's a sound, I can hear something |
| {声|こえ}がする | I can hear a voice |
| へんな{味|あじ}がする | it tastes strange |
| 〜{気|き}がする | I have a feeling (that) |

{台所|だいどころ}からいいにおいがします。 — There's a lovely smell coming from the kitchen.
にかいで{音|おと}がしました。 — There was a noise upstairs.
{何|なに}かわすれている{気|き}がします。 — I have a feeling I've forgotten something.

{気|き}がする is also a soft way to give an opinion: その{答|こた}えはちがう{気|き}がします (I have a
feeling that answer is wrong).

## Five ways to say "seems"

| Ending | Evidence | Joins | Style |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜そう (16) | how it looks right now | おいしそう, ふりそう | any |
| 〜そうだ (17) | someone told you | おいしいそうだ, ふるそうだ | any |
| 〜ようだ | your own clues | おいしいようだ, しずかなようだ, {雨|あめ}のようだ | polite, written |
| 〜みたい | your own clues | おいしいみたい, しずかみたい, {雨|あめ}みたい | casual |
| 〜らしい | what you heard or read | おいしいらしい, しずからしい, {雨|あめ}らしい | any |

A quick way to choose: if you're looking at it right now, そう. If someone told you or you read it,
and you can name the source, そうだ. If you worked it out from clues, ようだ or みたい. If you picked it up second-hand and
aren't sure, らしい. The reference sheet for this module has the full table.

## Colour, light and impression words

| Japanese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| きいろい | yellow |
| {真|ま}っ{赤|か} | bright red |
| {真|ま}っ{青|さお} | deep blue; pale (of a face) |
| {青空|あおぞら} | blue sky |
| {光|ひかり}, {光|ひか}る | light, shine |
| かげ | shadow |
| におい | smell |
| {足音|あしおと} | footsteps |
| はっきり | clearly |
| なんだか | somehow, for some reason |
| ふしぎ, へん | mysterious; strange, odd |
| あやしい | suspicious |
| こわい | scary |
| ようす, {見|み}た{目|め} | the state of things; looks |
| {気持|きも}ち | feeling, mood |

{真|ま}っ{青|さお} is also a face gone pale with fear or shock: {顔|かお}が{真|ま}っ{青|さお}になった. {真|ま}っ{赤|か}
is a face red with anger or embarrassment.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 色 | colour | ショク, シキ | いろ | 6 | {色|いろ}, {茶色|ちゃいろ} |
| 青 | blue, green | セイ | あお(い) | 8 | {青|あお}い, {青空|あおぞら}, {真|ま}っ{青|さお} |
| 赤 | red | セキ | あか(い) | 7 | {赤|あか}い, {赤|あか}ちゃん, {真|ま}っ{赤|か} |
| 黒 | black | コク | くろ(い) | 11 | {黒|くろ}い |
| 光 | light | コウ | ひかり, ひか(る) | 6 | {光|ひかり}, {光|ひか}る |
| 暗 | dark | アン | くら(い) | 13 | {暗|くら}い |
| 明 | bright, clear | メイ, ミョウ | あか(るい) | 8 | {明|あか}るい, {明日|あした}, {明後日|あさって} |

Several N5 words now get their kanji: {色|いろ}, {青|あお}い, {赤|あか}い, {黒|くろ}い, {明|あか}るい,
{暗|くら}い, {赤|あか}ちゃん, and {茶色|ちゃいろ} (茶 is from lesson 27).

Special readings to learn as whole words:

- {明日|あした} (tomorrow) and {明後日|あさって} (the day after tomorrow): the kanji give the meaning,
  not the sound. In formal speech {明日|あす} and {明日|みょうにち} are heard too.
- {真|ま}っ{赤|か} (bright red) and {真|ま}っ{青|さお} (deep blue): {真|ま} (true, really; lesson 3) +
  a small っ + a special reading of the colour.

{青|あお}い covers blue and some greens: a green traffic light is {青|あお}, and so are fresh young
leaves. みどり is the colour green as such.

Memory notes:

- 明 is the sun (日) and the moon (月) side by side: as bright as it gets.
- 暗 is the sun (日) next to 音 (sound, lesson 3): the sun has gone and only sounds are left.
- 光 is a fire burning above a person's legs: someone carrying a torch.
- 赤 is earth (土) on top of flames: the ground glowing red.
- 青 is a young plant above the moon (月): a fresh, clear colour.
- 黒 is a field (田) over fire: blackened by smoke.
- 色 is one person bending over another: the colour that comes into someone's face.

```trace
色青赤黒光暗明
```

## Reading: the light upstairs

> {土曜日|どようび}の{夜|よる}、{私|わたし}は{一人|ひとり}で{家|いえ}にいた。{父|ちち}と{母|はは}は{旅行|りょこう}に{行|い}っていて、
> {兄|あに}はアルバイトだった。{十時|じゅうじ}ごろ、にかいで{音|おと}がした。だれかが{歩|ある}いているような
> {音|おと}だった。{家|いえ}にはだれもいないと{思|おも}っていたので、{私|わたし}はこわくなった。かいだんの
> {上|うえ}を{見|み}ると、{兄|あに}のへやのドアの{下|した}から{光|ひかり}が{見|み}えた。{電気|でんき}がついているようだ。
> それに、なんだかカレーのようなにおいもする。「どろぼう…？」{顔|かお}が{真|ま}っ{青|さお}になった。
> でも、どろぼうがカレーを{食|た}べるだろうか。{私|わたし}はそっとドアを{開|あ}けた。{中|なか}では、{兄|あに}が
> カレーのカップラーメンを{食|た}べていた。「あれ、アルバイトは？」「{店|みせ}が{早|はや}くしまったんだ。
> でも、かぎをわすれちゃって」{兄|あに}は{少|すこ}し{前|まえ}に{帰|かえ}ってきて、まどから{入|はい}ったそうだ。
> ほんとうにふしぎな{兄|あに}だ。

かいだん = stairs; どろぼう = burglar; そっと = quietly; カップラーメン = cup noodles;
わすれちゃって = わすれてしまって (lesson 9); {帰|かえ}ってくる = come back home; 〜ので = because
(lesson 26); 〜だろうか = would (a burglar eat curry)?

On Saturday night I was home alone. Mum and Dad were away on a trip, and my brother was at
his part-time job. Around ten I heard a noise upstairs. It sounded like someone walking. I'd
thought nobody else was home, so I got scared. When I looked up the stairs, I could see light
under the door of my brother's room. The light seemed to be on. On top of that, there was
somehow a smell like curry. "A burglar…?" My face went pale. But would a burglar eat curry? I
opened the door quietly. Inside, my brother was eating curry-flavoured cup noodles. "Huh,
what about your job?" "The shop closed early. But I forgot my key." He'd come home a little
earlier and climbed in through the window, he said. My brother really is a mystery.

Notice the endings: ような{音|おと} and カレーのようなにおい are the narrator's impressions; {電気|でんき}が
ついているようだ is her inference; {入|はい}ったそうだ is what her brother told her.

## Pronunciation

- におい is three morae, に・お・い, with the pitch falling after the second: [におい:2].
- みたい: the い is short and light; don't make it "mitaai".
- {真|ま}っ{赤|か}: the small っ is a full beat of silence, ma-k-ka.

```speak
だれかいるようです。
= Someone seems to be in.
{今日|きょう}は{休|やす}みみたい。
= Seems it's closed today.
{山田|やまだ}さんは{会社|かいしゃ}をやめるらしいですよ。
= Apparently Mr Yamada is leaving the company.
まるでゆめのようです。
= It's just like a dream.
いいにおいがしますね。
= Something smells good.
{何|なに}かわすれている{気|き}がします。
= I have a feeling I've forgotten something.
```

## Common mistakes

- Joining みたい like ようだ: ×しずかなみたい, ×かぜのみたい. It's しずかみたい, かぜみたい.
- Joining ようだ like みたい: ×かぜようです. It's かぜのようです.
- Using らしい for something you're looking at: if the curry is in front of you, it's
  おいしそう, not おいしいらしい.
- まるで with a plain statement: ×まるでゆめです. Add ようだ or みたい: まるでゆめのようです.
- 〜がする with a sight: ×{光|ひかり}がする. Light is {見|み}える; がする is for smells, sounds,
  voices, tastes and feelings.
- Forgetting く with an い-adjective before {見|み}える: ×わかいに{見|み}える. It's わかく{見|み}える.

## Key points

- ようだ: it seems (from clues). Verb/い-adj + ようだ; な-adj + なようだ; noun + のようだ.
- みたい: the casual ようだ. な-adj and nouns join directly: しずかみたい, かぜみたい.
- らしい: apparently (from what you heard). Noun + らしい also means "typical of": {春|はる}らしい.
- のような / みたいな + noun, のように / みたいに + verb: like. まるで makes it stronger.
- 〜く/に{見|み}える: looks. におい・{音|おと}・{声|こえ}・{味|あじ}・{気|き}がする.
- New kanji: 色 青 赤 黒 光 暗 明, and the special readings {明日|あした}, {明後日|あさって}, {真|ま}っ{赤|か},
  {真|ま}っ{青|さお}.

lessons.title: Should be, might be: はずだ, かもしれない
topics: How sure you are (はず / かもしれない)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 16–18 were about evidence: what you see, what you heard, what the clues suggest.
This lesson is about how sure you are. "The bus should be here at ten", "it might be late",
"she can't possibly have forgotten". Japanese has a whole scale of these endings, from almost
certain to only just possible, and you'll need them whenever a plan depends on someone else
being on time.

The lesson also covers the time words that go with plans: 〜までに (by) and 〜まで (until),
〜{間|あいだ} and 〜{間|あいだ}に (during), and {以上|いじょう}, {以下|いか}, {以外|いがい}. The theme is
schedules, deadlines, being on time, arriving and waiting.

## Should be: はずだ

はずだ (polite はずです) means "it should be so; I have good reason to expect it". The reason
is something you know: a timetable, a promise, how things normally work.

はず is a noun, so it joins the plain form the way a noun does:

| Before はず | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| verb | バスは{十時|じゅうじ}に{来|く}るはずです | the bus should come at ten |
| verb, past | もう{着|つ}いたはずです | they should have arrived by now |
| verb, negative | {今日|きょう}は{来|こ}ないはずです | they're not expected today |
| い-adjective | あの{店|みせ}は{安|やす}いはずです | that shop should be cheap |
| な-adjective + な | {日曜日|にちようび}はひまなはずです | he should be free on Sunday |
| noun + の | {休|やす}みのはずです | it should be a holiday |

{山田|やまだ}さんは{九時|くじ}の{電車|でんしゃ}に{乗|の}ったから、もうすぐ{着|つ}くはずです。 — Mr Yamada took
the nine o'clock train, so he should arrive soon.
ミーティングは{三時|さんじ}からのはずです。 — The meeting should start at three.
かぎはかばんに{入|い}れたはずなんですが…。 — I'm sure I put the key in my bag, but…

The last example shows はず about your own actions: you remember doing it, so it "should" be
true, but the key isn't there.

### Can't possibly: はずがない

はずがない (polite はずがありません) is the strong opposite: "there's no way that…".

{田中|たなか}さんは{今|いま}アメリカにいるから、ここにいるはずがありません。 — Ms Tanaka is in America
now, so she can't possibly be here.
あのまじめな{人|ひと}が、ちこくするはずがない。 — Someone as conscientious as him can't be late.

Compare the two negatives:

| | Meaning | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| {来|こ}ないはずです | they're not expected to come | an expectation |
| {来|く}るはずがありません | there's no way they'll come | a strong denial |

### Was supposed to: はずだった

はずだった (polite はずでした) is an expectation that didn't come true: "was supposed to".

バスは{八時|はちじ}に{着|つ}くはずでしたが、じゅうたいで{三十分|さんじゅっぷん}おくれました。 — The bus was
supposed to arrive at eight, but it was thirty minutes late because of a traffic jam.
{今日|きょう}は{休|やす}みのはずだったんですが、{急|きゅう}に{仕事|しごと}が{入|はい}りました。 — Today was supposed
to be my day off, but some work came up suddenly.

## Might: かもしれない

かもしれない (polite かもしれません, casual かも) means "may, might, perhaps". It joins plain
forms, and な-adjectives and nouns drop だ:

| Before かもしれない | Example |
|---|---|
| verb | {雨|あめ}がふるかもしれない |
| verb, past | もう{出|で}たかもしれない |
| い-adjective | ちょっと{高|たか}いかもしれない |
| な-adjective | ひまかもしれない |
| noun | {休|やす}みかもしれない |

{電車|でんしゃ}がおくれるかもしれないから、{早|はや}く{出|で}ましょう。 — The train might be late, so let's
leave early.
あの{人|ひと}は{先生|せんせい}かもしれません。 — That person might be a teacher.
{間|ま}に{合|あ}わないかも。 — We might not make it. (casual)

## A scale of certainty

From most sure to least sure, roughly, with the strong negative はずがない at the end:

| Pattern | Meaning | Based on |
|---|---|---|
| きっと〜 (でしょう / と{思|おも}います) | surely, I'm sure | your own conviction |
| 〜はずだ | should | facts you know |
| 〜でしょう / 〜だろう | probably | your judgment |
| たぶん〜 (でしょう) | probably | your judgment |
| 〜かもしれない | might, maybe | a possibility |
| 〜はずがない | can't possibly | facts you know |

きっと and たぶん are adverbs at the start; the sentence still needs an ending:
きっと{来|く}るでしょう (he'll surely come), たぶん{来|く}ると{思|おも}います (I think he'll probably
come). The difference between きっと and はず is the reason: きっと is how sure you feel, はず is
what the facts say. You can hope with きっと (きっとだいじょうぶですよ, I'm sure it'll be fine),
but not with はず.

{一時|いちじ}に{家|いえ}を{出|で}たから、もう{着|つ}いたはずです。 — He left home at one, so he should be
there by now. (facts)
{二人|ふたり}ともよくがんばったから、きっとうまくいきますよ。 — You've both worked hard, so I'm sure
it'll go well. (feeling)

## By and until: までに, まで

まで (N5) is "until": the action goes on up to that time. までに is "by": a deadline for
something that happens once, at some point before then.

| | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| まで | {五時|ごじ}まで{待|ま}ちます | I'll wait until five (waiting the whole time) |
| までに | {五時|ごじ}までに{帰|かえ}ります | I'll be back by five (coming back once, at any time up to five) |

The verb decides: actions that last ({待|ま}つ, いる, {働|はたら}く, ねる, {勉強|べんきょう}する) take まで;
one-time actions ({出|だ}す, {着|つ}く, {終|お}わる, {帰|かえ}る, きめる…) take までに.

レポートは{金曜日|きんようび}までに{出|だ}してください。 — Please hand in the report by Friday.
{金曜日|きんようび}まで{東京|とうきょう}にいます。 — I'll be in Tokyo until Friday.
しめきりは{明日|あした}の{正午|しょうご}です。それまでに{送|おく}ってください。 — The deadline is noon tomorrow.
Please send it by then.

## During: {間|あいだ}, {間|あいだ}に

〜{間|あいだ} is "while, during: the whole time". 〜{間|あいだ}に is "while, during: at some point
within that time". It follows a noun with の, or a verb, usually in the 〜ている form:

| | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {間|あいだ} | {夏休|なつやす}みの{間|あいだ}、ずっと{国|くに}に{帰|かえ}っていました | I was back home for the whole summer holiday |
| {間|あいだ}に | {夏休|なつやす}みの{間|あいだ}に、{一度|いちど}{国|くに}に{帰|かえ}りました | I went home once during the summer holiday |

It's the same idea as まで and までに: {間|あいだ} goes with something that lasts the whole time,
{間|あいだ}に with something that happens once inside it.

{電車|でんしゃ}を{待|ま}っている{間|あいだ}、{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んでいました。 — I read a book the whole time I was
waiting for the train.
{母|はは}がねている{間|あいだ}に、ケーキを{作|つく}りました。 — While Mum was asleep, I made a cake.

N5 taught あいだ as "between": {銀行|ぎんこう}とスーパーの{間|あいだ}. It's the same word, now with its
kanji.

## Or more, or less, except: {以上|いじょう}, {以下|いか}, {以外|いがい}

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {以上|いじょう} | … or more, at least | {十八|じゅうはっ}さい{以上|いじょう}: 18 and over (18 included) |
| {以下|いか} | … or less, at most | {千円|せんえん}{以下|いか}: 1,000 yen or less |
| {以外|いがい} | except, other than | {日曜日|にちようび}{以外|いがい}: every day except Sunday |

{以上|いじょう} and {以下|いか} include the number itself, unlike English "over" and "under". For
"under 18, not including 18", Japanese uses a different word, みまん (its kanji aren't on the
list).

この{店|みせ}は{日曜日|にちようび}{以外|いがい}、{毎日|まいにち}{開|あ}いています。 — This shop is open every day
except Sunday.
{五人|ごにん}{以上|いじょう}のグループは、よやくしてください。 — Groups of five or more, please book.
{以上|いじょう}です。 — That's all. (the end of an announcement or a presentation)

## Time and schedule words

| Japanese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {時間|じかん}, {一週間|いっしゅうかん} | time, hours; one week |
| {間|ま}に{合|あ}う | be in time |
| おくれる, ちこく | be late, be delayed; lateness |
| しめきり | deadline |
| {着|つ}く, とうちゃく | arrive; arrival |
| {待|ま}ち{合|あ}わせ | arrangement to meet |
| じゅうたい | traffic jam |
| なかなか | (not) easily; quite |
| たしか | if I remember rightly |
| {電気代|でんきだい} | electricity bill |
| {時代|じだい} | era, days, times |
| {代|か}わりに | instead |
| {人間|にんげん} | human being |

{間|ま}に{合|あ}う takes に for what you're in time for: {電車|でんしゃ}に{間|ま}に{合|あ}う (catch the train),
しめきりに{間|ま}に{合|あ}う (make the deadline). おくれる is being late or delayed: {電車|でんしゃ}が
{十分|じゅっぷん}おくれた. ちこく is a person arriving late for school or work: {学校|がっこう}にちこくする.
なかなか with a negative is "just won't": バスがなかなか{来|こ}ない (the bus just isn't coming).
{時代|じだい} is an era, or a period of your life: {学生|がくせい}{時代|じだい} (one's student days).

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 間 | interval, between | カン, ケン | あいだ, ま | 12 | {時間|じかん}, {一週間|いっしゅうかん}, {間|あいだ}, {間|ま}に{合|あ}う, {人間|にんげん} |
| 度 | degree, time | ド | — | 9 | {一度|いちど}, {何度|なんど}, {今度|こんど}, {三十度|さんじゅうど} |
| 以 | by means of, from | イ | — | 5 | {以上|いじょう}, {以下|いか}, {以外|いがい} |
| 去 | leave, past | キョ, コ | さ(る) | 5 | {去年|きょねん} |
| 代 | replace, era, fee | ダイ, タイ | か(わる) | 5 | {時代|じだい}, {電気代|でんきだい}, {代|か}わりに |
| 着 | arrive, wear | チャク | つ(く), き(る) | 12 | {着|つ}く, {着|き}る, {着物|きもの} |

N5 words that now get their kanji: {去年|きょねん}, {一度|いちど}, {何度|なんど}, {今度|こんど} and {着|き}る (to
wear). {着物|きもの} (kimono) uses 物 from lesson 25.

Three readings of 間 to keep apart: カン in {時間|じかん} and {一週間|いっしゅうかん}, あいだ for "between,
during", and ま in {間|ま}に{合|あ}う. 度 counts times ({一度|いちど}, once) and measures degrees
({三十度|さんじゅうど}, thirty degrees). 着 is つく "arrive" and also きる "wear": {駅|えき}に{着|つ}く,
コートを{着|き}る.

Memory notes:

- 間 is the sun (日) seen through a gate (門, lesson 8): the gap between the doors.
- 度 is a roof with a hand (the bottom part) measuring underneath: measuring degrees, counting
  times.
- 以 is a plough next to a person: getting something done by means of a tool.
- 去 is earth (土) above a small closed shape: someone walking away and leaving the place
  behind. {去年|きょねん} is the year that has gone.
- 代 is a person (the left side, as in 休) next to a post: one person standing in for another.
  A {時代|じだい} is one age taking over from the last.
- 着 has a sheep on top (wool) over an eye (目): clothes you put on. Arriving uses the same
  kanji: you and your things have reached their place.

```trace
間度以去代着
```

## Dialogue: waiting at the station

Three friends are meeting to see a film. Two of them are waiting. Casual speech.

```dialogue
# Waiting at the station
さき: ゆうと、{来|こ}ないね。もう{十時十分|じゅうじじゅっぷん}だよ。
= Yuto's not here. It's already ten past ten.
りく: {十時|じゅうじ}にここで{待|ま}ち{合|あ}わせのはずだよね。
= We were supposed to meet here at ten, right?
さき: うん。{九時半|くじはん}の{電車|でんしゃ}に{乗|の}るって{言|い}ってたから、もう{着|つ}いているはずなんだけど。
= Yeah. He said he'd get the 9:30 train, so he should be here by now.
りく: {電車|でんしゃ}がおくれているのかもしれないね。…あ、じこで{十五分|じゅうごふん}ぐらいおくれてるみたい。
= Maybe the train's running late. …Oh, it looks like it's about fifteen minutes late because of an accident.
さき: じゃあ、{映画|えいが}に{間|ま}に{合|あ}わないかも。{十時半|じゅうじはん}からだよね。
= Then we might miss the film. It starts at half past ten, doesn't it?
りく: {映画館|えいがかん}まで{歩|ある}いて{十分|じゅっぷん}だから、ぎりぎり{間|ま}に{合|あ}うはずだよ。
= It's a ten-minute walk to the cinema, so we should just about make it.
さき: ゆうとを{待|ま}っている{間|あいだ}に、チケットを{買|か}っておこうか。
= Shall we buy the tickets while we're waiting for Yuto?
りく: いいね。あ、ゆうとからメッセージ。「ごめん！あと{五分|ごふん}で{着|つ}く！」
= Good idea. Oh, a message from Yuto: "Sorry! I'll be there in five minutes!"
さき: よかった。{十時二十分|じゅうじにじゅっぷん}までに{来|く}れば、だいじょうぶだね。
= Phew. If he's here by twenty past, we'll be fine.
```

じこ = accident; ぎりぎり = only just; {買|か}っておく = buy in advance (lesson 5); {来|く}れば = if he
comes (lesson 12).

## Pronunciation

- はず is two short morae, ha-zu, and flat: [はず:0].
- {間|ま}に{合|あ}う is four morae, ma-ni-a-u; say the a and the u separately.
- かもしれない is often cut to かも in casual speech: {間|ま}に{合|あ}わないかも.

```speak
バスはもうすぐ{来|く}るはずです。
= The bus should come soon.
{雨|あめ}がふるかもしれません。
= It might rain.
そんなはずはありません。
= That can't be right.
{五時|ごじ}までに{出|だ}してください。
= Please hand it in by five.
{間|ま}に{合|あ}いました！
= I made it!
```

そんなはずはない (polite そんなはずはありません) is a set phrase: "that can't be (true)".

## Common mistakes

- まで for a deadline: ×{金曜日|きんようび}まで{出|だ}してください. Handing in happens once: までに.
- ×{休|やす}みはずです. A noun needs の: {休|やす}みのはずです; a な-adjective needs な: ひまなはずです.
- ×{雨|あめ}だかもしれない. かもしれない drops だ: {雨|あめ}かもしれない.
- はず for a hope: ×{明日|あした}はいい{天気|てんき}のはずです when you have no reason to think so. Use
  きっと or たぶん: たぶんいい{天気|てんき}でしょう.
- Mixing up ないはず and はずがない: {来|こ}ないはず is "not expected to come"; {来|く}るはずがない
  is "there's no way he'll come".
- {間|あいだ} for a single event: ×{夏休|なつやす}みの{間|あいだ}、{一度|いちど}{帰|かえ}りました. One event inside a
  period takes {間|あいだ}に.
- Forgetting that {以上|いじょう} and {以下|いか} include the number: {十八|じゅうはっ}さい{以上|いじょう} includes
  18-year-olds.

## Key points

- はずだ: should (from facts). Verb/い-adj + はず, な-adj + なはず, noun + のはず.
- はずがない: no way. はずだった: was supposed to (but didn't).
- かもしれない (casual かも): might. な-adjectives and nouns drop だ.
- Certainty: きっと, はず > でしょう, たぶん > かもしれない; はずがない is "certainly not".
- まで (until) vs までに (by); {間|あいだ} (the whole time) vs {間|あいだ}に (at some point during).
- {以上|いじょう} and {以下|いか} include the number; {以外|いがい} is "except".
- New kanji: 間 度 以 去 代 着.
