lessons.title: Do you know when…? Indirect questions
topics: Something and someone (なにか / だれか)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

"What time does it start?" is a question. "Do you know what time it starts?" and "I don't
know what time it starts" have the same question inside a bigger sentence. That inner
question is an **[[indirect question]]**, and you need it constantly when you ask for
information: at a tourist office, at the lost-property counter, on the phone. It's also how
you say you're not sure: "I wonder if…".

This lesson covers question word + か inside a sentence, 〜かどうか (whether), 〜かな (I
wonder), {何|なに}か, だれか, どこか, いつか (something, someone…), the 〜のは〜だ pattern for
putting the important part last, and 〜のをわすれる (forget to do). It closes the module: after
lessons 16–19 on what you've seen, heard and guessed, this is how you ask about what you
don't know.

## Questions inside sentences

Take a question in the plain form, keep its question word and its か, and put it before a
verb such as {知|し}る, {分|わ}かる, {教|おし}える, {聞|き}く, しらべる or おぼえている:

| Direct question | Inside a sentence | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {映画|えいが}は{何時|なんじ}に{始|はじ}まりますか。 | {映画|えいが}が{何時|なんじ}に{始|はじ}まるか{知|し}っていますか。 | Do you know what time the film starts? |
| だれが{来|き}ましたか。 | だれが{来|き}たか{分|わ}かりません。 | I don't know who came. |
| どこでのりかえますか。 | どこでのりかえるか{教|おし}えてください。 | Please tell me where to change trains. |
| あの{人|ひと}はだれですか。 | あの{人|ひと}がだれか{知|し}っていますか。 | Do you know who that is? |

What changes:

- The inner question is in the plain form: {始|はじ}まるか, not {始|はじ}まりますか. Politeness goes
  on the main verb at the end.
- だ drops before か: だれか, {何曜日|なんようび}か. (You'll hear だれだか in casual speech, but the
  standard form has no だ.)
- A subject inside the question usually takes が: だれが{来|き}たか, {映画|えいが}が{何時|なんじ}に….
  ({映画|えいが}は at the very start, as the topic of the whole sentence, is fine too.)
- を or が after the か is usually left out: {何時|なんじ}に{始|はじ}まるか{知|し}っていますか.

{駅|えき}までどのぐらいかかるか{分|わ}かりますか。 — Do you know how long it takes to the station?
この{料理|りょうり}に{何|なに}が{入|はい}っているか{教|おし}えてください。 — Please tell me what's in this dish.
{何時|なんじ}に{家|いえ}を{出|で}たか、おぼえていません。 — I don't remember what time I left home.

For a polite request for information, use 〜か{教|おし}えていただけませんか (lesson 7):
つぎのバスが{何時|なんじ}に{来|く}るか、{教|おし}えていただけませんか。 — Could you tell me when the next bus
comes?

## Whether: 〜かどうか

A yes/no question has no question word. Inside a sentence it takes かどうか, "whether (or
not)":

{明日|あした}{来|く}るかどうか、まだ{分|わ}かりません。 — I don't know yet whether he's coming tomorrow.
この{電車|でんしゃ}が{京都|きょうと}に{止|と}まるかどうか{知|し}っていますか。 — Do you know whether this train
stops at Kyoto?
ほんとうかどうか、たしかめてください。 — Please check whether it's true.

It joins the same way: plain form, with だ dropped after nouns and な-adjectives (ほんとうかどうか,
しずかかどうか). か alone also works for yes/no ({来|く}るか{分|わ}かりません), and 〜か〜ないか spells
out both sides ({来|く}るか{来|こ}ないか{分|わ}かりません), but かどうか is the clearest.

## I wonder: 〜かな, 〜かしら

At the end of a sentence, plain form + かな is "I wonder…", said mostly to yourself or to
close friends:

{明日|あした}は、はれるかな。 — I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.
かぎ、どこにおいたかな。 — Now where did I put my keys?
これ、おいしいかな。 — I wonder if this is any good.

As in indirect questions, だ drops: {雨|あめ}かな (I wonder if it'll rain). かしら means the same,
but it now sounds old-fashioned and feminine; you'll meet it in older films and books more
than in conversation. In polite speech, use 〜でしょうか: {雨|あめ}はやむでしょうか (I wonder if
the rain will stop).

## Something, someone, somewhere: {何|なに}か, だれか, どこか

A question word + か, with no question around it, makes an indefinite word:

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {何|なに}か | something, anything | {何|なに}か{飲|の}みませんか。 Would you like something to drink? |
| だれか | someone, anyone | だれかいますか。 Is anyone there? |
| どこか | somewhere, anywhere | どこかで{会|あ}いましたね。 We've met somewhere, haven't we? |
| いつか | sometime, someday | いつか{京都|きょうと}に{行|い}きたいです。 I'd like to go to Kyoto someday. |

が and を usually drop after these words: {何|なに}か{食|た}べたい, だれか{来|き}ました. Other particles
stay: どこかに{行|い}きたい (I want to go somewhere), だれかと{話|はな}したい (I want to talk to
someone).

Compare N5's question word + も + a negative, "nothing, nobody":

{何|なに}か{食|た}べましたか。 — いいえ、{何|なに}も{食|た}べませんでした。 — Did you eat anything? — No, I
didn't eat anything.
だれかいましたか。 — いいえ、だれもいませんでした。 — Was anyone there? — No, nobody was there.

## The important part last: 〜のは〜だ

Japanese puts the most important information near the end. To move it there, turn the rest
of the sentence into a noun with の, make it the topic with は, and finish with the key part:

{私|わたし}はこの{店|みせ}のラーメンが{好|す}きです。 → {私|わたし}が{好|す}きなのは、この{店|みせ}のラーメンです。 —
What I like is this shop's ramen.
きのう{山田|やまだ}さんが{来|き}ました。 → きのう{来|き}たのは{山田|やまだ}さんです。 — It was Mr Yamada who
came yesterday.

The part before のは is in the plain form, with な after な-adjectives ({好|す}きなのは). The
pattern is common when you correct someone: 「{田中|たなか}さんが{来|き}たんですか。」「いいえ、{来|き}たの
は{山田|やまだ}さんです。」 — "Did Ms Tanaka come?" "No, it was Mr Yamada who came."

{大事|だいじ}なのは… (what matters is…) is a common opening: {大事|だいじ}なのは、{毎日|まいにち}{少|すこ}しずつ
{勉強|べんきょう}することです。 — What matters is studying a little every day. ({大事|だいじ} =
important.)

## Forgetting to: 〜のをわすれる

To forget to do something, put の after the dictionary form and make it the object:
〜のをわすれる.

{電気|でんき}をけすのをわすれました。 — I forgot to turn the light off.
{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}くのをわすれないでください。 — Please don't forget to write your name.

Without の, わすれる takes a thing: かさをわすれました (I forgot my umbrella; I left it
somewhere). The の turns the action into something you can forget.

## Words for asking for information

| Japanese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| あんない, あんないじょ | guidance, information; information office |
| かんこう | sightseeing |
| パンフレット | brochure, leaflet |
| {問|と}い{合|あ}わせ | enquiry |
| たずねる | ask, enquire |
| しらべる | look up, check |
| たしかめる | make sure, confirm |
| {知|し}らせる | let someone know |
| {考|かんが}える, {考|かんが}え | think about, consider; idea |
| {思|おも}い{出|だ}す | remember, recall |
| {知|し}り{合|あ}い | acquaintance |
| かかり | person in charge |
| かたち, なかみ | shape; contents |
| まよう | get lost, be unsure |
| {話題|わだい} | topic (of conversation) |

かんこうあんないじょ (tourist information office) is the sign to look for at a station.
{問|と}い{合|あ}わせ is the formal word for an enquiry, on websites and forms: お{問|と}い{合|あ}わせはこちら
(enquiries here). {道|みち}にまよう is "get lost". At a counter, ask for かかりの{人|ひと}, the person
in charge.

{考|かんが}える and {思|おも}う both translate as "think". {思|おも}う is an opinion or a feeling you have;
{考|かんが}える is thinking something through: よく{考|かんが}えてください (please think it over
carefully). {思|おも}い{出|だ}す is bringing something back to mind: {名前|なまえ}が{思|おも}い{出|だ}せません
(I can't remember the name).

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 問 | question, ask | モン | と(う), とい | 11 | {問題|もんだい}, {質問|しつもん}, {問|と}い{合|あ}わせ |
| 題 | topic, title | ダイ | — | 18 | {問題|もんだい}, {話題|わだい} |
| 答 | answer | トウ | こた(える), こた(え) | 12 | {答|こた}える, {答|こた}え |
| 知 | know | チ | し(る), し(らせる) | 8 | {知|し}る, お{知|し}らせ, {知|し}り{合|あ}い |
| 考 | think | コウ | かんが(える) | 6 | {考|かんが}える, {考|かんが}え |
| 思 | think, feel | シ | おも(う) | 9 | {思|おも}う, {思|おも}い{出|だ}す |

N5 words that now get their kanji: {問題|もんだい}, {質問|しつもん} (質 is from lesson 28),
{答|こた}え, {答|こた}える, {知|し}る and お{知|し}らせ. {思|おも}う you've been using since lesson 3.

{問題|もんだい} is both "a question on a test" (N5) and "a problem": {問題|もんだい}ありません (no
problem).

Memory notes:

- 問 is a mouth (口) inside a gate (門, lesson 8): calling out a question at the gate.
- 題 has, on the right, the same "head" part as 頭 and 顔 (lesson 12): the title at the head of
  a page.
- 答 is bamboo on top over 合 (fit, lesson 26): the answer that fits the question.
- 知 is an arrow on the left next to a mouth (口): knowing means saying it straight, like an
  arrow hitting the mark.
- 考 is an old person bent over a stick: thinking things over slowly.
- 思 is a field (田) on top of a heart (心, lesson 9): thoughts filling your heart.

```trace
問題答知考思
```

## Dialogue: at the lost-property office

ソフィア left her backpack on a train. She asks at the station office; it's polite speech.

```dialogue
# At the lost-property office
ソフィア: すみません。{電車|でんしゃ}にリュックをわすれてしまったんですが…。
= Excuse me. I left my backpack on a train…
えきいん: そうですか。どの{電車|でんしゃ}だったか、おぼえていますか。
= I see. Do you remember which train it was?
ソフィア: みどり{台|だい}を{十時|じゅうじ}ごろ{出|で}た{電車|でんしゃ}です。いちばん{前|まえ}に{乗|の}っていました。
= The one that left Midoridai at about ten. I was right at the front.
えきいん: どんなリュックですか。{色|いろ}やかたちを{教|おし}えてください。
= What kind of backpack is it? Please tell me its colour and shape.
ソフィア: {黒|くろ}くて{小|ちい}さいリュックです。なかみは{青|あお}いさいふと{日本語|にほんご}の{本|ほん}です。
= It's a small black one. Inside there's a blue wallet and a Japanese book.
えきいん: {分|わ}かりました。ほかの{駅|えき}にとどいているかどうか、{電話|でんわ}で{聞|き}いてみますね。
= All right. I'll phone and ask whether it's been handed in at another station.
えきいん: お{待|ま}たせしました。{黒|くろ}いリュックがさくら{山|やま}{駅|えき}にとどいているそうです。
= Sorry to keep you waiting. They say a black backpack has been handed in at Sakurayama.
ソフィア: よかった！いつまでに{行|い}けばいいですか。
= Thank goodness! By when should I go?
えきいん: {来週|らいしゅう}の{金曜日|きんようび}までに{行|い}ってください。それまではさくら{山|やま}{駅|えき}にあるはずです。
= Please go by next Friday. It should be at Sakurayama until then.
ソフィア: あのう、さくら{山|やま}{駅|えき}にはどうやって{行|い}くか、{教|おし}えていただけませんか。
= Um, could you tell me how to get to Sakurayama?
えきいん: むこうのホームの{電車|でんしゃ}で、{二|ふた}つ{目|め}の{駅|えき}ですよ。
= Take the train from the platform opposite. It's the second stop.
ソフィア: ほんとうにありがとうございました。
= Thank you so much.
```

えきいん = station staff ({駅員|えきいん}); リュック = backpack; とどく = arrive, be handed in;
お{待|ま}たせしました = sorry to keep you waiting (a set phrase); {行|い}けばいい = should go
(lesson 12).

## Pronunciation

- In an indirect question the inner か doesn't rise: it isn't a question by itself. Only the
  end of the whole sentence rises when you're asking: {何時|なんじ}に{始|はじ}まるか{知|し}っていますか？
- かな stays level or falls: it's a thought, not a question to someone.
- {何|なに}か is three morae, na-ni-ka, with the pitch falling after the first: {何|なに:1}か.

```speak
{何時|なんじ}に{始|はじ}まるか{知|し}っていますか。
= Do you know what time it starts?
この{電車|でんしゃ}が{京都|きょうと}に{止|と}まるかどうか{教|おし}えてください。
= Please tell me whether this train stops at Kyoto.
{明日|あした}は、はれるかな。
= I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.
{何|なに}か{飲|の}みませんか。
= Would you like something to drink?
{名前|なまえ}が{思|おも}い{出|だ}せません。
= I can't remember the name.
```

## Common mistakes

- Keeping ます inside: ×{何時|なんじ}に{始|はじ}まりますか{知|し}っていますか. The inner question is
  plain: {始|はじ}まるか.
- Forgetting か: ×{何時|なんじ}に{始|はじ}まる{知|し}っていますか. The か is what makes it a question.
- Keeping だ before か in careful speech: the standard form is だれか{分|わ}かりません,
  ほんとうかどうか.
- Mixing up {何|なに}か and {何|なに}も: {何|なに}か goes in questions and positive sentences; with a
  negative it's {何|なに}も.
- ×{電気|でんき}をけすをわすれました. A verb needs の first: けすのをわすれました.
- Using かしら in polite conversation: it sounds dated and feminine. かな is the everyday choice,
  and 〜でしょうか the polite one.

## Key points

- Indirect question: question word + plain form + か + {知|し}る / {分|わ}かる / {教|おし}える…:
  {何時|なんじ}に{始|はじ}まるか{知|し}っていますか. だ drops before か.
- Yes/no inside a sentence: 〜かどうか.
- 〜かな: I wonder (casual); 〜かしら is dated; polite 〜でしょうか.
- {何|なに}か, だれか, どこか, いつか: something, someone, somewhere, sometime; が and を drop
  after them.
- 〜のは〜だ puts the key part last. 〜のをわすれる: forget to do.
- New kanji: 問 題 答 知 考 思.

That's the end of module 4. The reference sheet "Seeming, hearsay and guessing" has all of its
endings in one table.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Reading easy news
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

News is one of the best things to read once you reach N4. The topics are real, the same
words come back every day, and there are news sites written in easy Japanese for learners and
children, such as NHK's NEWS WEB EASY, with furigana and audio. This honors lesson shows how
news Japanese works: how headlines leave words out, the だ/である style of written reports,
and how reporters use this module's endings (そうだ, ということだ, 〜と{話|はな}しています) to show
where each piece of information came from. It ends with an original easy-news article to
read.

## Headlines

Headlines ({見出|みだ}し) save space, so they leave out words a normal sentence needs.

| Headline | As a full sentence | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {市|し}の{図書館|としょかん}、{日曜日|にちようび}も{開|あ}く | {市|し}の{図書館|としょかん}は{日曜日|にちようび}も{開|あ}きます。 | City library to open on Sundays too |
| {大雨|おおあめ}で{電車|でんしゃ}とまる | {大雨|おおあめ}で{電車|でんしゃ}がとまりました。 | Heavy rain stops trains |
| {新|あたら}しい{駅|えき}、{来年|らいねん}{春|はる}{開業|かいぎょう} | {新|あたら}しい{駅|えき}が{来年|らいねん}の{春|はる}に{開業|かいぎょう}します。 | New station to open next spring |
| {夜|よる}の{火事|かじ}　{台所|だいどころ}から{火|ひ}か | {夜|よる}の{火事|かじ}は、{台所|だいどころ}から{火|ひ}が{出|で}たようです。 | Night fire: started in kitchen? |
| {駅前|えきまえ}のビル、{建|た}てかえへ | {駅前|えきまえ}のビルを{建|た}てかえるよていです。 | Station-front building to be rebuilt |

What headlines do:

- They drop は, が and を. A comma or a space often stands where は would be.
- They often use the dictionary form for things that have already happened: {電車|でんしゃ}とまる
  means the trains stopped. Context gives the tense.
- They often end with a noun, especially a する-noun without する: {開業|かいぎょう} (from
  {開業|かいぎょう}する, open for business).
- か at the end means "possibly, it's thought": the cause hasn't been confirmed yet.
- へ at the end often means "heading for, planned": {建|た}てかえへ, "to be rebuilt"
  ({建|た}てかえる = rebuild).

## だ and である: the written style

Ordinary newspapers write in the plain form, not です/ます. Where a spoken sentence would end
in だ, written reports often use である, which sounds more formal and impersonal.

| Polite | Plain | Formal written |
|---|---|---|
| {雨|あめ}です | {雨|あめ}だ | {雨|あめ}である |
| しずかでした | しずかだった | しずかであった |
| {学生|がくせい}ではありません | {学生|がくせい}ではない | {学生|がくせい}ではない |
| {行|い}きます | {行|い}く | {行|い}く |
| {高|たか}いです | {高|たか}い | {高|たか}い |

である only replaces だ, after nouns and な-adjectives. Verbs and い-adjectives have nothing to
replace, so they simply use the plain form. Easy news for learners usually keeps です/ます,
which is part of what makes it easy; newspapers, many websites, essays and textbooks use the
plain style, with である in places.

## Where the information comes from

News is careful about sources, and these endings tell you who said what:

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜によると、〜そうです | according to …, … | けいさつによると、けがをした{人|ひと}はいないそうです。 |
| 〜ということです | it is reported that | {電車|でんしゃ}は{夜|よる}まで{動|うご}かないということです。 |
| 〜と{話|はな}しています | (someone interviewed) says | 「とてもこわかったです」と{話|はな}していました。 |
| 〜とはっぴょうしました | announced that | {市|し}は、{新|あたら}しい{図書館|としょかん}を{作|つく}るとはっぴょうしました。 |
| 〜という。 | it is said (newspaper style) | {火事|かじ}は{午前|ごぜん}{二時|にじ}ごろだったという。 |

けが = injury: けがをした{人|ひと}, injured people. {動|うご}く = move, run (of trains).

The examples mean: according to the police, nobody was hurt; trains are reported not to be
running until the evening; "It was really scary," (the person) said; the city announced that it
will build a new library; the fire is said to have been at around 2 a.m.

らしい is rare in news reports. It sounds like something picked up second-hand and doesn't name
a source, so reporters prefer a named source with そうだ or ということだ. In conversation about
the news, らしい is perfectly natural: {駅前|えきまえ}で{火事|かじ}があったらしいよ (apparently there
was a fire in front of the station).

## News words

| Japanese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {見出|みだ}し | headline |
| きじ | article (in a newspaper or online) |
| はっぴょう, はっぴょうする | announcement; announce |
| けいさつ | the police |
| じこ | accident |
| {火事|かじ} | fire (a building burning) |

{火事|かじ} is a building or a forest on fire; a flame, as on a stove, is {火|ひ}.

## Reading: an easy-news article

This article is written for this course in the style of an easy-news site. It isn't based on
a real story.

> {中学生|ちゅうがくせい}が{町|まち}のかんこう{地図|ちず}を{作|つく}る
>
> {山|やま}の{近|ちか}くにある{小|ちい}さい{町|まち}、みどり{町|まち}で、{中学生|ちゅうがくせい}がかんこうに{来|く}る{人|ひと}のための
> {地図|ちず}を{作|つく}りました。
>
> みどり{町|まち}には{古|ふる}いおてらや{大|おお}きい{池|いけ}があって、{秋|あき}にはたくさんの{人|ひと}が{来|き}ます。
> でも、{町|まち}によると、{駅|えき}からの{道|みち}が{分|わ}かりにくくて、まよう{人|ひと}が{多|おお}いということです。
>
> そこで、{町|まち}の{中学校|ちゅうがっこう}の{二年生|にねんせい}{三十人|さんじゅうにん}が、{夏休|なつやす}みの{間|あいだ}に{町|まち}を{歩|ある}いて、
> {地図|ちず}を{作|つく}りました。{地図|ちず}には{店|みせ}やトイレのほかに、「ここから{見|み}る{夕日|ゆうひ}がきれい」
> 「この{店|みせ}のおだんごがおいしい」など、{中学生|ちゅうがくせい}のおすすめも{書|か}いてあります。
>
> {地図|ちず}は{日本語|にほんご}と{英語|えいご}の{二|ふた}つがあって、{駅|えき}のあんないじょでもらうことができます。
> {地図|ちず}を{作|つく}った{中学生|ちゅうがくせい}の{一人|ひとり}は「{町|まち}に{来|き}た{人|ひと}に、みどり{町|まち}をもっと
> {好|す}きになってほしいです」と{話|はな}していました。

〜のための = for (lesson 24); {分|わ}かりにくい = hard to work out (lesson 25); そこで = so, for
that reason; {夕日|ゆうひ} = the setting sun; おだんご = sweet rice dumplings; 〜てほしい = want
someone to (lesson 7).

Junior high school students make a sightseeing map of their town. In Midori, a small
town near the mountains, junior high school students have made a map for visitors. Midori has
old temples and a large pond, and many people come in autumn. But according to the town, the
way from the station is hard to work out, and many people get lost. So thirty second-year
students from the town's junior high school walked around the town during the summer holidays
and made a map. As well as shops and toilets, the map has the students' recommendations, such
as "The sunset you can see from here is beautiful" and "The dumplings at this shop are
delicious." There are two versions, in Japanese and English, and you can pick one up at the
station information office. One of the students who made it said, "I'd like visitors to like
Midori even more."

The same story in newspaper style would read like this:

> みどり{町|まち}の{中学生|ちゅうがくせい}が、かんこうに{来|く}る{人|ひと}のための{地図|ちず}を{作|つく}った。{町|まち}によると、
> {駅|えき}からの{道|みち}が{分|わ}かりにくいという{声|こえ}が{多|おお}かったという。

Notice the plain past {作|つく}った, and という twice: first before a noun (という{声|こえ}, voices
saying that…) and then at the end of the sentence (it is said).

## How to read a news article

1. Read the headline and guess: who did what, where?
2. The first sentence of an easy-news article usually sums up the whole story: who, what,
   where.
3. Look for the sources: {町|まち}によると…ということです, …と{話|はな}していました.
4. Don't stop at every new word. Read to the end once, then go back for the details.

## Key points

- Headlines drop は, が and を, use the dictionary form for past events, and often end in a
  noun; か at the end means "possibly", へ "planned".
- Written reports use the plain form; である replaces だ after nouns and な-adjectives.
- Sources: 〜によると…そうです, 〜ということです, 〜と{話|はな}しています, 〜とはっぴょうしました, and
  newspaper 〜という.
- らしい sounds like gossip in a report; it's for conversation.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Luck, fortune and folk beliefs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Many people in Japan who wouldn't call themselves religious still buy a good-luck charm
before an exam, draw a paper fortune at New Year, or glance at the calendar before choosing a
wedding date. This honors lesson looks at some of these customs, and at the language for
talking about beliefs without stating them as facts, which is exactly what this module's
endings are for: そうだ, らしい, かもしれない.

Some of the words for luck are written with kanji that are outside N4. They're shown with
furigana so you can recognize them on a slip or a calendar; you don't need to learn them.

## おみくじ: fortune slips

At many shrines (じんじゃ) and temples (おてら) you can draw an おみくじ, a paper slip that tells
your fortune, for a small fee. It's especially popular at はつもうで, the first visit to a
shrine or temple in the New Year. The slip gives an overall rank of luck, then short notes on
topics such as health, travel, study, work, love and lost things.

| Rank | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {大吉|だいきち} | great luck |
| {吉|きち} | good luck |
| {中吉|ちゅうきち} | moderate luck |
| {小吉|しょうきち} | a little luck |
| {末吉|すえきち} | luck to come later |
| {凶|きょう} | bad luck |
| {大凶|だいきょう} | very bad luck |

The order of the middle ranks differs from shrine to shrine, and not every shrine uses all of
them. {大凶|だいきょう} is rare, and some places leave it out altogether.

What do you do with the slip? A common custom is to tie a bad fortune to a rack or a branch at
the shrine, leaving the bad luck behind, and to keep a good one, for example in your wallet.
Customs vary, though: some people tie up every slip, good or bad.

## おまもり: good-luck charms

おまもり are small cloth bags sold at shrines and temples, each for a purpose:

| Charm | For |
|---|---|
| こうつうあんぜん | road safety (you'll see them hanging in cars) |
| ごうかく | passing an exam |
| けんこう | good health |
| あんざん | a safe birth |
| えんむすび | finding a partner |

Many people keep a charm for about a year and then take it back to a shrine or temple, where
old charms are collected, and buy a new one.

## Lucky and unlucky days: ろくよう

Many Japanese calendars print one of six words on each day: the ろくよう, a six-day cycle of
lucky and unlucky days that is said to have come from China.

| Day | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {大安|たいあん} | the luckiest day; very popular for weddings |
| {友引|ともびき} | "pulls a friend along"; fine for celebrations, but funerals are avoided |
| {先勝|せんしょう} | lucky in the morning, unlucky in the afternoon |
| {先負|せんぶ} | unlucky in the morning, lucky in the afternoon |
| {赤口|しゃっこう} | unlucky except around noon |
| {仏滅|ぶつめつ} | the unluckiest day; weddings are avoided |

Note the reading: {大安|たいあん}, with た, not だ. Many couples choose a たいあん for their wedding,
and some wedding halls offer lower prices on a ぶつめつ. On ともびき, funerals are avoided (the
idea is that the dead person might "pull a friend along"), and many crematoriums close that
day. Plenty of people today pay no attention to any of this, but the words are still on the
calendar.

## まねきねこ: the beckoning cat

The cat with one paw raised, in the windows of shops and restaurants, is a まねきねこ, a
"beckoning cat": it invites customers and money in. It's often said that a raised right paw
invites money and a raised left paw invites people, but explanations differ. The paw isn't
waving goodbye: it copies the Japanese gesture for "come here", made with the hand raised and the
fingers flapping downwards.

## Lucky and unlucky numbers and things

- し (4) sounds like the word for death, and く (9) like the word for suffering. Some hospitals
  and hotels have no room 4 or 9, and gifts aren't usually given in fours. It's one reason
  often given for よん and きゅう being the everyday readings.
- {八|はち} (8) is lucky: the kanji 八 opens out towards the bottom, like a future that grows
  wider.
- A tea stalk floating upright in your green tea, ちゃばしら, is said to bring good luck.
- Some people avoid sleeping with their head to the north (きたまくら), because the dead are
  traditionally laid that way.
- やくどし are ages traditionally thought to be unlucky. The best known are 42 for men and 33
  for women, counted in the old way, in which a baby is one year old at birth. Many people visit
  a shrine for a blessing in those years.

## Talking about beliefs

When people describe a belief, they rarely state it as a plain fact. They use this module's
endings, which put a little distance between the speaker and the belief:

| Ending | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 〜そうです | ちゃばしらが{立|た}つと、いいことがあるそうです。 | They say something good happens if a tea stalk stands up. |
| 〜らしいです | {大安|たいあん}の{日|ひ}は、けっこんしきが{多|おお}いらしいです。 | Apparently there are a lot of weddings on taian days. |
| 〜と{言|い}われています | {八|はち}はえんぎがいいと{言|い}われています。 | Eight is said to be lucky. |
| 〜かもしれません | おまもりがあると、{安心|あんしん}できるかもしれません。 | Having a charm might put your mind at ease. |
| 〜としんじている{人|ひと}もいます | {四|し}はえんぎがわるいとしんじている{人|ひと}もいます。 | Some people believe four is unlucky. |

〜と{言|い}われています is a passive (lesson 21), "it is said"; learn it as a phrase for now.
けっこんしき = wedding; {安心|あんしん}する = feel at ease.

To say where you stand yourself, add a plain statement: {私|わたし}はあまりしんじていませんが、
おみくじは{楽|たの}しいです (I don't really believe in it, but fortune slips are fun).

## Luck words

| Japanese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {運|うん} | luck: {運|うん}がいい (lucky), {運|うん}がわるい (unlucky) |
| えんぎ | omen: えんぎがいい (a good sign), えんぎがわるい (a bad sign) |
| おみくじ, おまもり | fortune slip; good-luck charm |
| しんじる | believe (in) |
| しあわせ | happiness; happy |

{運|うん} (luck) sounds just like the casual うん (yeah). Context tells you which: {運|うん}がいい is
"lucky"; うん、いいよ is "yeah, sure".

## Dialogue: New Year at the shrine

Two friends, ひな and そうた, on their first shrine visit of the year. Casual speech.

```dialogue
# New Year at the shrine
ひな: そうた、おみくじ{引|ひ}こうよ。
= Sota, let's draw fortunes.
そうた: いいね。…あ、{大吉|だいきち}だ！
= Sure. …Oh, great luck!
ひな: すごい！{私|わたし}は…{凶|きょう}…。
= Wow! Mine's… bad luck…
そうた: {凶|きょう}って、あまり{出|で}ないらしいよ。ある{意味|いみ}で{運|うん}がいいかも。
= Apparently bad luck hardly ever comes up. In a way, you're lucky.
ひな: そうかな。「{旅行|りょこう}：{急|いそ}がないほうがいい」だって。
= You think? "Travel: better not to rush," it says.
そうた: {凶|きょう}のおみくじは、ここにむすんで{帰|かえ}るといいらしいよ。
= Apparently you should tie bad ones up here before you go home.
ひな: じゃあ、むすんでいこう。それから、{試験|しけん}のおまもりも{買|か}いたいな。
= Let's tie it up, then. And I want to buy a charm for my exams too.
そうた: {春|はる}の{試験|しけん}？おまもりがあれば、きっとだいじょうぶだよ。
= The spring exams? With a charm, I'm sure you'll be fine.
ひな: おまもりより{勉強|べんきょう}かもしれないけどね。{今年|ことし}もしあわせな{一年|いちねん}になるといいな。
= Though studying might matter more than charms. I hope this year's a happy one too.
```

{引|ひ}く = draw (a slip); ある{意味|いみ}で = in a sense; 〜ないほうがいい = it's better not to;
むすぶ = tie; 〜といい = it's good to, I hope (lesson 11); 〜ば = if (lesson 12).

Notice how much of the dialogue is hearsay and guessing: らしいよ (twice), かも, だって, きっと,
かもしれない. Nobody says "bad luck is rare" or "you must tie it up" as plain facts.

## Key points

- おみくじ: fortune slips, ranked from {大吉|だいきち} to {凶|きょう}; bad ones are often tied up at the
  shrine.
- おまもり: charms for a purpose (exams, health, road safety), usually replaced after a year.
- ろくよう on calendars: {大安|たいあん} (luckiest; weddings), {仏滅|ぶつめつ} (unluckiest),
  {友引|ともびき} (no funerals).
- まねきねこ beckons customers and money; 4 and 9 are avoided, 8 is lucky.
- Talk about beliefs with そうです, らしいです, 〜と{言|い}われています, かもしれません,
  〜としんじている{人|ひと}もいます.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The passive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Until now, the subject of your sentences has always been the one who acts: {先生|せんせい}が{私|わたし}をほめました (the teacher praised me). Japanese can also turn this round and start from the person or thing the action happens to: {私|わたし}は{先生|せんせい}にほめられました (I was praised by the teacher). That form of the verb is the **[[passive]]**.

The Japanese passive does two jobs. The first is the one English has: "the castle was built in 1610", "this book is read all over the world". The second has no direct English equivalent: Japanese can use the passive to say that something happened *to you* and you were affected by it, usually for the worse: {雨|あめ}にふられた (I got rained on), {弟|おとうと}にケーキを{食|た}べられた (my brother ate my cake, and I'm not happy). This lesson covers both, and this module builds on the passive: lesson 22 adds the causative (make or let someone do), lesson 23 combines the two (be made to do).

The theme is animals and nature, and history and famous buildings, where passives are everywhere.

## Making the passive

Group 1 verbs change their last sound to the あ row and add れる; group 2 verbs drop る and add られる; する and {来|く}る are irregular.

| Group | Rule | Dictionary form | Passive |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | u → a + れる | {書|か}く | {書|か}かれる |
| 1 | | {読|よ}む | {読|よ}まれる |
| 1 | | {待|ま}つ | {待|ま}たれる |
| 1 | | {話|はな}す | {話|はな}される |
| 1 | う → わ + れる | {言|い}う, {買|か}う | {言|い}われる, {買|か}われる |
| 1 | | よぶ, しぬ | よばれる, しなれる |
| 2 | る → られる | {食|た}べる, {見|み}る | {食|た}べられる, {見|み}られる |
| 3 | | する | される |
| 3 | | {来|く}る | {来|こ}られる |

The ない form is a good guide for group 1: {書|か}かない → {書|か}かれる, {待|ま}たない → {待|ま}たれる, {言|い}わない → {言|い}われる. Swap ない for れる. Verbs in う take わ in both forms, never あ: {言|い}われる, not {言|い}あれる.

Every passive verb is a group 2 verb. Once you have {書|か}かれる, it conjugates like {食|た}べる: {書|か}かれます, {書|か}かれて, {書|か}かれない, {書|か}かれた, {書|か}かれました. The passive is now one of the forms in your conjugation drills.

### The same shape as the potential

For group 2 verbs the passive and the potential are identical: {食|た}べられる can mean "can eat" or "be eaten", and {来|こ}られる "can come" or, as a suffering passive (below), "have someone come". Context almost always settles it:

{私|わたし}は{生|なま}の{魚|さかな}が{食|た}べられます。 — I can eat raw fish. (potential: が marks what I can eat)
{私|わたし}のケーキが{弟|おとうと}に{食|た}べられました。 — My cake was eaten by my brother. (passive: に marks who did it)

Group 1 verbs keep them apart: {読|よ}める (can read) but {読|よ}まれる (be read). If you hear an あ-row sound before れる, it's a passive.

## The direct passive: AはBにVられる

In a **[[direct passive]]**, the object of an ordinary sentence becomes the subject, and the doer is marked with に:

| Active | Passive |
|---|---|
| {先生|せんせい}が{私|わたし}をほめた。 — The teacher praised me. | {私|わたし}は{先生|せんせい}にほめられた。 — I was praised by the teacher. |
| {父|ちち}が{弟|おとうと}をしかった。 — Father scolded my brother. | {弟|おとうと}は{父|ちち}にしかられた。 — My brother was scolded by Father. |
| {犬|いぬ}が{子|こ}どもをかんだ。 — The dog bit the child. | {子|こ}どもが{犬|いぬ}にかまれた。 — The child was bitten by the dog. |

The person or thing that does the action is called the **[[agent]]**, and in a passive it takes に. Keep the に straight in your head: in {先生|せんせい}にほめられた, the teacher is the one praising, not the one receiving. Lesson 7's 〜てもらう also had the giver on に; the passive works the same way.

Why choose a passive? Mostly to keep talking about the same person. If the story is about you, Japanese prefers to keep you as the subject:

{今日|きょう}、{作文|さくぶん}を{出|だ}したら、{先生|せんせい}にほめられました。 — I handed in my essay today, and the teacher praised it.

Verbs of being praised, scolded, invited, asked and told are the everyday passives: ほめられる, しかられる, おこられる (to get told off), よばれる (to be called; to be invited), {聞|き}かれる (to be asked), {言|い}われる (to be told), さそわれる (to be invited; さそう = to invite).

With verbs of telling and sending, the agent can also take から: {先生|せんせい}から{言|い}われた (I was told by the teacher). に is always correct for this course's sentences.

## Body parts and belongings: Nを Vられる

When the action happens to *part* of you or to something of yours, the person stays the subject and the part or the thing keeps を:

{犬|いぬ}に{手|て}をかまれました。 — I was bitten on the hand by a dog.
{電車|でんしゃ}で{足|あし}をふまれました。 — Someone stepped on my foot on the train.
ハチに{足|あし}をさされました。 — I was stung on the leg by a bee.
{電車|でんしゃ}でさいふをぬすまれました。 — I had my wallet stolen on the train.

Notice that English says "my foot" or "my wallet", but Japanese doesn't say {私|わたし}の{足|あし}が…: the person who was affected is the subject (often left out), and the foot or the wallet is the object. {私|わたし}の{足|あし}がふまれました is understandable but sounds like a report about the foot.

Mosquitoes and bees さす (sting, pierce), they don't かむ: かにさされた (I got bitten by a mosquito; か = mosquito).

## The indirect (suffering) passive

Here Japanese does something English can't. Even a verb with no object, such as ふる (fall, of rain) or なく (cry), can be made passive. The subject is someone who wasn't part of the action but was affected by it, almost always unpleasantly. This is the **[[indirect passive]]**, also called the **[[suffering passive]]**:

{雨|あめ}にふられました。 — I got caught in the rain. (literally "I was rained on")
{夜|よる}、{赤|あか}ちゃんになかれて、ねられませんでした。 — The baby cried at night, and I couldn't sleep.
{出|で}かける{前|まえ}に{友|とも}だちに{来|こ}られて、{電車|でんしゃ}に{間|ま}に{合|あ}いませんでした。 — A friend turned up just before I went out, and I missed my train. ({間|ま}に{合|あ}う = to be in time)

It works with verbs that have an object, too. The object stays with を, and the person who suffers is the subject:

{弟|おとうと}にケーキを{食|た}べられました。 — My brother ate my cake (and I'm annoyed).
となりの{人|ひと}に{夜|よる}おそくまでピアノをひかれて、こまっています。 — My neighbour plays the piano until late at night, and it's a problem for me.

Compare a neutral sentence with a suffering passive:

{雨|あめ}がふりました。 — It rained. (a fact)
{雨|あめ}にふられました。 — It rained on me. (I got wet; my plans were spoiled)

A good English test: if you could say "on me" ("he ate my cake on me", "the baby cried on me"), the suffering passive is probably right. The thing that happens is marked by に (the rain, the baby, my brother), just as in the direct passive.

## Things, history and "it is said": 〜と{言|い}われている

When the subject is a thing, the passive often has no agent at all. This is the passive of notices, guidebooks and history:

この{建物|たてもの}は{百年|ひゃくねん}{前|まえ}に{建|た}てられました。 — This building was built a hundred years ago.
{英語|えいご}は{世界中|せかいじゅう}で{使|つか}われています。 — English is used all over the world.
この{池|いけ}の{鳥|とり}は、{町|まち}の{人|ひと}たちに{大切|たいせつ}にされています。 — The birds on this pond are well looked after by the townspeople.

With 〜ている, a passive describes how something generally is: {使|つか}われている (is used), {知|し}られている (is known), {読|よ}まれている (is read).

〜と{言|い}われている (it is said that…) is how Japanese reports something many people believe, without vouching for it:

このしろは{日本|にほん}でいちばん{古|ふる}いと{言|い}われています。 — This castle is said to be the oldest in Japan.
さるは{頭|あたま}がいい{動物|どうぶつ}だと{言|い}われています。 — Monkeys are said to be clever animals.

### によって: made, written or discovered by

When a thing is created, written, built, invented or discovered by someone, the agent takes によって instead of に. You mostly need to recognize it, in writing and on signs:

このおてらは{有名|ゆうめい}なおぼうさんによって{建|た}てられました。 — The temple was built by a famous monk. (おぼうさん = Buddhist monk)
{電話|でんわ}はベルによって{発明|はつめい}されたと{言|い}われています。 — The telephone is generally said to have been invented by Bell.

Why not に? {有名|ゆうめい}なおぼうさんに{建|た}てられた sounds as if the temple was affected by him, like a person being scolded. For creations, によって is the standard choice.

## Reading: the castle in Midori Town

みどり{町|まち}の{北|きた}に、{古|ふる}いしろがあります。このしろは{四百年|よんひゃくねん}ぐらい{前|まえ}に{建|た}てられたと{言|い}われています。{町|まち}の{人|ひと}たちには「さくらじょう」とよばれています。{春|はる}になると、しろのまわりのさくらがとてもきれいだからです。

{百五十年|ひゃくごじゅうねん}ぐらい{前|まえ}に、しろは{火事|かじ}で{一度|いちど}、もえてしまいました。でも、{町|まち}の{人|ひと}たちが{集|あつ}めたお{金|かね}で、また{建|た}てられました。{今|いま}は{有名|ゆうめい}になって、{日本中|にほんじゅう}から{人|ひと}が{来|き}ます。

しろの{前|まえ}には{大|おお}きい{池|いけ}があって、{鳥|とり}がたくさんいます。でも、{気|き}をつけてください。{池|いけ}のまわりで{食|た}べ{物|もの}を{持|も}っていると、{鳥|とり}にとられることがあります。{私|わたし}の{弟|おとうと}も{去年|きょねん}、サンドイッチを{大|おお}きい{鳥|とり}にとられて、ないていました。

しろの{中|なか}に{入|はい}るのは{有料|ゆうりょう}で、{大人|おとな}は{五百円|ごひゃくえん}です。{子|こ}どもはむりょうです。

> North of Midori Town there's an old castle. It's said to have been built about four hundred years ago. The townspeople call it "Cherry Castle", because in spring the cherry trees around it are beautiful.
>
> About a hundred and fifty years ago the castle burned down in a fire. But it was built again with money the townspeople collected. Now it's famous, and people come from all over Japan.
>
> In front of the castle there's a big pond with lots of birds. But be careful: if you're holding food near the pond, the birds sometimes take it. Last year a big bird snatched my little brother's sandwich, and he cried.
>
> There's a charge to go inside the castle: 500 yen for adults. Children go in free.

〜じょう = castle (in names); {火事|かじ} = a fire (in a building); もえる = to burn; とる = to take.

## Dialogue: at the zoo

```dialogue
# At the zoo
はると: ゆいちゃん、どうしたの？{元気|げんき}ないね。
= Yui, what's up? You look down.
ゆい: さっき、さるにパンをとられちゃった。
= A monkey just snatched my bread.
はると: えっ、さるに？ここのさるはよく{人|ひと}の{食|た}べ{物|もの}をとるって{言|い}われてるよ。
= What, a monkey? People say the monkeys here often steal food.
ゆい: {知|し}らなかった。それに、{手|て}もかまれそうになったの。
= I didn't know. And it nearly bit my hand, too.
はると: だいじょうぶ？かかりの{人|ひと}に{言|い}った？
= Are you OK? Did you tell one of the staff? (かかりの{人|ひと} = the person in charge)
ゆい: うん。「パンを{見|み}せないでください」って{言|い}われた。
= Yes. They told me "Please don't show the monkeys your bread."
はると: そうか。じゃあ、ぞうを{見|み}に{行|い}こうよ。ぞうは{世界中|せかいじゅう}の{子|こ}どもに{好|す}かれている{動物|どうぶつ}だからね。
= I see. Well, let's go and see the elephants. Kids all over the world love elephants.
ゆい: うん。でも、{今度|こんど}はパンをかばんに{入|い}れておくね。
= OK. But this time I'll put my bread away in my bag.
```

とられちゃった is the casual 〜てしまった (lesson 9) of the passive とられる. かまれそうになった = nearly got bitten (〜そう, lesson 16).

## Pronunciation: two kinds of かう and two kinds of しろ

Some words in this lesson share their sound with an N5 word and differ only in pitch:

- [かう:0] (to buy) is flat; [かう:1] (to keep an animal) is high on か and falls: いぬを[かう:1] (to keep a dog).
- [しろ:1] (white) falls after し; [しろ:0] (castle) is flat, and a following particle stays high: [しろ:0]が{見|み}える.

Context almost always tells you which is meant, but saying them right makes you easier to follow.

## Kanji

Seven kanji for the world, animals and buildings. With them you can write five N5 words you've used in kana: {世界|せかい}, {有名|ゆうめい}, {犬|いぬ}, {池|いけ} and {建物|たてもの}.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 建 | build | ケン, コン | た(てる), た(つ) | 9 | {建|た}てる, {建|た}つ, {建物|たてもの} |
| 世 | world; generation | セ, セイ | よ | 5 | {世界|せかい}, {世話|せわ} (lesson 22) |
| 界 | boundary; world | カイ | — | 9 | {世界|せかい}, {世界中|せかいじゅう} |
| 有 | have, exist | ユウ, ウ | あ(る) | 6 | {有名|ゆうめい}, {有料|ゆうりょう} |
| 犬 | dog | ケン | いぬ | 4 | {犬|いぬ}, {小犬|こいぬ} (puppy) |
| 鳥 | bird | チョウ | とり | 11 | {鳥|とり}, {小鳥|ことり} |
| 池 | pond | チ | いけ | 6 | {池|いけ}, {電池|でんち} (battery) |

Memory notes:

- 犬 is 大 (big) with an extra dot: a big friend with a dot of a nose. Don't confuse it with 太 (fat, lesson 12), whose dot is inside, at the bottom.
- 鳥 is a picture of a bird: the head at the top, the body in the middle, and four dots for the feet or tail feathers at the bottom.
- 池 has the water radical on the left: three drops of water, the same as in 海 (sea, lesson 3) and 洗 (wash, lesson 10).
- 界 has a field (田) on top: borders between fields, and by extension the world.
- 建 has the long sweeping stroke at the bottom left, which is written last: draw the right-hand part first, then the sweep under it.

The kun'yomi of 有 (あ(る)) is rarely written with this kanji; ある stays in kana, as this course always writes it.

```trace
建世界有犬鳥池
```

## Say it

```speak
{雨|あめ}にふられました。
= I got caught in the rain.
{先生|せんせい}にほめられました。
= I was praised by the teacher.
{電車|でんしゃ}で{足|あし}をふまれました。
= Someone stepped on my foot on the train.
このしろは{四百年|よんひゃくねん}{前|まえ}に{建|た}てられました。
= This castle was built four hundred years ago.
{英語|えいご}は{世界中|せかいじゅう}で{使|つか}われています。
= English is used all over the world.
```

## Common mistakes

- Mixing up who did what. In {私|わたし}は{兄|あに}にしかられた, the brother (に) did the scolding. If you translate に as "to", you'll get it backwards.
- う verbs with あ. {言|い}う → {言|い}われる, {買|か}う → {買|か}われる, never {言|い}あれる.
- {来|く}る. The passive is {来|こ}られる, read こられる, the same as the potential.
- The owner as subject. Say ({私|わたし}は)さいふをぬすまれた, not {私|わたし}のさいふがぬすまれた when you're telling what happened to you.
- Overusing the suffering passive. It nearly always means you were bothered. {友|とも}だちに{来|こ}られた means the visit was unwelcome; if you were glad, say {友|とも}だちが{来|き}てくれた (lesson 7).
- に for a creator. For who built, wrote or invented something, use によって in writing: ベルによって{発明|はつめい}された.

## Key points

- Passive: group 1 あ row + れる ({書|か}かれる, {言|い}われる); group 2 〜られる (same as the potential); される; {来|こ}られる. All passives conjugate like group 2 verbs.
- The agent (the doer) takes に: {先生|せんせい}にほめられた.
- Body parts and belongings keep を: {足|あし}をふまれた, さいふをぬすまれた.
- The suffering passive: something happens and you're affected: {雨|あめ}にふられた, {弟|おとうと}にケーキを{食|た}べられた.
- Things: {建|た}てられた, {使|つか}われている; 〜と{言|い}われている (it's said that); によって for the creator.
- New kanji: 建 世 界 有 犬 鳥 池.

lessons.title: Making and letting: the causative
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Parents make children eat their vegetables; bosses have staff write reports; good teachers let students choose. Japanese says all of these with one form of the verb, the **[[causative]]**: {食|た}べさせる (make or let eat), {書|か}かせる (make or let write), えらばせる (make or let choose).

The causative is the second building block of this module. Lesson 21 turned "the teacher praised me" into "I was praised by the teacher"; this lesson adds a new person who causes someone else to act. Lesson 23 then combines the two: "I was made to…". You'll also learn the most useful causative of all, the polite way to ask to be allowed to do something: {帰|かえ}らせてください (please let me go home), {休|やす}ませていただけませんか (could I possibly take the day off?).

The theme is parents and children at home, and bosses and staff at work.

## Making the causative

The causative is built like the passive, with せる in place of れる:

| Group | Rule | Dictionary form | Causative |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | u → a + せる | {書|か}く | {書|か}かせる |
| 1 | | {読|よ}む | {読|よ}ませる |
| 1 | | {待|ま}つ | {待|ま}たせる |
| 1 | | {話|はな}す | {話|はな}させる |
| 1 | う → わ + せる | {言|い}う, {買|か}う | {言|い}わせる, {買|か}わせる |
| 1 | | {行|い}く, あそぶ | {行|い}かせる, あそばせる |
| 2 | る → させる | {食|た}べる, {見|み}る | {食|た}べさせる, {見|み}させる |
| 3 | | する | させる |
| 3 | | {来|く}る | {来|こ}させる |

Again the ない form helps with group 1: {書|か}かない → {書|か}かせる, {言|い}わない → {言|い}わせる. Two endings to watch: verbs in す give 〜させる ({話|はな}させる, かえさせる), which looks like group 2's させる but is just the あ-row さ + せる; and verbs in う give わせる.

Every causative verb is a group 2 verb: {書|か}かせます, {書|か}かせて, {書|か}かせない, {書|か}かせた. The causative is now one of the forms in your conjugation drills. In some casual speech you'll also hear a shorter form ({書|か}かす); learn to recognize it, but use the せる form.

## Who makes whom: を or に

A causative sentence has two people: the one who causes (the subject, with は or が) and the one who does the action (the "causee"). The causee takes を or に, depending on the verb.

With a verb that has its own を object ({食|た}べる something, {書|か}く something), the causee takes に. A Japanese sentence doesn't like two を for one verb:

{母|はは}は{弟|おとうと}に{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べさせました。 — Mother made my brother eat his vegetables.
ぶちょうは{社員|しゃいん}にレポートを{書|か}かせます。 — The department head has the staff write reports.

With a verb that has no object ({行|い}く, {来|く}る, {走|はし}る, なく), the causee usually takes を. {待|ま}たせる (keep someone waiting) works the same way:

{親|おや}は{私|わたし}をじゅくに{行|い}かせました。 — My parents sent me to cram school.
{弟|おとうと}をなかせてしまいました。 — I made my little brother cry.
{友|とも}だちを{一時間|いちじかん}も{待|ま}たせてしまいました。 — I kept my friend waiting a whole hour.

With these verbs に is possible too, and then the sentence tends to mean "let": the person wanted to do it and was allowed to:

{子|こ}どもに{好|す}きなだけあそばせました。 — I let the children play as much as they liked.

This を/に difference is a tendency, not a strict rule; with a verb that already has a を object, only に is possible, and context alone tells make from let.

## Make or let?

The causative itself doesn't say whether the person wanted to act. Context does:

{父|ちち}は{私|わたし}に{車|くるま}を{洗|あら}わせました。 — Father made me wash the car. (probably a chore)
{父|ちち}は{私|わたし}に{車|くるま}を{運転|うんてん}させました。 — Father let me drive the car. (probably a treat)

When you want to be clear that it was "let", add the giving verbs from lesson 7. 〜させてくれる and 〜させてもらう are always "let", and grateful:

{父|ちち}は{私|わたし}に{車|くるま}を{運転|うんてん}させてくれました。 — Father let me drive the car (kindly).
じょうしに{早|はや}く{帰|かえ}らせてもらいました。 — My boss let me go home early.
{親|おや}は{私|わたし}をアメリカにりゅうがくさせてくれました。 — My parents let me study in America.

And 〜させてあげる is "let someone do" from your side: {子|こ}どもにゲームをさせてあげました (I let my child play a game).

A few more from home and work:

むすめにおこづかいで{好|す}きなおもちゃを{買|か}わせました。 — I let my daughter buy the toy she wanted with her pocket money.
むすこには{毎日|まいにち}{犬|いぬ}の{世話|せわ}をさせています。 — I have my son look after the dog every day.
かいぎの{前|まえ}に、{新人|しんじん}にしりょうをコピーさせました。 — Before the meeting, I had the new employee copy the handouts. (しりょう = handouts, materials)

When the boss simply orders, Japanese can also say めいれいする (to give an order): ぶちょうはめいれいするだけで、{自分|じぶん}では{何|なに}もしない (the department head only gives orders and does nothing himself).

### Causing feelings

With verbs of feeling, the causative means "make someone feel": しんぱいさせる (make someone worry), びっくりさせる (surprise), わらわせる (make laugh), なかせる (make cry), おこらせる (make angry).

{夜|よる}おそくまで{帰|かえ}らなくて、{親|おや}をしんぱいさせてしまいました。 — I didn't come home until late at night and made my parents worry.
{弟|おとうと}はいつもおもしろいことを{言|い}って、みんなをわらわせます。 — My brother always says funny things and makes everyone laugh.

The person whose feeling it is takes を.

## Asking to be allowed: 〜させてください

The causative's て form + ください means "please let me…". It's one of the most useful patterns in polite Japanese, because it asks for permission and offers to do something at the same time:

ちょっと{考|かんが}えさせてください。 — Let me think about it for a moment.
{私|わたし}にはらわせてください。 — Please let me pay. (はらう = to pay)
その{仕事|しごと}、{私|わたし}にやらせてください。 — Please let me do that job.

For more politeness, use the request forms from lesson 7:

| Pattern | Feels like | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜させてください | please let me | {帰|かえ}らせてください |
| 〜させてもらえませんか | could you let me | {早|はや}く{帰|かえ}らせてもらえませんか |
| 〜させていただけませんか | could I possibly (very polite) | {明日|あした}、{休|やす}ませていただけませんか |
| 〜させていただきます | I will (humbly announced) | {今日|きょう}は{早|はや}く{帰|かえ}らせていただきます |

The last one doesn't ask; it announces what you're going to do, as if with the listener's kind permission. You'll hear it constantly in shops and offices: {本日|ほんじつ}は{休|やす}ませていただきます (we are closed today). Many speakers feel it's overused, so for yourself keep it for formal announcements.

Remember that {休|やす}む is group 1: {休|やす}ませる, not {休|やす}めさせる. And {帰|かえ}る is group 1 too: {帰|かえ}らせる.

## Dialogue: asking the manager

```dialogue
# In the back room of a café
たむら: {店長|てんちょう}、ちょっといいですか。
= Manager, have you got a moment?
てんちょう: はい、どうしたんですか。
= Yes, what's the matter?
たむら: すみません、{明日|あした}{病院|びょういん}に{行|い}かなければならないので、{午後|ごご}から{休|やす}ませていただけませんか。
= I'm sorry, I have to go to the hospital tomorrow, so could I possibly have the afternoon off?
てんちょう: ああ、いいですよ。じゃあ、{午前|ごぜん}は{新|あたら}しいアルバイトの{人|ひと}に{仕事|しごと}を{教|おし}えてくれますか。
= Ah, that's fine. Then in the morning, could you teach the new part-timer the job?
たむら: はい。レジは{私|わたし}がやってみせて、そうじはやらせてみます。
= Sure. I'll show them the till myself, and I'll have them try the cleaning.
てんちょう: おねがいします。それから、{来週|らいしゅう}のシフトも{田村|たむら}さんにきめさせてあげますよ。
= Thanks. And I'll let you decide next week's shifts, too.
たむら: えっ、いいんですか。ありがとうございます。
= Oh, really? Thank you.
てんちょう: いつもがんばってくれているからね。
= You always work so hard for us.
```

{田村|たむら} is a family name. やってみせる = to show how (do it in front of someone). シフト = shift (work schedule). きめる = to decide.

## Kanji

Six kanji for work and the people who do it. With them you can write N5 words you've used in kana: {働|はたら}く, {使|つか}う, {作|つく}る, {店員|てんいん}, {会社員|かいしゃいん}.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 働 | work | ドウ | はたら(く) | 13 | {働|はたら}く, {働|はたら}き{方|かた} (way of working) |
| 使 | use; messenger | シ | つか(う) | 8 | {使|つか}う, {使|つか}い{方|かた} (lesson 25) |
| 作 | make | サク, サ | つく(る) | 7 | {作|つく}る, {作業|さぎょう}, {作文|さくぶん} (lesson 23) |
| 主 | main; master | シュ, ス | おも, ぬし | 5 | {主人|しゅじん}, {主|おも}に |
| 員 | member | イン | — | 10 | {店員|てんいん}, {社員|しゃいん}, {会社員|かいしゃいん} |
| 業 | business; work; deed | ギョウ, ゴウ | わざ | 13 | {作業|さぎょう}, {工業|こうぎょう} (industry) |

Memory notes:

- 働 is the person radical next to 動 (move, lesson 2): a person who moves is working. It's one of the few kanji created in Japan rather than China.
- 使 is the person radical next to a shape for an official: someone sent with a message, who is used by others.
- 作 is the person radical next to a shape like a saw cutting wood: a person making something.
- 主 is a lamp with a flame (the dot) on top: the master of the house keeps the lamp.
- 員 is a mouth (口) over a shell (shells were once used as money): one mouth, one member, counted like coins.

業 also appears in じゅぎょう (class) and そつぎょう (graduation); this course writes those in kana, because their first kanji are outside the course list.

```trace
働使作主員業
```

## Say it

```speak
ちょっと{考|かんが}えさせてください。
= Let me think about it for a moment.
{明日|あした}、{休|やす}ませていただけませんか。
= Could I possibly take tomorrow off?
{友|とも}だちを{待|ま}たせてしまいました。
= I kept my friend waiting.
{私|わたし}にやらせてください。
= Please let me do it.
{親|おや}をしんぱいさせてしまいました。
= I made my parents worry.
```

## Common mistakes

- させる on group 1 verbs. {書|か}かせる, not {書|か}きさせる or {書|か}くさせる; {休|やす}ませる, not {休|やす}めさせる.
- Missing さ with す verbs. {話|はな}す → {話|はな}させる (はな-さ-せる), not {話|はな}せる, which is the potential.
- Two を in one sentence. {母|はは}は{弟|おとうと}を{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べさせた is wrong: with a を object, the causee takes に.
- Using the causative for "have something done" by a professional. "I had my hair cut" isn't びよういんでかみを{切|き}らせた (that sounds as if you ordered someone around). Say かみを{切|き}ってもらった (lesson 7).
- 〜させていただきます everywhere. It's an announcement, not a request. To ask, use 〜させていただけませんか.

## Key points

- Causative: group 1 あ row + せる ({書|か}かせる, {言|い}わせる, {話|はな}させる); group 2 〜させる; させる; {来|こ}させる. All causatives conjugate like group 2 verbs.
- The causee takes に when the verb has a を object, and usually を when it doesn't (に there leans towards "let").
- Make or let comes from context; 〜させてくれる / 〜させてもらう mean "let", gratefully.
- Feelings: しんぱいさせる, わらわせる, なかせる (the person takes を).
- Asking permission: 〜させてください, 〜させてもらえませんか, 〜させていただけませんか; 〜させていただきます announces.
- New kanji: 働 使 作 主 員 業.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Being made to: the causative-passive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Think back to school: the essays you had to write, the laps you had to run, the songs you had to sing in front of everyone. Japanese has one verb form for exactly this, "I was made to do it (and didn't want to)": the **[[causative-passive]]**.

You already have both halves. Lesson 22 gave you the causative ({母|はは}は{私|わたし}に{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べさせた, Mother made me eat vegetables). Lesson 21 gave you the passive, which makes the person on the receiving end the subject. Put them together and the person who was made to act becomes the subject: {私|わたし}は{母|はは}に{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べさせられた (I was made to eat vegetables by Mother).

The theme is school, clubs and exams, and the things you were made to do as a child.

## From causative to causative-passive

Start from the causative, which is always a group 2 verb ending in せる, and make its passive the group 2 way: せる → せられる.

| Verb | Causative | Causative-passive |
|---|---|---|
| {食|た}べる | {食|た}べさせる | {食|た}べさせられる |
| おぼえる | おぼえさせる | おぼえさせられる |
| する | させる | させられる |
| {来|く}る | {来|こ}させる | {来|こ}させられる |
| {書|か}く | {書|か}かせる | {書|か}かせられる, short: {書|か}かされる |

Group 2 verbs, する and {来|く}る have only this one form. Group 1 verbs have two.

### Group 1: the short form 〜される

For group 1 verbs, the long form ({書|か}かせられる) is correct but heavy, and in everyday Japanese people almost always shorten せられ to され: {書|か}かされる. The short form is simply the verb's あ row + される:

| Verb | ない form | Short (everyday) | Long (also correct) |
|---|---|---|---|
| {書|か}く | {書|か}かない | {書|か}かされる | {書|か}かせられる |
| {待|ま}つ | {待|ま}たない | {待|ま}たされる | {待|ま}たせられる |
| {飲|の}む | {飲|の}まない | {飲|の}まされる | {飲|の}ませられる |
| {歌|うた}う | {歌|うた}わない | {歌|うた}わされる | {歌|うた}わせられる |
| {走|はし}る | {走|はし}らない | {走|はし}らされる | {走|はし}らせられる |
| {行|い}く | {行|い}かない | {行|い}かされる | {行|い}かせられる |

This course uses the short form for group 1 verbs and accepts the long one in answers.

The exception: verbs in す. The short form would give さされる ({話|はな}さされる), two さ in a row, which Japanese avoids. Verbs in す use only the long form:

{話|はな}す → {話|はな}させられる, not {話|はな}さされる
かえす → かえさせられる
{出|だ}す → {出|だ}させられる

Like every passive, the causative-passive conjugates as a group 2 verb: {書|か}かされます, {書|か}かされて, {書|か}かされた, {書|か}かされなかった. It isn't a separate drill form in this course; your conjugation drills practise the causative, and you add られる (or the short される) yourself.

## The sentence: who was made to do what

The person who was made to act is the subject (with は or が, often left out), the one who made them takes に, and the verb's own object keeps を:

| Causative | Causative-passive |
|---|---|
| {先生|せんせい}は{私|わたし}に{作文|さくぶん}を{書|か}かせた。 — The teacher made me write an essay. | {私|わたし}は{先生|せんせい}に{作文|さくぶん}を{書|か}かされた。 — I was made to write an essay by the teacher. |
| せんぱいはこうはいを{走|はし}らせた。 — The older students made the younger ones run. | こうはいはせんぱいに{走|はし}らされた。 — The younger students were made to run by the older ones. |

As in the passive, に marks the one who made it happen. In {私|わたし}は{母|はは}にピアノを{習|なら}わされた, the mother did the making and I did the learning.

More examples:

{小学生|しょうがくせい}のとき、{毎日|まいにち}{漢字|かんじ}を{十回|じゅっかい}ずつ{書|か}かされました。 — In primary school I was made to write each kanji ten times every day.
{駅|えき}で{一時間|いちじかん}も{待|ま}たされました。 — I was kept waiting a whole hour at the station.
{飲|の}み{会|かい}で、おさけを{飲|の}まされました。 — At the drinking party I was made to drink alcohol.
クラスのみんなの{前|まえ}で{歌|うた}わされて、はずかしかったです。 — I was made to sing in front of the whole class, and it was embarrassing.
{夏休|なつやす}みに{毎朝|まいあさ}そうじさせられました。 — During the summer holidays I was made to clean every morning.

Clubs and school life are full of them:

がっしゅくでは、かんとくに{朝|あさ}から{夜|よる}まで{走|はし}らされました。 — At training camp the coach made us run from morning to night.
{国語|こくご}の{時間|じかん}には、たんにんの{先生|せんせい}に{一人|ひとり}ずつ{音読|おんどく}させられました。 — In Japanese class, our class teacher made us read aloud one by one. ({国語|こくご} = Japanese, as a school subject)
{入学|にゅうがく}した{日|ひ}は、{校長先生|こうちょうせんせい}の{長|なが}い{話|はなし}を{一時間|いちじかん}も{聞|き}かされました。 — On our first day at school, we were made to listen to the head teacher's long speech for a whole hour.

{待|ま}たされる (be kept waiting) is so common that it's almost a word of its own: お{待|ま}たせしました (sorry to have kept you waiting) comes from its causative, {待|ま}たせる.

## How it feels: unwilling, not grateful

The causative-passive almost always means the person didn't want to. Compare three ways of saying "I learned the piano because of my mother":

| Sentence | How it feels |
|---|---|
| {母|はは}は{私|わたし}にピアノを{習|なら}わせた。 | Mother made (or let) me learn the piano. (her side) |
| {母|はは}にピアノを{習|なら}わせてもらった。 | Mother let me learn the piano. (I'm grateful; lesson 22) |
| {母|はは}にピアノを{習|なら}わされた。 | I was made to learn the piano by Mother. (I didn't want to) |

So the causative-passive is the form for complaints and memories of chores. If you liked it, use 〜させてもらう; if you hated it, use the causative-passive. Often both feelings come in one story: as a child you were made to do something, and now you're glad. Then the 〜てよかった from lesson 1 does the rest:

{子|こ}どものころはいやだったけど、{毎日|まいにち}ピアノをれんしゅうさせられて、{今|いま}はよかったと{思|おも}っています。 — I hated it as a child, but now I'm glad I was made to practise the piano every day.

## Don't confuse it with the passive or the causative

Three similar forms of {書|か}く, three different meanings:

| Form | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {書|か}かれる | be written (passive) | この{本|ほん}は{英語|えいご}で{書|か}かれています。 — This book is written in English. |
| {書|か}かせる | make/let someone write (causative) | {先生|せんせい}は{学生|がくせい}に{作文|さくぶん}を{書|か}かせた。 |
| {書|か}かされる | be made to write (causative-passive) | {学生|がくせい}は{作文|さくぶん}を{書|か}かされた。 |

Listen for the sound before れる: か-れる is the passive, か-さ-れる and か-せ-られる are the causative-passive. For group 2 verbs it's させられる (two morae longer than the passive), so it's hard to miss: {食|た}べられる (passive or potential) vs {食|た}べさせられる.

## Reading: Kenji's school memories

{私|わたし}の{中学校|ちゅうがっこう}は、ルールがとても{多|おお}い{学校|がっこう}でした。{毎朝|まいあさ}{八時|はちじ}{前|まえ}に{学校|がっこう}に{来|こ}させられて、グラウンドを{走|はし}らされました。{雨|あめ}の{日|ひ}も{走|はし}らされたので、みんないやがっていました。

いちばんこわかったのは、{一年生|いちねんせい}のときの{英語|えいご}の{先生|せんせい}です。その{先生|せんせい}は{毎週|まいしゅう}、せいとに{英語|えいご}の{文|ぶん}を{二十|にじゅう}あんきさせて、テストをしました。てんが{悪|わる}かったせいとは、{教室|きょうしつ}にのこされて、{同|おな}じ{文|ぶん}をノートに{十回|じゅっかい}ずつ{書|か}かされました。

{私|わたし}もよくのこされて、{友|とも}だちに「また？」とわらわれました。でも、そのおかげで、{今|いま}は{英語|えいご}の{文|ぶん}がすぐ{口|くち}から{出|で}てきます。{去年|きょねん}、{会社|かいしゃ}の{英語|えいご}の{試験|しけん}にごうかくしたとき、その{先生|せんせい}を{思|おも}い{出|だ}しました。あのとき{書|か}かされた{文|ぶん}は、{今|いま}もぜんぶおぼえています。

> My middle school was a school with a lot of rules. Every morning we were made to come in before eight and run round the sports ground. We were made to run even on rainy days, so everyone hated it.
>
> The scariest was my English teacher in the first year. Every week she made the pupils memorize twenty English sentences and then tested us. Pupils who got bad marks were kept behind in the classroom and made to write the same sentences ten times each in their notebooks.
>
> I was often kept behind too, and my friends laughed at me: "Again?" But thanks to that, English sentences come straight out of my mouth now. Last year, when I passed my company's English exam, I remembered that teacher. I still remember every sentence I was made to write back then.

{一年生|いちねんせい} = first-year student; せいと = pupil (at a school; {学生|がくせい} is mainly used for university students); のこす = to keep behind (passive のこされる); いやがる = to show you hate something (lesson 25); そのおかげで = thanks to that; {思|おも}い{出|だ}す = to remember, recall.

## Dialogue: club memories

```dialogue
# Two colleagues at lunch
さき: {高校|こうこう}のとき、ぶかつは{何|なに}をしていたんですか。
= What club were you in at high school?
はると: サッカーです。でも、{一年生|いちねんせい}のときは、ボールはあまりさわらせてもらえませんでした。
= Football. But in my first year they hardly let us touch the ball.
さき: えっ、どうしてですか。
= What? Why not?
はると: {毎日|まいにち}{走|はし}らされて、せんぱいたちのボールを{集|あつ}めさせられていたんです。{試合|しあい}にも{出|だ}させてもらえませんでした。
= We were made to run every day and to collect the seniors' balls. They wouldn't let us play in matches either.
さき: たいへんでしたね。{私|わたし}はブラスバンドで、{毎朝|まいあさ}{六時|ろくじ}かられんしゅうさせられました。
= That sounds tough. I was in the brass band, and we were made to practise from six every morning.
はると: {六時|ろくじ}！{早|はや}いですね。
= Six! That's early.
さき: でも、{三年生|さんねんせい}のときに{大|おお}きい{大会|たいかい}でいちばんになって、みんなでないてよろこびました。
= But in our third year we came first in a big competition, and we all cried for joy.
はると: いい{思|おも}い{出|で}ですね。
= What a great memory.
```

さわる = to touch; ブラスバンド = brass band; {大会|たいかい} = competition, tournament; {思|おも}い{出|で} = a memory. さわらせてもらえませんでした and {出|だ}させてもらえませんでした are the causative + もらえない: they wouldn't let us.

## Kanji

Six kanji for study and exams. With them you can write the N5 words {英語|えいご} and {試験|しけん}, and the word {漢字|かんじ} itself.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 英 | England; excellent | エイ | — | 8 | {英語|えいご}, {英会話|えいかいわ} |
| 漢 | China (Han) | カン | — | 13 | {漢字|かんじ} |
| 字 | character, letter | ジ | — | 6 | {字|じ}, {漢字|かんじ}, {文字|もじ} (letter, character) |
| 文 | writing, sentence | ブン, モン | ふみ | 4 | {文|ぶん}, {作文|さくぶん}, {文学|ぶんがく}, {注文|ちゅうもん} |
| 試 | test, try | シ | ため(す) | 13 | {試験|しけん}, {試合|しあい}, {試|ため}す |
| 験 | test, effect | ケン, ゲン | — | 18 | {試験|しけん} |

Memory notes:

- 字 is a child (子) under a roof: children at home learning their letters.
- 文 is a person with a pattern drawn on the chest: marks, and so writing. It's only four strokes: a dot, a horizontal line and two crossing sweeps.
- 試 has words (言) on the left: a test is done with words. 験 has the kanji for horse on the left: picture a horse being put to the test. It's one of the most complicated kanji in the course, so trace it slowly.
- 漢 has the water radical on the left: it was first the name of a river, the Han, which gave its name to a region and to the Han dynasty of China.
- 英 has the grass radical (two short crosses) on top, as in 花 (flower) and 茶 (tea, lesson 27).

{文字|もじ} uses モ, a shortened form of the rarer reading モン; most words use ブン.

```trace
英漢字文試験
```

## Say it

```speak
{駅|えき}で{一時間|いちじかん}も{待|ま}たされました。
= I was kept waiting a whole hour at the station.
{子|こ}どものころ、{毎日|まいにち}ピアノをれんしゅうさせられました。
= As a child I was made to practise the piano every day.
みんなの{前|まえ}で{歌|うた}わされました。
= I was made to sing in front of everyone.
{先生|せんせい}に{作文|さくぶん}を{書|か}かされました。
= The teacher made me write an essay.
いやでしたが、がまんしました。
= I hated it, but I put up with it.
```

## Common mistakes

- Mixing up who made whom. In {私|わたし}は{兄|あに}に{歌|うた}わされた, the brother made me sing. The に person is the one in control.
- ×{話|はな}さされる: verbs in す have only the long form: {話|はな}させられる, かえさせられる.
- The short form with group 2 verbs. {食|た}べさせられる can't be shortened: {食|た}べさされる is wrong. Only group 1 verbs (not in す) have 〜される.
- Using it for something you wanted. If you were glad, say 〜させてもらった: {父|ちち}に{車|くるま}を{運転|うんてん}させてもらった.
- Confusing {書|か}かれる and {書|か}かされる. The first is "be written", the second "be made to write".

## Key points

- Causative-passive = causative + passive: 〜させられる ({食|た}べさせられる, させられる, {来|こ}させられる).
- Group 1: short あ row + される ({書|か}かされる, {待|ま}たされる, {飲|の}まされる) is everyday; the long 〜せられる is also correct. Verbs in す: long only ({話|はな}させられる).
- The one who was made to act is the subject; the one who made them takes に.
- It sounds unwilling. For gratitude, use 〜させてもらう.
- New kanji: 英 漢 字 文 試 験.
