lessons.title: Becoming, habits and goals: ようになる, ようにする, ように, ために
topics: ように and ために
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is about change and effort: things you can do now that you couldn't before, things you've started or stopped doing, habits you're trying to build, and what you do them for. Japanese has a small family of patterns for this, most of them built on よう (a grammar noun meaning roughly "way, manner") and ため (sake, purpose):

- {漢字|かんじ}が{読|よ}めるようになりました。 — I can read kanji now.
- {毎朝|まいあさ}{歩|ある}くようにしています。 — I make a point of walking every morning.
- わすれないように、メモします。 — I'll make a note so that I don't forget.
- {日本|にほん}で{働|はたら}くために、{日本語|にほんご}を{勉強|べんきょう}しています。 — I'm studying Japanese in order to work in Japan.

You'll also learn 〜のに "for (a purpose)", how to say "make it brighter / quieter" (〜くする, 〜にする), and 〜てくる / 〜ていく for change over time. よう and ため are grammar words, so they're always written in kana. The theme is health, exercise and study habits.

## 〜ようになる: can now, have come to

Dictionary form + ようになる describes a change that happened gradually, often after effort: "I've come to…", "I've started…", "now I…".

With the potential form (lesson 2), it means "can now", a new ability:

{三|さん}か{月|げつ}れんしゅうして、およげるようになりました。 — After three months of practice, I can swim now.
{日本語|にほんご}のニュースが{少|すこ}し{分|わ}かるようになりました。 — I've started to understand the news in Japanese a little.
{子|こ}どもが{一人|ひとり}で{自転車|じてんしゃ}に{乗|の}れるようになりました。 — My child can ride a bike on their own now.

With an ordinary verb, it means a new habit or a change in what you do:

{犬|いぬ}をかってから、{毎朝|まいあさ}{早|はや}く{起|お}きるようになりました。 — Since getting a dog, I've started getting up early every morning.
{日本|にほん}に{来|き}て、{魚|さかな}をよく{食|た}べるようになりました。 — Since coming to Japan, I've started eating a lot of fish.

Compare N5's なる after nouns and adjectives ({元気|げんき}になる, {大|おお}きくなる): ようになる is the same idea, after a verb.

### The negative: 〜なくなる

For "can't any more" or "don't any more", put the ない form into なくなる (ない → なく + なる):

{目|め}が{悪|わる}くなって、{小|ちい}さい{字|じ}が{読|よ}めなくなりました。 — My eyes have got worse, and I can't read small print any more.
{子|こ}どもが{大|おお}きくなって、{家族|かぞく}で{旅行|りょこう}しなくなりました。 — Now that the children are older, we don't go on family trips any more.

〜ないようになる also exists, but 〜なくなる is the everyday choice. Use it.

## 〜ようにする: make a point of

Dictionary form (or ない form) + ようにする means "make an effort to, make sure that". 〜ようにしている is the ongoing habit: "I make a point of…".

{毎日|まいにち}{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べるようにしています。 — I make a point of eating vegetables every day.
けんこうのために、エレベーターを{使|つか}わないようにしています。 — For my health, I try not to use lifts.
{明日|あした}から、{夜|よる}{十一時|じゅういちじ}{前|まえ}にねるようにします。 — From tomorrow, I'll make sure I go to bed before eleven.
{毎朝|まいあさ}、{起|お}きたらたいそうかストレッチをするようにしています。 — I make a point of doing some exercises or stretches when I get up every morning.
{野菜|やさい}も{肉|にく}も{食|た}べて、バランスのいい{食事|しょくじ}をするようにしています。 — I try to eat a balanced diet, with vegetables and meat.

It's softer than a firm decision (for that, use 〜ことにする from lesson 4): ようにする is about trying, not about deciding.

〜ようにしてください is a polite instruction, "please make sure to": {薬|くすり}は{毎日|まいにち}{飲|の}むようにしてください (please make sure you take the medicine every day). Doctors and teachers use it a lot.

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜ようになる | a change happened | {走|はし}れるようになった — I can run now |
| 〜なくなる | stopped, or can't any more | {走|はし}れなくなった — I can't run any more |
| 〜ようにする | try to, make sure | {走|はし}るようにする — I'll make sure I run |
| 〜ようにしている | a habit you keep up | {走|はし}るようにしている — I make a point of running |

## So that, in order to: 〜ように and 〜ために

Both join a purpose to an action, but they don't go with the same verbs.

### 〜ために: in order to

Dictionary form + ために: "in order to". The verb is something you decide to do, and the person doing the main action is the one with the goal:

{医者|いしゃ}になるために、{大学|だいがく}で{勉強|べんきょう}しています。 — I'm studying at university to become a doctor.
やせるために、{毎朝|まいあさ}{走|はし}っています。 — I run every morning to lose weight. (やせる = to lose weight)
きんにくを{強|つよ}くするために、ヨガを{始|はじ}めました。 — I've started yoga to strengthen my muscles.
{日本|にほん}の{会社|かいしゃ}で{働|はたら}くために、{日本語|にほんご}を{習|なら}っています。 — I'm learning Japanese in order to work for a Japanese company.

After a noun, のために means "for (the sake of)": {家族|かぞく}のために{料理|りょうり}を{作|つく}ります (I cook for my family), けんこうのために (for my health). In formal writing it can also mean "because of": {雨|あめ}のために{電車|でんしゃ}がおくれました (the trains were delayed because of the rain). Lesson 26 comes back to this use.

### 〜ように: so that

〜ように is "so that": a result you hope for, which you can't simply decide. Use it

- with the potential: {聞|き}こえるように, {読|よ}めるように, {話|はな}せるように;
- with verbs nobody controls: {分|わ}かる, {見|み}える, {聞|き}こえる, なる;
- with the ない form: わすれないように, おくれないように;
- when the person who benefits is someone else.

{後|うし}ろの{人|ひと}にも{聞|き}こえるように、{大|おお}きい{声|こえ}で{話|はな}してください。 — Please speak up so that the people at the back can hear too.
かぜをひかないように、{手|て}をよく{洗|あら}って、うがいをしています。 — I wash my hands well and gargle so that I don't catch a cold.
{子|こ}どもも{読|よ}めるように、ひらがなで{書|か}きました。 — I wrote it in hiragana so that children can read it too.

The same goal can often take either, with a different verb:

| ために (a decision) | ように (a hoped-for result) |
|---|---|
| {日本|にほん}に{行|い}くために、お{金|かね}をためています。 — I'm saving money to go to Japan. | {日本|にほん}に{行|い}けるように、お{金|かね}をためています。 — I'm saving money so that I'll be able to go to Japan. |
| {研究者|けんきゅうしゃ}になるために、{大学|だいがく}に{入|はい}りました。 | ×{研究者|けんきゅうしゃ}になるように… (sounds as if it isn't up to you) |
| ×{聞|き}こえるために… | {聞|き}こえるように、{前|まえ}にすわりました。 — I sat at the front so that I could hear. |

ためる = to save (money). A quick test: if the verb before it is a potential, a ない form or {分|わ}かる/{見|み}える/{聞|き}こえる, choose ように.

You'll also see ように at shrines, on the little wooden prayer boards: ごうかくできますように (may I pass), みんなが{元気|げんき}でいられますように (may everyone stay well). 〜ますように on its own is a wish.

## 〜のに: used for

Dictionary form + のに, followed by a word like {使|つか}う, いい, べんり, ひつよう (necessary) or {時間|じかん}がかかる, means "for doing":

はさみは{紙|かみ}を{切|き}るのに{使|つか}います。 — Scissors are used for cutting paper.
このアプリはたんごをおぼえるのにべんりです。 — This app is handy for learning vocabulary.
{駅|えき}まで{歩|ある}くのに{二十分|にじゅっぷん}かかります。 — It takes twenty minutes to walk to the station.

The の turns 「{紙|かみ}を{切|き}る」 into a noun, "cutting paper", which then takes the particle に. A word that does this is a **[[nominalizer]]**: the same の you met in N5's {読|よ}むのが{好|す}き (I like reading), and こと does the same job in 〜ことができる. With a plain noun you don't need の: このかばんは{旅行|りょこう}にいいです (this bag is good for travelling).

Don't confuse it with the のに of lesson 26 ("even though"), which comes after a whole sentence and expresses surprise or complaint. The のに here is always followed by a word of using, needing or taking time.

## Making it: 〜くする and 〜にする

In N5 you learned 〜くなる and 〜になる (become). Swap なる for する and the meaning becomes "make it so": someone causes the change.

| Word | become (なる) | make (する) |
|---|---|---|
| {明|あか}るい | {明|あか}るくなる — get lighter | {明|あか}るくする — make lighter |
| {小|ちい}さい | {小|ちい}さくなる — get smaller | {小|ちい}さくする — make smaller |
| いい | よくなる — get better | よくする — make better |
| しずか | しずかになる — get quiet | しずかにする — make quiet, be quiet |
| きれい | きれいになる — become clean | きれいにする — clean up, tidy |

テレビの{音|おと}を{小|ちい}さくしてください。 — Please turn the TV down.
すみません、しずかにしてください。 — Excuse me, please be quiet.
{体|からだ}をじょうぶにするために、{毎日|まいにち}{運動|うんどう}しています。 — I exercise every day to make my body strong.

You already know Nにする for choosing (コーヒーにします, lesson 4); it's the same shape, "make it N".

## Change over time: 〜てくる and 〜ていく

The て form + くる or いく can describe a change that moves through time. くる is a change that has come up to now; いく is a change that will go on from now:

{寒|さむ}くなってきましたね。 — It's been getting colder, hasn't it.
{日本語|にほんご}がだんだんおもしろくなってきました。 — Japanese has been getting more and more interesting.
これから、{日本|にほん}に{住|す}む{外国人|がいこくじん}はもっとふえていくでしょう。 — From now on, the number of foreigners living in Japan will probably keep growing. (ふえる = to increase)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: てきた and ていく on a time line
  accDescr: A line from the past to the future. The part from the past up to now is labelled てきた, change that has happened up to now. The part from now into the future is labelled ていく, change that will go on.
  A[past] -- "〜てきた: change up to now" --> B((now))
  B -- "〜ていく: change from now on" --> C[future]
```

The same two verbs also keep their everyday meaning of coming and going after doing something:

ちょっと{飲|の}み{物|もの}を{買|か}ってきます。 — I'll just go and buy a drink (and come back).
かさを{持|も}っていってください。 — Please take an umbrella with you.

As auxiliary verbs after て, くる and いく are written in kana.

## Dialogue: getting fit

```dialogue
# Two colleagues in the office
マヤ: けんさん、このごろ{元気|げんき}そうですね。
= Ken, you're looking well these days.
けん: ありがとう。{去年|きょねん}、{医者|いしゃ}に「もっと{運動|うんどう}するようにしてください」と{言|い}われて、ジムに{行|い}くようになったんです。
= Thanks. Last year my doctor told me to make sure I exercise more, so I started going to the gym.
マヤ: へえ。{毎日|まいにち}{行|い}っているんですか。
= Really? Do you go every day?
けん: {毎日|まいにち}はむりですけど、{週|しゅう}に{三回|さんかい}は{行|い}くようにしています。それから、あまい{物|もの}を{食|た}べないようにしています。
= Every day is too much, but I make a point of going three times a week. And I try not to eat sweet things.
マヤ: すごいですね。{体重|たいじゅう}もへりましたか。
= Impressive. Have you lost weight, too?
けん: {五|ご}キロへりました。かいだんを{上|のぼ}っても、つかれなくなりました。
= I've lost five kilos. I don't get tired any more, even going up stairs.
マヤ: いいですね。{私|わたし}も{運動|うんどう}しなきゃ。でも、{仕事|しごと}がいそがしくて……
= Great. I should exercise too. But work's so busy…
けん: じゃあ、エレベーターを{使|つか}わないようにするのはどうですか。それだけでも、ずいぶんちがいますよ。
= Then how about trying not to use the lift? Even that makes quite a difference.
マヤ: そうですね。{明日|あした}からやってみます。
= You're right. I'll try it from tomorrow.
```

へる = to go down, decrease; かいだん = stairs; ずいぶん = quite, very.

## Reading: a year of Japanese

{日本語|にほんご}の{勉強|べんきょう}を{始|はじ}めて、{一年|いちねん}になりました。はじめはひらがなも{読|よ}めませんでしたが、{今|いま}は{漢字|かんじ}が{二百|にひゃく}ぐらい{読|よ}めるようになりました。

{私|わたし}が{気|き}をつけていることは{三|みっ}つあります。{一|ひと}つ{目|め}は、{毎日|まいにち}{少|すこ}しでも{勉強|べんきょう}するようにしていることです。いそがしい{日|ひ}も、{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}でたんごを{十|じゅう}おぼえます。{二|ふた}つ{目|め}は、{発音|はつおん}がよくなるように、{声|こえ}に{出|だ}して{読|よ}むことです。{三|みっ}つ{目|め}は、{勉強|べんきょう}に{集中|しゅうちゅう}できるように、スマホを{別|べつ}のへやにおいておくことです。

{来年|らいねん}のもくひょうは、{日本|にほん}の{大学|だいがく}で{研究|けんきゅう}するために、もっとむずかしい{本|ほん}が{読|よ}めるようになることです。{勉強|べんきょう}がだんだんおもしろくなってきたので、これからもつづけていきたいです。

> It's been a year since I started studying Japanese. At first I couldn't even read hiragana, but now I can read about two hundred kanji.
>
> There are three things I'm careful about. The first is that I make a point of studying every day, even a little. Even on busy days I learn ten words on the train. The second is that I read aloud so that my pronunciation gets better. The third is that I leave my phone in another room so that I can concentrate on studying.
>
> My goal for next year is to be able to read harder books, so that I can do research at a Japanese university. Studying has been getting more and more interesting, so I want to keep it up.

{声|こえ}に{出|だ}して{読|よ}む = to read aloud; {別|べつ} = another, separate; つづける = to continue.

## Kanji

Six kanji for study and effort. With them you can write the N5 words {勉強|べんきょう}する, {習|なら}う, {注意|ちゅうい}, {注文|ちゅうもん} and {集|あつ}める.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 勉 | effort | ベン | — | 10 | {勉強|べんきょう} |
| 習 | learn | シュウ | なら(う) | 11 | {習|なら}う, {学習|がくしゅう}, {習|なら}い{事|ごと} |
| 研 | polish, sharpen | ケン | と(ぐ) | 9 | {研究|けんきゅう}, {研究者|けんきゅうしゃ} |
| 究 | investigate | キュウ | きわ(める) | 7 | {研究|けんきゅう} |
| 注 | pour; attention | チュウ | そそ(ぐ) | 8 | {注意|ちゅうい}, {注文|ちゅうもん} |
| 集 | gather | シュウ | あつ(まる), あつ(める) | 12 | {集|あつ}まる, {集|あつ}める, {集中|しゅうちゅう} |

Memory notes:

- 勉 has 力 (power, lesson 2) on the right: studying takes effort.
- 習 is two wings over 白 (white): a young white bird beating its wings again and again until it learns to fly.
- 集 is a small bird on top of 木 (tree): birds gathering in a tree.
- 注 has the water radical on the left and 主 (lesson 22) on the right: pouring oil into the master's lamp.
- 研 has the kanji for stone on the left: polishing on a stone until it's sharp. 究 has a hole on top: searching to the bottom of a hole. Together, 研究 is "research".

The kun'yomi と(ぐ), きわ(める) and そそ(ぐ) are for recognition only; at N4 you'll meet these kanji mostly in their on'yomi words.

```trace
勉習研究注集
```

## Say it

```speak
{漢字|かんじ}が{読|よ}めるようになりました。
= I can read kanji now.
{毎朝|まいあさ}{歩|ある}くようにしています。
= I make a point of walking every morning.
わすれないように、メモします。
= I'll make a note so that I don't forget.
{日本|にほん}で{働|はたら}くために、{日本語|にほんご}を{勉強|べんきょう}しています。
= I'm studying Japanese in order to work in Japan.
{寒|さむ}くなってきましたね。
= It's been getting colder, hasn't it.
しずかにしてください。
= Please be quiet.
```

## Common mistakes

- ために with a potential or a ない form. ×{聞|き}こえるために, ×わすれないために (in the sense "so that I don't forget"): use ように.
- ように with a plain decision of your own. {医者|いしゃ}になるために{勉強|べんきょう}する is the natural "in order to".
- ようになる after a noun. "I became a doctor" is {医者|いしゃ}になった; {医者|いしゃ}のようになった means "I became like a doctor".
- 〜ないようになる for "not any more". It exists, but 〜なくなる is what people say: {食|た}べなくなった.
- 〜くなる vs 〜くする. へやが{明|あか}るくなった (the room got lighter by itself) vs へやを{明|あか}るくした (I made the room lighter). する takes を.
- Mixing up the two のに. "For doing" is followed by {使|つか}う/いい/べんり/ひつよう/かかる; "even though" isn't.

## Key points

- 〜ようになる: a gradual change, "can now" with the potential; 〜なくなる for "not any more".
- 〜ようにする / ようにしている: make an effort to, make a point of; 〜ようにしてください: please make sure to.
- 〜ために: in order to (a verb you decide; same person); Nのために: for N.
- 〜ように: so that (potentials, {分|わ}かる/{見|み}える/{聞|き}こえる, ない forms, someone else benefits). 〜ますように: a wish.
- 〜のに + {使|つか}う/いい/べんり/かかる: for doing (の is a nominalizer).
- 〜くする / 〜にする: make it…; 〜てくる / 〜ていく: change up to now / from now on.
- New kanji: 勉 習 研 究 注 集.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Easy, hard, too much, how to: やすい, にくい, すぎる, かた, さ, がる
topics: やすい and にくい
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Online shops and reviews are full of short, packed descriptions: {使|つか}いやすい (easy to use), {重|おも}すぎる (too heavy), {使|つか}い{方|かた}が{分|わ}かりにくい (it's hard to work out how to use it). This lesson gives you the word-building endings that make them, all of which attach to a stem you already know:

| Ending | Attaches to | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| やすい | ます stem | easy to | {使|つか}いやすい |
| にくい | ます stem | hard to | {読|よ}みにくい |
| すぎる | ます stem, adjective stem | too (much) | {食|た}べすぎる, {高|たか}すぎる |
| {方|かた} | ます stem | way of, how to | {使|つか}い{方|かた} |
| さ | adjective stem | -ness (a measurable quality) | {重|おも}さ, {長|なが}さ |
| がる | adjective stem, 〜たい stem | (someone else) shows a feeling | ほしがる, {行|い}きたがる |

To finish, 〜と{同|おな}じ and 〜とちがう for saying what's the same and what's different. The theme is products, online shopping and reviews.

## Easy and hard to: 〜やすい, 〜にくい

The ます stem (the form before ます: {使|つか}い, {読|よ}み, {食|た}べ) + やすい means "easy to do", and + にくい "hard to do":

このかばんは{軽|かる}くて{使|つか}いやすいです。 — This bag is light and easy to use.
{先生|せんせい}の{説明|せつめい}はいつも{分|わ}かりやすいです。 — The teacher's explanations are always easy to understand.
この{字|じ}は{小|ちい}さくて{読|よ}みにくいです。 — This writing is small and hard to read.
このくつは{歩|ある}きにくいです。 — These shoes are hard to walk in.

The result is an ordinary い-adjective, so it conjugates like one: {使|つか}いやすくない (not easy to use), {使|つか}いやすかった (was easy to use), {使|つか}いやすくて (easy to use, and…), and it can go before a noun: {使|つか}いやすいパソコン (an easy-to-use computer).

With verbs of things happening by themselves, やすい means "tend to, easily": このコップはわれやすいです (this glass breaks easily; われる = to break, of glass), {冬|ふゆ}はかぜをひきやすいです (you catch colds easily in winter).

This やすい is written in kana: it isn't {安|やす}い (cheap), though it sounds the same. にくい is in kana too.

## Too much: 〜すぎる

すぎる on its own means "to go past" ({十二時|じゅうにじ}をすぎる, to be past twelve). After a stem it means "too much": too far past the right amount.

| Word | Stem | 〜すぎる |
|---|---|---|
| {食|た}べる | {食|た}べ | {食|た}べすぎる — eat too much |
| {飲|の}む | {飲|の}み | {飲|の}みすぎる — drink too much |
| {働|はたら}く | {働|はたら}き | {働|はたら}きすぎる — work too much |
| {高|たか}い | {高|たか} | {高|たか}すぎる — too expensive |
| {重|おも}い | {重|おも} | {重|おも}すぎる — too heavy |
| いい | (よ) | よすぎる — too good |
| ない | (な) | なさすぎる — too little (of something) |
| しずか | しずか | しずかすぎる — too quiet |
| べんり | べんり | べんりすぎる — too convenient |

い-adjectives drop the い; な-adjectives just add すぎる. Two irregulars: いい becomes よすぎる (the よ of よくない), and ない becomes なさすぎる ({時間|じかん}がなさすぎる, there's far too little time).

すぎる is a group 2 verb: {高|たか}すぎます, {高|たか}すぎて, {高|たか}すぎた, {高|たか}すぎない.

このスーツケースは{大|おお}きすぎて、{電車|でんしゃ}に{持|も}って{乗|の}れません。 — This suitcase is too big to take on the train.
きのうは{飲|の}みすぎて、{今朝|けさ}は{頭|あたま}がいたいです。 — I drank too much yesterday, and I have a headache this morning.
ねだんは{安|やす}いけど、{品質|ひんしつ}が{低|ひく}すぎます。 — It's cheap, but the quality is far too low.

The verb stem alone, with すぎ, is also a noun: {食|た}べすぎ (overeating), {飲|の}みすぎ (drinking too much), {働|はたら}きすぎ (overwork). {飲|の}みすぎに{注意|ちゅうい}しましょう (take care not to drink too much) is a classic poster line.

## How to: stem + {方|かた}

The ます stem + {方|かた} is "the way of doing", "how to":

{使|つか}う → {使|つか}い{方|かた} (how to use)
{読|よ}む → {読|よ}み{方|かた} (how to read; the reading of a kanji)
{作|つく}る → {作|つく}り{方|かた} (how to make; a recipe)
{行|い}く → {行|い}き{方|かた} (how to get there)

The result is a noun, so the verb's object takes の, not を:

この{漢字|かんじ}の{読|よ}み{方|かた}を{教|おし}えてください。 — Please tell me how to read this kanji.
すみません、このアプリの{使|つか}い{方|かた}が{分|わ}かりません。 — Excuse me, I don't know how to use this app.
{駅|えき}までの{行|い}き{方|かた}を{聞|き}きました。 — I asked the way to the station.

For する verbs, use Nの{仕方|しかた}: {注文|ちゅうもん}の{仕方|しかた} (how to order), へんぴんの{仕方|しかた} (how to return something). {仕方|しかた} is する's stem し + {方|かた}, written with 仕.

## -ness: 〜さ

An い-adjective's stem + さ makes a noun for the quality, usually something you can measure:

| Adjective | Noun | |
|---|---|---|
| {重|おも}い | {重|おも}さ | weight |
| {長|なが}い | {長|なが}さ | length |
| {高|たか}い | {高|たか}さ | height (also: how expensive) |
| {大|おお}きい | {大|おお}きさ | size |
| {寒|さむ}い | {寒|さむ}さ | (how) cold |
| いい | よさ | good points, merit |
| べんり | べんりさ | convenience |

このスーツケースの{重|おも}さはどのぐらいですか。 — How heavy is this suitcase?
{日本|にほん}の{冬|ふゆ}の{寒|さむ}さにおどろきました。 — I was surprised by how cold Japanese winters are. (おどろく = to be surprised)

Online shops also love a few short nouns from this lesson's word list: {新品|しんぴん} (brand new), {中古|ちゅうこ} (second-hand), {品切|しなぎ}れ (sold out), ポイント (loyalty points), {送料|そうりょう}むりょう (free shipping).

When you shop online, the product page usually lists {大|おお}きさ, {重|おも}さ, {長|なが}さ and {高|たか}さ, so these are worth knowing by sight.

## Other people's feelings: 〜がる, 〜たがる

Japanese speakers are careful about stating someone else's feelings directly. {私|わたし}はほしい (I want it) is fine, but {弟|おとうと}はほしい sounds odd: you can't feel your brother's wanting. N5 got round this with 〜と{言|い}っていました. Another way is 〜がる, "show signs of feeling": it describes the feeling you can see from the outside.

| Feeling word | 〜がる |
|---|---|
| ほしい (want) | ほしがる |
| 〜たい ({行|い}きたい) | 〜たがる ({行|い}きたがる) |
| こわい (scared) | こわがる |
| いや (unpleasant) | いやがる |
| {寒|さむ}い (cold) | {寒|さむ}がる |

Drop an い-adjective's い and add がる; a な-adjective such as いや just adds がる. The result is a group 1 verb: ほしがります, ほしがって, ほしがった. For what someone feels now, it's usually in the ている form:

{弟|おとうと}は{新|あたら}しいゲームをほしがっています。 — My little brother wants the new game.
{子|こ}どもたちはどうぶつえんに{行|い}きたがっています。 — The children want to go to the zoo.
うちの{犬|いぬ}はかみなりをこわがります。 — Our dog is scared of thunder. (かみなり = thunder)

Two things to notice. With ほしがる and 〜たがる, the thing wanted takes を, not が: ゲームをほしがる. And 〜がる is for other people, often children, family and animals; using it about your teacher or boss sounds as if you're reporting on them, so in polite talk about superiors, avoid it.

## Same and different: 〜と{同|おな}じ, 〜とちがう

{同|おな}じ (same) behaves unusually: it goes straight before a noun, without な or の:

{同|おな}じ{色|いろ} — the same colour (not ×{同|おな}じな{色|いろ}, ×{同|おな}じの{色|いろ})
{同|おな}じ{店|みせ} — the same shop

To say "the same as N", use Nと{同|おな}じ; "different from N" is Nとちがう. ちがう is a group 1 verb (ちがいます, ちがって, ちがった):

このかばんは{私|わたし}のと{同|おな}じです。 — This bag is the same as mine.
とどいた{品物|しなもの}は、{写真|しゃしん}とちがいました。 — The item that arrived was different from the photo.
AとBは{大|おお}きさは{同|おな}じですが、{重|おも}さがちがいます。 — A and B are the same size but different in weight.
このつくえは、あのつくえと{同|おな}じぐらいの{高|たか}さです。 — This desk is about the same height as that one.

ちがう also means "to be wrong": {答|こた}えがちがいます (the answer is wrong). Context tells you which.

## Reading: three reviews

「かるいリュック」のレビュー

★★★★★ ゆうと（{二十代|にじゅうだい}）
ほんとうに{軽|かる}いです。{重|おも}さは{五百|ごひゃく}グラムしかありません。ポケットが{多|おお}くて、{物|もの}を{入|い}れやすいです。{毎日|まいにち}{会社|かいしゃ}に{持|も}っていっています。

★★★☆☆ みき（{三十代|さんじゅうだい}）
{使|つか}いやすいですが、{私|わたし}には{少|すこ}し{小|ちい}さすぎました。パソコンが{入|はい}りにくいです。{色|いろ}は{写真|しゃしん}と{同|おな}じで、きれいでした。

★☆☆☆☆ ひろし（{五十代|ごじゅうだい}）
{注文|ちゅうもん}してから{二週間|にしゅうかん}もとどきませんでした。とどいたリュックは、{写真|しゃしん}と{色|いろ}がちがいました。へんぴんの{仕方|しかた}も{分|わ}かりにくくて、さいていでした。{子|こ}どもはほしがっていましたが、もう{買|か}いません。

> Reviews of the "Light Rucksack"
>
> ★★★★★ Yuto (20s): It really is light. It weighs only 500 grams. It has lots of pockets, so it's easy to put things in. I take it to work every day.
>
> ★★★☆☆ Miki (30s): It's easy to use, but it was a bit too small for me. It's hard to get a laptop into it. The colour was the same as in the photo, and pretty.
>
> ★☆☆☆☆ Hiroshi (50s): It didn't arrive for two whole weeks after I ordered it. The rucksack that came was a different colour from the photo. And it was hard to work out how to return it. Terrible. My child wanted it, but I won't buy from them again.

リュック = rucksack, backpack; 〜{代|だい} = in one's …s (age); ポケット = pocket.

## Dialogue: which suitcase?

```dialogue
# Shopping online
あや: ねえ、{旅行|りょこう}のスーツケース、どっちがいいと{思|おも}う？
= Hey, which suitcase do you think is better for the trip?
りく: {見|み}せて。こっちは{安|やす}いけど、{重|おも}さが{五|ご}キロもあるね。ちょっと{重|おも}すぎない？
= Show me. This one's cheap, but it weighs five kilos. Isn't that a bit too heavy?
あや: そうなんだよね。こっちは{三|さん}キロで{軽|かる}いんだけど、ねだんが{高|たか}すぎて……
= That's the thing. This one's only three kilos, but it's way too expensive…
りく: レビューは？
= What do the reviews say?
あや: {軽|かる}いほうは「{引|ひ}きやすい」って{書|か}いてある。{安|やす}いほうは「すぐこわれた」って。
= For the light one they say "easy to pull". For the cheap one, "broke straight away".
りく: こわれやすいのはこまるね。{大|おお}きさは{同|おな}じ？
= Breaking easily is no good. Are they the same size?
あや: うん、{大|おお}きさは{同|おな}じだけど、{色|いろ}がちがう。{軽|かる}いほうは{三|さん}しゅるいからえらべるよ。
= Yes, the same size, but different colours. The light one comes in three colours.
りく: じゃあ、{軽|かる}いほうがいいよ。{長|なが}く{使|つか}えるから。{送料|そうりょう}は？
= Then get the light one. You'll be able to use it for a long time. What about shipping?
あや: {一万円|いちまんえん}{以上|いじょう}だとむりょうだって。よし、これにする！
= Free over ten thousand yen, it says. Right, I'll take this one!
```

{引|ひ}く = to pull; 〜って{書|か}いてある = it says (in writing) that…

## Kanji

Seven kanji for things and how they feel in your hand. With them you can write many N5 words you've written in kana: {重|おも}い, {軽|かる}い, {短|みじか}い, {低|ひく}い, {同|おな}じ, and every word with {物|もの}: {食|た}べ{物|もの}, {飲|の}み{物|もの}, {買|か}い{物|もの}.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 物 | thing | ブツ, モツ | もの | 8 | {物|もの}, {動物|どうぶつ}, {品物|しなもの}, {買|か}い{物|もの} |
| 品 | goods; quality | ヒン | しな | 9 | {品物|しなもの}, {食品|しょくひん}, {作品|さくひん}, {品質|ひんしつ} |
| 重 | heavy | ジュウ, チョウ | おも(い) | 9 | {重|おも}い, {重|おも}さ, {体重|たいじゅう} |
| 軽 | light (not heavy) | ケイ | かる(い) | 12 | {軽|かる}い, {気軽|きがる} |
| 短 | short | タン | みじか(い) | 12 | {短|みじか}い |
| 低 | low | テイ | ひく(い) | 7 | {低|ひく}い |
| 同 | same | ドウ | おな(じ) | 6 | {同|おな}じ |

Memory notes:

- 品 is three mouths, or three boxes piled up: goods stacked in a shop.
- 物 has 牛 (cow, lesson 16) on the left: in the old days a cow was the most valuable thing a family owned.
- 軽 has 車 (vehicle) on the left: a light cart is easy to pull.
- 短 has the kanji for arrow on the left: an arrow is short compared with a spear.
- 同 is a frame with 一 and 口 inside: everyone speaking with one mouth, the same.
- 重 has 日 and the lines of a heavy load stacked through the middle: count the horizontal strokes carefully when you trace it.

物 has two on'yomi: ブツ in {動物|どうぶつ}, and モツ in にもつ (luggage), which this course writes in kana because its first kanji is outside the list.

```trace
物品重軽短低同
```

## Say it

```speak
このかばんは{使|つか}いやすいです。
= This bag is easy to use.
この{字|じ}は{読|よ}みにくいです。
= This writing is hard to read.
ちょっと{高|たか}すぎますね。
= It's a bit too expensive, isn't it.
きのうは{食|た}べすぎました。
= I ate too much yesterday.
このアプリの{使|つか}い{方|かた}を{教|おし}えてください。
= Please show me how to use this app.
{写真|しゃしん}とちがいます。
= It's different from the photo.
```

## Common mistakes

- The full adjective before すぎる. ×{高|たか}いすぎる: drop the い, {高|たか}すぎる. And いい → よすぎる, not ×いすぎる.
- The dictionary form before やすい / すぎる / {方|かた}. ×{使|つか}うやすい, ×{食|た}べるすぎる: use the ます stem, {使|つか}いやすい, {食|た}べすぎる.
- を before {方|かた}. ×{漢字|かんじ}を{読|よ}み{方|かた}: {方|かた} makes a noun, so it's {漢字|かんじ}の{読|よ}み{方|かた}.
- な after {同|おな}じ. ×{同|おな}じな{色|いろ}: just {同|おな}じ{色|いろ}.
- がる about yourself. {私|わたし}はほしがっています sounds as if you're describing yourself from outside. Say ほしいです.
- やすい "easy" vs {安|やす}い "cheap". {使|つか}いやすい is always "easy to use", never "cheap to use".

## Key points

- ます stem + やすい / にくい: easy / hard to (an い-adjective).
- 〜すぎる: too much. Verb stem, adjective stem (い dropped), な-adjective; いい → よすぎる, ない → なさすぎる. Noun: {食|た}べすぎ.
- ます stem + {方|かた}: how to; the object takes の: {漢字|かんじ}の{読|よ}み{方|かた}. する verbs: Nの{仕方|しかた}.
- Adjective stem + さ: {重|おも}さ, {長|なが}さ, {大|おお}きさ, よさ.
- 〜がる / 〜たがる: other people's visible feelings (often 〜がっている); the object takes を.
- {同|おな}じ + noun (no な); Nと{同|おな}じ, Nとちがう.
- New kanji: 物 品 重 軽 短 低 同.

lessons.title: School life in Japan
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Almost every Japanese adult can tell you stories about school: the club that practised every morning, the senior students who had to be obeyed, the sports day, the entrance exams. These stories are full of the forms from this module: {走|はし}らされた (we were made to run), そうじさせられた (we were made to clean), {好|す}きなことをさせてもらった (they let us do what we liked). This lesson gives you the background to understand them, and the words to tell your own.

The details below are typical, not universal: Japan has public and private schools, and rules differ from school to school and from region to region.

## The school year

The Japanese school year starts in April and ends in March. Most schools divide it into three terms, with a summer holiday from late July to the end of August, a short winter holiday over the New Year and a short spring holiday before the new year begins. Some schools use two terms instead.

The year opens with an entrance ceremony (にゅうがくしき) in early April, often under the cherry blossoms, and ends with a graduation ceremony (そつぎょうしき) in March. That's why spring in Japan is linked to new beginnings: new schools, new classes, and for many people new jobs, which also start in April.

| School | Ages (roughly) | Years | |
|---|---|---|---|
| {小学校|しょうがっこう} | 6–12 | 6 | compulsory |
| {中学校|ちゅうがっこう} | 12–15 | 3 | compulsory |
| {高校|こうこう} | 15–18 | 3 | not compulsory, but almost everyone goes |
| {大学|だいがく} / せんもんがっこう | 18– | 4 / 2 or so | university / vocational college |

{一年生|いちねんせい}, {二年生|にねんせい}… means first-year, second-year student at any level; the numbers start again at each school.

## Entrance exams

At the end of middle school, most students take a high school entrance exam ({高校入試|こうこうにゅうし}), and many high school students later take university entrance exams ({大学入試|だいがくにゅうし}). Some children also take exams to get into a private middle school. Taking an entrance exam is じゅけん, and a student preparing for one is a じゅけんせい.

Many students prepare at じゅく (cram school) in the evenings and holidays, on top of their school homework. Exams are in winter, and at shrines you'll see wooden boards with wishes such as ごうかくできますように (may I pass), written in the 〜ますように form from lesson 24.

## Clubs: ぶかつ

Middle and high schools have clubs after school, called ぶかつ: sports clubs (サッカー, やきゅう, バスケットボール…) and culture clubs (ブラスバンド, {茶道|さどう} tea ceremony, {書道|しょどう} calligraphy, {写真|しゃしん}…). At many schools almost everyone joins one, and keen clubs practise every day, early in the morning, and at weekends. In recent years many areas have started to limit club hours, to give students and teachers more rest.

Clubs are where students learn the せんぱい / こうはい relationship. A せんぱい is anyone who started before you (older students in the club, colleagues who joined the company before you); a こうはい started after you. こうはい usually speak politely to せんぱい and, in some clubs, are expected to do the chores: carrying equipment, collecting balls, cleaning up. The relationship carries on into working life, and it explains many causative-passive memories:

{一年生|いちねんせい}のときは、せんぱいにボールを{集|あつ}めさせられました。 — In my first year, the seniors made us collect the balls.
{毎朝|まいあさ}{六時|ろくじ}に{来|こ}させられて、グラウンドを{何回|なんかい}も{走|はし}らされました。 — We were made to come in at six every morning and run round the sports ground again and again.

## School events

Two events fill the calendar of most schools.

{運動会|うんどうかい} (sports day). Races, relays and team games, with the whole school divided into teams, often red and white. Families come to watch and eat a packed lunch together on mats. Many schools hold it in autumn, and some in spring.

ぶんかさい (school festival). Mainly at middle and high schools, usually in autumn. Each class or club runs something for a day or two: a café, a haunted house, a play, a concert or an exhibition. Visitors, including families and students from other schools, can often come in.

Most schools also take each year group on one longer school trip (しゅうがくりょこう) at elementary, middle and high school, often to Kyoto and Nara or, for high schools, sometimes abroad.

## Uniforms, cleaning and lunch

Uniforms. Most middle and high schools have a せいふく (uniform); public elementary schools usually don't. Inside the building, students change into indoor shoes (うわばき) at the entrance, just as people take their shoes off at home.

Cleaning. At most schools, students clean their own classrooms, corridors and toilets in a short cleaning time every day, in groups that take turns. Many people say it taught them to look after shared places.

Lunch. At elementary school, and at many public middle schools, a school lunch (きゅうしょく) is served in the classroom, and the students take turns to serve it to each other, in white coats and caps.

## Talking about school memories

The forms from lessons 22 and 23 let you say how you felt:

| You want to say | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| They made us (and we didn't like it) | causative-passive | {毎日|まいにち}そうじさせられました。 |
| They let us (and we were glad) | causative + もらう/くれる | {先生|せんせい}が{好|す}きな{歌|うた}を{歌|うた}わせてくれました。 |
| What someone made others do | causative | せんぱいはこうはいにボールを{集|あつ}めさせました。 |
| Something done to us | passive | {先生|せんせい}によくほめられました。 |

## Dialogue: comparing schools

```dialogue
# A student from abroad and a Japanese friend
エミリー: {日本|にほん}の{学校|がっこう}では、せいとがそうじをするってほんとう？
= Is it true that students do the cleaning in Japanese schools?
たいち: うん、{毎日|まいにち}そうじさせられたよ。トイレのそうじもさせられた。
= Yeah, we were made to clean every day. Even the toilets.
エミリー: たいへんだったね。ぶかつは{何|なに}をしていたの？
= That sounds hard. What club were you in?
たいち: やきゅう。{一年生|いちねんせい}のときは、せんぱいのボールを{集|あつ}めさせられてばかりだった。
= Baseball. In my first year, all we did was get made to collect the seniors' balls.
エミリー: {試合|しあい}には{出|で}られた？
= Did you get to play in matches?
たいち: {三年生|さんねんせい}になってから、やっと{出|だ}させてもらえた。
= Only in my third year did they finally let me play.
エミリー: {私|わたし}の{国|くに}にはぶかつがあまりないから、ちょっとうらやましいな。
= We don't really have school clubs in my country, so I'm a little jealous.
たいち: でも、{運動会|うんどうかい}やぶんかさいは{楽|たの}しかったよ。いい{思|おも}い{出|で}だね。
= But sports day and the school festival were fun. Good memories.
```

せいと = pupil, school student; ほんとう = true; 〜てばかり = do nothing but (lesson 14); やっと = finally; うらやましい = envious.

## Say it

```speak
{毎日|まいにち}そうじさせられました。
= We were made to clean every day.
せんぱいに{走|はし}らされました。
= The seniors made us run.
{先生|せんせい}が{好|す}きなことをさせてくれました。
= The teacher let us do what we liked.
ぶかつは{何|なに}をしていましたか。
= What club were you in?
ごうかくできますように。
= May I pass.
```

## Key points

- The school year runs from April to March. {小学校|しょうがっこう} (6 years) and {中学校|ちゅうがっこう} (3) are compulsory; almost everyone goes on to {高校|こうこう} (3).
- {入試|にゅうし} (entrance exams) at the end of middle and high school; many students go to じゅく.
- ぶかつ (clubs) and the せんぱい / こうはい relationship.
- Events: {運動会|うんどうかい}, ぶんかさい, しゅうがくりょこう. Most middle and high schools have せいふく; students clean their schools.
- For memories: causative-passive for what you were made to do, 〜させてもらう/くれる for what you were allowed to do.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Working in Japan
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Many learners first use their Japanese at work: a part-time job in a café or a convenience store, an office, a lab. Japanese workplaces have their own habits and their own set phrases, and they're also where you'll hear the forms from this module every day: {休|やす}ませていただけませんか (could I take the day off?), ざんぎょうさせられた (I was made to work overtime), {店長|てんちょう}にほめられた (the manager praised me).

This lesson describes common practice in general terms. Workplaces differ a lot: a start-up in Tokyo and a family factory in the countryside feel very different, and things have been changing quickly.

## Part-time jobs and interviews

Part-time work, アルバイト (often just バイト), is very common among students: in convenience stores, restaurants, supermarkets, cram schools and warehouses. Pay is usually by the hour (じきゅう, hourly wage), and you work shifts (シフト) agreed in advance. Students from abroad who want to work usually need permission first and can only work a limited number of hours a week; check the current rules before you look for a job.

Getting a job usually starts with a short めんせつ (interview). You bring a りれきしょ, a résumé on a fixed form (sold in convenience stores, or downloaded) with your photo, education and work history. Typical interview manners:

- Knock, open the door, and say しつれいします as you go in.
- Wait to be asked to sit down: どうぞ、おかけください (please have a seat; a polite phrase to recognize).
- Answer clearly: which days and hours you can work, when you can start, why you want the job.
- When you leave, stand, bow and say ありがとうございました、しつれいします.

Many of the questions use the potential (lesson 2): {週|しゅう}に{何日|なんにち}{働|はたら}けますか (how many days a week can you work?), {何時|なんじ}から{来|こ}られますか (from what time can you come?).

## ほうれんそう: report, contact, consult

New employees in Japan are often taught the word ほうれんそう. It sounds like the word for spinach, but here it's made from three words of office life:

| | Word | Meaning | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| ほう | ほうこく(する) | report | tell your boss how a task went, good or bad |
| れん | れんらく(する) | contact, let know | pass on information: you'll be late, a customer called |
| そう | そうだん(する) | consult | ask for advice before you decide |

The idea is that bad news should travel fast and nobody should make big decisions alone. Even in a part-time job, if you break something or make a mistake, report it straight away: すみません、コップをわってしまいました (sorry, I broke a glass).

## Drinking after work

The {飲|の}み{会|かい} (drinking party) after work, with colleagues and the boss, has long been part of Japanese office life. At the start everyone waits until all glasses are full and someone calls かんぱい (cheers); people often pour drinks for each other rather than for themselves. Office parties at the end of the year and in spring, to welcome new staff, are common.

Many companies hold fewer drinking parties than before, and many younger workers say they'd rather not go, or go without drinking alcohol. Saying no politely is normal: すみません、{今日|きょう}はちょっと…… is understood.

## Overtime and paid leave

Long working hours and ざんぎょう (overtime) have long been a known problem in Japan, and in recent years laws have limited how much overtime companies can ask for. By law, workers also get ゆうきゅう (paid leave), which grows with the years they've worked. Many people don't take all of it, partly so as not to burden colleagues; since 2019, companies have had to make sure that most full-time workers take at least five days a year.

When you ask for time off, the causative from lesson 22 is the polite way:

{来週|らいしゅう}の{金曜日|きんようび}、ゆうきゅうをとらせていただけませんか。 — Would it be all right if I took paid leave next Friday?
すみません、かぜをひいたので、{今日|きょう}は{休|やす}ませてください。 — I'm sorry, I've caught a cold, so please let me take today off.

And when you complain to a friend afterwards, the causative-passive from lesson 23: きのうも{夜|よる}{九時|くじ}までざんぎょうさせられたよ (they made me work overtime until nine again yesterday).

## Set phrases at work

Japanese workplaces run on a handful of fixed phrases. They're said so often that leaving one out is noticed.

| Phrase | When | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| おはようございます | arriving | good morning (in some workplaces, such as restaurants, at the start of any shift, whatever the time) |
| よろしくおねがいします | starting work together, asking for something | I'm in your hands; thanks in advance |
| おつかれさまです | greeting a colleague, opening an email or call to a colleague | thanks for your hard work (a general greeting at work) |
| お{先|さき}にしつれいします | leaving before others | excuse me for leaving first |
| しつれいします | entering a room, ending a phone call | excuse me |
| もうしわけありません | apologizing to a customer or your boss | I'm very sorry (more formal than すみません) |
| かしこまりました | a customer or boss asks for something | certainly (lesson 28 shows more phrases like it) |

When someone leaves with お{先|さき}にしつれいします, the usual reply is おつかれさまでした.

## Dialogue: a job interview

```dialogue
# At a café, after closing time
てんちょう: どうぞ、すわってください。
= Please, have a seat.
リン: しつれいします。リンです。よろしくおねがいします。
= Thank you. I'm Lin. Thank you for seeing me.
てんちょう: {週|しゅう}に{何日|なんにち}ぐらい{働|はたら}けますか。
= About how many days a week can you work?
リン: {大学|だいがく}がありますので、{週|しゅう}に{三日|みっか}{働|はたら}けます。{土曜日|どようび}と{日曜日|にちようび}は、{朝|あさ}から{来|こ}られます。
= I have university, so I can work three days a week. On Saturdays and Sundays I can come from the morning.
てんちょう: そうですか。{前|まえ}にもアルバイトをしたことがありますか。
= I see. Have you had a part-time job before?
リン: はい、{国|くに}でレストランで{働|はたら}いていました。{店長|てんちょう}によくほめられました。
= Yes, I worked in a restaurant back home. The manager often praised me.
てんちょう: いいですね。うちでは、ミスをしたら、すぐほうこくしてください。
= Good. Here, if you make a mistake, please report it straight away.
リン: はい、{分|わ}かりました。それから、テストの{前|まえ}は、{少|すこ}し{休|やす}ませていただけませんか。
= Yes, of course. Also, before exams, could I possibly take a little time off?
てんちょう: いいですよ。そのときは、{早|はや}めにれんらくしてくださいね。
= That's fine. Just let me know early when that happens.
リン: ありがとうございます。がんばります。
= Thank you. I'll do my best.
```

ので is a softer から (lesson 26); {早|はや}めに = early, in good time.

## Say it

```speak
{来週|らいしゅう}、{休|やす}ませていただけませんか。
= Could I possibly take a day off next week?
お{先|さき}にしつれいします。
= Excuse me for leaving before you.
おつかれさまでした。
= Thanks for your hard work. (reply)
すぐほうこくします。
= I'll report it straight away.
よろしくおねがいします。
= Thank you in advance; I look forward to working with you.
```

## Key points

- アルバイト is common among students; interviews (めんせつ) need a りれきしょ and polite manners. Students from abroad need permission to work.
- ほうれんそう: ほうこく (report), れんらく (contact), そうだん (consult).
- {飲|の}み{会|かい} after work are traditional but less common than before; saying no politely is fine.
- ざんぎょう (overtime) is limited by law; workers have ゆうきゅう (paid leave), and employers must make sure most full-time workers take at least five days of it.
- Ask for time off with the causative: {休|やす}ませていただけませんか, ゆうきゅうをとらせていただけませんか.
- Set phrases: おはようございます, よろしくおねがいします, おつかれさまです, お{先|さき}にしつれいします.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Reasons and contrasts: ので, のに, し, とか
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You have given reasons with から since N5, and you can say "but" with が and けど. That is
enough to explain yourself, but it can sound blunt: から puts your own reason up front, and
けど says nothing about how you feel about the contrast. Japanese has more precise tools, and
you need them for the situations this lesson is about: making excuses, apologizing,
complaining, and talking about the people in your life.

This lesson teaches four of them:

- ので, a softer "because", the one you use when you apologize or ask a favour;
- のに, "even though", which adds surprise, disappointment or a complaint;
- 〜し〜し, for giving several reasons at once;
- 〜とか〜とか, for giving examples ("things like … and …").

All four, like から, けど and が, are **[[conjunctive particles]]**: they end one clause and join it
to the next. The lesson also reviews ため as a formal "because of". This is the first lesson of the last module.
Lessons 27 and 28 then turn to keigo, the respectful and humble language you need with
customers, teachers and companies.

## ので: a softer "because"

ので joins a reason to a result, like から: reason first, then ので, then what follows from it.

| Before ので | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| verb, plain form | {電車|でんしゃ}がおくれたので | because the train was late |
| い-adjective | {頭|あたま}がいたいので | because I have a headache |
| な-adjective + な | {不安|ふあん}なので | because I'm worried |
| noun + な | {日曜日|にちようび}なので | because it's Sunday |

The last two rows are the trap. Before から, a plain noun or な-adjective takes だ
({日曜日|にちようび}だから). Before ので it takes な: {日曜日|にちようび}なので, never
\*{日曜日|にちようび}だので.

{電車|でんしゃ}がおくれたので、ちこくしました。 — The train was late, so I was late.

{明日|あした}は{試験|しけん}なので、{今夜|こんや}は{出|で}かけません。 — I have an exam tomorrow, so
I'm not going out tonight.

{道|みち}がよく{分|わ}からないので、{地図|ちず}を{送|おく}ってもらえませんか。 — I don't really know
the way, so could you send me a map?

すみません、ねつがあるので、{今日|きょう}は{休|やす}ませていただけませんか。 — I'm sorry, I have a
temperature, so could I take today off? (ねつ = fever; 〜させていただけませんか, lesson 22.)

In formal speech the polite form can come before ので: {雨|あめ}がふっていますので、お{足|あし}もとに
ご{注意|ちゅうい}ください (it's raining, so please watch your step). You'll hear this in
announcements and from shop staff.

### ので or から?

Both are correct in most sentences. The difference is in the feeling.

| | から | ので |
|---|---|---|
| Sounds like | my reason, stated plainly | a natural result, an explanation |
| Typical use | casual talk, opinions, commands | apologies, excuses, polite requests, notices |
| Can end a sentence | yes: 〜からです (it's because…) | no: \*〜のでです |
| Before it | plain or polite form | plain form (polite form in formal speech) |

When you explain why you are late, why you can't come, or why you are asking for something,
ので makes the reason sound like a fact you had no control over, which is exactly what an
excuse needs. から is more natural when the main clause is your own strong opinion, an
invitation between friends, or an order: あぶないから、さわるな！ (It's dangerous, so don't
touch!) would sound odd with ので.

To answer どうして with a reason, only から works: 「どうして{来|こ}なかったんですか。」「ねぼうしたからです。」
or, between friends, ねぼうしたから.

In speech many people also start a sentence with なので ("so", "that's why"). It is common,
but in careful writing だから, ですから or そのため are safer.

## のに: even though

のに joins two facts that don't fit together: "A, and yet B". It carries a feeling: surprise,
disappointment, frustration, or a complaint. Grammar books call a clause like this
**[[concessive]]**: it concedes a fact that ought to have changed the outcome. のに attaches like ので: plain form, and な after
nouns and な-adjectives.

{毎日|まいにち}{勉強|べんきょう}しているのに、{漢字|かんじ}がなかなかおぼえられません。 — Even though I study
every day, I just can't remember kanji. (なかなか + negative = "just won't"; potential, lesson 2.)

やくそくしたのに、かれは{来|こ}なかった。 — He promised, and yet he didn't come.

{日曜日|にちようび}なのに、{仕事|しごと}に{行|い}かなければなりません。 — It's Sunday, but I still
have to go to work.

この{店|みせ}は{高|たか}いのに、あまりおいしくない。 — This place is expensive, and it isn't even
very good.

{春|はる}なのに、{寒|さむ}いですね。 — It's spring, but it's so cold.

### のに or けど?

Both can translate as "but". けど (and が) just set two things side by side. のに adds "and that
isn't what should happen":

- {雨|あめ}だけど、{出|で}かけます。 — It's raining, but I'm going out. (a plain fact)
- {雨|あめ}なのに、{出|で}かけるの？ — It's raining, and you're going out? (surprise)

Because のに reports something that has already turned out a certain way, the second half
must be a fact. It can't be a request, an invitation, an order or what you intend to do.
Use けど or でも for those:

- ✗ {雨|あめ}なのに、{出|で}かけましょう。
- ✓ {雨|あめ}だけど、{出|で}かけましょう。 — It's raining, but let's go out anyway.

### のに at the end of a sentence

Leave the second half unsaid and のに becomes a sigh or a complaint: せっかく{作|つく}ったのに……
(and I made it specially…, せっかく = "going to the trouble"). With ばよかった (lesson 12) it
is "you should have…" or "if only…":

{言|い}ってくれればよかったのに。 — You could have told me.

もっと{早|はや}く{来|く}ればよかったのに。 — You should have come earlier.

### Not the のに of lesson 24

Lesson 24 taught another のに, "for (a purpose)": はさみは{紙|かみ}を{切|き}るのに{使|つか}います.
That one follows a dictionary form and comes before words like {使|つか}う, いい, べんり or
{時間|じかん}がかかる. The のに of this lesson joins two clauses that clash. If you can put
"even though" in the English, it's this one.

### それなのに

At the start of a sentence, それなのに is "and yet", "even so":

{二時間|にじかん}{待|ま}ちました。それなのに、だれも{来|き}ませんでした。 — I waited two hours.
And yet nobody came.

## 〜し〜し: one reason, and another

し lists reasons, usually two, with the feeling "and there are others too". Put it after the
plain form (in polite speech, after です and ます). Nouns and な-adjectives take だ before し.

このアパートは{駅|えき}に{近|ちか}いし、{広|ひろ}いし、それにやちんも{安|やす}いです。 — This flat is
near the station, it's roomy, and what's more the rent is low. (やちん = rent.)

{今日|きょう}は{雨|あめ}だし、つかれているし、{家|いえ}にいよう。 — It's raining today and I'm tired,
so let's stay home.

かれはやさしいし、おもしろいし、みんなに{好|す}かれています。 — He's kind and he's fun, and
everyone likes him. (passive, lesson 21)

One し on its own is common too. It gives one reason and hints that there are more, so it
sounds gentler than から:

もうおそいし、そろそろ{帰|かえ}ります。 — It's late (and so on), so I'll head home soon.

Notice that the reasons often end with も instead of が: やちんも{安|やす}い. も adds "also", which
fits a list. それに (besides, what's more) adds one more point at the start of a sentence:
{駅|えき}に{近|ちか}いです。それに、{安|やす}いです。

## 〜とか〜とか: things like

とか gives examples from a longer list, like や…など, but it belongs to casual speech. It can
follow nouns or plain-form verbs.

{休|やす}みの{日|ひ}は、{映画|えいが}とか{音楽|おんがく}とか、{好|す}きなことをしています。 — On my days off
I do things I like: films, music, that kind of thing.

しゅうまつは、そうじをするとか{買|か}い{物|もの}に{行|い}くとか、いろいろ{用事|ようじ}があります。 — At the
weekend I've got all sorts of things to do, like cleaning and going shopping.

A single とか softens a suggestion, like "or something" in English:

{今度|こんど}、{映画|えいが}とか{行|い}かない？ — Do you want to go to a film or something sometime?

In writing and polite speech, use や…など for nouns: {映画|えいが}や{音楽|おんがく}など.

## ため: because of (formal)

Lesson 24 taught ために for purpose ("in order to") and noun + のために for "because of". In
notices and the news, ため(に) is the usual formal "because": noun + のため, or a plain verb +
ため.

{大雨|おおあめ}のため、{今日|きょう}の{試合|しあい}は{中止|ちゅうし}になりました。 — Because of heavy rain, today's
match has been cancelled.

じこがあったため、{電車|でんしゃ}がおくれています。 — Trains are delayed because there has been
an accident.

So the reason words run from casual to formal: から, ので, ため. You'll meet all three in
lesson 29's notices and messages.

## Kanji

Six kanji for feelings and relationships. Two N5 words can now be written with kanji:
すき → {好|す}き and わるい → {悪|わる}い. (ふべん stays in kana: its second kanji isn't on the course list.)

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 好 | like, fond of | コウ | す(き), この(む) | 6 | {好|す}き, {大好|だいす}き, {好物|こうぶつ} (favourite food) |
| 悪 | bad | アク | わる(い) | 11 | {悪|わる}い, {悪口|わるぐち}, {気分|きぶん}が{悪|わる}い (to feel unwell) |
| 別 | separate, other | ベツ | わか(れる) | 7 | {別|べつ}の, {別|べつ}に, {別|わか}れる, {特別|とくべつ} (special) |
| 不 | not, un- | フ, ブ | — | 4 | {不安|ふあん}, {不親切|ふしんせつ} (unkind), {不足|ふそく} (shortage) |
| 合 | fit, come together | ゴウ, ガッ | あ(う) | 6 | {合|あ}う, {間|ま}に{合|あ}う, {都合|つごう}, {試合|しあい} (match, game) |
| 送 | send | ソウ | おく(る) | 9 | {送|おく}る, {見送|みおく}る, {送料|そうりょう} (postage) |

Memory notes:

- 好 is a woman (女) next to a child (子): the picture of fondness.
- 悪 has a heart (心, lesson 9) at the bottom, weighed down by the shape above it: a bad heart.
- 別 has the knife radical 刂 on the right: something cut apart, so "separate". {別|わか}れる,
  to part from someone, is the same idea.
- 不 is a line laid across the top of a shoot, blocking it: "not". It goes before a word like
  English un-: {不安|ふあん} (not at ease, anxious), {不親切|ふしんせつ} (unkind).
- 合 is a lid that fits on top of a pot (口): things that fit. {合|あ}う is "to fit, suit,
  match", and {間|ま}に{合|あ}う ("to fit in the time") is "to be in time".
- 送 has the road radical 辶 at the bottom left, the one in {道|みち} and {近|ちか}い: sending
  something off down the road.

{別|べつ} and {別|べつ}に are worth knowing as words. {別|べつ}の + noun is "another, a different":
{別|べつ}の{日|ひ} (another day). {別|べつ}に + negative is "not particularly": 「どうしたの？」
「{別|べつ}に{何|なに}も。」 ("What's up?" "Nothing much.") On its own, {別|べつ}に can sound curt, a bit
like "whatever".

```trace
好悪別不合送
```

## Dialogue: late again

Misaki and Yuto have been going out for a year. Yuto is late. This is casual speech between
a couple.

```dialogue
# Late again
みさき: もう{七時|しちじ}{半|はん}だよ。{六時|ろくじ}って{言|い}ったのに。
= It's half past seven. We said six.
ゆうと: ごめん！{仕事|しごと}がなかなか{終|お}わらなかったし、{電車|でんしゃ}もおくれたし……。
= Sorry! Work just wouldn't finish, and then the train was late…
みさき: {先週|せんしゅう}も{同|おな}じこと{言|い}ってたよね。
= You said exactly the same thing last week.
ゆうと: ほんとうなんだよ。かいぎが{長|なが}くなっちゃって。
= It's true! The meeting ran on.
みさき: {電話|でんわ}してくれればよかったのに。ずっと{待|ま}ってたんだよ。
= You could have phoned me. I've been waiting all this time.
ゆうと: しようと{思|おも}ったんだけど、スマホの{電池|でんち}が{切|き}れちゃって……。
= I was going to, but my phone battery died…
みさき: それ、いいわけでしょう。
= That's an excuse, isn't it?
ゆうと: ……うん、ごめん。おわびに、{今日|きょう}はぼくがごちそうするよ。{何|なん}でも{好|す}きなもの{食|た}べて。
= …Yeah, sorry. To make up for it, dinner's on me tonight. Have whatever you like.
みさき: じゃあ、{前|まえ}から{行|い}きたかったイタリア{料理|りょうり}の{店|みせ}にしよう。ちょっと{高|たか}いけど。
= Then let's go to that Italian place I've been wanting to try. It's a bit pricey, though.
ゆうと: え……。いいよ。{今日|きょう}はぼくが{悪|わる}かったから。
= Uh… OK. Today was my fault.
みさき: よし。ゆるしてあげる。
= Right. You're forgiven.
```

かいぎ = meeting; {電池|でんち}が{切|き}れる = a battery runs out; おわび = an apology (おわびに, "by
way of apology"); ごちそうする = to treat someone to a meal; ゆるす = to forgive. Notice where
each pattern does its work: Misaki complains with のに twice, Yuto piles up his reasons with し,
and his last line uses plain から, not ので, because it is a casual admission between a couple.

## Reading: a letter to an advice column

Advice columns (なやみそうだん) are a staple of Japanese magazines and websites. Read the
letter first for the main problem, then again for the details.

> {大学|だいがく}{二年生|にねんせい}の{女|おんな}の{子|こ}です。{同|おな}じサークルに、{一年|いちねん}{前|まえ}からつきあっているかれがいます。かれはやさしいし、おもしろいし、さいしょはいっしょにいるのがとても{楽|たの}しかったです。
>
> でも、さいきん、かれはよくやくそくの{時間|じかん}におくれます。{先週|せんしゅう}も、{映画|えいが}を{見|み}に{行|い}くやくそくをしていたのに、{三十分|さんじゅっぷん}もおくれて{来|き}ました。りゆうを{聞|き}くと、「ねぼうした」とか「{電車|でんしゃ}がこんでいた」とか、いつも{同|おな}じようないいわけです。
>
> {私|わたし}がもんくを{言|い}うと、かれは「そんなにおこらなくてもいいのに」と{言|い}います。わたしは{待|ま}つのがきらいなので、そう{言|い}われると、とてもいやな{気持|きも}ちになります。
>
> かれのことは{今|いま}も{好|す}きなので、{別|わか}れたくはありません。でも、このままでいいのか、{不安|ふあん}です。どうすればいいでしょうか。

The columnist's answer:

> {待|ま}たされるのはつらいですね。かれは{悪|わる}い{人|ひと}ではないと{思|おも}いますが、あなたの{気持|きも}ちに{気|き}がついていないのかもしれません。おこってもんくを{言|い}うより、「{待|ま}っている{時間|じかん}がさびしい」と、すなおに{話|はな}してみてはどうでしょうか。{二人|ふたり}でよく{話|はな}し{合|あ}えば、きっといいほうほうが{見|み}つかりますよ。

A second-year university student writes that she has been going out with someone from her
club for a year. He's kind and fun, and at first she loved being with him. Lately, though, he
is often late; last week he turned up thirty minutes late for a film, though they'd arranged
it, and his excuses are always the same kind of thing: "I overslept", "the train was
packed". When she complains, he says, "You don't have to get that angry." She hates waiting,
so being told that makes her feel awful. She still likes him and doesn't want to break up,
but she is uneasy about leaving things as they are, and asks what she should do. The
columnist answers that being kept waiting is hard; he probably isn't a bad person, but he may
not have noticed how she feels. Rather than getting angry and complaining, she could try
telling him honestly that the time spent waiting makes her feel lonely. If they talk it over
properly, they will surely find a way.

New in the text: サークル = a (university) club; さいしょ = at first; さいきん = lately; 〜も after a
number = as much as (さんじゅっぷんも, "a whole thirty minutes"); こむ = to be crowded; おこる = to get
angry; さびしい = lonely; すなおに = honestly, openly; {話|はな}し{合|あ}う = to talk something over;
ほうほう = a way, method. Find each pattern: two し reasons in the first paragraph, のに for
what should have happened, とか…とか for his excuses, ので for her reasons, and a のに at the
end of his remark, which is what upsets her: it turns "you don't need to" into "you're making
a fuss".

## Pronunciation

ので and のに differ only in their last mora. Neither has an accent of its own: both take
their pitch from the word before them. In fast speech, ので often becomes んで: おくれたんで. When you hear のに, listen
for the tone: it usually carries a note of complaint.

[ひどい:2] (awful) falls after its second mora: hi-DO-i. {都合|つごう:0} is flat, and so is
{気持|きも:0}ち: no fall at all, and the particle after them stays high.

## Say it

```speak
おそくなってすみません。{電車|でんしゃ}がおくれたので。
= Sorry I'm late. The train was delayed.
ちょっと{用事|ようじ}があるので、{今日|きょう}はしつれいします。
= I have something to do, so I'll be off now.
{言|い}ってくれればよかったのに。
= You could have told me.
{時間|じかん}もないし、お{金|かね}もないし……。
= I've got no time, and no money either…
{別|べつ}にいいよ。
= It's fine, really.
{都合|つごう}が{悪|わる}いので、{別|べつ}の{日|ひ}にしてもいいですか。
= That day doesn't suit me. Could we make it another day?
```

{都合|つごう}が{悪|わる}い ("the circumstances are bad") is the standard polite way to say a time
doesn't suit you; {都合|つごう}がいい is the opposite. It's softer than {行|い}けません and gives no
details, which is the point.

## Common mistakes

- \*{日曜日|にちようび}だので. Nouns and な-adjectives take な before ので and のに: なので, なのに.
- \*〜のでです. To say "it's because…", use からです.
- のに before a request, invitation or plan: \*{雨|あめ}なのに、{行|い}きましょう. Use けど or でも.
- Using のに for a neutral "but". のに complains; けど doesn't. {高|たか}いのに、{買|か}った sounds
  like you regret it; {高|たか}いけど、{買|か}った is just a fact.
- Forgetting だ with し: \*{雨|あめ}し → {雨|あめ}だし.
- とか in a formal email or essay. Use や…など there.
- Mixing up the two のに: purpose (lesson 24) follows a dictionary form and goes before
  {使|つか}う, いい, {時間|じかん}がかかる; "even though" joins two clauses that clash.

## Key points

- ので: a softer, more objective "because" for excuses, apologies and polite requests. Nouns
  and な-adjectives take な: なので. It can't end a sentence (\*のでです).
- のに: "even though", with surprise or complaint. Also な after nouns and な-adjectives. The
  second half must be a fact, not a request or plan. At the end of a sentence, 〜ばよかったのに =
  "you should have…".
- 〜し〜し lists reasons ("and…, and…, so"); one し hints at more. それに adds one more point.
- 〜とか〜とか gives examples in casual speech; や…など is the neutral, written version.
- ため(に) is the formal "because of", common in notices: {大雨|おおあめ}のため.
- New kanji: 好 悪 別 不 合 送.
