complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Respectful language: sonkeigo
topics: お〜になる and お〜ください
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In N5 you learned to recognize the polite Japanese of shops and stations: いらっしゃいませ,
しょうしょうお{待|ま}ちください, かしこまりました. At N4 you start to use it. You don't need to speak like a
hotel receptionist, but you do need a handful of respectful forms for talking to a teacher, a
host family's parents, a customer or anyone you'd address with さま, and you need to
understand them when they're used to you.

This lesson covers respectful language, the forms that raise the person you're talking about.
Lesson 28 covers the other side, the humble forms that lower yourself. Together they are the
core of what the JLPT expects at N4.

## What keigo is

**[[Keigo]]** (けいご) is the general name for Japanese language that shows respect. Most
grammars divide it into three kinds:

| Kind | Japanese name | What it does | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[[polite language]]** | ていねいご | polite to the listener; raises and lowers nobody | です, ます, ございます |
| **[[honorific language]]** | そんけいご | raises the person who does the action | いらっしゃる, お{待|ま}ちになる |
| **[[humble language]]** | けんじょうご | lowers yourself (or your side) as the one who acts | まいる, お{持|も}ちする |

You have used polite language since your first lesson. The other two work in opposite
directions, and the key question is always: *who does the action?*

- Someone you respect does it → honorific: {先生|せんせい}がいらっしゃいました (the teacher came).
- You do it, for or towards them → humble: {私|わたし}がまいりました (I came; lesson 28).

You never use an honorific verb about yourself. \*{私|わたし}はいらっしゃいます is not "politer";
it's wrong, because it raises you.

(An official guide published in 2007 by an advisory council of Japan's Agency for Cultural
Affairs splits keigo into five kinds instead of three, by separating out two smaller groups.
You'll meet one of them, **[[beautifying お/ご]]**, at the end of this lesson, and the other in
lesson 28.)

### Who gets keigo?

Keigo follows two things: status (age, position, being a customer) and distance (how well you
know someone, whether they are in your group). In practice:

- Use honorific forms about teachers, bosses, customers, older people you don't know well, and
  the families of people you're visiting.
- Use plain or ordinary polite speech with friends, family and people of your own age and
  status.
- Staff use keigo to customers, whatever their age. Customers answer in ordinary です/ます.

Lesson 6 introduced in-group and out-group (uchi and soto). It matters here too: you don't use
honorific forms about your own family or, when talking to outsiders, about your own company.
Lesson 28 shows what to do instead.

## Special honorific verbs

The most common verbs have their own honorific partners. Learn these as words:

| Ordinary verb | Honorific | ます form | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| いる, {行|い}く, {来|く}る | いらっしゃる | いらっしゃいます | {先生|せんせい}は{研究室|けんきゅうしつ}にいらっしゃいます。 |
| {言|い}う | おっしゃる | おっしゃいます | {先生|せんせい}は{何|なん}とおっしゃいましたか。 |
| {食|た}べる, {飲|の}む | めしあがる | めしあがります | どうぞめしあがってください。 |
| {見|み}る | ごらんになる | ごらんになります | この{写真|しゃしん}、もうごらんになりましたか。 |
| する | なさる | なさいます | しゅうまつは{何|なに}をなさいますか。 |
| くれる | くださる | くださいます | {先生|せんせい}が{本|ほん}をくださいました。 |
| {知|し}っている | ごぞんじだ | ごぞんじです | この{店|みせ}をごぞんじですか。 |

{先生|せんせい}は{研究室|けんきゅうしつ}にいらっしゃいます。 — The professor is in her office.

{社長|しゃちょう}は{明日|あした}、{京都|きょうと}へいらっしゃいます。 — The company president is going to
Kyoto tomorrow.

{先生|せんせい}は{何|なん}とおっしゃいましたか。 — What did the teacher say?

この{写真|しゃしん}、もうごらんになりましたか。 — Have you seen this photo yet?

しゅうまつは{何|なに}をなさいますか。 — What are you doing at the weekend?

{先生|せんせい}が{本|ほん}をくださいました。 — My teacher gave me a book. (くださる, lesson 6)

この{店|みせ}をごぞんじですか。 — Do you know this shop?

いらっしゃる has three meanings, like the three verbs it replaces. Context decides: {研究室|けんきゅうしつ}に
いらっしゃいます (is in), {京都|きょうと}へいらっしゃいます (is going to), {日本|にほん}にいらっしゃいました
(came to Japan, or was in Japan).

### Watch the ます form

いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, なさる and くださる look like ordinary group 1 verbs, but their ます form
has い where you'd expect り:

| Verb | ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|---|
| いらっしゃる | いらっしゃります | いらっしゃいます |
| おっしゃる | おっしゃります | おっしゃいます |
| なさる | なさります | なさいます |
| くださる | くださります | くださいます |

Their other forms are regular: いらっしゃらない, いらっしゃった, いらっしゃって, おっしゃった,
なさって. And you already know their command forms from set phrases: いらっしゃい(ませ),
なさい (lesson 15) and ください. That's where those words come from.

めしあがる and ごらんになる are ordinary group 1 verbs (めしあがります, ごらんになります), so they join
your conjugation drills (in the forms that make sense for them: not the potential, volitional,
passive or causative); the four irregular ones above don't, because the drills can't generate
their ます forms. Practise them with this lesson's questions instead.

ごぞんじ is a noun used with です: ごぞんじですか (do you know?). For "don't you know?" say
ごぞんじないですか or, more politely, ごぞんじありませんか.

## お + ます stem + になる

For most other verbs, honorific forms are made with a pattern: お + the ます stem + になる.

| Verb | ます stem | Honorific |
|---|---|---|
| {待|ま}つ | {待|ま}ち | お{待|ま}ちになる |
| {帰|かえ}る | {帰|かえ}り | お{帰|かえ}りになる |
| {書|か}く | {書|か}き | お{書|か}きになる |
| {読|よ}む | {読|よ}み | お{読|よ}みになる |
| {使|つか}う | {使|つか}い | お{使|つか}いになる |
| {持|も}つ | {持|も}ち | お{持|も}ちになる |

ぶちょうは{何時|なんじ}ごろお{帰|かえ}りになりますか。 — Around what time will the department
manager be back?

{先生|せんせい}はもうお{帰|かえ}りになりました。 — The teacher has already gone home.

この{本|ほん}をお{読|よ}みになったことがありますか。 — Have you ever read this book?

Verbs made from a noun + する take ご + noun + になる: ごりようになる (to use, of a service),
ご{説明|せつめい}になる (to explain). なさる is the other option: {説明|せつめい}なさる.

The pattern doesn't work everywhere:

- Not with verbs that have a special form: \*お{行|い}きになる and \*おいになる are wrong;
  use いらっしゃる. \*お{見|み}になる → ごらんになる. \*お{言|い}いになる → おっしゃる.
- Most verbs whose ます stem is a single mora ({見|み}る, {来|く}る, ねる) use a special verb
  instead: ごらんになる, いらっしゃる, and おやすみになる for ねる (to go to bed).

### The short form: お + stem + です

In shops and hotels you'll often hear a shorter honorific: お + ます stem + です. It describes
what the customer is doing or has: ポイントカードはお{持|も}ちですか (do you have a points card?),
お{帰|かえ}りですか (are you leaving?), {何|なに}かおさがしですか (are you looking for something?).
Recognize it; you don't need to produce it.

## Respectful requests: お〜ください

To ask a customer or a guest to do something, staff use お + ます stem + ください (or ご + noun +
ください). It is politer than 〜てください.

| 〜てください | お〜ください |
|---|---|
| {待|ま}ってください | お{待|ま}ちください |
| {入|はい}ってください | お{入|はい}りください |
| {使|つか}ってください | お{使|つか}いください |
| {書|か}いてください | お{書|か}きください |
| りようしてください | ごりようください |
| {注意|ちゅうい}してください | ご{注意|ちゅうい}ください |

こちらにお{名前|なまえ}とご{住所|じゅうしょ}をお{書|か}きください。 — Please write your name and address
here.

よろしければ、このかさをお{使|つか}いください。 — Please use this umbrella, if you like.

ドアがしまります。ご{注意|ちゅうい}ください。 — The doors are closing. Please be careful.

The same limits apply: {見|み}る gives ごらんください (please look), not \*お{見|み}ください, and
"please come" is おこしください or いらっしゃってください. またおこしください (please come again) is a
phrase every shop uses.

お〜ください is polite, but it is still an instruction. It suits notices and staff speaking to
customers. To ask a favour of your teacher, a request is kinder: {見|み}ていただけませんか
(lesson 7) rather than ごらんください.

## The honorific 〜られる (to recognize)

There is a third, lighter way to show respect: the same form as the passive (lesson 21).
{書|か}かれる, {帰|かえ}られる, {来|こ}られる, される.

{社長|しゃちょう}は{何時|なんじ}に{来|こ}られますか。 — What time is the president coming?

{先生|せんせい}はどう{思|おも}われますか。 — What do you think, professor?

It is common at work, in the news and in letters, and it is easy to make, but it looks like a
passive (or a potential), so context has to show it's honorific: usually the subject is a
respected person and nobody is acting on them. Recognize it; when you speak, use the special
verbs and お〜になる.

## Polite words for people and things

Keigo isn't only verbs. A few everyday words have polite partners, and staff use them all the
time:

| Ordinary | Polite | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {人|ひと} | {方|かた} | person: この{方|かた}, あの{方|かた} |
| だれ | どなた | who |
| どこ, ここ | どちら, こちら | where, here; also "which way", "this way" |
| どう | いかが | how |
| いいですか | よろしいですか | is it all right? |
| ちょっと | しょうしょう | a little, a moment |
| 〜さん | 〜さま | Mr, Ms (to customers, in letters) |
| {今|いま} | ただいま | now, at the moment |

こちらでよろしいですか。 — Is this all right? / Is this the one?

お{飲|の}み{物|もの}はいかがですか。 — Would you like something to drink?

On the phone, どちらさまですか is the usual polite "may I ask who's calling?"; どなたですか is
correct but sounds a little more direct.

## Beautifying お and ご

Some お and ご don't raise anyone. They just make a word sound more refined: お{茶|ちゃ},
お{水|みず}, お{金|かね}, ご{飯|はん}, お{手洗|てあら}い (toilet), おさけ, おべんとう, おみやげ. This is
beautifying お/ご. You can use these words about your own things, and many of them are
the normal words in everyday speech: hardly anyone says {茶|ちゃ} for green tea.

A respectful お/ご is different: it marks something as belonging to the person you respect, so
you never use it for your own things: ご{家族|かぞく} (your family), お{名前|なまえ} (your name),
ご{住所|じゅうしょ} (your address). Talking about yourself: {私|わたし}の{名前|なまえ}, {私|わたし}の{家族|かぞく}.

Which one, お or ご? A rule of thumb:

- お + native Japanese words (words with kun'yomi, written in kana or read the Japanese way):
  お{名前|なまえ}, お{手紙|てがみ}, お{休|やす}み.
- ご + words borrowed from Chinese (two kanji read in on'yomi): ご{家族|かぞく}, ご{住所|じゅうしょ},
  ご{注文|ちゅうもん} (order), ご{意見|いけん} (opinion).
- Common exceptions take お: お{電話|でんわ}, お{時間|じかん}, お{食事|しょくじ}, お{料理|りょうり},
  お{元気|げんき}ですか.
- Katakana loanwords usually take neither: コーヒー, not \*おコーヒー.

## Kanji

Four kanji for places and things you meet as a customer. Three N5 words can now be written
with kanji: おちゃ → お{茶|ちゃ}, ちゃいろ → {茶色|ちゃいろ} and ふく → {服|ふく}.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 茶 | tea | チャ, サ | — | 9 | お{茶|ちゃ}, {茶色|ちゃいろ}, {茶道|さどう} (the tea ceremony; also read ちゃどう) |
| 洋 | ocean; Western | ヨウ | — | 9 | {洋服|ようふく}, {洋食|ようしょく}, {西洋|せいよう} (the West) |
| 服 | clothes | フク | — | 8 | {服|ふく}, {洋服|ようふく} |
| 堂 | hall | ドウ | — | 11 | {食堂|しょくどう}, {本堂|ほんどう} (the main hall of a temple) |

Memory notes:

- 茶 has the grass radical 艹 at the top and a person (人) standing over a tree (木): a plant
  whose leaves people pick.
- 洋 is water (氵, three drops) beside a shape that pictures a sheep: a wide sea, and the countries across
  it. That's why it means "Western": {洋服|ようふく} (Western clothes, now just "clothes"),
  {洋食|ようしょく} (Western food), {洋室|ようしつ} (a Western-style room).
- 服 has the moon/flesh shape 月 on the left, as in many body words: what you put on your
  body.
- 堂 has 土 (earth) at the bottom, under a roof with light shining above it: a big building on
  solid ground, a hall. {食堂|しょくどう} is literally "eating hall": a canteen or a simple
  restaurant.

茶 is read ちゃ in most words, but さ in {茶道|さどう} and a few others. お{茶|ちゃ} on its own means
green tea; black tea is こうちゃ.

```trace
茶洋服堂
```

## Dialogue 1: at a hotel

Oliver checks in. The receptionist uses keigo; Oliver uses ordinary です/ます, which is exactly
right for a guest.

```dialogue
# At the front desk
フロント: いらっしゃいませ。チェックインですか。お{名前|なまえ}をおねがいします。
= Good evening. Checking in? May I have your name, please?
オリバー: スミスです。{今日|きょう}から{二|に}はくで、よやくしています。
= Smith. I've booked two nights from today.
フロント: スミスさまですね。しょうしょうお{待|ま}ちください。……はい、ございました。{朝食|ちょうしょく}つきのごよやくですね。
= Mr Smith… One moment, please. …Yes, here it is. A booking with breakfast included.
オリバー: はい、そうです。
= That's right.
フロント: では、こちらにお{名前|なまえ}とご{住所|じゅうしょ}をお{書|か}きください。
= Then please write your name and address here.
オリバー: はい。……あのう、{朝食|ちょうしょく}は{何時|なんじ}からですか。
= Sure. …Um, what time is breakfast?
フロント: {七時|しちじ}から{十時|じゅうじ}まででございます。{二|に}かいのレストランをごりようください。
= From seven to ten. Please use the restaurant on the second floor.
オリバー: {分|わ}かりました。それから、{明日|あした}の{朝|あさ}、タクシーをよんでもらえますか。
= OK. And could you call me a taxi tomorrow morning?
フロント: かしこまりました。{何時|なんじ}ごろお{出|で}かけになりますか。
= Certainly. Around what time will you be going out?
オリバー: {九時|くじ}ごろです。{京都|きょうと}{駅|えき}まで{行|い}きたいんですが。
= Around nine. I'd like to go to Kyoto Station.
フロント: では、{八時|はちじ}{五十分|ごじゅっぷん}にロビーでお{待|ま}ちください。タクシーをよんでおきます。
= Then please wait in the lobby at ten to nine. I'll have a taxi called for you.
フロント: こちらがおへやのかぎでございます。どうぞごゆっくり。
= Here is your room key. Enjoy your stay.
```

{二|に}はく = two nights (〜はく counts nights at a hotel); よやく = booking; {朝食|ちょうしょく}つき =
with breakfast (〜つき, "included"); ございました = here it is (literally "there was"); ロビー = lobby;
ごゆっくり = take your time, make yourself at home. Count the honorific forms: お{名前|なまえ},
ごよやく, ご{住所|じゅうしょ}, お{書|か}きください, ごりようください, お{出|で}かけになる, お{待|ま}ちください,
and the very polite でございます (lesson 28).

## Dialogue 2: talking to a teacher

Saki, a university student, needs to see her professor. She is polite and uses a few honorific
forms; the professor answers in plain polite Japanese.

```dialogue
# Outside the professor's office
さき: {先生|せんせい}、{今|いま}ちょっとよろしいですか。
= Professor, do you have a moment?
{先生|せんせい}: はい、どうぞ。
= Yes, go ahead.
さき: {来週|らいしゅう}のはっぴょうのことなんですが、{先生|せんせい}は{何曜日|なんようび}に{研究室|けんきゅうしつ}にいらっしゃいますか。
= It's about my presentation next week. Which days are you in your office?
{先生|せんせい}: {火曜日|かようび}と{木曜日|もくようび}はいますよ。
= I'm in on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
さき: では、{火曜日|かようび}にしりょうを{見|み}ていただけませんか。
= Then could you look at my materials on Tuesday?
{先生|せんせい}: いいですよ。{何時|なんじ}ごろ{来|き}ますか。
= Sure. What time will you come?
さき: {午後|ごご}{二時|にじ}はいかがですか。
= How about two in the afternoon?
{先生|せんせい}: {二時|にじ}ですね。{分|わ}かりました。
= Two o'clock. Fine.
さき: ありがとうございます。あ、{先生|せんせい}がおっしゃった{本|ほん}、{図書館|としょかん}にありました。
= Thank you. Oh, the book you mentioned, I found it in the library.
{先生|せんせい}: そうですか。よかったですね。
= Did you? Good.
```

はっぴょう = presentation; しりょう = materials, handouts. Saki uses honorific forms for what the
professor does (いらっしゃる, おっしゃった) and a polite request for the favour (〜ていただけませんか),
and for her own visit she simply suggests a time (いかがですか). The professor speaks plainly
politely and says います about himself: nobody uses いらっしゃる for their own actions.

## Pronunciation

The keigo verbs are long, so say them slowly at first. [いらっしゃる:4] has five morae
(い・ら・っ・しゃ・る: the small っ counts as one, しゃ is one): low on い, high from ら to しゃ,
then down on る. [おっしゃる:3] (お・っ・しゃ・る) falls after しゃ too, and [なさる:2] after さ.
[めしあがる:0] is flat. In the ます form the
fall moves to ま, as in every verb: いらっしゃいます, なさいます.

## Say it

```speak
{先生|せんせい}、{今|いま}ちょっとよろしいですか。
= Excuse me, professor, do you have a moment?
どうぞ、めしあがってください。
= Please, help yourself.
しょうしょうお{待|ま}ちください。
= One moment, please.
{先生|せんせい}は{何|なん}とおっしゃいましたか。
= What did the teacher say?
この{本|ほん}をごぞんじですか。
= Do you know this book?
{何時|なんじ}ごろお{帰|かえ}りになりますか。
= Around what time will you be back?
```

## Common mistakes

- Honorific verbs about yourself: \*{私|わたし}は{明日|あした}いらっしゃいます. Use {行|い}きます (or the
  humble まいります, lesson 28).
- \*いらっしゃります, \*おっしゃります, \*なさります. The ます forms end in います.
- \*お{見|み}になる, \*お{行|い}きになる, \*お{言|い}いになる: verbs with special forms don't take the
  pattern.
- Stacking two honorifics: \*おっしゃられる. おっしゃる is already honorific; adding られる on top is
  a common slip, even among native speakers, but it's considered wrong.
- ご{家族|かぞく} or お{名前|なまえ} for your own family or name. The respectful お/ご is for the other
  person's.
- Using keigo with friends. It sounds cold or sarcastic, not polite.

## Key points

- Keigo has three main kinds: polite (です/ます), honorific (raises the person who acts) and
  humble (lowers you, lesson 28).
- Special honorific verbs: いらっしゃる (いる/{行|い}く/{来|く}る), おっしゃる ({言|い}う), めしあがる
  ({食|た}べる/{飲|の}む), ごらんになる ({見|み}る), なさる (する), くださる (くれる), ごぞんじ
  ({知|し}っている). ます forms: いらっしゃいます, おっしゃいます, なさいます, くださいます.
- Other verbs: お + ます stem + になる (お{待|ま}ちになる); する nouns: ご + noun + になる.
- Requests: お + ます stem + ください, ご + noun + ください (お{待|ま}ちください, ご{注意|ちゅうい}ください).
- 〜られる (same as the passive) is a lighter honorific: recognize it.
- Beautifying お/ご (お{茶|ちゃ}, ご{飯|はん}) can be used for your own things; respectful お/ご
  (ご{家族|かぞく}) can't.
- New kanji: 茶 洋 服 堂.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Humble language: kenjōgo
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 27 raised the other person. This lesson lowers you. Humble language (けんじょうご) is
what you use about your own actions when they involve someone you respect: visiting a
teacher, carrying a customer's bag, introducing yourself at a job interview, answering the
phone at work. With it, the honorific forms of lesson 27 and the very polite でございます, you
can follow the situations where Japanese people themselves use keigo every day: the office,
phone calls, visits to another company and interviews.

## How humble language works

The question is still "who does the action?". When you (or someone on your side) do something
that involves a person you respect, you describe it in humble form:

- {先生|せんせい}がいらっしゃいました。 — The teacher came. (honorific: the teacher acts)
- {私|わたし}が{先生|せんせい}のところへまいりました。 — I went to see the teacher. (humble: I act)

Both sentences show respect for the teacher, in opposite ways. Mixing them up is the classic
keigo mistake: never use a humble form for what the other person does
(\*{先生|せんせい}がまいりました), and never an honorific form for what you do.

## Special humble verbs

As with honorific verbs, the most common ones have their own forms. いただく and さしあげる,
which you met in lesson 6, are humble verbs too.

| Ordinary verb | Humble | ます form | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {行|い}く, {来|く}る | まいる | まいります | {明日|あした}、{三時|さんじ}にそちらへまいります。 |
| いる | おる | おります | {夜|よる}は{家|いえ}におります。 |
| {言|い}う | もうす | もうします | {田中|たなか}ともうします。 |
| する | いたす | いたします | {私|わたし}がごあんないいたします。 |
| {食|た}べる, {飲|の}む, もらう | いただく | いただきます | おかしをいただきました。 |
| {見|み}る | はいけんする | はいけんします | お{手紙|てがみ}、はいけんしました。 |
| {聞|き}く (ask), {行|い}く (visit) | うかがう | うかがいます | ちょっとうかがいたいんですが。 |
| {知|し}っている | ぞんじている | ぞんじております | その{話|はなし}はぞんじております。 |
| {会|あ}う | お{目|め}にかかる | お{目|め}にかかります | {明日|あした}お{目|め}にかかれますか。 |
| あげる | さしあげる | さしあげます | {先生|せんせい}にお{茶|ちゃ}をさしあげました。 |

{明日|あした}、{三時|さんじ}にそちらへまいります。 — I'll come to your office at three tomorrow.

{夜|よる}は{家|いえ}におります。 — I'm at home in the evenings.

はじめまして。{田中|たなか}ともうします。 — How do you do? My name is Tanaka.

{私|わたし}がごあんないいたします。 — I'll show you round. (あんない = guiding, showing the way)

おかしをいただきました。 — I was given some sweets. (or "I had some sweets": context decides)

お{手紙|てがみ}、はいけんしました。 — I have read your letter.

{先生|せんせい}、ちょっとうかがいたいことがあるんですが。 — Professor, there's something I'd like to
ask you.

{明日|あした}、おたくにうかがってもよろしいですか。 — May I visit you at home tomorrow?
(おたく = your home, polite)

{明日|あした}お{目|め}にかかれますか。 — Could I see you tomorrow?

{先生|せんせい}にお{茶|ちゃ}をさしあげました。 — I served the teacher some tea.

The negative of ぞんじている is ぞんじません: もうしわけありません、そのことはぞんじませんでした (I'm
very sorry, I wasn't aware of that). To a customer this sounds far better than {知|し}りません,
which can come across as "not my business".

All of these verbs are regular. まいる, おる, もうす, いたす and うかがう are group 1 (まいって,
おって, もうして, いたして, うかがって), and はいけんする is a する verb, so they join your
conjugation drills. The drills leave out forms that don't suit a humble verb (the volitional,
passive and causative, and for most of them the potential; うかがえる and はいけんできる are
fine). おる is drilled only in its polite forms, the て form and the ば form: in standard
Japanese its plain forms (おらない, おった) sound dialectal.

### Humble, or just courteous?

Four of these verbs, まいる, おる, もうす and いたす, are also used when the action involves nobody
you need to raise, simply to be courteous to the person you're speaking to:

{電車|でんしゃ}がまいります。 — The train is arriving. (station announcement)

{雨|あめ}がふってまいりました。 — It has started to rain.

{父|ちち}は{銀行|ぎんこう}で{働|はたら}いております。 — My father works at a bank.

The 2007 guide mentioned in lesson 27 calls this use **[[courteous language]]** (ていちょうご) and
counts it as a separate group. You don't need the label: in formal speech, 〜ております,
〜てまいります and 〜いたします sound right whoever the action is for.

## お/ご + ます stem + する

Other verbs become humble with a pattern that mirrors lesson 27's: お + ます stem + する
(humbler still: + いたす), or ご + noun + する for する nouns.

| Verb | Humble | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {持|も}つ | お{持|も}ちする | おにもつ、お{持|も}ちしましょうか。 (Shall I carry your bags?) |
| {待|ま}つ | お{待|ま}ちする | お{待|ま}ちしております。 (We look forward to seeing you.) |
| {送|おく}る | お{送|おく}りする | しりょうをメールでお{送|おく}りします。 (I'll email you the documents.) |
| {貸|か}す | お{貸|か}しする | かさをお{貸|か}ししましょうか。 (Shall I lend you an umbrella?) |
| {知|し}らせる | お{知|し}らせする | けっかは{後|あと}でお{知|し}らせします。 (We'll let you know the results later.) |
| {説明|せつめい}する | ご{説明|せつめい}する | {私|わたし}がご{説明|せつめい}します。 (Let me explain.) |
| れんらくする | ごれんらくする | {明日|あした}ごれんらくします。 (I'll contact you tomorrow.) |
| {電話|でんわ}する | お{電話|でんわ}する | {後|あと}でお{電話|でんわ}いたします。 (I'll call you later.) |

Two rules:

1. *Your action must involve the other person.* You carry their bags, you send them the
   documents. If nobody else is involved, the pattern is wrong: \*{毎朝|まいあさ}{七時|しちじ}にお{起|お}きします
   makes no sense. Just say {起|お}きます.
2. *Not with verbs that have a special humble form*: \*お{見|み}する → はいけんする, \*お{言|い}いする
   → もうす (or もうしあげる, "to say to someone above you").

お{電話|でんわ}する takes お, not ご, just as お{電話|でんわ} did in lesson 27.

## でございます and the politest teineigo

At the top of polite language sit two forms you heard in N5:

- ある → ございます: お{手洗|てあら}いはあちらにございます (the toilets are over there).
- です → でございます: うけつけは{一|いっ}かいでございます (reception is on the ground floor).

いい has a politer form too, よろしい: こちらでよろしいでしょうか (would this be all right?).

Don't confuse でございます with でいらっしゃいます. Both are "very polite です", but でいらっしゃる is
honorific, for the other person, while でございます is for things or for yourself:

- {田中|たなか}さまでいらっしゃいますか。 — Would you be Mr Tanaka? (about the listener)
- はい、{田中|たなか}でございます。 — Yes, this is Tanaka. (about yourself)

## Inside and outside: talking about your own side

Lesson 6 introduced in-group and out-group (uchi and soto). Keigo makes the line strict. When
you talk to an outsider (a customer, another company, a visitor), everyone on your side is
treated like you, even people above you:

- Your own family: {父|ちち}, {母|はは}, {兄|あに}, never お{父|とう}さん; humble verbs; no さん.
- Your colleagues, your boss, even the company president: the surname alone, no さん, and humble
  verbs.
- The outsider and their side: さん or さま, and honorific verbs.

So the same person is spoken of in two ways, depending on who is listening:

| Speaking to | About the manager, Mr Yamada |
|---|---|
| a colleague (inside) | {山田|やまだ}ぶちょうはいらっしゃいますか。 (Is Mr Yamada in?) |
| a customer (outside) | ぶちょうの{山田|やまだ}は{今|いま}{出|で}かけております。 (Yamada, our manager, is out at the moment.) |

The titles ぶちょう (department manager) and {社長|しゃちょう} (company president) work like
{先生|せんせい}: inside the company they replace さん ({山田|やまだ}ぶちょう). To outsiders the title
goes before the name instead: ぶちょうの{山田|やまだ}.

{母|はは}がよろしくともうしておりました。 — My mother sends her regards.

In formal speech, {私|わたし} is often read わたくし. For "your company" and "our company" there are
special words to recognize from interviews and business emails: おんしゃ (your company, spoken),
へいしゃ (our company) and わたくしども (we, our side).

## On the phone

Telephone Japanese is built from set phrases. Learn them as blocks.

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| はい、ミドリ{工業|こうぎょう}でございます。 | Hello, Midori Industries. (answering) |
| いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております。 | Thank you for your continued support. (the standard opening) |
| {田中|たなか}さんはいらっしゃいますか。 | Is Mr/Ms Tanaka there? |
| しょうしょうお{待|ま}ちください。 | One moment, please. |
| お{待|ま}たせいたしました。 | Sorry to keep you waiting. |
| {田中|たなか}はただいませきを{外|はず}しております。 | Tanaka is away from his desk at the moment. |
| {田中|たなか}はかいぎ{中|ちゅう}でございます。 | Tanaka is in a meeting. |
| おりかえしお{電話|でんわ}いたしましょうか。 | Shall I have him call you back? |
| でんごんをおねがいできますか。 | Could I leave a message? |
| もう{一度|いちど}おねがいします。 | Could you say that again, please? |
| お{電話|でんわ}が{少|すこ}し{遠|とお}いようなんですが。 | Sorry, I can't hear you very well. (literally "the phone seems a little far away") |
| しつれいいたします。 | Goodbye. (ending a call politely) |

お{世話|せわ}になっております ("you always look after us") opens almost every business call and
email, whether or not you have actually worked together. {世話|せわ} is care, looking after:
お{世話|せわ}になりました is how you thank a host family or a workplace when you leave.

## Dialogue 1: a phone call

Ms Kato from another company phones Midori Industries. The receptionist talks about her own
colleague Tanaka without さん; Ms Kato, an outsider, uses さん and いらっしゃる for him.

```dialogue
# A phone call
うけつけ: はい、ミドリ{工業|こうぎょう}でございます。
= Hello, Midori Industries.
かとう: いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております。サクラ{電気|でんき}のかとうともうします。えいぎょうぶの{田中|たなか}さんはいらっしゃいますか。
= Hello, this is Kato from Sakura Electric. Is Mr Tanaka from Sales there?
うけつけ: {田中|たなか}でございますね。しょうしょうお{待|ま}ちください。
= Tanaka? One moment, please.
うけつけ: お{待|ま}たせいたしました。もうしわけございません。{田中|たなか}はただいまかいぎ{中|ちゅう}でございます。
= Sorry to keep you waiting. I'm very sorry, Tanaka is in a meeting at the moment.
かとう: そうですか。{何時|なんじ}ごろ{終|お}わりますか。
= I see. Around what time will it finish?
うけつけ: {十一時|じゅういちじ}ごろには{終|お}わると{思|おも}います。おりかえしお{電話|でんわ}いたしましょうか。
= I think it will finish around eleven. Shall I have him call you back?
かとう: では、おねがいします。それから、でんごんをおねがいできますか。
= Yes, please. And could I leave a message?
うけつけ: はい、どうぞ。
= Of course.
かとう: {来週|らいしゅう}の{工場|こうじょう}{見学|けんがく}の{時間|じかん}がかわりましたので、メールをお{送|おく}りしました、とおつたえください。
= Please tell him that the time of next week's factory visit has changed, and that I've sent him an email.
うけつけ: {工場|こうじょう}{見学|けんがく}のお{時間|じかん}がかわったので、メールをお{送|おく}りいただいた、ということですね。かしこまりました。{田中|たなか}にもうしつたえます。
= So the time of the factory visit has changed and you've sent him an email. Certainly. I'll pass that on to Tanaka.
かとう: よろしくおねがいいたします。
= Thank you very much.
うけつけ: サクラ{電気|でんき}のかとうさまですね。お{電話|でんわ}ありがとうございました。しつれいいたします。
= Ms Kato of Sakura Electric. Thank you for calling. Goodbye.
```

えいぎょうぶ = the sales department; かいぎ{中|ちゅう} = in a meeting; {工場|こうじょう}{見学|けんがく} = a
factory visit; おつたえください = please tell (つたえる, to pass on a message); もうしつたえる = the
humble "pass a message on". Notice Kato's かわりましたので: in formal speech the polite form can
come before ので (lesson 26). The receptionist's お{送|おく}りいただいた ("you kindly sent") is
humble: it describes the receptionist's side receiving a favour from Kato.

## Dialogue 2: a job interview

Lin, a graduate student, has an interview at a car company. The interviewer uses polite and
honorific forms (〜られる, なさる); Lin answers in humble forms.

```dialogue
# A job interview
めんせつかん: どうぞ、おかけください。
= Please, have a seat.
リン: しつれいいたします。リン・ウェイともうします。{本日|ほんじつ}はよろしくおねがいいたします。
= Thank you. My name is Lin Wei. Thank you for seeing me today.
めんせつかん: よろしくおねがいします。リンさんは、どうしてこの{会社|かいしゃ}で{働|はたら}きたいと{思|おも}われたんですか。
= Nice to meet you. Ms Lin, why did you decide you'd like to work for this company?
リン: {大学|だいがく}で{自動車|じどうしゃ}の{研究|けんきゅう}をしております。{去年|きょねん}、おんしゃの{工場|こうじょう}を{見学|けんがく}させていただいて、ここで{働|はたら}きたいと{思|おも}いました。
= I'm doing research on cars at university. Last year I was allowed to visit your factory, and I decided I wanted to work here.
めんせつかん: そうですか。{日本語|にほんご}はどのぐらい{勉強|べんきょう}なさいましたか。
= I see. How long have you studied Japanese?
リン: {三年|さんねん}ぐらいです。{今|いま}も{毎日|まいにち}{勉強|べんきょう}しております。
= About three years. I still study every day.
めんせつかん: {入社|にゅうしゃ}したら、どんな{仕事|しごと}をしてみたいですか。
= If you join us, what kind of work would you like to try?
リン: {新|あたら}しいエンジンの{開発|かいはつ}にさんかしたいと{思|おも}っております。
= I'd like to take part in developing new engines.
めんせつかん: {分|わ}かりました。{何|なに}か{質問|しつもん}はありますか。
= All right. Do you have any questions?
リン: はい。{入社|にゅうしゃ}の{前|まえ}に{勉強|べんきょう}しておいたほうがいいことがあれば、{教|おし}えていただけませんか。
= Yes. If there's anything I should study before joining, could you tell me?
めんせつかん: そうですね。{工場|こうじょう}のきかいについて、{少|すこ}ししらべておくといいですよ。
= Let me see. It would be good to read up a little on the machines in the factory.
リン: {分|わ}かりました。{本日|ほんじつ}はありがとうございました。しつれいいたします。
= I will. Thank you very much for today. Goodbye.
```

めんせつかん = interviewer; {本日|ほんじつ} = today (formal); {自動車|じどうしゃ} = car (the formal word);
{入社|にゅうしゃ}する = to join a company; {開発|かいはつ} = development; きかい = machine; しらべる =
to look into, look up. Lin never uses an honorific form for herself, calls the company おんしゃ,
and asks her question with 〜ていただけませんか. The interviewer, who has the higher status here,
still speaks politely, with a light honorific {思|おも}われた.

## Kanji

Four kanji for work and explanations. One N5 word can now be written in kanji: しつもん →
{質問|しつもん}.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 工 | craft, construction | コウ, ク | — | 3 | {工場|こうじょう}, {工業|こうぎょう} (industry), {工事|こうじ} (construction work), {大工|だいく} (carpenter) |
| 場 | place | ジョウ | ば | 12 | {場所|ばしょ}, {工場|こうじょう}, {会場|かいじょう} (venue), {売|う}り{場|ば} (sales floor) |
| 質 | quality; matter | シツ | — | 15 | {質問|しつもん}, {品質|ひんしつ} (quality) |
| 説 | explain; theory | セツ | — | 14 | {説明|せつめい}, {小説|しょうせつ} (novel) |

Memory notes:

- 工 is a carpenter's tool, a beam with a flat top and base: making and building.
- 場 has 土 (earth) on the left, and on the right the sun (日) rising over the horizon: a piece
  of open ground in the sun, a place. On'yomi ジョウ is for places where something is done
  ({工場|こうじょう}, {会場|かいじょう}); kun'yomi ば is the everyday "place" ({場所|ばしょ}, {売|う}り{場|ば}).
- 質 has two axes on top and, underneath, the shape for a shell, which once meant money:
  weighing up what something is worth, its quality.
- 説 has the speech radical 言 on the left, as in 話, 読 and 語: explaining in words.

{工場|こうじょう} has a second reading, こうば, for a small workshop. ジョウ is the usual one.

```trace
工場質説
```

## Pronunciation

[まいる:1] and [もうす:1] fall after their first mora: MA-i-ru, MO-o-su. [うかがう:0] is flat.
{工場|こうじょう:3} falls after こうじょ, so the particle after it is low: こうじょうに.
{説明|せつめい:0} is flat.

When you read {私|わたくし} as わたくし in formal speech, say all four morae clearly: わ・た・く・し.

## Say it

```speak
はじめまして。{田中|たなか}ともうします。
= How do you do? My name is Tanaka.
いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております。
= Thank you for your continued support.
しょうしょうお{待|ま}ちください。
= One moment, please.
おにもつ、お{持|も}ちしましょうか。
= Shall I carry your bags?
{明日|あした}、{三時|さんじ}にうかがいます。
= I'll come and see you at three tomorrow.
おりかえしお{電話|でんわ}いたします。
= I'll call you back.
```

## Common mistakes

- Humble verbs for the other person's actions: \*{先生|せんせい}がまいりました → いらっしゃいました.
- Asking a customer \*{何|なに}をいただきますか for "what will you have?". いただく is humble; the
  customer's eating is めしあがる: {何|なに}をめしあがりますか.
- \*{田中|たなか}さんはただいま{出|で}かけていらっしゃいます, said by Tanaka's colleague to a caller. To
  outsiders, your own colleagues get no さん and humble forms: {田中|たなか}はただいま{出|で}かけて
  おります.
- お〜する for actions that don't involve the other person: \*{毎朝|まいあさ}お{起|お}きします.
- \*お{見|み}する, \*お{言|い}いする: use はいけんする and もうす (もうしあげる).
- \*{私|わたし}は{田中|たなか}でいらっしゃいます. でいらっしゃる is for the other person; for yourself
  it's でございます (or just です).

## Key points

- Humble language lowers you and your side when your action involves someone you respect.
- Special humble verbs: まいる ({行|い}く, {来|く}る), おる (いる), もうす ({言|い}う), いたす
  (する), いただく ({食|た}べる, {飲|の}む, もらう), はいけんする ({見|み}る), うかがう ({聞|き}く,
  visit), ぞんじる ({知|し}る), お{目|め}にかかる ({会|あ}う), さしあげる (あげる).
- まいる, おる, もうす, いたす are also courteous to the listener in formal speech: {電車|でんしゃ}
  がまいります.
- Other verbs: お + ます stem + する/いたす, ご + noun + する: お{持|も}ちします, ご{説明|せつめい}します.
- でございます (for things and yourself) vs でいらっしゃいます (for the other person).
- To outsiders, your family and colleagues get no さん and humble verbs.
- Phone phrases: …でございます, いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております, おりかえしお{電話|でんわ}いたします.
- New kanji: 工 場 質 説.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Reading and listening practice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson has no new grammar. It puts the whole course to work on the kinds of Japanese
you'll actually meet: a notice from your neighbourhood, an email from a teacher,
instructions on a machine, a blog post, a change to the train timetable. Each text is a little
longer than the readings in earlier lessons, and each one is followed by questions in the quiz.
The second half is about listening, and especially about the short casual forms that friends
use, which you've learned one by one since lesson 1 but which can be hard to catch at full
speed.

Read each text twice: once quickly for the main point, then slowly for the details. The quiz
asks the kind of questions the JLPT asks.

## Reading strategies

At N4 the texts are longer, but the same three habits from N5 still work:

1. **[[Skimming]]**. Look at the title, the headings and the first and last lines first. They
   usually say what the text is and what it wants you to do.
2. *Read the question first.* In a test, the question tells you what to look for: a date, a
   place, a reason, what someone must do.
3. **[[Scanning]]**. Then run your eyes over the text for that one piece of information: numbers,
   days of the week, place names, words like 〜まで or 〜までに.

Notices and messages also have their own vocabulary. These words come up again and again:

| Word | Meaning | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|
| {日時|にちじ} | date and time | at the top of event notices |
| {場所|ばしょ}, {会場|かいじょう} | place, venue | where it happens |
| {中止|ちゅうし} | cancellation | {雨天|うてん}{中止|ちゅうし}: cancelled if it rains |
| えんき | postponement | moved to a later date |
| へんこう | change | a change of time or place |
| むりょう, {有料|ゆうりょう} | free of charge, not free | prices and entry |
| ていいん | capacity | the maximum number of people |
| ただし | however, but (an exception) | before a condition or exception |
| ※ | note | a mark before extra information, often important |

ただし is worth watching for. It introduces the exception that a test question is often about:
{入場|にゅうじょう}むりょう。ただし、{子|こ}どもは{大人|おとな}といっしょに{来|き}てください (admission free;
however, children must come with an adult).

Also notice the reason words from lesson 26: notices say 〜のため, polite emails say 〜ので, and
friends say 〜から or 〜し.

## Text 1: a neighbourhood notice

> さくら{町|ちょう}　{夏|なつ}まつりのお{知|し}らせ
>
> {今年|ことし}も{夏|なつ}まつりを{行|おこな}います。みなさん、ぜひ{来|き}てください。
>
> {日時|にちじ}：{八月|はちがつ}{二十三日|にじゅうさんにち}（{土|ど}）{午後|ごご}{四時|よじ}〜{九時|くじ}
>
> {場所|ばしょ}：さくらこうえん
>
> ※{雨天|うてん}の{場合|ばあい}は、つぎの{日|ひ}（{二十四日|にじゅうよっか}・{日|にち}）にえんきします。
>
> ・{花火|はなび}は{午後|ごご}{八時|はちじ}からです。
>
> ・ゆかたを{着|き}て{来|き}た{方|かた}には、ジュースを{一本|いっぽん}さしあげます。
>
> ・{会場|かいじょう}には{車|くるま}で{来|こ}ないでください。{近|ちか}くのちゅうしゃじょうも{使|つか}えません。
>
> ・ボランティアをぼしゅうしています。さんかしたい{方|かた}は、{八月|はちがつ}{十日|とおか}までに、{町|ちょう}のじむしょにごれんらくください。
>
> さくら{町|ちょう}

{行|おこな}う = to hold (an event); ゆかた = a light summer kimono; ちゅうしゃじょう = car park;
ボランティア = volunteers; ぼしゅうする = to recruit, invite applications; じむしょ = office.
Notice the keigo: {方|かた} for the readers, さしあげる (humble, lesson 28) for what the organizers
give, and ごれんらくください (lesson 27).

## Text 2: an email from a teacher

The subject line of a Japanese email is called けんめい.

> けんめい：{来週|らいしゅう}{月曜日|げつようび}のじゅぎょうについて
>
> {日本語|にほんご}クラスのみなさん
>
> こんにちは。{山本|やまもと}です。
>
> {来週|らいしゅう}の{月曜日|げつようび}（{十月|じゅうがつ}{六日|むいか}）は、{私|わたし}が{大学|だいがく}のかいぎに{出|で}なければならないので、じゅぎょうを{休|やす}みにします。そのかわりに、{木曜日|もくようび}（{九日|ここのか}）の{午後|ごご}{三時|さんじ}から{四時|よじ}{半|はん}まで、205{教室|きょうしつ}でじゅぎょうをします。いつもの{教室|きょうしつ}とちがうので、{気|き}をつけてください。
>
> {木曜日|もくようび}に{来|こ}られない{人|ひと}は、{金曜日|きんようび}までにメールでれんらくしてください。じゅぎょうで{使|つか}うしりょうを{送|おく}ります。
>
> それから、しゅくだいのしめきりはかわりません。{月曜日|げつようび}の{夜|よる}までに{出|だ}してください。
>
> よろしくおねがいします。
>
> {山本|やまもと}

そのかわりに = instead; しめきり = deadline. The teacher writes in ordinary polite Japanese, not
keigo: teachers write to students this way. Notice ので for her reason, and the two
deadlines: 〜までに (by) Friday for the email, Monday night for the homework.

## Text 3: instructions

A sign beside the washing machines in a coin laundry:

> コインランドリーの{使|つか}い{方|かた}
>
> 1. {洗|あら}うものを{入|い}れて、ドアをしっかりしめてください。
> 2. コースをえらんでください。ふつう：{三十分|さんじゅっぷん}・{五百円|ごひゃくえん}　もうふ：{四十分|よんじゅっぷん}・{八百円|はっぴゃくえん}
> 3. お{金|かね}を{入|い}れると、すぐに{始|はじ}まります。{百円|ひゃくえん}だましか{使|つか}えません。りょうがえきは{入|い}り{口|ぐち}のよこにあります。
> 4. {終|お}わったら、なるべく{早|はや}く{出|だ}してください。つぎの{人|ひと}が{待|ま}っています。
>
> ※ドアは{終|お}わるまで{開|あ}けられません。
>
> ※せんざいは{自動|じどう}で{入|はい}ります。{自分|じぶん}で{入|い}れないでください。

コース = a programme (on a machine); もうふ = blanket; {百円|ひゃくえん}だま = a 100-yen coin;
りょうがえき = change machine; なるべく = as … as possible; せんざい = detergent; {自動|じどう}で =
automatically. Instructions use the と conditional (lesson 11) for what a machine does,
〜てください and 〜ないでください for what you must do, and the potential {開|あ}けられません for what
you can't.

## Text 4: a blog post

Blogs are usually written in the plain style (だ, plain verb forms), like a diary.

> はじめてのひとり{旅|たび}
>
> {先週|せんしゅう}、はじめてひとり{旅|たび}をした。{行|い}き{先|さき}は{長野|ながの}の{小|ちい}さな{村|むら}だ。{東京|とうきょう}から{電車|でんしゃ}とバスで{四時間|よじかん}ぐらいかかった。バスをおりると、{目|め}の{前|まえ}に{大|おお}きな{山|やま}が{見|み}えて、{空気|くうき}がとてもおいしかった。
>
> {村|むら}には{店|みせ}が{少|すく}ないし、{夜|よる}は{暗|くら}いし、さいしょはちょっと{不安|ふあん}だった。でも、とまった{古|ふる}い{家|いえ}のおばあさんがとても{親切|しんせつ}で、{夕飯|ゆうはん}に、はたけでとれた{野菜|やさい}を{料理|りょうり}してくれた。{東京|とうきょう}で{食|た}べる{野菜|やさい}より、ずっと{味|あじ}がこかった。
>
> つぎの{日|ひ}は{雨|あめ}だったので、{山|やま}にはのぼれなかった。{楽|たの}しみにしていたのに、ざんねん！ そのかわり、おばあさんにそばの{作|つく}り{方|かた}を{教|おし}えてもらった。はじめて{作|つく}ったそばはかたちが{悪|わる}かったけど、{二人|ふたり}でわらいながら{食|た}べた。
>
> {帰|かえ}るとき、おばあさんは「また{来|き}てね」と{言|い}って、バスが{見|み}えなくなるまで{手|て}をふってくれた。{今度|こんど}は{友|とも}だちとか{家族|かぞく}といっしょに{来|こ}ようと{思|おも}う。

{行|い}き{先|さき} = destination; {空気|くうき} = air; とまる = to stay (at a hotel or house); はたけ =
vegetable field; {味|あじ}がこい = to have a strong, rich taste; のぼる = to climb; そば = buckwheat
noodles; かたち = shape; わらう = to laugh; {手|て}をふる = to wave. Find lesson 26's patterns:
し…し for her worries, ので for the rain, のに for her disappointment, とか for who she'll
bring next time.

## Text 5: a timetable change

> みどりせん　{工事|こうじ}のお{知|し}らせ
>
> せんろの{工事|こうじ}のため、{十一月|じゅういちがつ}{十五日|じゅうごにち}（{土|ど}）と{十六日|じゅうろくにち}（{日|にち}）の{午後|ごご}{十時|じゅうじ}から{終電|しゅうでん}まで、{北町|きたまち}{駅|えき}と{南町|みなみまち}{駅|えき}の{間|あいだ}で{電車|でんしゃ}が{止|と}まります。
>
> この{間|あいだ}は、{代|か}わりのバスが{走|はし}ります。バス{乗|の}り{場|ば}は、それぞれの{駅|えき}の{東口|ひがしぐち}にあります。
>
> バスは{電車|でんしゃ}より{三十分|さんじゅっぷん}ぐらい{多|おお}く{時間|じかん}がかかりますので、ご{注意|ちゅうい}ください。{工事|こうじ}は{雨|あめ}の{日|ひ}も{行|おこな}います。
>
> ごめいわくをおかけしますが、ごりかいとごきょうりょくをおねがいいたします。

〜せん = line (railway); せんろ = track; {代|か}わりの = replacement; {乗|の}り{場|ば} = stop (where you
board); それぞれ = each; ごりかいとごきょうりょく = your understanding and cooperation. The last
line is a fixed formula on every notice about works or delays, and it's pure keigo: ご〜をおかけ
します (humble), ご〜をおねがいいたします (humble). The reason comes first, with the formal ため.

## Casual contractions

Friends and family don't say 〜ている or 〜てしまう in full. You have met each short form in the
lesson that taught the full one. Here they are together, because in listening they come thick
and fast:

| Full form | **[[Contraction]]** | Example | Taught in |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜ている | 〜てる | {何|なに}{見|み}てるの？ | 1 |
| 〜ておく / 〜でおく | 〜とく / 〜どく | {買|か}っとく、{読|よ}んどく | 5 |
| 〜てしまう / 〜でしまう | 〜ちゃう / 〜じゃう | わすれちゃった、{飲|の}んじゃった | 9 |
| 〜なければ / 〜なくては | 〜なきゃ / 〜なくちゃ | もう{行|い}かなきゃ | 15 |
| 〜と / 〜という / 〜と{言|い}っていた | 〜って | {来|く}るって | 17 |
| 〜ていく | 〜てく | かさ{持|も}ってく？ | (new) |
| 〜ては / 〜では | 〜ちゃ / 〜じゃ | さわっちゃだめ | (new) |
| 〜じゃないか | 〜じゃん | いいじゃん | (new) |
| 〜のだ / 〜のです | 〜んだ / 〜んです | {行|い}きたいんだ | 1 |

Three are new:

- 〜てく is 〜ていく with the い dropped, like 〜てる: {持|も}ってく (take it with you).
- 〜ちゃ/〜じゃ is 〜ては/〜では, mostly in 〜ちゃだめ / 〜ちゃいけない ("you mustn't", from N5's 〜てはいけない): ここで{写真|しゃしん}をとっちゃだめだよ.
- じゃん is a casual sentence ending from じゃないか ("isn't it?"). It invites agreement or points
  something out: いいじゃん (that's nice, isn't it / what's wrong with that?), {言|い}ったじゃん (I
  told you!). It's very common among young people; just recognize it.

These belong to casual speech. Don't write them in an email to a teacher or use them in an
interview, but expect them in every conversation between friends, in dramas and in the JLPT
listening section.

### Dialogue: running late

Ken and Aya, friends, are going out together. Listen first with the words hidden, and count the
contractions.

```dialogue
# Running late
けん: もう{七時|しちじ}じゃん！{早|はや}く{行|い}かなきゃ。
= It's already seven! We've got to go.
あや: え、まだきがえてる。ちょっと{待|ま}って。
= What? I'm still getting changed. Hang on.
けん: じゃあ、{先|さき}に{駅|えき}に{行|い}っとくね。きっぷ{買|か}っとくから。
= Then I'll go on ahead to the station. I'll get the tickets.
あや: ありがとう。あ、{雨|あめ}ふってる？
= Thanks. Oh, is it raining?
けん: うん、ちょっと。かさ{持|も}ってかないと。
= Yeah, a bit. We'd better take umbrellas.
あや: {分|わ}かった。そういえば、ゆうこも{来|く}るって。
= OK. Oh, by the way, Yuko's coming too, she says.
けん: え、ほんと？じゃあ、きっぷ{三|さん}まい{買|か}っとかなきゃ。
= Really? Then I'd better get three tickets.
あや: あ、ゆうこは{自分|じぶん}で{買|か}うって{言|い}ってたよ。
= Oh, Yuko said she'd buy her own.
けん: そっか。じゃ、{先|さき}{行|い}っちゃうね。
= Right. I'll head off, then.
あや: うん、あとでね！
= OK, see you there!
```

きがえる = to get changed; そういえば = speaking of which, by the way; ほんと = ほんとう; そっか =
そうか (I see). The full forms: {七時|しちじ}じゃないか, {行|い}かなければ, きがえている, {行|い}っておく,
{買|か}っておく, ふっている, {持|も}っていかないと, {来|く}ると{言|い}っていた, {買|か}っておかなければ,
{行|い}ってしまう.

## Listening strategies

- *Before you listen*, read the choices (or look at the pictures) and guess what the question
  will be about: a time, a place, what someone will do.
- *Listen for the change.* JLPT conversations often make one plan and then change it. The
  words that signal it: でも, じつは (actually), やっぱり (after all; going back to the first idea
  or doing what you thought), それより (rather than that). 「バスで{行|い}こうか。」「でも、{雨|あめ}だし……。
  やっぱり、タクシーにしよう。」: the answer is the taxi.
- *Listen for the signposts.* それで (and so, and then) moves the story on; つまり (in other
  words) gives the summary, often the answer; ところで (by the way) changes the subject, so what
  came before is finished.
- *Who does what?* Keigo is a clue in listening: honorific verbs mean the other person acts,
  humble verbs mean the speaker does. {私|わたし}がまいります: the speaker will go.
- *Don't translate.* Listen for the facts the question needs; you don't have to understand
  every word.

## Say it

Casual reactions and fillers you'll hear in every conversation. Say them with a friend's
intonation:

```speak
ほんと？
= Really?
そっか。
= I see. / Right.
やっぱり。
= I knew it. / Just as I thought.
いいじゃん。
= That's nice! / What's wrong with that?
もう{行|い}かなきゃ。
= I've got to go.
ちょっと{待|ま}ってて。
= Wait a sec. ({待|ま}っていて)
```

## Key points

- Reading: skim first, read the question, then scan for the detail. Watch for ※ and ただし.
- Notice words: {日時|にちじ}, {会場|かいじょう}, {中止|ちゅうし}, えんき, へんこう, むりょう, {有料|ゆうりょう},
  ていいん.
- Register tells you the text type: notices use ため and keigo formulas; emails to students use
  です/ます and ので; blogs use the plain style.
- Casual contractions: てる, とく/どく, ちゃう/じゃう, なきゃ/なくちゃ, って, てく, ちゃ/じゃ, じゃん.
- Listening: read the choices first, listen for changes (でも, やっぱり, じつは) and signposts
  (それで, つまり, ところで), and use keigo to tell who acts.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The JLPT N4 and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for This is the last core lesson of the course. It explains the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test at level N4: what the level means, how the test is built and scored, and how to prepare. It then reviews the grammar of the whole course by what it does (explaining, asking, giving, guessing, being polite), so you can see what you know and where to go back. It ends with a plan for moving on towards N3. The quiz at the end mixes questions from every module: treat it as a final check. ## The JLPT and the level N4 The **[[JLPT]]** (Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, {日本語|にほんご}のうりょく{試験|しけん}) has five levels, from N5, the easiest, to N1. N4 is the second step, and it is the level this course has taught. In this course's own words, someone who has reached N4 can understand basic Japanese: - they can read passages about familiar everyday topics, written with basic vocabulary and kanji; - they can follow conversations from daily life, as long as they are spoken fairly slowly. That is a step up from N5 in three ways: the texts are longer (a few paragraphs rather than a few lines), there are more kanji and more words, and the grammar includes everything from the verb forms of this course to the first keigo. The test still checks only reading and listening. There is no speaking or writing section, and every question is multiple choice. The JLPT has published no official lists of words, kanji or grammar for each level since the test was revised in 2010. Courses and books (this one included) follow the scope that has become standard: about 1,500 words and roughly 300 kanji in all for N4, counting N5's. ## How the N4 test is built The test is taken in one sitting, in three timed parts: ```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: The three parts of the JLPT N4 accDescr: The N4 test has three timed parts taken in order. First, language knowledge (vocabulary), 25 minutes. Second, language knowledge (grammar) and reading, 55 minutes. Third, listening, 35 minutes. The first two parts are scored together out of 120 points, and listening out of 60, for a total of 180. A["1. Vocabulary
25 min"] --> B["2. Grammar and reading
55 min"] B --> C["3. Listening
35 min"] A -.-> S1["Scored together: 0 to 120"] B -.-> S1 C -.-> S2["Scored: 0 to 60"] ``` | Part | Time | What it tests | |---|---|---| | Language knowledge: vocabulary | 25 minutes | reading kanji words; choosing how a word is written; the word that fits a sentence; a sentence with the same meaning; how a word is used | | Language knowledge: grammar, and reading | 55 minutes | the right form or particle; word order; gaps in a text; short and medium-length texts; finding information in a notice or timetable | | Listening | 35 minutes | what someone will do; a key detail; what to say in a situation; the right quick reply | These are the times since the December 2020 test. Before that the first two parts were 30 and 60 minutes, so older books may give different figures. Here is each part, described in this course's own words. ### Vocabulary (25 minutes) - *Kanji readings.* A word in kanji inside a sentence; you choose its reading. Expect near misses: a long vowel dropped, a small っ missing, a voiced sound added or dropped ({工場|こうじょう} or こうしょう?). - *Writing.* The reverse: a word in hiragana, and you choose its kanji. Lookalikes are the trap: {待|ま}つ and {持|も}つ, {体|からだ} and {休|やす}む, and the kanji inside a gate: {間|あいだ}, {問題|もんだい}, {聞|き}く, {開|あ}ける. - *Words in context.* A sentence with a gap; one word fits the meaning. - *Paraphrase.* A sentence and four others; you choose the one with the same meaning. Many of these test pairs like {不安|ふあん}だ = しんぱいだ. - *Usage.* New at N4: one word and four sentences that use it; you choose the sentence where it's used correctly. This tests whether you know how a word behaves, not just its English meaning. For example, {間|ま}に{合|あ}う is used for time ({電車|でんしゃ}に{間|ま}に{合|あ}った), not for meeting people. ### Grammar and reading (55 minutes) - *Choosing the form.* Which particle, verb form or expression fits the gap? The traps are the pairs this course has contrasted: ので and のに, そう and そうだ, ように and ために, the four conditionals, あげる and くれる, passive and causative. - *Word order.* Four pieces to put in order, and you report the one in a marked position (★). Build the whole sentence before you answer. - *Text grammar.* A short passage with gaps, often for linking words (それに, それなのに, だから) and sentence endings. - *Reading.* Short texts of a few lines (a note, an email) with one question each; longer texts of a few paragraphs with several questions; and an information text, such as a notice, a timetable or a price list, where you answer a practical question. These are the text types of lesson 29. ### Listening (35 minutes) - *What to do.* A conversation, then a question about what someone will do (or do first). Listen for changes of plan: でも, やっぱり, じつは. - *Key detail.* You hear the question first, then the conversation, and choose a detail: a reason, a time, a place. Read the choices before the audio starts. - *What do you say?* A picture shows a situation and you choose what the person marked with an arrow would say. Many of these are about politeness: asking a favour, offering help, apologizing. - *Quick reply.* One short sentence, then three spoken replies; nothing is printed. This is where keigo and casual contractions both turn up. Each recording is played once, and you mark one circle per question on a mark sheet. ## Scoring | Scoring section | Score range | Minimum to pass | |---|---|---| | Language knowledge (vocabulary and grammar) and reading | 0–120 | 38 | | Listening | 0–60 | 19 | | Total | 0–180 | 90 | You need *both* a total of at least 90 *and* at least the minimum in each section. That minimum is the **[[sectional pass mark]]**: with 110 points overall but 15 in listening, you fail. The scores are **[[scaled scores]]**, adjusted so that the same score means the same ability on every test date, so don't try to work out a percentage of questions you need. The test is usually held in July and December, in Japan and in many other countries (some places hold it only once a year), and registration closes months in advance. Dates, fees and rules can change, so check the official website and your local test centre: - [The official JLPT website](https://www.jlpt.jp/e/) - [Official sample questions for learners](https://www.jlpt.jp/e/samples/forlearners.html) The official samples show the real layout of each question type, with audio. Save them for the last weeks and do them under timed conditions. ## Strategies ### Before the test - *Words and kanji every day.* Keep your vocabulary reviews going to the end; the vocabulary section and much of the reading depend on them. Go through the kanji list in the Study tools box with the readings covered. - *Turn furigana off.* The test prints readings only over kanji beyond the level. Reread this course's texts (lessons 26–29) without furigana. - *Read whole texts.* N4 reading is longer than N5. Read lesson 29's texts, and graded readers from the reading list, at your own speed, and then against the clock. - *Listen daily, including casual speech.* Replay this course's dialogues with the words hidden. Learn the contractions of lesson 29 until you hear 〜とかなきゃ as 〜ておかなければ without thinking. ### During the test - *Vocabulary:* it's quick, so don't linger. For kanji readings check the small details: long vowels, っ, voiced sounds. - *Grammar:* look at what comes right before and after the gap. Is it a stem (ながら, すぎる, やすい, そう "looks"), a plain form (そうだ "I hear", はず, かもしれない) or a noun with の or な (のに, ので: なのに, なので)? The form often decides the answer. - *Reading:* read the question first, then scan. In information texts, check the conditions: ただし, ※ and 〜までに. - *Listening:* use keigo to tell who acts (honorific: the other person; humble: the speaker), and listen to the end before you choose: the plan may change in the last line. - *Always answer.* There's no penalty for a wrong answer. ## The whole course by function Use this table to decide what to review. If a pattern doesn't feel familiar, go back to its lesson. | What you want to do | Patterns | Lessons | |---|---|---| | Explain, give reasons | 〜んです; て form for causes (〜てすみません); ので, のに, し, とか; ため | 1, 24, 26 | | Say what you can do | potential ({書|か}ける, {食|た}べられる); 〜ことができる | 2 | | Plans and intentions | 〜(よ)うと{思|おも}う; つもり, よてい; ことにする, ことになる | 3, 4 | | Try and prepare | 〜てみる; 〜ておく | 5 | | Give, receive, ask favours | あげる, くれる, もらう; 〜てあげる/くれる/もらう; 〜ていただけませんか; 〜てほしい | 6, 7 | | Describe states and changes | transitive/intransitive pairs; 〜ている vs 〜てある; 〜てしまう; 〜ようになる, 〜なくなる | 8, 9, 24 | | Talk about timing | 〜ながら; 〜ところ; 〜たばかり; 〜まま; 〜ないで; 〜までに; 〜あいだ(に) | 10, 19 | | Conditions | と; ば; たら; なら; 〜ても | 11–14 | | Rules and obligations | 〜なければならない; 〜なくてもいい; 〜なさい; the imperative | 15 | | Appearance, hearsay, guesses | 〜そう (looks); 〜そうだ (I hear); 〜って; ようだ, みたい, らしい; はず, かもしれない | 16–19 | | Questions inside sentences | 〜か; 〜かどうか | 20 | | Who does what to whom | passive; causative; causative-passive | 21–23 | | Purpose and manner | 〜ように, 〜ために; やすい, にくい, すぎる; 〜{方|かた}; 〜さ; 〜がる | 24, 25 | | Be polite | honorific (いらっしゃる, お〜になる, お〜ください); humble (まいる, お〜する); でございます | 27, 28 | ### Seven things to check These are the points that cost N4 learners the most marks: 1. *The four conditionals.* たら is the safest all-rounder. と can't be followed by a request or a plan (\*{駅|えき}に{着|つ}くと、{電話|でんわ}してください → {着|つ}いたら). なら takes up what the other person just said ({京都|きょうと}なら…). ば is for general conditions and advice (どうすればいいですか). 2. *そう or そうだ.* Stem + そう is "looks like": おいしそう. Plain form + そうだ is "I hear": おいしいそうだ. いい gives よさそう; ない gives なさそう. 3. *Giving verbs.* Things that come to you or your side take くれる, never あげる: {友|とも}だちが ({私|わたし}に) {本|ほん}をくれた. With もらう, the giver takes に or から. 4. *Passive, causative, causative-passive.* {母|はは}にしかられた (I was scolded by my mother); {子|こ}どもに{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べさせた (I made the child eat vegetables); {母|はは}に{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べさせられた (I was made to eat vegetables by my mother). Ask who acts and who wants it. 5. *Transitive and intransitive.* を + transitive, が + intransitive: ドアを{開|あ}ける / ドアが{開|あ}く. 〜てある needs a transitive verb (まどが{開|あ}けてある, someone left it open); 〜ている after an intransitive verb describes the state (まどが{開|あ}いている). 6. *ので, のに and the な.* {雨|あめ}なので, {雨|あめ}なのに, never \*{雨|あめ}だので. のに can't be followed by a request. 7. *Keigo direction.* Honorific for what others do (いらっしゃる, めしあがる), humble for what you do (まいる, いただく). \*{先生|せんせい}がまいりました and \*{私|わたし}がいらっしゃいます are both wrong. ## Words for the exam | Word | Meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | ごうかくする | to pass (an exam) | N4にごうかくしました。 (I passed N4.) | | てんすう | score, points | ちょうかいのてんすうが{低|ひく}かった。 (My listening score was low.) | | けっか | result | {試験|しけん}のけっかはいつ{分|わ}かりますか。 (When do the exam results come out?) | | もうしこみ | application, registration | もうしこみは{九月|くがつ}までです。 (Applications close in September.) | | じゅけんする | to sit (an exam) | {十二月|じゅうにがつ}にじゅけんするつもりです。 (I plan to sit it in December.) | | ぶんぽう | grammar | ぶんぽうのもんだい (grammar questions) | | ごい | vocabulary | ごいをふやす (to build up your vocabulary) | | どっかい | reading (comprehension) | どっかいは{時間|じかん}がたりなかった。 (I ran out of time on reading.) | | ちょうかい | listening (comprehension) | ちょうかいは{一回|いっかい}しか{聞|き}けない。 (You can only hear the listening once.) | | じつりょく | real ability | じつりょくを{試|ため}す (to test what you can really do) | | もくひょう | goal, target | {来年|らいねん}のもくひょうはN3です。 (Next year my goal is N3.) | | {計画|けいかく} | plan | {勉強|べんきょう}の{計画|けいかく}を{立|た}てる (to make a study plan) | ごうかくする, ぶんぽう, もくひょう and {計画|けいかく} are from earlier lessons and are here as a reminder; the others are new. ぶんぽう, ごい, どっかい and ちょうかい are the Japanese names of the test's parts, and you'll see them on study books and in the score report. じゅけんする and the N5 word うける both mean "to take an exam"; じゅけん is the formal word, and it's the usual one for entrance exams. {計画|けいかく}を {立|た}てる (literally "stand up a plan") is the set phrase for making a plan. ## A study plan for the last month | Week | What to do | |---|---| | 1 | Modules 1–2: reread each lesson's Key points and redo the module quizzes. Every day: vocabulary reviews, one dialogue with the words hidden. | | 2 | Modules 3–4 the same way, with the conditionals and seeming/hearsay tables in the Study tools box. | | 3 | Modules 5–6. Reread lesson 29's texts with furigana off and against the clock (about one minute per 100 characters). Ten minutes of listening a day. | | 4 | The official sample questions, timed. Go back to the lesson behind each mistake. Rest the day before. | ## After N4: towards N3 N3 is the bridge between basic and intermediate Japanese, and the jump from N4 is bigger than the jump from N5. Commonly cited lists roughly double the vocabulary and kanji again, the texts are longer and closer to real Japanese (newspaper-style summaries, explanations, essays), and the listening is closer to natural speed. A plan that works for many learners: - *Read a lot of easy text.* Extensive reading, at a level where you know nearly every word, is the fastest way to grow vocabulary. Start with the graded readers in this course's reading list one level above where you feel comfortable, then move to easy news. - *Keep kanji tied to words.* Learn new kanji inside words you meet in your reading, not from a list alone. - *Listen to natural speech.* Podcasts and videos for learners first, then dramas and vlogs with Japanese subtitles. Casual contractions (lesson 29) are everywhere. - *Expect new grammar patterns.* N3 adds many patterns, often built from words you know: 〜ば〜ほど (the more … the more, mentioned in lesson 12), 〜わけだ (that's why), 〜ついでに (while you're at it), 〜くせに (even though, critical) and many more. With the verb forms of N4 behind you, they are much easier to pick up. - *Use keigo for real.* Write a polite email (lesson 30h2), and practise the phone phrases of lesson 28 out loud. ## Dialogue: after the test Two friends who sat N4 together compare notes on the way home. ```dialogue # After the test エマ: やっと{終|お}わったね。どうだった？ = Finally over. How did it go? たくや: ぶんぽうはできたと{思|おも}うけど、どっかいは{時間|じかん}がたりなかったよ。さいごのもんだい、{読|よ}めなかった。 = I think grammar went OK, but I ran out of time on reading. I couldn't read the last question. エマ: {私|わたし}も。お{知|し}らせのもんだいはかんたんだったのに、{長|なが}いぶんしょうがむずかしかった。 = Me too. The notice one was easy, but the long passage was hard. たくや: ちょうかいは？ = What about listening? エマ: さいしょはよく{分|わ}かったんだけど、けいごの{会話|かいわ}で、だれが{来|く}るのか{分|わ}からなくなっちゃった。 = At first I understood well, but in the keigo conversation I lost track of who was coming. たくや: ああ、「まいります」と「いらっしゃいます」のもんだいだね。まいりますって{言|い}ったのは{店|みせ}の{人|ひと}だから、{来|く}るのは{店|みせ}の{人|ひと}だよ。 = Oh, the まいります and いらっしゃいます one. It was the shop assistant who said まいります, so it's the shop assistant who's coming. エマ: あ、そうか！やっぱりまちがえた。 = Oh, of course! I knew I'd got it wrong. たくや: でも、{一|ひと}つや{二|ふた}つまちがえても、だいじょうぶだよ。 = But you'll be fine even if you got one or two wrong. エマ: そうだといいけど。けっかが{出|で}るまで、まだ{何|なん}か{月|げつ}もあるんだよね。 = I hope so. And it's still months until the results come out, isn't it? たくや: うん。だから、もうN3の{計画|けいかく}を{立|た}てようかな。 = Yeah. So maybe I'll start planning for N3 already. エマ: え、もう？じゃあ、{今日|きょう}だけは{休|やす}もうよ。おいしいものでも{食|た}べに{行|い}こう！ = What, already? Then let's at least take today off. Let's go and eat something nice! ``` たりない = not enough; さいご = last; かんたん = easy; ぶんしょう = a text, a passage; さいしょ = at first; {会話|かいわ} = conversation; そうだといいけど = I hope so; {何|なん}か{月|げつ}も = (for) months. Takuya's explanation is the listening strategy from lesson 29 in action: まいります is humble, so the speaker is the one who comes. ## Can you do this? By the end of this course you should be able to do everything below. If something feels shaky, the numbers show where to go back. - Explain why something happened, apologize and make excuses politely (1, 26). - Say what you can and can't do, and what you intend or have decided to do (2–4). - Ask for, offer and thank people for favours, and talk about gifts (6, 7). - Describe what has happened to things around the house, and accidents and mishaps (8, 9). - Talk about conditions, advice and rules (11–15). - Say how things look, what you've heard and what you guess (16–19). - Ask for information politely (20). - Talk about what was done to you, and what you made or let others do (21–23). - Talk about habits, goals and products (24, 25). - Speak politely to teachers, customers and companies, and follow keigo on the phone and in shops (27, 28). - Read notices, emails, instructions and blog posts, and follow casual conversation (29). ## Common mistakes - Studying only grammar. Listening has its own pass mark (19 of 60), and missing it means failing, whatever your total. - Running out of time in the grammar and reading part. Do the grammar questions quickly; the reading needs the time. - Choosing a listening answer before the conversation ends. The plan often changes in the last line. - Reading every word of an information text. Read the question, then scan. - Leaving questions blank. A guess can score; a blank can't. ## Key points - N4 has three timed parts: vocabulary (25 minutes), grammar and reading (55 minutes) and listening (35 minutes). - Two scoring sections: language knowledge and reading (0–120, at least 38) and listening (0–60, at least 19). You pass with 90 of 180 *and* both minimums. Scores are scaled. - Vocabulary at N4 adds a usage question: which sentence uses the word correctly. - Review with the table by function and the seven things to check: conditionals, そう/そうだ, giving verbs, passive and causative, transitive and intransitive, ので/のに, keigo direction. - Check jlpt.jp for dates, rules and sample questions. The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: A longer story: the Saturday bakery
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is one story, about 1,400 characters long, written for this course. It uses only
words and grammar from N5 and N4, plus a few words glossed before each part. Read it the way
you'd read a graded reader: for the story first, without stopping at every word. Then read it
again, slowly, and answer the questions in the quiz.

Try reading it with furigana off. The kanji are all from this course's list.

## Before you read

The story is told in the plain style (だ, plain verb forms), like most fiction. Conversations
are in 「」 quotation marks; the old baker speaks in a gentle, slightly old-fashioned casual
style (〜わ, 〜のよ, 〜かしら).

Words you may not know yet:

| Part | Words |
|---|---|
| 1 | パン{屋|や} = bakery; やく = to bake; やきたて = freshly baked; さくさく = crisp, flaky |
| 2 | はりがみ = a notice stuck up on paper; たつ = (time) to pass; けがをする = to get hurt; {入院|にゅういん}する = to go into hospital; むすこ = son |
| 3 | おどろく = to be surprised; わざわざ = taking the trouble; こな = flour; だまる = to fall silent; やがて = before long, eventually |
| 4 | {言|い}われたとおりに = just as (she) told him; はかる = to measure; ちょうし = condition, the way something is going (そのちょうし = "that's it, keep going"); れつ = a queue; {頭|あたま}を{下|さ}げる = to bow |

## 1. Melon bread every morning

> はるとが{大学|だいがく}に{入|はい}って、この{町|まち}に{住|す}み{始|はじ}めたのは{四月|しがつ}だった。{駅|えき}までの{道|みち}に、{小|ちい}さなパン{屋|や}がある。{店|みせ}の{名前|なまえ}は「こむぎ」。{朝|あさ}{七時|しちじ}に{開|あ}く{店|みせ}で、{山口|やまぐち}さんというおばあさんが{一人|ひとり}でパンをやいている。
>
> はるとは{毎朝|まいあさ}、そこでメロンパンを{一|ひと}つ{買|か}うことにしていた。やきたてのメロンパンは、{外|そと}がさくさくしていて、{中|なか}がやわらかい。{山口|やまぐち}さんはパンをわたしながら、いつも「いってらっしゃい」と{言|い}ってくれた。{一人|ひとり}で{住|す}んでいるはるとには、それがとてもうれしかった。

## 2. The notice on the door

> {十月|じゅうがつ}のある{朝|あさ}、「こむぎ」のドアが{開|あ}いていなかった。ドアには「しばらく{休|やす}みます」と{書|か}いたはりがみがしてあった。つぎの{日|ひ}も、そのつぎの{日|ひ}も、{店|みせ}は{休|やす}みだった。
>
> {一週間|いっしゅうかん}たって、はるとはとなりの{花屋|はなや}の{主人|しゅじん}に{聞|き}いてみた。
>
> 「{山口|やまぐち}さん、どうしたんですか。」
>
> 「{店|みせ}で{転|ころ}んで、けがをしたそうだよ。{今|いま}は{駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くの{病院|びょういん}に{入院|にゅういん}しているらしい。」
>
> {主人|しゅじん}は{少|すこ}しさびしそうに{言|い}った。「おおさかに{住|す}んでいるむすこさんが、もう{店|みせ}をやめたほうがいいと{言|い}っているそうだ。{四十年|よんじゅうねん}もつづいた{店|みせ}なのに、ざんねんだね。」

## 3. At the hospital

> その{週|しゅう}の{土曜日|どようび}、はるとは{花|はな}を{持|も}って{病院|びょういん}へ{行|い}った。{山口|やまぐち}さんはベッドの{上|うえ}で{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んでいたが、はるとを{見|み}ると、おどろいた{顔|かお}をした。
>
> 「まあ、メロンパンの{学生|がくせい}さん！わざわざ{来|き}てくれたの？」
>
> 「はい。お{店|みせ}が{開|あ}かないので、しんぱいで……。けがはだいじょうぶですか。」
>
> 「ありがとう。{足|あし}はもうすぐよくなるのよ。でも、むすこが、{一人|ひとり}で{店|みせ}をつづけるのはもうむりだって。たしかに、{朝|あさ}{四時|よじ}に{起|お}きて、{重|おも}いこなのふくろを{運|はこ}ぶのは、もうたいへんなの。」
>
> {山口|やまぐち}さんはまどの{外|そと}を{見|み}た。
>
> 「{近所|きんじょ}の{子|こ}どもたちが、{小|ちい}さいときから{買|か}いに{来|き}てくれてね。その{子|こ}たちが{大人|おとな}になって、{今度|こんど}は{自分|じぶん}の{子|こ}どもをつれて{来|く}るの。それが{私|わたし}の{楽|たの}しみだったのに……。」
>
> はるとは{少|すこ}し{考|かんが}えてから、{言|い}った。
>
> 「あのう、{私|わたし}にてつだわせていただけませんか。{高校|こうこう}のとき、パン{屋|や}でアルバイトをしていたので、{少|すこ}しはできます。{重|おも}いものも{運|はこ}べます。」
>
> 「でも、{学生|がくせい}さんにそんなことはさせられないわ。」
>
> 「{朝|あさ}はどうせ{早|はや}く{起|お}きますから。それに、こむぎのメロンパンが{食|た}べられないと、{一日|いちにち}が{始|はじ}まらないんです。」
>
> {山口|やまぐち}さんはしばらくだまっていたが、やがてわらって{言|い}った。
>
> 「じゃあ、{土曜日|どようび}だけ、おねがいしようかしら。」

## 4. The Saturday bakery

> {十一月|じゅういちがつ}から、「こむぎ」は{土曜日|どようび}だけ{開|ひら}くことになった。
>
> はるとは{朝|あさ}{四時|よじ}に{店|みせ}に{行|い}って、{山口|やまぐち}さんに{言|い}われたとおりに、こなをはかったり、パンのかたちを{作|つく}ったりした。{山口|やまぐち}さんはいすにすわって、「もう{少|すこ}しやさしく」「そう、そのちょうし」と{教|おし}えてくれた。さいしょのメロンパンはかたちがへんで、{二人|ふたり}で{大|おお}きな{声|こえ}でわらった。
>
> 「はるとくんのメロンパン、{見|み}た{目|め}は{悪|わる}いけど、{味|あじ}はいいわよ。」
>
> {三回目|さんかいめ}の{土曜日|どようび}には、{店|みせ}の{前|まえ}にれつができるようになった。{店|みせ}が{休|やす}みの{間|あいだ}も、「こむぎはいつ{開|あ}くの？」と{聞|き}きに{来|く}る{人|ひと}が{多|おお}かったそうだ。
>
> ある{土曜日|どようび}、おおさかからむすこさんが{来|き}た。{店|みせ}の{中|なか}で{楽|たの}しそうにおきゃくさんと{話|はな}している{母|はは}を{見|み}て、むすこさんはしばらく{何|なに}も{言|い}わなかった。それから、はるとに{頭|あたま}を{下|さ}げた。
>
> 「{母|はは}がこんなに{元気|げんき}なのは、ひさしぶりです。ありがとうございます。{土曜日|どようび}だけなら、つづけてもいいと{思|おも}います。」
>
> つぎの{土曜日|どようび}、{小|ちい}さな{女|おんな}の{子|こ}が、お{母|かあ}さんといっしょにメロンパンを{買|か}いに{来|き}た。はるとはパンをわたしながら、{山口|やまぐち}さんと{同|おな}じように{言|い}った。
>
> 「いってらっしゃい。」

## In English

Haruto moved to the town in April, when he started university. On the way to the station there
is a small bakery called Komugi ("wheat"), where an old woman, Mrs Yamaguchi, bakes bread by
herself. Every morning he buys one melon bread, and every morning she hands it over saying
"いってらっしゃい", "off you go, have a good day", which means a lot to someone living alone.

One October morning the shop is shut, with a notice saying it will be closed for a while. After
a week Haruto asks the florist next door, who has heard that she fell in the shop, was hurt, and
seems to be in hospital; her son in Osaka is saying she should give up the shop. "Such a shame,
after forty years."

That Saturday Haruto visits her with flowers. She is surprised and touched. Her leg will soon
heal, she says, but her son says she can't go on alone: getting up at four and carrying heavy
sacks of flour is too much now. The children of the neighbourhood have bought her bread since
they were small, and now they bring their own children; that was her joy. Haruto thinks, then
asks to be allowed to help: he worked part-time in a bakery in high school, and he can carry
heavy things. She says she couldn't ask a student to do that. He answers that he gets up early
anyway, and that his day doesn't start without Komugi's melon bread. After a silence she smiles:
then perhaps just on Saturdays.

From November, Komugi opens on Saturdays only. Haruto arrives at four and weighs the flour and
shapes the bread as she tells him, while she sits on a chair and coaches him. His first melon
breads are a funny shape and they laugh out loud: "It doesn't look good, but it tastes good."
By the third Saturday there is a queue outside; while the shop was closed, many people had come
to ask when it would open. One Saturday the son comes from Osaka. Seeing his mother chatting
happily with customers, he says nothing for a while, then bows to Haruto: it's a long time since
his mother was this well; if it's only Saturdays, she can carry on. The next Saturday, a little
girl comes in with her mother to buy melon bread, and Haruto, handing it over, says just what Mrs
Yamaguchi always said: "いってらっしゃい."

## Grammar to notice

The story uses patterns from every module. Find them as you reread:

| Pattern | In the story | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| 〜ことにしている | {買|か}うことにしていた (made a habit of buying) | 4 |
| 〜ながら | わたしながら | 10 |
| 〜てある | はりがみがしてあった | 8 |
| 〜そうだ (hearsay) | けがをしたそうだ, {言|い}っているそうだ | 17 |
| らしい | {入院|にゅういん}しているらしい | 18 |
| のに | {四十年|よんじゅうねん}もつづいた{店|みせ}なのに; {楽|たの}しみだったのに | 26 |
| ので | {開|あ}かないので; していたので | 26 |
| causative + いただけませんか | てつだわせていただけませんか | 22 |
| causative + potential | させられない (I can't make you do that) | 2, 22 |
| potential + と | {食|た}べられないと、{一日|いちにち}が{始|はじ}まらない | 2, 11 |
| ことになる | {開|ひら}くことになった | 4 |
| passive | {言|い}われたとおりに | 21 |
| 〜ようになる | れつができるようになった | 24 |
| 〜そう (looks) | {楽|たの}しそうに | 16 |
| 〜かしら | おねがいしようかしら | 20 |

Notice also how the people speak. Haruto uses polite Japanese with Mrs Yamaguchi and asks for a
favour with the politest request in the course, 〜させていただけませんか. She speaks casually to
him, as an older person to a young one. Her son, a stranger to Haruto, uses です/ます.

The words in the table above are glossed for this story; the five listed below (はりがみ, どうせ,
だまる, やがて, れつ) join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Writing polite emails and letters
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Sooner or later you'll need to write to someone in polite Japanese: an email to your teacher
because you'll miss a class, a thank-you letter to the family you stayed with, an apology for
something you forgot. Written Japanese has fixed frames for these, and once you know the frame,
the keigo of lessons 27 and 28 fills it in. This lesson shows the frame for a polite email and
for a traditional letter, the phrases for asking and apologizing, and the seasonal greetings
that open a letter.

## A polite email

A polite email to a teacher, a host family or a company has six parts, in this order:

| Part | What goes in it | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. けんめい (subject) | short and specific; students often add their name | {来週|らいしゅう}のじゅぎょうについて（リン） |
| 2. The reader's name | name + {先生|せんせい} or さま, on its own line | {山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい} |
| 3. Greeting and who you are | a set opening, then your class or company and your name | いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております。{日本語|にほんご}クラスのリンです。 |
| 4. The main point | what you're asking first, then why, then any details | (see the examples) |
| 5. Closing | a set phrase | よろしくおねがいいたします。 |
| 6. Your name | your name, and your class or contact details | リン・ウェイ |

Two habits make an email polite in Japanese eyes. First, *say who you are near the top*: the
reader should never have to guess. Second, *put the main point early*, in a sentence or two,
before the details.

### Example 1: asking to miss a class

> けんめい：{来週|らいしゅう}{月曜日|げつようび}のじゅぎょうについて（リン・ウェイ）
>
> {山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい}
>
> いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております。{日本語|にほんご}クラスのリン・ウェイです。
>
> もうしわけありませんが、{来週|らいしゅう}{月曜日|げつようび}のじゅぎょうを{休|やす}ませていただけないでしょうか。{国|くに}からりょうしんが{来|く}ることになり、その{日|ひ}にくうこうへむかえに{行|い}かなければならないためです。
>
> じゅぎょうで{使|つか}うしりょうがありましたら、メールで{送|おく}っていただけるとたすかります。しゅくだいは{金曜日|きんようび}までに{出|だ}します。
>
> おいそがしいところ、もうしわけありません。よろしくおねがいいたします。
>
> リン・ウェイ（{日本語|にほんご}クラス）

りょうしん = parents; くうこう = airport; むかえに{行|い}く = to go to meet someone; たすかる = to be a
help. The request comes first, in the politest form in the course (〜させていただけないでしょうか);
the reason follows, with the formal ため; then a helpful detail and the closing.

Notice {来|く}ることになり, not {来|く}ることになって. In polite writing, a clause that would end in
the て form often ends in the ます stem instead: 〜てしまい, 〜ことになり, 〜ており. It sounds more
formal, and you'll see it in every business email.

### Example 2: apologizing

> けんめい：しゅくだいがおくれたおわび（リン・ウェイ）
>
> {山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい}
>
> いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております。リン・ウェイです。
>
> きのうがしめきりだったしゅくだいを、まだ{出|だ}していませんでした。もうしわけありません。{日|ひ}にちをまちがえてしまい、{今朝|けさ}{気|き}がつきました。
>
> しゅくだいは、このメールにつけてお{送|おく}りします。ごめいわくをおかけして、たいへんもうしわけありませんでした。これからは、しめきりをよくかくにんするようにします。
>
> リン・ウェイ

{日|ひ}にち = the date; まちがえる = to get wrong; つける = to attach; かくにんする = to check. The
apology comes first and is plain about what happened; the promise at the end (〜ようにします,
lesson 24) matters as much as the apology.

The teacher's reply (へんしん) is short, and less formal: teachers write to students this way.

> リンさん
>
> しゅくだい、うけとりました。ていねいなメールをありがとう。つぎから{気|き}をつけてくださいね。
>
> {山本|やまもと}

うけとる = to receive.

## Phrases for asking and apologizing

| Phrase | Meaning and use |
|---|---|
| 〜ていただけないでしょうか | Could you possibly…? The politest request; でしょうか softens いただけませんか (lesson 7). |
| 〜させていただけないでしょうか | Could I possibly be allowed to…? (lesson 22) |
| 〜ていただけるとたすかります | It would be a great help if you could… |
| 〜がありましたら | If there is/are… (polite たら) |
| おいそがしいところ、もうしわけありません | Sorry to trouble you when you're busy. |
| ごめいわくをおかけして、もうしわけありません | I'm sorry for the trouble I've caused. |
| 〜てしまい、もうしわけありませんでした | I'm sorry that I… (for a mistake) |
| おわびもうしあげます | I sincerely apologize. (very formal; companies) |
| これからは〜ようにします | From now on I'll make sure to… |
| よろしくおねがいいたします | The closing of almost every polite email. |

おわび is the noun "apology": a subject line like 〜のおわび says at once that the email apologizes.

## A traditional letter

A letter on paper (to a host family, a teacher, an older relative) has a more formal frame. Emails
and cards usually leave the opening and closing words out, but they keep the order.

1. はいけい, the opening word ("Dear…", formal).
2. A **[[seasonal greeting]]**: a line about the season or the weather.
3. Asking after the reader: みなさまお{元気|げんき}でいらっしゃいますか.
4. さて ("now", "well then"), which turns to the main point of the letter.
5. Closing wishes for the reader's health: お{体|からだ}を{大切|たいせつ}になさってください.
6. けいぐ, the closing word ("Yours sincerely"), which always pairs with はいけい.
7. The date and your name, and then the name of the person you're writing to.

The pair はいけい … けいぐ is to recognize: they're formal, and modern personal letters often
start straight with the seasonal greeting. Some women close a letter with かしこ instead of けいぐ.

### Seasonal greetings

A Japanese letter opens with the season the way an English one might open with "I hope you're
well". These are simple, all-purpose ones:

| Season | Greeting | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| spring | さくらの{花|はな}がきれいなきせつになりました。 | It's the season of the lovely cherry blossoms. |
| rainy season (June) | {雨|あめ}の{日|ひ}がつづいていますが、いかがおすごしですか。 | It's been raining day after day; how are you? |
| summer | {暑|あつ}い{日|ひ}がつづいていますが、お{元気|げんき}ですか。 | It's been hot day after day; are you well? |
| autumn | すずしくなってまいりました。 | It has turned cool. |
| winter | {寒|さむ}さがきびしくなってまいりました。 | The cold has become severe. |

いかがおすごしですか (how are you spending your days?) is the polite "how are you?" of letters.
Notice the courteous 〜てまいりました (lesson 28): it's typical of letters.

### Example 3: a thank-you letter to a host family

> はいけい
>
> {秋|あき}もふかくなり、{朝|あさ}{夕|ゆう}はすっかり{寒|さむ}くなりました。{田中|たなか}さんご{家族|かぞく}のみなさま、お{元気|げんき}でいらっしゃいますか。
>
> {夏|なつ}のホームステイでは、たいへんお{世話|せわ}になりました。{毎日|まいにち}おいしいご{飯|はん}を{作|つく}っていただいたり、おまつりにつれて{行|い}っていただいたりして、ほんとうに{楽|たの}しい{一|いっ}か{月|げつ}でした。とくに、おばあさまに{教|おし}えていただいたゆかたの{着方|きかた}は、{今|いま}も{友|とも}だちにじまんしています。
>
> {国|くに}に{帰|かえ}ってから、{前|まえ}よりもっと{日本語|にほんご}を{勉強|べんきょう}するようになりました。{来年|らいねん}は、N3をうけるつもりです。
>
> さて、{先日|せんじつ}、こちらのおかしを{少|すこ}しお{送|おく}りしました。お{口|くち}に{合|あ}うとうれしいです。
>
> これから{寒|さむ}くなりますので、どうぞお{体|からだ}を{大切|たいせつ}になさってください。また{日本|にほん}に{行|い}ったときに、お{目|め}にかかれるのを{楽|たの}しみにしております。
>
> けいぐ
>
> {十一月|じゅういちがつ}{三日|みっか}
>
> サラ・ジョンソン
>
> {田中|たなか}さま　ご{家族|かぞく}のみなさま

{秋|あき}もふかくなり = as autumn deepens; {朝|あさ}{夕|ゆう} = mornings and evenings; すっかり =
completely; おばあさま = (your) grandmother, very polite; {着方|きかた} = how to put on; じまんする
= to show off, be proud of; {先日|せんじつ} = the other day; お{口|くち}に{合|あ}う = to suit your
taste. Find the keigo: honorific for the family (でいらっしゃいますか, なさってください), humble for
Sarah (お{送|おく}りしました, お{目|め}にかかれる, しております), and 〜ていただく for every kindness she
received.

### Example 4: a short thank-you card

Cards are simpler: no frame, just thanks, one detail, and a good wish.

> {山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい}
>
> {一年間|いちねんかん}、ほんとうにありがとうございました。{先生|せんせい}のおかげで、{日本語|にほんご}が{大好|だいす}きになりました。N4にもごうかくできました。これからもがんばります。
>
> どうぞお{元気|げんき}で。
>
> リン

〜のおかげで = thanks to. A specific detail (here, passing N4) makes a short card feel personal.

## Common mistakes

- Starting with the reason and reaching the request at the end. Put the request (or apology) first.
- Forgetting to say who you are. Even if the teacher knows you, write your class and name.
- Mixing styles: one casual line (〜てね, 〜けど) in a keigo email stands out. Keep to です/ます and
  keigo throughout.
- Using honorific forms for yourself: \*{私|わたし}がお{送|おく}りになりました → お{送|おく}りしました.
- はいけい without けいぐ (or the reverse). They come as a pair.

## Key points

- Email: subject, the reader's name, お{世話|せわ}になっております + who you are, the main point first,
  よろしくおねがいいたします, your name.
- Asking: 〜ていただけないでしょうか, 〜させていただけないでしょうか, 〜ていただけるとたすかります.
- Apologizing: ごめいわくをおかけして, 〜てしまい, もうしわけありませんでした; おわび (noun).
- Written style links clauses with the ます stem: 〜てしまい, 〜ことになり.
- A letter: はいけい, seasonal greeting, asking after the reader, さて + main point, wishes, けいぐ,
  date and names.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you

sections.name: Giving, receiving and getting things done
Polite Japanese and the N4 exam

questions.stem: Complete the explanation: {明日|あした}は{休|やす}み___。 (Tomorrow is my day off, you see.)
questions.explanation: Nouns and な-adjectives take な before ん: {休|やす}みなんです. だ can't stand before ん (×{休|やす}みだんです), and ん can't follow a noun directly (×{休|やす}みんです).

questions.stem: A colleague looks pale and keeps sighing. What do you say?
questions.explanation: どうしたんですか asks for an explanation of something you've noticed: "What's the matter?" どうしますか is "What will you do?", どうでしたか is "How was it?", and どうしてですか ("Why?") needs something to ask why about.

questions.stem: You want a map of the town at the tourist office. Which is the most natural way to start?
choices: {町|まち}の{地図|ちず}がほしいんですが……
{町|まち}の{地図|ちず}がほしいです。ください。
{町|まち}の{地図|ちず}がほしかったんです。
{町|まち}の{地図|ちず}をほしがります。
questions.explanation: 〜んですが…… gives the background and leaves the request unsaid, the polite way to open. ほしいです。ください。 is abrupt, ほしかったんです puts the wish in the past, and ほしがる describes someone else's wishes.

questions.stem: Which is the casual way to ask どこに{行|い}くんですか？
questions.explanation: Casual questions with the explanatory の are plain form + の: どこ{行|い}くの？ な comes only after nouns and な-adjectives (テストなの？), and だ never goes before の.

questions.stem: What is the て form of {近|ちか}い (near)?
questions.explanation: い-adjectives drop the final い and add くて: {近|ちか}い → {近|ちか}くて. ×{近|ちか}いくて keeps the い, and で is the て form for な-adjectives and nouns.

questions.stem: Type the て form of いい (good): ___
questions.explanation: いい uses its older stem よ in every form except the dictionary form: よくない, よかった, and the て form よくて. ×いくて is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Choose the word for the blank: この{町|まち}はしずか___、きれいです。
questions.explanation: しずか is a な-adjective, so its て form is しずかで: "quiet and pretty". くて is for い-adjectives, なくて would mean "not quiet", and に makes an adverb.

questions.stem: What does this mean? {車|くるま}がなくて、こまっています。
choices: I'm in trouble without using the car.
Please don't take the car; I'm in trouble.
I had no car, but I was fine.
I don't have a car, so I'm stuck.
questions.explanation: なくて is the て form of ない and gives a reason: "there's no car, so". こまっています is "I'm in a fix". A request (please don't) would be 〜ないでください.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT natural?
choices: おそくなって、すみません。
{雨|あめ}がふって、{出|で}かけないでください。
{日本|にほん}に{来|き}て、よかったです。
ニュースを{見|み}て、びっくりしました。
questions.explanation: A て form reason must be followed by a feeling or reaction, not a request. For "It's raining, so please don't go out", use から: {雨|あめ}がふっているから、{出|で}かけないでください. The other three are natural cause + feeling sentences.

questions.stem: Your friend arrives twenty minutes late. What does she say?
choices: おそくなって、すみません。
おそくて、すみませんでした。
おそくなったら、すみません。
questions.explanation: Verb て form + すみません apologizes for what happened: おそくなって, "I became late". おそいで isn't a form; おそくて would apologize for being slow in general; 〜たら (lesson 13) means "if".

questions.stem: What does this mean? {母|はは}の{声|こえ}を{聞|き}いて、{安心|あんしん}しました。
choices: I listened to my mother's voice, then calmed her down.
Please listen to my mother; she's worried.
My mother was relieved to hear my voice.
I was relieved to hear my mother's voice.
questions.explanation: The て form gives the cause of the feeling: hearing her voice, then relief. {安心|あんしん}する is "to be relieved", and the one relieved is the speaker; it's the mother's voice that was heard.

questions.stem: Which is the most natural way to say "This town has a lot of greenery"?
choices: この{町|まち}はみどりが{多|おお}いです。
この{町|まち}がみどりは{多|おお}いです。
この{町|まち}をみどりが{多|おお}いです。
この{町|まち}のみどりを{多|おお}いです。
questions.explanation: AはBが〜: the town is the topic (は) and みどり, the part being described, takes が. The other choices swap the particles or use を, which never marks the subject of {多|おお}い.
