questions.stem: Read: {近|ちか}くに{大|おお}きい{病院|びょういん}がなくて、ちょっとふべんです。バスも{少|すく}ないんです。 What does the writer find inconvenient?
choices: The hospital is too big and the buses are full.
There are many hospitals but no buses.
There's no big hospital nearby, and there aren't many buses.
The buses are expensive and slow.
questions.explanation: {病院|びょういん}がなくて means "there's no hospital, and so"; バスも{少|すく}ない adds that there are few buses too. ふべん = inconvenient.

questions.stem: How is 近所 read in this sentence? {家|いえ}の近所にスーパーがあります。
questions.explanation: 近所 (neighbourhood) uses the on'yomi of both kanji: 近 キン + 所 ジョ. ちか is the kun'yomi of 近, used in {近|ちか}い.

questions.stem: Match each kanji to its meaning.
questions.explanation: 町 town, 村 village, 森 forest (three trees), 遠 far. "Near" is 近 and "ground, land" is 地.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker's problem?

audio.text: すみません、道にまよったんです。

questions.explanation: すみません、{道|みち}にまよったんです: I've got lost. まよう is to lose your way; "late" would be おそくなった, and "unwell" ぐあいが{悪|わる}い.

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?

audio.text: この町はしずかで、きれいです。

choices: この{町|まち}はしずかじゃなくて、きれいです。
この{町|まち}はしずかで、きれいでした。
この{町|まち}はしずかなんです。
この{町|まち}はしずかで、きれいです。
questions.explanation: この{町|まち}はしずかで、きれいです: quiet and pretty, in the present. しずかで is the て form of the な-adjective; only the last word, きれいです, shows the tense.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker asking?

audio.text: あの店、知ってる？

choices: Did you go to that shop?
Shall we go to that shop?
questions.explanation: あの{店|みせ}、{知|し}ってる？ {知|し}ってる is the casual short form of {知|し}っている (the い of 〜ている drops): "Do you know that shop?"

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: This town is quiet and has a lot of greenery.
questions.explanation: この{町|まち}は is the topic, しずかで joins the first description, and みどりが{多|おお}いです is the second (AはBが〜). ×しずかくて doesn't exist: しずか is a な-adjective.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Why are you studying Japanese?
questions.explanation: "Why" questions take 〜んですか: どうして{日本語|にほんご}を{勉強|べんきょう}しているんですか. どうして can also come after the object. After a verb the ending is んですか, not なんですか.

questions.stem: What is the potential form of {書|か}く (to write)?
questions.explanation: Group 1: move the last kana to the え-row and add る: く → け, {書|か}ける. ×{書|か}けれる adds an extra れ; {書|か}かれる is the passive (lesson 21).

questions.stem: What is the potential form of {食|た}べる (to eat)?
questions.explanation: Group 2: drop る and add られる: {食|た}べられる. {食|た}べれる is the "ら-less" form heard in casual speech but not used in writing or on the test; {食|た}べさせる is the causative (lesson 22).

questions.stem: Type the potential form of する (to do): ___
questions.explanation: The potential of する is a different verb, できる. Every する verb follows it: {運転|うんてん}する → {運転|うんてん}できる.

questions.stem: What is the potential form of {来|く}る (to come)?
questions.explanation: {来|く}る takes the こ vowel, as in {来|こ}ない: {来|こ}られる. Its ら-less casual form is これる; くれる is a different verb (to give, lesson 6).

questions.stem: Type the potential form of {話|はな}す (to speak): ___
questions.explanation: す → せ, then る: {話|はな}せる. It conjugates like a group 2 verb: {話|はな}せます, {話|はな}せない.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its potential form.
questions.explanation: Group 1 verbs go to the え-row + る: む → める, つ → てる, う → える, る → れる. {帰|かえ}る looks like group 2 but is group 1, so not ×{帰|かえ}られる; ×{買|か}われる is the passive.

questions.stem: You're busy tomorrow. How do you say "I can't come tomorrow"?
choices: {明日|あした}は{来|こ}ないです。
{明日|あした}は{来|こ}られません。
{明日|あした}は{来|こ}られます。
questions.explanation: The potential negative {来|こ}られません says you're unable to come. {来|き}ません and {来|こ}ないです just say you won't come, and {来|こ}られます is "I can come".

questions.stem: Which particle can replace を in this sentence? {漢字|かんじ}を{読|よ}めますか。
questions.explanation: The object of a potential verb can take が or を: {漢字|かんじ}が{読|よ}めますか is the traditional choice. に, で and へ mark places and directions, not objects.

questions.stem: From the window you can see the mountains. Choose the most natural verb: このまどから{山|やま}が___。
questions.explanation: {見|み}える is for things that come into view by themselves: the mountains are simply there. {見|み}られます suggests having the chance to see them (like a brochure); {見|み}せます is "show".

questions.stem: Choose the verb: このアプリで{日本|にほん}のラジオが___。 (You can listen to Japanese radio with this app.)
questions.explanation: The app gives you the means to listen, so it's the ordinary potential {聞|き}けます. {聞|き}こえます is for sounds that reach your ears by themselves, like a train passing.

questions.stem: Which sentence means the same as ここで{写真|しゃしん}がとれます？
choices: ここで{写真|しゃしん}をとったことがあります。
ここで{写真|しゃしん}をとることができます。
ここで{写真|しゃしん}をとることにします。
ここで{写真|しゃしん}をとってみます。
questions.explanation: Dictionary form + ことができる is the formal version of the potential: "You can take photos here." たことがある is experience, ことにする a decision (lesson 4), and てみる "try" (lesson 5).

questions.stem: Listen to your friend's question. What is the standard (written) form of the verb you heard?

audio.text: これ、たべれる？

questions.explanation: これ、{食|た}べれる？ {食|た}べれる is the ら-less potential, very common in speech. The standard form keeps ら: {食|た}べられる.

questions.stem: Which verb has no potential form?
questions.explanation: ある (there is) has no potential: ×あれる. {書|か}ける, {来|こ}られる and {見|み}られる are all fine. {分|わ}かる and できる have none either, because they already mean "can".

questions.stem: Read: スポーツセンターは{月曜日|げつようび}が{休|やす}みです。テニスコートは{一時間|いちじかん}{五百円|ごひゃくえん}で、ラケットはセンターで{借|か}りられます。{車|くるま}は{二十台|にじゅうだい}{止|と}められます。 Which is true?
choices: You can borrow a racket at the centre.
The centre is open on Mondays.
You can't park a car there.
questions.explanation: {借|か}りられます is the potential of {借|か}りる (borrow): you can borrow a racket. The centre is closed ({休|やす}み) on Mondays, courts are 500 yen an hour ({一時間|いちじかん}), and twenty cars can park ({止|と}められます).

questions.stem: How is 運動 read? {毎朝|まいあさ}、運動しています。
questions.explanation: 運動 (exercise) is ウン + ドウ, both on'yomi. うんてん is {運転|うんてん} (driving) and どうぶつ is {動物|どうぶつ} (animal); うごき uses the kun'yomi of 動.

questions.stem: Which kanji is used to write よわい (weak)?
questions.explanation: 弱 is weak (two bent bows), 強 is strong, 力 is power and 走 is run.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: すみません、あしたはこられません。

questions.explanation: {明日|あした}はこられません: こられません is the potential negative of {来|く}る, "can't come". Can come would be こられます.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: ここから海が見えます。

choices: You can watch the sea on TV here.
Let's go and see the sea.
You can't see the sea from here.
You can see the sea from here.
questions.explanation: ここから{海|うみ}が{見|み}えます: the sea is visible from here. Can't see would be {見|み}えません.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I can read a little kanji.
questions.explanation: {読|よ}む → {読|よ}める (group 1). {少|すこ}し can go before or after {漢字|かんじ}が. ×{読|よ}められます adds an extra られ.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: My big brother is strong, so he can carry heavy things too.
questions.explanation: {力|ちから}が{強|つよ}くて gives the reason with the adjective て form; {持|も}つ → {持|も}てる is the potential. {持|も}たれます would be a passive form.

questions.stem: What is the volitional form of {行|い}く (to go)?
questions.explanation: Group 1 verbs move to the お-row and add う: く → こ, {行|い}こう. ×{行|い}きよう adds the group 2 ending to the ます stem.

questions.stem: What is the volitional form of {食|た}べる (to eat)?
questions.explanation: Group 2: drop る and add よう: {食|た}べよう. The お-row change is only for group 1 verbs.

questions.stem: Type the volitional form of する (to do): ___
questions.explanation: する → しよう, and every する verb follows it: {旅行|りょこう}しよう, {運動|うんどう}しよう.

questions.stem: What is the volitional form of {来|く}る (to come)?
questions.explanation: {来|く}る takes the こ vowel, as in {来|こ}ない and {来|こ}られる: {来|こ}よう.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its volitional form.
questions.explanation: Group 1: つ → とう, す → そう, う → おう, る → ろう. {帰|かえ}る is group 1, so not ×{帰|かえ}よう; and う becomes お, not わ.

questions.stem: Which is the casual way to say {写真|しゃしん}をとりましょう？
questions.explanation: The plain volitional is the casual "let's": とる → とろう. {写真|しゃしん}をとって is a casual request ("take a photo"), not "let's".

questions.stem: What does this mean? {夏休|なつやす}みに{旅|たび}をしようと{思|おも}います。
choices: I think someone will travel in the summer.
I travelled in the summer holidays.
I think I'll go travelling in the summer holidays.
I want someone to travel in the summer.
questions.explanation: Volitional + と{思|おも}います states your own intention: "I think I'll travel." A guess about someone else would use the plain form: {旅|たび}をすると{思|おも}います.

questions.stem: Which sentence states the speaker's own intention ("I mean to go")?
choices: {明日|あした}、{山|やま}に{行|い}こうと{思|おも}います。
{明日|あした}、{山|やま}に{行|い}くと{思|おも}います。
{明日|あした}、{山|やま}に{行|い}ったと{思|おも}います。
{明日|あした}、{山|やま}に{行|い}くでしょう。
questions.explanation: {行|い}こうと{思|おも}う is a decision or intention. {行|い}くと{思|おも}う is a guess ("I think (they'll) go", or at most "I'll probably go"), {行|い}ったと{思|おも}う is about the past, and でしょう is "probably".

questions.stem: Your brother has been planning to buy a car. Which sentence is correct?
choices: {兄|あに}は{車|くるま}を{買|か}おうと{思|おも}います。
{兄|あに}は{車|くるま}を{買|か}うと{思|おも}いましょう。
{兄|あに}は{車|くるま}を{買|か}いようと{思|おも}っています。
{兄|あに}は{車|くるま}を{買|か}おうと{思|おも}っています。
questions.explanation: For someone else's intention use 〜と{思|おも}っています; 〜と{思|おも}います can only be the speaker's own thought. ×{買|か}いよう mixes the ます stem with the group 2 ending.

questions.stem: Which means "I'd like to go abroad" (a wish, not a plan)?
choices: {海外|かいがい}に{行|い}こうと{思|おも}います。
{海外|かいがい}に{行|い}きたいと{思|おも}います。
{海外|かいがい}に{行|い}くと{思|おも}います。
{海外|かいがい}に{行|い}きましょう。
questions.explanation: 〜たいと{思|おも}う is a wish; 〜(よ)うと{思|おも}う is an intention ("I think I'll go"); the plain form + と{思|おも}う is a guess.

questions.stem: What does this mean? {出|で}かけようとしたとき、{電話|でんわ}がなりました。
choices: After I went out, the phone rang.
Just as I was about to go out, the phone rang.
I tried going out to see, and the phone rang.
Whenever I want to go out, the phone rings.
questions.explanation: Volitional + とする means "be about to" or "try to": {出|で}かけようとしたとき, just as I was about to leave. なる here means "to ring".

questions.stem: You're carrying a heavy box. Listen to your friend. What is she offering?

audio.text: おもそうだね。もとうか？

choices: To try lifting it to see how heavy it is
To buy you a new box
questions.explanation: {重|おも}そうだね。{持|も}とうか？ {持|も}とうか is the volitional of {持|も}つ + か, "shall I carry it?". Trying to lift it would be {持|も}ってみる.

questions.stem: Read Ken's blog: {去年|きょねん}は{何回|なんかい}も{走|はし}るのを{始|はじ}めようとしたけど、{寒|さむ}くてやめた。{今年|ことし}こそ！ What happened last year?
choices: He tried to start running several times but gave up because of the cold.
He ran every day in spite of the cold.
He started running many times and enjoyed it.
He decided not to run because he dislikes the cold.
questions.explanation: {始|はじ}めようとした = tried to start (and it didn't last); {寒|さむ}くてやめた = it was cold, so he stopped. 〜こそ means "this time for sure".

questions.stem: How is 旅行 read? {夏休|なつやす}みに旅行します。
questions.explanation: 旅行 is リョ + コウ, both on'yomi: りょこう, with a short りょ. たび is the kun'yomi of 旅, used on its own ({旅|たび}).

questions.stem: In which word is 楽 read らく?
questions.explanation: The な-adjective {楽|らく} (easy, comfortable) is read らく. In {楽|たの}しい and {楽|たの}しみ it's たの, and in {音楽|おんがく} it's ガク.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "sound"?
questions.explanation: 音 (おと, オン) is sound: "stand" (立) over "sun" (日). 歌 is song, 写 is copy and 海 is sea.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker suggesting?

audio.text: いっしょにいこう。

questions.explanation: いっしょにいこう: いこう is the volitional of {行|い}く, the casual "let's". A request would be {行|い}って(ください).

questions.stem: Listen. What do you learn about the speaker?

audio.text: らいねん、かいがいにいこうとおもっています。

choices: They're thinking of going abroad next year.
Their friend is going abroad next year.
They want to go abroad but can't.
questions.explanation: {来年|らいねん}、{海外|かいがい}に{行|い}こうと{思|おも}っています: {来年|らいねん} next year, {海外|かいがい} abroad, {行|い}こうと{思|おも}っています, I'm thinking of going.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I'm thinking of going to Kyoto by train over the long weekend.
questions.explanation: The plan is volitional + と{思|おも}っています at the end. The means ({電車|でんしゃ}で) and the destination ({京都|きょうと}へ) can come in either order before the verb.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: My big brother is thinking of buying a new car.
questions.explanation: Someone else's intention takes 〜と{思|おも}っています; ×{兄|あに}は〜と{思|おも}います is only for the speaker's own thoughts.

questions.topic: つもり and よてい
questions.stem: How do you say "I intend not to buy a car"?
choices: {車|くるま}を{買|か}うないつもりです。
{車|くるま}を{買|か}わないつもりです。
{車|くるま}を{買|か}わなかったつもりです。
{車|くるま}を{買|か}いつもりません。
questions.explanation: A plan not to do something is the ない form + つもりです: {買|か}わないつもりです. ×{買|か}うない isn't a form, and the past {買|か}わなかった doesn't fit a plan.

questions.topic: つもり and よてい
questions.stem: Someone asks: {会社|かいしゃ}をやめるんですか。 Which answer firmly denies any such intention?
choices: いいえ、やめたつもりです。
いいえ、やめることがあります。
いいえ、やめることになりました。
いいえ、やめるつもりはありません。
questions.explanation: つもりはありません denies the intention itself: "I have no intention of quitting." ことがあります is "I sometimes quit", and ことになりました says it has been decided that you will.

questions.topic: つもり and よてい
questions.stem: Choose the word: {電車|でんしゃ}は{十時|じゅうじ}に{着|つ}く___です。 (The train is due at ten.)
questions.explanation: A timetable is an arrangement, so it's よてい. つもり is a person's intention, and a train has none. ことに needs する or なる after it.

questions.topic: ことにする and ことになる
questions.stem: Your company is transferring you to Kyoto. Which do you say?
choices: {京都|きょうと}で{働|はたら}くことにしました。
{京都|きょうと}で{働|はたら}くつもりでした。
{京都|きょうと}で{働|はたら}くことになりました。
{京都|きょうと}で{働|はたら}いたことがあります。
questions.explanation: The company decided, not you, so it's ことになりました ("it's been decided that I'll work in Kyoto"). ことにしました would mean you chose it yourself; つもりでした is "I meant to"; たことがあります is past experience.

questions.topic: ことにする and ことになる
questions.stem: What does this mean? まいばん、にっきを{書|か}くことにしています。
choices: I've just decided to write a diary tonight.
I'm supposed to write a diary; it's a rule.
I make a point of writing my diary every night.
I sometimes write a diary at night.
questions.explanation: ことにしている is a habit you've set yourself and keep. A rule set by others would be ことになっている, and "sometimes" is ことがある.

questions.topic: ことにする and ことになる
questions.stem: What does this mean? このりょうでは、{夜|よる}{十一時|じゅういちじ}までに{帰|かえ}ることになっています。
choices: In this dorm you're supposed to be back by 11 p.m.
I've decided to come back to the dorm by 11 p.m.
I sometimes come back to the dorm at 11 p.m.
I intend to leave the dorm at 11 p.m.
questions.explanation: ことになっている describes a rule or arrangement that stands. "I've decided" would be ことにしました, and "sometimes" ことがあります.

questions.stem: At a café the waiter asks {何|なに}にしますか。 You want coffee. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Noun + にする is "choose, go with": コーヒーにします, "I'll have coffee". を, が and で don't make this meaning.

questions.stem: Choose the ending: {朝|あさ}は{電車|でんしゃ}がおくれる___。 (The trains are sometimes late in the morning.)
questions.explanation: Dictionary form + ことがある is "it sometimes happens that". ことにします is a decision, つもりです an intention (trains have none), and ことになります "it will be decided".

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: きょうとにいくことがあります。

choices: They have been to Kyoto before.
They have decided to go to Kyoto.
They meant to go to Kyoto.
questions.explanation: {京都|きょうと}に{行|い}くことがあります: dictionary form + ことがある, "I sometimes go to Kyoto". "Have been" would be {行|い}ったことがあります, with the た form.

questions.topic: つもり and よてい
questions.stem: Complete: ___、{仕事|しごと}が{終|お}わりませんでした。 (I meant to go home early, but my work didn't get finished.)
choices: {早|はや}く{帰|かえ}ったつもりでしたが
{早|はや}く{帰|かえ}るつもりですが
{早|はや}く{帰|かえ}ることがありましたが
{早|はや}く{帰|かえ}るつもりでしたが
questions.explanation: The intention is in the past, not the going: dictionary form + つもりでした. {帰|かえ}ったつもり means "I was sure I'd gone home", a different idea.

questions.topic: ことにする and ことになる
questions.stem: Type the missing word in hiragana: {大学|だいがく}のりょうに{住|す}む___にしました。 (I've decided to live in the university dorm.)
questions.explanation: Dictionary form + ことにする is "decide to": {住|す}むことにしました. The grammar word こと is written in kana.

questions.stem: Read: じつは、{仕事|しごと}で{京都|きょうと}に{住|す}むことになりました。{二十日|はつか}にひっこすよていです。アパートは{店|みせ}の{近|ちか}くにしました。 Which is true?
choices: He's moving to Kyoto because of his work.
He moved on the 20th of last month.
He chose by himself to change jobs.
questions.explanation: {仕事|しごと}で…ことになりました: it was decided because of work. The move is scheduled for the 20th (よていです), and he has already chosen (にしました) a flat near the shop.

questions.stem: How is 住所 read? {新|あたら}しい住所を{教|おし}えてください。
questions.explanation: 住所 (address) is ジュウ + ショ, both on'yomi. す is the kun'yomi of 住 in {住|す}む, and ところ the kun'yomi of 所.

questions.stem: How is 終わりました read? {仕事|しごと}が終わりました。
questions.explanation: 終 is お(わる), end: {終|お}わりました, "finished". "Began" would be {始|はじ}まりました, with 始.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "begin"?
questions.explanation: 始 (はじ(める), はじ(まる)) is begin; 終 is end, 引 is pull and 事 is thing, matter.

questions.stem: How is 用事 read? {急|きゅう}に用事ができました。
questions.explanation: 用事 (an errand, something to do) is ヨウ + ジ. 事 is こと on its own (ごと in {仕事|しごと}) and ジ in compounds such as {食事|しょくじ} and 用事.

questions.stem: Listen. What do you learn about the speaker?

audio.text: らいげつ、きょうとにひっこすことになりました。

choices: They moved to Kyoto last month.
They're going to move to Kyoto next month.
They've decided not to move to Kyoto.
questions.explanation: {来月|らいげつ}、{京都|きょうと}にひっこすことになりました: next month, it's been settled that I'll move to Kyoto.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker mean?

audio.text: コーヒーにします。

questions.explanation: コーヒーにします: noun + にする is choosing, "I'll have coffee". Making coffee would be コーヒーをいれます.

questions.topic: ことにする and ことになる
questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I've decided to save ten thousand yen every month.
questions.explanation: Your own decision is ことにしました. With なりました it would mean the decision was made for you.

questions.topic: つもり and よてい
questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I'm due to move house next Monday.
questions.explanation: Dictionary form + よていです: a scheduled plan. The topic {私|わたし}は can come first or after the time. ×ひっこすつもりのです isn't a form.

questions.stem: In a shoe shop, you say このくつ、はいてみてもいいですか。 What are you asking?
choices: May I wear these shoes home?
May I try these shoes on?
Have you ever worn these shoes?
questions.explanation: て form + みる is "do it and see": はいてみる, try them on. 〜てもいいですか asks permission.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I tried writing my name in kanji (and I did write it)"?
choices: {漢字|かんじ}で{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}こうとしました。
{漢字|かんじ}で{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}いておきました。
{漢字|かんじ}で{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}くことにしました。
{漢字|かんじ}で{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}いてみました。
questions.explanation: 〜てみる is doing the action to see what it's like. 〜(よ)うとしました is an attempt that may not have succeeded; 〜ておきました is "wrote it in advance", and ことにしました "decided to write it".

questions.stem: What does this mean? ホテルをよやくしておきました。
choices: I've booked the hotel in advance.
I'm going to book the hotel.
I left the hotel booking alone.
questions.explanation: て form + おく is doing something in advance, as preparation: よやくしておきました, I've booked it (so we're ready). "Tried" would be 〜てみました.

questions.stem: Choose the form: この{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んで___ください。 (Please read this book beforehand.)
questions.explanation: おく is a group 1 verb in く, so its て form is おいて: 〜ておいてください. ×おきて treats it as group 2.

questions.stem: What is the casual form of {買|か}っておく?
questions.explanation: 〜ておく shrinks to 〜とく, keeping the っ: {買|か}っとく. どく is only after a て form in で ({読|よ}んどく), and {買|か}ってく is short for {買|か}っていく, "buy and take along", a different meaning.

questions.stem: Type the casual form of {読|よ}んでおく (read beforehand): ___
questions.explanation: After a て form ending in で, 〜でおく becomes 〜どく: {読|よ}んどく.

questions.stem: You offer to copy the map for everyone before the trip. What do you say?
choices: {地図|ちず}をコピーしておきましょうか。
{地図|ちず}をコピーしてみたいですか。
{地図|ちず}をコピーしようとしましょうか。
{地図|ちず}をコピーしておいてください。
questions.explanation: 〜ておきましょうか offers to prepare something: "Shall I copy the map (for later)?" 〜ておいてください asks someone else to do it.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker asking?

audio.text: まどはあけておいてください。

questions.explanation: 〜ておく can also mean "leave something as it is": keep the window open. "Try opening" would be {開|あ}けてみてください.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I'd like to try travelling on my own some time"?
choices: {一度|いちど}、{一人|ひとり}で{旅行|りょこう}したことがあります。
{一度|いちど}、{一人|ひとり}で{旅行|りょこう}してみたいです。
{一度|いちど}、{一人|ひとり}で{旅行|りょこう}しようとしました。
{一度|いちど}、{一人|ひとり}で{旅行|りょこう}しておきました。
questions.explanation: 〜てみたい is "I'd like to try": {旅行|りょこう}してみたいです. したことがあります is "I have travelled", しようとしました "I tried to", and しておきました "I travelled in advance".

questions.stem: Your friend asks: きっぷ、もう{買|か}った？ Which reply fits?
choices: うん、きのう{買|か}ってみるよ。
うん、きのう{買|か}っといたよ。
うん、きのう{買|か}おうとするよ。
うん、きのう{買|か}っておくよ。
questions.explanation: きのう needs a past form: {買|か}っといた (casual for {買|か}っておいた), "I bought them yesterday, so we're set". The others are non-past.

questions.stem: Read: {新|あたら}しいくつを{一度|いちど}はいてみる。たくさん{歩|ある}くから。 Why will Natsumi try on her new shoes before the trip?
choices: Because she'll be walking a lot.
questions.explanation: たくさん{歩|ある}くから: because she'll walk a lot, she wants to see how the shoes feel first (はいてみる).

questions.stem: Read Natsumi's list: パスポートをたしかめておく。くうこうで{少|すこ}しりょうがえしておく。{新聞|しんぶん}を{止|と}めておく。 Which is NOT on the list?
choices: Change some money at the airport.
questions.explanation: たしかめる = check, りょうがえする = change money, {新聞|しんぶん}を{止|と}める = stop the newspaper. There's nothing about a guidebook (ガイドブック).

questions.stem: How is 乗ります read? バスに乗ります。
questions.explanation: 乗 is の(る), to ride or get on: {乗|の}ります. ジョウ is its on'yomi, used in compounds; のぼる is "to climb".

questions.stem: How is 早く read? {明日|あした}は早く{起|お}きます。
questions.explanation: 早 is はや(い), early: {早|はや}く{起|お}きます, I'll get up early. ソウ is the on'yomi.

questions.stem: How is 急いで read? 急いでください。
questions.explanation: 急 is いそ(ぐ), hurry: {急|いそ}いでください. キュウ is the on'yomi, as in {急|きゅう}に (suddenly).

questions.stem: Match each word to its reading.
questions.explanation: 用意 (preparation) ヨウ + イ; 意味 (meaning) イ + ミ; 乗り物 (vehicle) の + もの; 気持ち (feeling) き + も. ようじ is 用事.

questions.stem: Listen. Where is the speaker most likely to be?

audio.text: このくつ、はいてみてもいいですか。

questions.explanation: このくつ、はいてみてもいいですか: may I try these shoes on? That's a shoe shop.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker asking you to do?

audio.text: でかけるまえに、でんきをけしておいてください。

choices: Turn on the lights when you come back.
Turn off the lights before you go out.
questions.explanation: {出|で}かける{前|まえ}に、{電気|でんき}をけしておいてください: before going out, turn the lights off (so they're off while you're away). けす = turn off.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I'll look up the train times before I go out.
questions.explanation: 〜ておきます goes on the verb at the end. The time phrase {出|で}かける{前|まえ}に can come before or after the object.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I'd like to try Japanese sweets.
questions.explanation: Try and see is て form + みる; "I'd like to try" is 〜てみたいです. 〜ておきたい would be "want to eat them in advance".

questions.stem: What is Japanese pitch accent?
choices: Saying one syllable louder and longer than the others
A pattern of high and low pitch on each mora of a word
The difference between long and short vowels
The rising voice at the end of a question
questions.explanation: In Japanese every mora keeps its length and loudness; what changes is pitch, high or low. Loud-and-long stress is how English marks syllables.

questions.stem: How many morae are there in がっこう (school)?
questions.explanation: が・っ・こ・う: the small っ and the second half of the long vowel (う) each count as a mora.

questions.stem: In standard (Tokyo) Japanese, if the first mora of a word is low, the second mora is…
choices: either, it depends on the speaker
always the same as the third
questions.explanation: The first two morae always differ: low-high, or high-low. So a word that starts low rises on the second mora.

questions.stem: {名前|なまえ:0} (name) is flat, accent 0. What happens to the particle が after it?
questions.explanation: In a flat (heiban) word the pitch never falls, not even onto the particle: な low, ま え が high.

questions.stem: What does the 3 in [せんせい:3] mean?
choices: The pitch falls after the third mora.
The pitch rises on the third mora.
questions.explanation: The number is the accent nucleus: the mora after which the pitch drops. せんせい: せ low, ん せ high, い low.

questions.stem: Which two words sound the same on their own but differ when a particle follows?
questions.explanation: An odaka word (はし, bridge, 2) and a flat word (はし, edge, 0) are both low-high alone. Only the particle tells them apart: low after "bridge", high after "edge".

questions.stem: Where does the pitch fall in ます forms such as [たべます:3] and [いきます:3]?
choices: Nowhere: ます forms are flat
questions.explanation: Every ます form falls after ま, whatever the verb: even a flat verb like いく becomes いきま↓す.

questions.stem: {雨|あめ:1} (rain) and [あめ:0] (candy): which one is high, then low?
questions.explanation: {雨|あめ} is atamadaka (1): あ high, め low. The candy is flat (0): あ low, め high.

questions.stem: Which statement about regional accents is true?
choices: Every Japanese speaker uses the Tokyo pattern.
The Kansai region has its own accent system, and many words sound different there.
Pitch accent exists only in Tokyo.
Kansai speakers can't understand Tokyo speakers.
questions.explanation: Kansai (Osaka, Kyoto, Kobe) has a different system, and some areas hardly distinguish words by pitch at all. Speakers understand each other across all of them.

questions.stem: How does pitch accent figure in the JLPT?
choices: Points are taken off for wrong pitch in the speaking part.
N4 has a separate pitch section.
The test has no questions on pitch.
questions.explanation: The JLPT tests vocabulary, grammar, reading and listening, with no speaking part and no pitch questions. Good pitch still helps you hear where words begin and end.

questions.stem: Listen to the sentence. After はな (flower), is the particle が high or low?

audio.text: 花がきれいです。

choices: Low: {花|はな:2} is odaka, so the pitch falls onto が.
High: はな is flat here, so が stays high.
questions.explanation: {花|はな} is accent 2, odaka: は low, な high, が low. The flat はな (0) is "nose", where が would stay high.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word do you hear?

audio.text: 発音

questions.explanation: {発音|はつおん}, pronunciation. It's flat (0): は low, つ お ん high.

questions.stem: What is れいきん?
choices: A deposit that is mostly returned
A payment to the landlord that you don't get back
questions.explanation: れいきん, "key money", is a thank-you payment to the landlord, not returned. The deposit is しききん, and the rent is やちん. Many flats now ask for no れいきん.

questions.stem: What usually happens to the しききん (deposit) when you move out?
choices: The landlord keeps all of it.
It's paid to the city office.
It's used as the last month's rent by law.
The cost of cleaning and repairs is taken out and the rest is returned.
questions.explanation: しききん is a deposit: the landlord takes out the costs of cleaning and repairs and returns the rest.

questions.stem: What does やちん mean?
questions.explanation: やちん is the rent you pay each month. The deposit is しききん, the contract けいやく, and the landlord {大家|おおや}(さん).

questions.stem: What does 2LDK mean in a listing?
choices: Two floors with a large kitchen
Two kitchens and a dining room
Two rooms plus a living, dining and kitchen area
questions.explanation: The number is the rooms, and L, D and K are living, dining and kitchen. A 1K is one room plus a small kitchen.

questions.stem: Which is true of rental contracts today, according to the lesson?
choices: A はんこ is always required by law.
Contracts never last more than a year.
Many agents accept a signature instead of a はんこ.
questions.explanation: Contracts were traditionally stamped with a はんこ, but many agents now accept a signature, and online contracts are spreading. Two-year contracts are common.

questions.stem: You're visiting your new neighbours to say hello. What's a typical small gift?
questions.explanation: A small, useful gift worth roughly 500 to 1,000 yen (a towel, washing powder, sweets) is traditional. Many people living alone in big blocks of flats now skip the visit.

questions.stem: In the landlord's notice, when should rubbish go out?
choices: The night before the collection day
Any time, at the collection point
By 8 a.m. on the collection day
questions.explanation: {朝|あさ}{八時|はちじ}までに…{出|だ}してください、{前|まえ}の{日|ひ}の{夜|よる}には{出|だ}さないでください: by 8 a.m., and not the night before.

questions.stem: In the landlord's notice, what goes out on Fridays?
questions.explanation: しげんごみ (recyclables: かん, びん, ペットボトル) goes out on Fridays. Kitchen waste is burnable (Mondays and Thursdays), umbrellas are non-burnable, and furniture is そだいごみ.

questions.stem: According to the notice, how do you get rid of an old desk?
choices: Put it out with the burnable rubbish.
Phone the city and book a collection; there's a fee.
Leave it at the collection point on Monday.
questions.explanation: {市|し}に{電話|でんわ}して、よやくしてください。お{金|かね}がかかります: phone the city, book, and pay.

questions.stem: How soon after moving must you register your new address at the city office?
questions.explanation: The law asks for registration within 14 days of moving in, for foreign residents too (their residence card is updated at the same time).

questions.stem: Listen to the estate agent. Which is true?

audio.text: しききんはいっかげつぶんです。れいきんはありません。

choices: The deposit is one month's rent, and there's no key money.
There's no deposit, but the key money is one month's rent.
Both the deposit and the key money are one month's rent.
The rent must be paid one month in advance.
questions.explanation: しききんは{一|いっ}か{月|げつ}{分|ぶん}です。れいきんはありません: the deposit is one month's worth; there is no key money.

questions.stem: At the estate agent's, how do you say you're looking for a flat near the station?
choices: {駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くでへやをさがしてみましょう。
{駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くにへやがさがしています。
{駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くでへやをさがしているんですが。
{駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くのへやに{住|す}んでいます。
questions.explanation: 〜ているんですが opens a request politely: "I'm looking for a flat near the station…". さがす takes を, not が, and {住|す}んでいます says you already live there.

questions.stem: Your older sister gave you a book for your birthday. Which sentence says this correctly?
choices: {姉|あね}が{本|ほん}をあげました。
{姉|あね}が{本|ほん}をくれました。
{姉|あね}が{本|ほん}をもらいました。
{私|わたし}は{姉|あね}に{本|ほん}をくれました。
questions.explanation: The book came inward, to you, so the verb is くれる with the giver as subject: {姉|あね}が{本|ほん}をくれました. あげました would send it outward, away from you, and もらいました needs the receiver (you) as the topic. {私|わたし}は{姉|あね}に{本|ほん}をくれました makes you the giver of くれる, which is never possible.

questions.stem: Choose the verb: {私|わたし}は{友|とも}だちにCDを___。 (I gave my friend a CD.)
questions.explanation: You are the giver and the CD goes outward to your friend: あげました. くれました is only for gifts coming to you or your side, くださいました is its respectful form, and もらいました would mean you received it.

questions.stem: {私|わたし}は{兄|あに}___カードをもらいました。 Which particle marks the person you got the card from?
questions.explanation: With もらう the giver takes に (or から): {兄|あに}にもらいました, "got it from my brother". It looks like the に of "to", but here it marks where the card came from. を marks the card itself, and で and へ don't mark a giver.

questions.stem: Your neighbour gave your little brother some sweets. Choose the verb: となりの{人|ひと}が{弟|おとうと}におかしを___。
questions.explanation: Your brother is in your family, on your side, so from where you stand the sweets came inward: くれました. あげました would treat your brother as an outsider. さしあげました is humble giving to a superior, and いただきました is humble receiving, with the receiver as subject.

questions.stem: The teacher gave you a dictionary. Which is correct?
choices: {先生|せんせい}がじしょをくださいました。
{先生|せんせい}がじしょをさしあげました。
{先生|せんせい}がじしょをくださりました。
{先生|せんせい}がじしょをいただきました。
questions.explanation: くださる is the respectful form of くれる, and its ます form is くださいます (past くださいました), not くださります. さしあげる is for giving to a superior, and いただく needs you as the receiver: {先生|せんせい}にいただきました.

questions.stem: You want to say humbly that you received some tea from your teacher. {先生|せんせい}にお{茶|ちゃ}を___。
questions.explanation: いただく is the humble form of もらう: the receiver (you) is the topic and the teacher takes に. くださいました would need the teacher as subject with が ({先生|せんせい}がくださいました), and あげました and くれました have the wrong direction or politeness.

questions.stem: Kenji and Saki are both people you know but neither is in your family. Kenji gave Saki some flowers. Which sentence is correct?
choices: けんじさんはさきさんに{花|はな}をくれました。
さきさんはけんじさんに{花|はな}をあげました。
けんじさんはさきさんに{花|はな}をあげました。
けんじさんはさきさんに{花|はな}をもらいました。
questions.explanation: Between two outsiders, the neutral verb with the giver as subject is あげる. くれる only works when the receiver is you or your side. さきさんはけんじさんに{花|はな}をあげました makes Saki the giver, and 〜にもらいました with けんじさんは makes Kenji the receiver.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT natural Japanese?
choices: {友|とも}だちがペンをくれました。
{私|わたし}は{友|とも}だちにペンをあげました。
{私|わたし}は{友|とも}だちにペンをもらいました。
{友|とも}だちは{私|わたし}にペンをあげました。
questions.explanation: あげる can never point at you as the receiver. When a friend gives you something, it's くれる: {友|とも}だちが（{私|わたし}に）ペンをくれました. The other three sentences are all correct.

questions.stem: Which verb fits a casual sentence about your plants? {毎朝|まいあさ}、{花|はな}に{水|みず}を___。
questions.explanation: やる is the casual "give" for plants and animals: {花|はな}に{水|みず}をやる, to water the flowers. (Many people say あげる here too.) くれる and くださる would mean the flowers gave water to you, and もらう that you received water from them.

questions.stem: Three friends are buying a present together. What does {一人|ひとり}{千円|せんえん}ずつ{出|だ}しましょう mean?
choices: Let's put in only a thousand yen.
Let's put in about a thousand yen.
Let's put in a thousand yen in total.
Let's each put in a thousand yen.
questions.explanation: ずつ after an amount means "each" or "so much at a time": {一人|ひとり}{千円|せんえん}ずつ is a thousand yen per person. "Only" would be だけ, "about" ぐらい, and "in total" ぜんぶで.

questions.stem: Type the verb (polite past): {兄|あに}が{時計|とけい}を___。 (My older brother gave me a watch.)
questions.explanation: The watch came to you, and the giver is the subject with が, so it's くれる: くれました. あげました would mean your brother gave it to someone else.

questions.stem: How is 家族 read in this sentence? 家族はみんな{元気|げんき}です。
questions.explanation: 家族 is かぞく (family), the N5 word now written with kanji: 家 is read カ here and 族 is ゾク. いえ is 家 alone (a house); 族 is never じょく.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "younger sister"?
questions.explanation: 妹 (いもうと) is younger sister. 姉 (あね) is older sister; both have 女 (woman) on the left. 弟 (おとうと) is younger brother and 兄 (あに) is older brother.

questions.stem: Match each giving verb to its polite partner.
questions.explanation: あげる → さしあげる (humble: you lower your own giving), くれる → くださる (respectful: you raise the giver), もらう → いただく (humble: you lower your own receiving). いらっしゃる is a respectful word for "be, come, go", not a giving verb.

questions.stem: How is this word read? お兄さん
questions.explanation: お兄さん is a special reading: おにいさん, someone else's older brother (or how you address your own). On its own 兄 is あに (my older brother); ケイ and キョウ are its on'yomi, as in 兄弟 (きょうだい).

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: あねがくれました。

choices: My older sister gave it to me.
I gave it to my older sister.
I got it for my older sister.
questions.explanation: あねがくれました: くれる means someone gave something to the speaker (or the speaker's side), so the older sister is the giver and the speaker the receiver. "I gave it to my sister" would be あねにあげました.

questions.stem: Listen. Who received the thing?

audio.text: せんせいにいただきました。

questions.explanation: せんせいにいただきました is the humble form of せんせいにもらいました: the speaker received it from the teacher. With もらう and いただく, the person with に is the giver.

questions.stem: Listen. What did the speaker get from their parents?

audio.text: りょうしんからカードとほんをもらいました。

questions.explanation: りょうしんからカードとほんをもらいました: "I got a card and a book from my parents". から marks the giver here, as に can; カードとほん is "a card and a book".

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Grandma gave each of us grandchildren three sweets.
questions.explanation: The giver (そぼは) comes first, the receivers take に, the gift を, and ずつ follows the number: {三|みっ}つずつ, three each. The verb is くれました because the speaker is one of the receivers. あげました can't have you among the receivers. The receivers and the gift can swap places, and {三|みっ}つずつ can come just before おかしを.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Yesterday the teacher kindly gave me a new book.
questions.explanation: The teacher is the giver and the subject (が), so the respectful verb is くださいました. いただきました would need the speaker as subject and {先生|せんせい}に. {新|あたら}しい goes straight before {本|ほん}を; きのう can come first or after the subject.

questions.stem: A friend drove you to the station. Which sentence says it with thanks?
choices: {友|とも}だちが{駅|えき}まで{送|おく}ってあげました。
{友|とも}だちに{駅|えき}まで{送|おく}ってくれました。
{友|とも}だちが{駅|えき}まで{送|おく}ってくれました。
{友|とも}だちが{駅|えき}まで{送|おく}ってもらいました。
questions.explanation: The favour came to you, so it's 〜てくれる with the friend as subject: {友|とも}だちが{送|おく}ってくれました. 〜てあげました sends the favour outward, to someone else. くれる can't take the doer with に, and {友|とも}だちが{送|おく}ってもらいました would mean the friend got someone else to drive them.

questions.stem: {私|わたし}は{兄|あに}に{写真|しゃしん}をとって___。 (I had my older brother take a photo.)
questions.explanation: The topic is you, the one who benefits, and the person who did the action takes に: that's 〜てもらう. くれました and くださいました need the doer as subject ({兄|あに}がとってくれました), and あげました would mean you did it for him.

questions.stem: {友|とも}だち___かばんを{持|も}ってあげました。 (I carried my friend's bag for them.)
questions.explanation: {持|も}つ has no slot for a person with に, so you show whose bag it is with の: {友|とも}だちのかばんを{持|も}ってあげました. ×{友|とも}だちにかばんを{持|も}ってあげました is a common learner's mistake. を already marks the bag, and が would make the friend the one who carried it.

questions.stem: Your teacher is carrying a pile of heavy books. What is the best thing to say?
choices: {先生|せんせい}、{持|も}ちましょうか。
{先生|せんせい}、{持|も}ってくれませんか。
{先生|せんせい}、{持|も}ってあげます。
{先生|せんせい}、{持|も}ってほしいです。
questions.explanation: To offer help, use 〜ましょうか: {持|も}ちましょうか, "shall I carry them?". Saying 〜てあげます to the person's face sounds like you're doing them a favour from above, which is rude to a teacher. The other two ask the teacher to carry something.

questions.stem: Which is the most polite way to ask your boss to look at a document?
choices: ちょっと{見|み}てくれる？
ちょっと{見|み}てください。
ちょっと{見|み}てもらえませんか。
ちょっと{見|み}ていただけませんか。
questions.explanation: 〜ていただけませんか (the potential of いただく, in a negative question) is the most polite of these. 〜てもらえませんか is polite but a step lower, 〜てください is direct, and 〜てくれる？ is casual, for friends and family.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I want my mother to get well soon"?
choices: {母|はは}は{早|はや}く{元気|げんき}になりたいです。
{母|はは}に{早|はや}く{元気|げんき}になってほしいです。
{母|はは}に{早|はや}く{元気|げんき}になってあげたいです。
{母|はは}が{早|はや}く{元気|げんき}になってもらいます。
questions.explanation: "I want someone to do" is person に + 〜てほしい: {母|はは}に{元気|げんき}になってほしいです. 〜たい is about your own wish to do something, so {母|はは}は{元気|げんき}になりたいです says the mother wants to get well (and states her feelings directly). The other two misuse あげる and もらう.

questions.stem: A sign in a museum says ここで{写真|しゃしん}をとらないでほしいです. What does it mean?
choices: We would like you to take photos here.
We would like you not to take photos here.
Please take a photo of us here.
questions.explanation: 〜ないでほしい is "I want you not to do": the negative of 〜てほしい. (A real sign would more often say ごえんりょください, please refrain.)

questions.stem: You want to borrow a classmate's pen. Which request is correct?
choices: ペンを{借|か}りてくれませんか。
ペンを{貸|か}してもいいですか。
ペンを{借|か}りてあげましょうか。
ペンを{貸|か}してもらえませんか。
questions.explanation: You ask the other person to lend ({貸|か}す): ペンを{貸|か}してもらえませんか, "could I have you lend me your pen?". ペンを{借|か}りてくれませんか asks them to borrow it, and {貸|か}してもいいですか asks permission for you to lend it. (To ask "may I borrow", say {借|か}りてもいいですか.)

questions.stem: {先生|せんせい}がていねいに{説明|せつめい}して___。 (The teacher kindly explained it carefully.)
questions.explanation: The teacher is the subject (が) and did the favour for you, so it's 〜てくださる, the respectful form of 〜てくれる. いただきました and もらいました need you as the topic and {先生|せんせい}に; さしあげました would mean you did it for the teacher.

questions.stem: You are at home with your younger brother. How do you ask him to pass you the remote control (リモコン)?
choices: リモコン、とってくれる？
リモコン、とっていただけませんか。
リモコン、とってあげる？
リモコン、とってもらいました。
questions.explanation: With family, a casual 〜てくれる？ (or 〜てくれない？) is natural. 〜ていただけませんか is far too formal for your brother, とってあげる？ offers to get it for him, and もらいました is a statement about the past.

questions.stem: Type the missing words (polite past): {友|とも}だちに{日本語|にほんご}を{教|おし}えて___。 (I had a friend teach me Japanese.)
questions.explanation: The topic is you and the friend who did the teaching takes に, so it's 〜てもらう: {教|おし}えてもらいました. くれました would need {友|とも}だちが as the subject.

questions.stem: A colleague helps you carry some boxes. Afterwards you say: ありがとうございます、たすかりました。 What does たすかりました mean here?
questions.explanation: たすかる is "to be helped, saved", and たすかりました is how people thank someone for a favour: "you saved me, that was a big help". It can mean being rescued, but not here. "I'm sorry to trouble you" would be すみません.

questions.stem: How is the verb read? かさを貸してください。
questions.explanation: 貸して is かして, from 貸す (to lend): "please lend me an umbrella". かりて would be 借りて (borrow), a different kanji. タイ is the on'yomi of 貸, but the verb uses the kun'yomi か(す).

questions.stem: Which kanji is used to write かりる (to borrow)?
questions.explanation: 借 is borrow: 借りる. 貸 is lend (貸す); the two are a pair and easy to mix up (lend has money, a shell, at the bottom; borrow has a person on the left). 待 is wait and 教 is teach.

questions.stem: How is the word read? これは大切な{写真|しゃしん}です。 (大切)
questions.explanation: 大切 is たいせつ (precious, important). 大 is read タイ here, not ダイ or おお, and 切 is セツ, as in 親切 (しんせつ). きり comes from the verb 切る, which isn't used in this word.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker want?

audio.text: すみません、ちょっとてつだってもらえませんか。

questions.explanation: てつだってもらえませんか is "could you help me?": 〜てもらえませんか asks the listener to do something for the speaker. Offering help would be てつだいましょうか. すみません here just means "excuse me".

questions.stem: Listen. What happened?

audio.text: ちちがえきまでむかえにきてくれました。

choices: The speaker went to the station to pick up their father.
The speaker and their father met at the station by chance.
The speaker asked their father to come to the station.
The speaker's father came to the station to pick the speaker up.
questions.explanation: むかえにきてくれました: the father came to meet (pick up) the speaker, and くれました shows it was a favour to the speaker. If the speaker had gone to pick up the father, it would be むかえにいきました.

questions.stem: Listen. Who is being asked to take the photo?

audio.text: しゃしんをとっていただけませんか。

choices: Nobody: the speaker wants to buy a photo
questions.explanation: 〜ていただけませんか is a very polite request: "might I ask you to take a photo (for us)?". The listener is asked to do it, for the speaker's benefit.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: My older sister looked after my dog for me.
questions.explanation: The doer ({姉|あね}が) comes first, 〜の{世話|せわ}をする is "look after", and the favour comes to you, so the auxiliary is くれました, straight after the て form して. あげました would mean she did it for someone outside your side.

questions.stem: Build the request in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Excuse me, could you lend me your dictionary for a moment?
questions.explanation: すみません opens the request, the object じしょを comes before the verb, and 〜てもらえませんか ends it. The verb is {貸|か}して (lend), because you're asking the other person to lend; {借|か}りてもらえませんか would ask them to borrow it. ちょっと can come before or after じしょを.

questions.stem: Choose the particle: {風|かぜ}でドア___あきました。 (The door opened in the wind.)
questions.explanation: {開|あ}く is intransitive: the door opens by itself, so the door is the subject with が. を goes with the transitive partner: ドアを{開|あ}けました (someone opened the door).

questions.stem: You just want to say that the light is on. Which sentence fits?
choices: {電気|でんき}をつけています。
{電気|でんき}がついています。
{電気|でんき}がついてあります。
questions.explanation: Intransitive つく + ている describes the state after the change: the light is on. {電気|でんき}をつけています is someone turning it on right now. 〜てある can't go on an intransitive verb, and つく can't take を.

questions.stem: Someone has opened the window on purpose, to air the room. Which sentence says this?
choices: まどが{開|あ}いています。
まどを{開|あ}いています。
まどが{開|あ}けています。
まどが{開|あ}けてあります。
questions.explanation: Transitive {開|あ}ける + てある is a state someone created deliberately: まどが{開|あ}けてあります. まどが{開|あ}いています only describes the state (maybe the wind did it). {開|あ}く can't take を, and {開|あ}ける + ている with が doesn't fit.

questions.stem: Which verb is the transitive partner of こわれる (to break, get broken)?
questions.explanation: こわす (to break something) is transitive; like most verbs in す, it takes を: パソコンをこわす. こわる isn't a word, and the other two aren't the partner verb.

questions.stem: Which of these verbs is intransitive?
questions.explanation: {止|と}まる ends in 〜aる, the typical intransitive shape: {車|くるま}が{止|と}まる (the car stops). {出|だ}す (す verb), {始|はじ}める and {入|い}れる all take を.

questions.stem: What does {父|ちち}がまどを{開|あ}けています mean?
choices: My father has left the window open.
My father is opening the window.
My father will open the window.
questions.explanation: A transitive verb + ている usually means an action in progress: he is opening it. "The window is open" would be まどが{開|あ}いています, and "has been left open" まどが{開|あ}けてあります.

questions.stem: Why is ×{電気|でんき}がついてあります wrong?
choices: てある must be in the past tense.
てある needs を, not が.
つく is intransitive, and てある only goes on transitive verbs.
It should be ついておきます.
questions.explanation: 〜てある describes something someone did on purpose, so it needs a transitive verb: {電気|でんき}がつけてあります. With intransitive つく, use ている: {電気|でんき}がついています. が is normal with 〜てある, and its tense isn't the problem.

questions.stem: The computer stopped working by itself. It isn't anyone's fault. Which is the natural report?
choices: パソコンをこわしました。
パソコンがこわしました。
パソコンがこわれました。
パソコンをこわれました。
questions.explanation: For something that broke by itself, use the intransitive こわれる with が: パソコンがこわれました. パソコンをこわしました says you broke it. The other two mix the particles: こわす needs を, こわれる needs が.

questions.stem: Choose the verb: じゅぎょうは{九時|くじ}に___。 (Class starts at nine.)
questions.explanation: The class is the subject and nobody is named as starting it, so the intransitive {始|はじ}まる fits: じゅぎょうは{九時|くじ}に{始|はじ}まります. {始|はじ}めます needs someone to start something (を). 〜てある doesn't express a timetable.

questions.stem: Choose the ending: ノートに{名前|なまえ}が{書|か}いて___。 (A name has been written in the notebook.)
questions.explanation: {書|か}く is transitive, and the thing written is now the subject with が: {名前|なまえ}が{書|か}いてあります, a state someone left there. {書|か}いています would mean someone is writing. おきます (do in advance) and しまいます (finish, regret) need を and a person doing it.

questions.stem: Type the intransitive partner of {止|と}める (to stop something), in the dictionary form.
questions.explanation: {止|と}める (transitive, 〜eる) pairs with {止|と}まる (intransitive, 〜aる): {車|くるま}を{止|と}める (stop the car) / {車|くるま}が{止|と}まる (the car stops).

questions.stem: Match each transitive verb to its intransitive partner.
questions.explanation: しめる/しまる (close), けす/きえる (turn off / go off), おとす/おちる (drop / fall), なおす/なおる (fix / get fixed). The transitive verbs are the ones in す or 〜eる here; けせる is the potential of けす ("can turn off"), not its partner.

questions.stem: How is the verb read? まどを開けてください。
questions.explanation: 開けて is あけて, from 開ける (to open something): "please open the window". 開 has another kun'yomi, ひら(く), but ひらける is a different verb and doesn't take を here; カイ is the on'yomi; しめて (close) is the opposite.

questions.stem: How is 八百屋 read?
questions.explanation: 八百屋 (greengrocer) has a special reading: やおや. The number reading はっぴゃく ("eight hundred") isn't used, and 屋 is や (shop) here, not its on'yomi オク.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "gate"?
questions.explanation: 門 (もん) is a gate: it's a picture of two doors. The others are built on it: 開 (open), 間 (between, interval: the sun showing through the gate) and 問 (question: a mouth at the gate).

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: まどがあいています。

choices: The window has been opened on purpose.
questions.explanation: まどがあいています: intransitive あく + ている, just the state: the window is open. "Someone is opening it" would be あけています, and "opened on purpose" あけてあります.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say about the light?

audio.text: でんきがけしてあります。

choices: Someone has turned it off (on purpose).
questions.explanation: けしてあります is transitive けす + てある: someone turned the light off and left it that way. If it had gone out by itself, the speaker would say きえています (or きえました).

questions.stem: Listen. What is the problem?

audio.text: エアコンがこわれています。

choices: The air conditioner is being repaired.
The air conditioner is too cold.
questions.explanation: こわれています: intransitive こわれる + ている, the state after it broke. "Someone broke it" would be こわしました, and "being repaired" しゅうりしています.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: The key has been put in the drawer in the entrance.
questions.explanation: {入|い}れる is transitive, so the state someone left on purpose is 〜てあります; the key, the thing put away, is the topic. 〜ています with a transitive verb would mean someone is putting it there now. The place phrase can also come first.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: The kitchen light is still on.
questions.explanation: つく is intransitive, so the light is the subject with が and the state is 〜ています. {電気|でんき}を needs the transitive つける, and 〜てある can't follow つく. まだ (still) can come first or just before the verb.

questions.stem: What does てしまいました add in さいふをなくしてしまいました?
choices: A plan to do something later
questions.explanation: With an accident like losing your wallet, 〜てしまう tells the listener you're upset about it: "I've gone and lost my wallet". さいふをなくしました is just the fact. (With a planned job, 〜てしまう can mean "finish it", but not here.)

questions.stem: What is the casual form of {食|た}べてしまった?
questions.explanation: て + しまった shortens to ちゃった: {食|た}べちゃった. じゃった is only for verbs whose て form ends in で ({読|よ}んで → {読|よ}んじゃった). The other two aren't real forms.

questions.stem: What is the casual form of {読|よ}んでしまった?
questions.explanation: で + しまった becomes じゃった: {読|よ}んじゃった. {読|よ}んちゃった forgets the voicing; {読|よ}みちゃった is built on the ます stem, not the て form.

questions.stem: You're writing an email to your boss to apologize for being late. Which is right?
choices: ちこくしちゃいました。すみません。
ちこくしてしまいました。もうしわけありません。
ちこくしちゃった。ごめん。
ちこくした。すみません。
questions.explanation: In writing and with a superior, use the full 〜てしまいました and a formal apology. 〜ちゃう forms are casual, even with ます, and ごめん and the plain ちこくした are for friends.

questions.stem: What does しゅくだいはもうぜんぶやってしまいました mean?
choices: I've already finished all my homework.
I'm going to do all my homework.
I forgot to do my homework.
questions.explanation: With a job you meant to do, 〜てしまう means "finish it off": もうぜんぶやってしまいました, I've already done all of it. Nothing here is a regret; "forgot" would be わすれてしまいました.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "It suddenly started to rain"?
choices: {雨|あめ}がふり{終|お}わりました。
{雨|あめ}がふって{出|だ}しました。
{急|きゅう}に{雨|あめ}がふり{出|だ}しました。
{雨|あめ}がふる{出|だ}しました。
questions.explanation: 〜{出|だ}す after the ます stem is "suddenly start": ふり{出|だ}しました. Compound verbs join to the ます stem, not the て form or the dictionary form. ふり{終|お}わりました would mean the rain finished (and is unusual).

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I've finished reading this book"?
choices: この{本|ほん}を{読|よ}み{始|はじ}めました。
この{本|ほん}を{読|よ}み{出|だ}しました。
この{本|ほん}を{読|よ}みつづけました。
この{本|ほん}を{読|よ}み{終|お}わりました。
questions.explanation: Stem + {終|お}わる is "finish doing": {読|よ}み{終|お}わりました. {始|はじ}める is start, つづける keep on, and {出|だ}す suddenly start.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT correct?
choices: {明日|あした}から{勉強|べんきょう}し{始|はじ}めます。
{赤|あか}ちゃんがなき{出|だ}しました。
{三時間|さんじかん}{歩|ある}きつづけました。
{明日|あした}から{勉強|べんきょう}し{出|だ}してください。
questions.explanation: 〜{出|だ}す is for something sudden and uncontrolled, so it doesn't fit a request or a plan. Ask with 〜{始|はじ}めてください instead. The other three are natural.

questions.stem: The glass fell off the shelf by itself and broke. Which sentence is correct?
choices: コップがおちて、われてしまいました。
コップがおとして、われてしまいました。
コップをおちて、われてしまいました。
コップがおちて、わってしまいました。
questions.explanation: Nobody did anything, so both verbs are intransitive with が: おちる (fall) and われる (break). おとす and わる are transitive and need someone as subject and the glass with を; おちる can't take を.

questions.stem: You broke a friend's umbrella. Which apology takes responsibility?
choices: かさがこわれていますよ。
かさがこわれてしまいましたね。
かさをこわしてしまって、すみません。
かさをこわしておきました。
questions.explanation: The transitive こわす says you did it, and 〜てしまって、すみません apologizes for it. The intransitive こわれる makes it sound as if it broke by itself, and 〜ておきました would mean you broke it on purpose, in advance.

questions.stem: Type the casual form of {行|い}ってしまった (went off, has gone).
questions.explanation: て + しまった → ちゃった: {行|い}って → {行|い}っちゃった. For example {電車|でんしゃ}が{行|い}っちゃった, "the train's gone".

questions.stem: Match each full form to its casual form.
questions.explanation: て + しま → ちゃ, で + しま → じゃ. {飲|の}んで ends in で, so it becomes {飲|の}んじゃった, never {飲|の}んちゃった; {書|か}いて, {来|き}て and して all end in て and take ちゃった.

questions.stem: How is the verb read? {毎朝|まいあさ}{六時|ろくじ}に起きます。
questions.explanation: 起きます is おきます, from 起きる (to get up): "I get up at six every morning". キ is the on'yomi of 起, but the verb uses the kun'yomi お(きる).

questions.stem: How is the verb read? バスで{学校|がっこう}に通っています。
questions.explanation: 通う is かよう (to go regularly, commute), so 通っています is かよっています: "I go to school by bus". 通 is also とお(る), to pass through, but going to school regularly is かよう. ツウ is the on'yomi.

questions.stem: Which kanji appears in both 自転車 (bicycle) and 運転 (driving)?
questions.explanation: 転 (turn, roll; テン) is in both: じてんしゃ and うんてん. 車 is only in 自転車, 運 only in 運転, and 自 only in 自転車.

questions.stem: Listen. What has happened?

audio.text: しまった！かぎをわすれちゃった。

choices: The speaker has forgotten the key.
The speaker has found the key.
The speaker has locked the door.
The speaker has lost a wallet.
questions.explanation: しまった！ is "oh no!", and わすれちゃった is the casual わすれてしまった: "I've forgotten my key". Finding would be みつけた, and locking かぎをかけた.

questions.stem: Listen. Why is the speaker apologizing?

audio.text: すみません、ねぼうしてしまいました。

questions.explanation: ねぼうしてしまいました: "I overslept (sorry)". ねぼうする is to oversleep. Spilling would be こぼして, getting lost みちにまよって, and breaking こわして.

questions.stem: Listen. What happened?

audio.text: きゅうにあめがふりだしました。

questions.explanation: ふりだしました is ふる + だす, "started to fall (suddenly)", and きゅうに means "suddenly". Stopping would be やみました, and "kept raining" ふりつづけました.

questions.stem: Build the apology in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I'm really sorry I spilled the coffee.
questions.explanation: The cause comes first in the て form, 〜てしまって, and the apology last: ほんとうにすみません. You did the spilling, so it's the transitive こぼす with を; こぼれる (spill by itself) can't take コーヒーを.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Yesterday I kept walking for three hours, all the way to the station.
questions.explanation: つづける joins to the ます stem: {歩|ある}きつづけました, kept on walking. {歩|ある}いてつづけました is wrong, because compounds don't use the て form. {駅|えき}まで and {三時間|さんじかん} can swap places.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I study while listening to music"?
choices: {勉強|べんきょう}しながら{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}きます。
{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}くながら{勉強|べんきょう}します。
{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}きながら{勉強|べんきょう}します。
{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}いてながら{勉強|べんきょう}します。
questions.explanation: ながら joins to the ます stem ({聞|き}き), and the main action goes last: studying is what you're doing, with music in the background. {勉強|べんきょう}しながら{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}きます is grammatical but puts listening in focus. ながら never follows the dictionary form or the て form.

questions.stem: Your friend asks you to come to the phone, but you're just about to go out. What do you say?
choices: {今|いま}、{出|で}かけたところです。
{今|いま}、{出|で}かけているところです。
{今|いま}、{出|で}かけたばかりです。
{今|いま}、{出|で}かけるところです。
questions.explanation: The dictionary form + ところ is "about to": {出|で}かけるところです. 〜たところ and 〜たばかり mean you have just done it, and 〜ているところ that you're in the middle of it.

questions.stem: You walked in through the front door a moment ago. Which sentence fits?
choices: {今|いま}、{帰|かえ}ったところです。
{今|いま}、{帰|かえ}るところです。
{今|いま}、{帰|かえ}っているところです。
questions.explanation: The た form + ところ is "have just done": {今|いま}、{帰|かえ}ったところです, I've just got home. {帰|かえ}るところ is about to leave for home, and {帰|かえ}っているところ on the way home.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I only came to Japan last month"?
choices: {先月|せんげつ}{日本|にほん}に{来|き}たところです。
{先月|せんげつ}{日本|にほん}に{来|き}たばかりです。
{先月|せんげつ}{日本|にほん}に{来|く}るところです。
{先月|せんげつ}{日本|にほん}に{来|き}ているところです。
questions.explanation: 〜たばかり is "only just", measured by how recent it feels, so it works with {先月|せんげつ}. 〜たところ is the moment right after the action and can't go with "last month". The other two mean "about to" and "in the middle of".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "Please don't come into the house with your shoes on"?
choices: くつをはくまま、{家|いえ}に{入|はい}らないでください。
くつをはいてまま、{家|いえ}に{入|はい}らないでください。
くつをはいたまま、{家|いえ}に{入|はい}らないでください。
くつをはかないで、{家|いえ}に{入|はい}らないでください。
questions.explanation: まま follows the た form: はいたまま, with your shoes still on. The dictionary form and the て form can't go before まま. はかないで…{入|はい}らないでください says "don't come in without putting your shoes on", the opposite.

questions.stem: Choose the form: {朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べ___、{学校|がっこう}に{行|い}きました。 (I went to school without eating breakfast.)
questions.explanation: 〜ないで is "without doing": {食|た}べないで{行|い}きました. 〜なくて is "because not", which needs a result you didn't choose (got hungry). ながら would mean eating on the way, and たばかりで "having only just eaten".

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT correct?
choices: {私|わたし}は{音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}きながら{料理|りょうり}をしました。
{父|ちち}はラジオを{聞|き}きながら{運転|うんてん}します。
{歩|ある}きながら{電話|でんわ}をしないでください。
{姉|あね}がテレビを{見|み}ながら、{私|わたし}はそうじをしました。
questions.explanation: 〜ながら needs one person doing both actions. "My sister watched TV while I cleaned" has two people, so it needs another pattern (〜あいだ, lesson 19). The other three each have a single subject.

questions.stem: A friend phones while you're eating dinner. What do you say?
choices: {今|いま}、ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べているところなんです。
{今|いま}、ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べたばかりなんです。
{今|いま}、ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べるところだったんです。
{今|いま}、ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べながらです。
questions.explanation: 〜ているところ is "in the middle of": {食|た}べているところなんです, with んです giving it as the reason you can't talk. 〜たばかり means you've already eaten, 〜るところだった that you were about to, and ながら can't end a sentence like this.

questions.stem: What does {電気|でんき}をつけたまま、ねてしまいました mean?
choices: I turned on the light and then went to bed.
I couldn't sleep with the light on.
I went to sleep after turning off the light.
I fell asleep with the light on.
questions.explanation: 〜たまま is "with the state left unchanged": the light stayed on while you slept. 〜てしまいました adds that you didn't mean to. "Turned on and then went to bed" would be つけてからねました.

questions.stem: Choose the form: {時間|じかん}が___、{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}が{食|た}べられませんでした。 (I didn't have time, so I couldn't eat breakfast.)
questions.explanation: "Because not" is なくて (lesson 1): {時間|じかん}がなくて. 〜ないで means "without doing" and follows verbs only; ない after a noun like {時間|じかん}が is the い-adjective-like ない, whose て form is なくて. なかって and ないながら aren't forms.

questions.stem: Type the ながら form of {歩|ある}く (while walking).
questions.explanation: Take the ます stem ({歩|ある}きます → {歩|ある}き) and add ながら: {歩|ある}きながら.

questions.stem: Match each pattern to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Dictionary form + ところ: about to; 〜ているところ: in the middle of; た form + ところ: just did; 〜ないで: without doing. "While eating" would be {食|た}べながら.

questions.stem: How is 今朝 read? 今朝は{寒|さむ}かったです。
questions.explanation: 今朝 is a special reading, けさ (this morning), the N5 word now written with kanji. The kanji's usual readings (いま, あさ, チョウ) don't apply here.

questions.stem: How is 七夕 read? (the Star Festival on 7 July)
questions.explanation: 七夕 is a special reading: たなばた. Neither kanji is read as usual; learn it as a word.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "wash"?
questions.explanation: 洗 (あら(う), to wash) has the three drops of water on the left and 先 on the right. 先 alone means ahead, 海 (sea) also has the water drops, and 飯 is meal.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker doing?

audio.text: いま、でかけるところです。

choices: They are about to go out.
They are out at the moment.
They went out an hour ago.
questions.explanation: でかけるところです: the dictionary form + ところ, "just about to go out". "Just come back" would be かえったところ.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: にほんにきたばかりです。

choices: They're about to come to Japan.
They've lived in Japan for a long time.
They came to Japan not long ago.
questions.explanation: きたばかりです is "have only just come": the speaker arrived in Japan recently. 〜たばかり can cover days or months, as long as it feels recent.

questions.stem: Listen. What did the speaker do?

audio.text: テレビをみながらゆうはんをたべました。

questions.explanation: みながら is "while watching", and the main action is ゆうはんをたべました, ate supper. "Made" would be つくりました, and "without watching" みないで.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I fell asleep with the window open.
questions.explanation: まま follows the た form ({開|あ}けたまま, with the window left open), and 〜てしまいました adds that you didn't mean to fall asleep. The dictionary form {開|あ}ける can't go before まま.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I'm in the middle of washing the dishes right now.
questions.explanation: "In the middle of" is 〜ているところです: {洗|あら}っているところです. {洗|あら}ったところ would mean you've just finished. {今|いま} usually comes first but can follow おさらを.

questions.stem: When is お{中元|ちゅうげん} usually sent around Tokyo?
questions.explanation: お{中元|ちゅうげん} is the summer gift, sent roughly in early to mid July around Tokyo (later in some regions). Early December is おせいぼ, the year-end gift, and 14 March is White Day.

questions.stem: What is おせいぼ?
choices: A gift to thank someone for their help over the year
A gift for a new baby
A return gift after a wedding
questions.explanation: おせいぼ is the year-end gift, sent in December to people who helped you during the year. A gift for a baby is おいわい, a return gift おかえし, and a souvenir おみやげ.

questions.stem: You're back at work after a trip. What kind of おみやげ is most usual for your colleagues?
choices: One expensive gift for your boss only
A box of local sweets, wrapped one by one, so everyone gets one
A potted plant for the office
questions.explanation: The usual office おみやげ is a box of local sweets, each wrapped separately and shared out one each. A gift for the boss alone would leave others out, and money isn't a souvenir.

questions.stem: Why do some people avoid giving sets of four?
choices: Four is an unlucky even number at weddings only.
Four things are hard to wrap.
Four is a number used only for the emperor.
questions.explanation: {四|し} can be read し, which sounds like {死|し} (death), so sets of four are often avoided. Even numbers are avoided for wedding money for a different reason (they can be divided).

questions.stem: You're visiting a friend in hospital. Which gift is traditionally avoided?
questions.explanation: A potted plant "takes root", which suggests staying in bed for a long time, so it's a traditional thing to avoid. Fruit, magazines and sweets are common get-well gifts (if the patient is allowed them).

questions.stem: Wedding gifts of money are usually an odd number of 10,000-yen notes. Why?
choices: Odd numbers are easier to count.
Even numbers are for funerals only.
Banks only give out notes in odd numbers.
An even number can be divided, like a couple splitting up.
questions.explanation: An even amount can be split in two, which suggests the couple might separate, so people prefer odd numbers of notes. The other reasons aren't part of the custom.

questions.stem: On which kind of gift would you NOT find のし?
choices: A gift for a new baby
A summer gift (お{中元|ちゅうげん})
A condolence gift for a funeral
questions.explanation: のし is a sign of a celebration gift, so it's left off gifts for sad occasions: condolence gifts have black and white or silver cords and no のし. Weddings, births and seasonal gifts can all have it.

questions.stem: How do you hand over a gift politely?
choices: With one hand, so the other is free to bow
Left on the table without a word
With both hands, the front of the gift facing the receiver
Still in the shop's bag, front facing you
questions.explanation: Use both hands (りょうて) and turn the gift so its front faces the receiver. Taking it out of the shop's bag is traditional, though many people now hand it over in the bag.

questions.stem: What does ほんの{気持|きも}ちですが mean, said when handing over a gift?
questions.explanation: ほんの{気持|きも}ちですが is "it's just a small token (of my feelings)": a modest, current way to hand over a gift. ほんの = merely, just; {気持|きも}ち = feeling.

questions.stem: Why do many people now avoid つまらないものですが?
choices: It's only used for funeral gifts.
It literally calls the gift boring, and some find that old-fashioned or odd.
It's a phrase only for gifts from children.
questions.explanation: つまらないものですが is a humble phrase ("this is a boring thing, but…"). It's still heard in formal settings, but many people now find it old-fashioned and prefer ほんの{気持|きも}ちですが or naming the gift.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: わざわざありがとうございます。

choices: Thank you, I'll open it now.
Thank you, but I can't accept this.
Thank you for going to so much trouble.
questions.explanation: わざわざ is "specially, taking the trouble", so わざわざありがとうございます thanks someone for going out of their way, for example to bring a gift.

questions.stem: Build what you say as you hand over a gift.
questions.prompt: It's just a small token, but here you are.
questions.explanation: ほんの (just, merely) goes before the noun {気持|きも}ち, ですが softens it ("it's…, but"), and どうぞ hands it over.

questions.stem: What is a でんぴょう when you send a parcel?
choices: The receipt you get after paying a bill
The waybill where you write the addresses and delivery time
The box the parcel goes in
The tracking app on your phone
questions.explanation: A でんぴょう is the waybill: names, addresses and phone numbers of sender and receiver, what's inside, and the day and time slot you want. Many companies also let you fill it in on an app.

questions.stem: You find a ふざいれんらくひょう in your postbox. What does it mean?
choices: Your parcel has been left outside your door.
A parcel came while you were out, and you can ask for redelivery.
You need to pay the delivery charge at the door.
questions.explanation: ふざい is absence: the slip says the driver came while you were out, and tells you how to ask for さいはいたつ (redelivery).

questions.stem: Read the missed-delivery slip in the lesson again. How long will the depot keep Lucas's parcel?
questions.explanation: えいぎょうしょで{一週間|いっしゅうかん}おあずかりします: "we will keep it at the depot for one week". 18:00 is the deadline for asking for delivery the same evening.

questions.stem: According to the slip, what happens if Lucas applies by 18:00?
choices: The parcel is delivered again that evening.
He can pick it up at a convenience store.
questions.explanation: {今日|きょう}の{十八時|じゅうはちじ}までにおもうしこみいただくと、{今日|きょう}の{夜|よる}にもう{一度|いちど}とどけられます: if you apply by 18:00, it can be delivered again tonight.

questions.stem: What does もとばらい mean on a parcel?
choices: You pay at a convenience store.
questions.explanation: もとばらい is "paid at the origin": the sender pays. ちゃくばらい is the opposite, payment by the receiver.

questions.stem: What are こうきょう{料金|りょうきん}?
choices: Bills for electricity, gas, water and similar services
questions.explanation: こうきょう{料金|りょうきん} are public-utility charges: electricity, gas, water and so on. You can pay them at a コンビニ with the barcode slip.

questions.stem: Read the notice in the lesson again. How will you know your online order has arrived at the shop?
choices: A slip is put in your postbox.
You have to keep checking at the till.
You get an email on the day it arrives.
questions.explanation: {品物|しなもの}が{店|みせ}にとどいた{日|ひ}に、メールでお{知|し}らせします: "we'll let you know by email on the day the item arrives at the shop".

questions.stem: Choose the verb: {国|くに}の{母|はは}から{手紙|てがみ}が___。 (A letter has arrived from my mother back home.)
questions.explanation: The letter is the subject with が and nobody is doing anything to it, so the intransitive とどく fits: とどきました. とどける (deliver) is its transitive partner and needs someone delivering something with を.

questions.stem: How do you ask, at the counter, for your parcel to be delivered tomorrow morning?
choices: {明日|あした}の{午前中|ごぜんちゅう}にとどいてもらえますか。
{明日|あした}の{午前中|ごぜんちゅう}にとどけてもらえますか。
{明日|あした}の{午前中|ごぜんちゅう}にとどけてあげますか。
{明日|あした}の{午前中|ごぜんちゅう}にとどけてしまいますか。
questions.explanation: You want the company to deliver it for you: transitive とどける + 〜てもらえますか. とどく is intransitive and can't be "done for you", 〜てあげますか offers a favour, and 〜てしまいますか doesn't make a request.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the customer asking?

audio.text: カードではらえますか。

questions.explanation: はらえますか is the potential of はらう (to pay): "can I pay?", and カードで is "by card".

questions.stem: Listen. What is the clerk saying?

audio.text: いま、レシートをだしているところです。

choices: The receipt has already been printed.
questions.explanation: だしているところです is 〜ているところ, "in the middle of": the receipt is coming out now. "Already printed" would be だしたところ or もうでています.

questions.stem: Type the transitive partner of とどく (to arrive, be delivered), in the dictionary form.
questions.explanation: とどく (intransitive: にもつがとどく) pairs with とどける (transitive: にもつをとどける), like {開|あ}く / {開|あ}ける.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says "When you press this button, the door opens"?
choices: このボタンをおしたと、ドアが{開|あ}きます。
このボタンをおすと、ドアが{開|あ}きます。
このボタンをおすと、ドアを{開|あ}けてください。
このボタンをおすだと、ドアが{開|あ}きます。
questions.explanation: と follows the plain non-past: おすと. ×おしたと puts a past form before と, which never happens; the tense goes on the last verb. ×おすだと adds だ, which only nouns and な-adjectives need. The third choice puts a request after と, which と can't take.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT natural Japanese?
choices: {春|はる}になると、さくらがさきます。
お{金|かね}を{入|い}れると、きっぷが{出|で}ます。
{駅|えき}に{着|つ}くと、{電話|でんわ}してください。
まっすぐ{行|い}くと、{銀行|ぎんこう}があります。
questions.explanation: After と the result happens by itself, so it can't be a request: ×{着|つ}くと、{電話|でんわ}してください. Use たら (lesson 13): {着|つ}いたら、{電話|でんわ}してください. The others are nature, a machine and directions, the three classic uses of と.

questions.stem: Fill the blank: "{雨|あめ}___、{道|みち}がこみます。" (When it rains, the roads get busy.)
questions.explanation: A noun needs だ before the conditional と: {雨|あめ}だと. {雨|あめ}と alone is the と of "and/with" (rain and…). な and の don't go before this と. (こむ = to be crowded.)

questions.stem: What does "まどを{開|あ}けると、ゆきがふっていました。" mean?
choices: When I opened the window, it was snowing.
If I open the window, it will snow.
I opened the window because it was snowing.
Please open the window when it snows.
questions.explanation: With a past verb at the end, 〜と、〜た tells what happened or what you found: when I opened the window, it was snowing. It isn't a reason (that would be から), and と never takes a request after it.

questions.stem: Read: "{駅|えき}を{出|で}て、{左|ひだり}にまっすぐ{行|い}くと、ふみきりがあります。ふみきりをわたって、{一|ひと}つ{目|め}のかどを{右|みぎ}にまがると、{左|ひだり}に{図書館|としょかん}があります。" Where is the library?
choices: Before the level crossing, on the left
Right at the second corner after the crossing, on the left
Right at the first corner after the crossing, on the right
Right at the first corner after the crossing, on the left
questions.explanation: Go left from the station to the level crossing (ふみきり), cross it, turn right at the first corner ({一|ひと}つ{目|め}のかど), and the library is on the left ({左|ひだり}に). The tempting wrong answer mixes up the direction you turn (right) with the side the library is on (left).

questions.stem: How is 時計 read? "この時計は{高|たか}いです。"
questions.explanation: {時計|とけい} (clock, watch) is a special reading: neither 時 nor 計 is read this way anywhere else. 計 is usually ケイ ({合計|ごうけい}), which is why じけい looks tempting.

questions.stem: How is 出発 read? "バスは{八時|はちじ}に出発します。"
questions.explanation: {出発|しゅっぱつ}: シュツ shortens to しゅっ and ハツ becomes ぱつ after it. しゅつはつ keeps both readings unchanged, which Japanese doesn't do here. (Typing: shuppatsu.)

questions.stem: Which kanji is in じぶん (oneself) and じどう (automatic)?
questions.explanation: 自 (self): {自分|じぶん}, {自動|じどう}, {自転車|じてんしゃ}. It looks like 目 (eye) with a stroke on top; 白 (white) and 百 (hundred) also have a stroke on top, but only one line inside the box.

questions.stem: Complete with the と conditional of {入|い}れる (to put in): "お{金|かね}を ___、きっぷが{出|で}ます。" (When you put the money in, the ticket comes out.)
questions.explanation: Dictionary form + と: {入|い}れると. Not {入|い}れたと (no past before と) and not {入|い}れますと in an everyday sentence: the と clause is plain.

questions.stem: What does "{父|ちち}は{家|うち}に{帰|かえ}ると、すぐテレビをつけます。" tell you about the father?
choices: He turned on the TV once, after coming home.
He wants to turn on the TV when he gets home.
He always turns on the TV as soon as he gets home.
He will turn on the TV if he gets home early.
questions.explanation: と with a non-past ending describes a habit: whenever he gets home, he turns on the TV straight away (すぐ). A single past event would end in つけました; a wish would need 〜たい, which と can't take.

questions.stem: Listen. What happens when you press the button?

audio.text: このボタンをおすと、おつりがでます。

questions.explanation: このボタンをおすと、おつりが{出|で}ます: when you press this button, the change (おつり) comes out. きっぷ (ticket) and ドア (door) aren't in the sentence.

questions.stem: Listen. Where is the bank?

audio.text: まっすぐいくと、みぎにぎんこうがあります。

choices: At the end of the road
questions.explanation: まっすぐ{行|い}くと、{右|みぎ}に{銀行|ぎんこう}があります: go straight on and there's a bank on the right. みぎ is right, ひだり left; "the end of the road" would be つきあたり.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear, in hiragana: ___

audio.text: しゅっぱつ

questions.explanation: しゅっぱつ ({出発|しゅっぱつ}, departure) has a small っ before ぱ: one beat of silence. Type it as shuppatsu.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: When you put the money in and press the button, a ticket comes out.
questions.explanation: お{金|かね}を{入|い}れて、ボタンをおすと、きっぷが{出|で}てきます。The two steps are joined with the て form, and と comes after the last one; what the machine does comes after と. おしてください is a request, which can't follow と.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Go straight along this road and there's a bank on the left.
questions.explanation: この{道|みち}をまっすぐ{行|い}くと、{左|ひだり}に{銀行|ぎんこう}があります。The と clause (the step) comes first and the main clause (what you'll find) last. Inside each part the order is free: まっすぐ can go before or after この{道|みち}を, and {左|ひだり}に before or after {銀行|ぎんこう}が.

questions.stem: Which word means "machine"?
questions.explanation: きかい is a machine. ボタン is a button, がめん a screen, カード a card: all parts of what you use at a ticket machine or ATM.

questions.stem: Fill the blank: "カードに{千円|せんえん}___しました。" (I put 1,000 yen on my card.)
questions.explanation: チャージする is to top up a card with money. タッチする is to tap the card on a reader, which doesn't add money. コピー (copy) and サイン (signature) don't fit.

questions.stem: What does "{明日|あした}はれるといいですね。" mean?
choices: When it is sunny tomorrow, it is good.
If it is sunny tomorrow, let's go out.
It was sunny yesterday, wasn't it?
questions.explanation: 〜といいですね is a set phrase for a hope: "it would be nice if…", "I hope…". The literal reading (when it's sunny, it's good) misses the meaning, and "let's go out" would need an invitation, which と can't take.

questions.stem: Match each word to its reading.
questions.explanation: {自分|じぶん} (oneself), {今回|こんかい} (this time), {合計|ごうけい} (total), {時計|とけい} (clock: a special reading). じかい (next time) is a real word, but it isn't written with 自.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: お{金|かね}を{入|い}れないと、{動|うご}きません。
{右|みぎ}に{回|まわ}すと、{音|おと}が{大|おお}きくなります。
{冬|ふゆ}になると、{寒|さむ}くなります。
ドアを{開|あ}けたと、ねこがいました。
questions.explanation: The verb before と must be non-past even when the story is in the past: ドアを{開|あ}けると、ねこがいました (when I opened the door, there was a cat). The others are correct: a negative before と ({入|い}れないと) is fine.

questions.stem: What is the ば form of {買|か}う (to buy)?
questions.explanation: Group 1: the last kana moves to the え row and ば is added: う → え, {買|か}えば. かわば borrows the わ of the ない form ({買|か}わない), which the ば form doesn't use.

questions.stem: What is the ば form of {来|く}る (to come)?
questions.explanation: {来|く}る → {来|く}れば, read くれば: the vowel stays く. きれば mixes in the ます form ({来|き}ます), これば the ない form ({来|こ}ない).

questions.stem: Fill the blank: "___、{買|か}います。" (If it's cheap, I'll buy it.)
questions.explanation: い-adjectives replace い with ければ: {安|やす}ければ. ×{安|やす}いれば treats the adjective like a group 2 verb.

questions.stem: Fill the blank: "{午後|ごご}にコーヒーを___、よくねむれますよ。" (If you don't drink coffee in the afternoon, you'll sleep well.)
questions.explanation: The ない form changes like an い-adjective: {飲|の}まない → {飲|の}まなければ. {飲|の}めなければ is the potential ("if you can't drink"), which changes the meaning.

questions.stem: You've lost your key and want advice. What do you ask?
choices: どうすればいいですか。
questions.explanation: どうすればいいですか: what should I do? どうしてですか asks "why?", どうしたんですか "what's wrong?" (what you ask someone else) and どうでしたか "how was it?".

questions.stem: What does "もっと{早|はや}く{来|く}ればよかった。" mean?
choices: If I come earlier, it will be good.
It was good that I came early.
questions.explanation: 〜ばよかった is regret: "it would have been good if…", so "I should have come earlier". It isn't about the future, and it says the opposite of "it was good that I came".

questions.stem: Which sentence is natural?
choices: {駅|えき}に{着|つ}けば、{電話|でんわ}してください。
{時間|じかん}があれば、{来|き}てください。
{十時|じゅうじ}になれば、{出|で}かけましょう。
{家|うち}に{帰|かえ}れば、{電話|でんわ}してね。
