questions.explanation: 〜ようにしている is a habit you work at: "I make a point of". 〜ようになっている describes a change or how something is set up, not an effort; the ために and のに versions aren't grammatical here.

questions.topic: ように and ために
questions.stem: Choose: 「{後|うし}ろの{人|ひと}にも{聞|き}こえる___、{大|おお}きい{声|こえ}で{話|はな}してください。」
questions.explanation: {聞|き}こえる is a verb nobody controls, and the people at the back are the ones who benefit, so it's ように (so that). ために needs a verb of deciding with the same person in both halves.

questions.topic: ように and ために
questions.stem: Choose: 「{日本|にほん}の{会社|かいしゃ}で{働|はたら}く___、{日本語|にほんご}を{習|なら}っています。」 (I'm learning Japanese in order to work for a Japanese company.)
questions.explanation: {働|はたら}く is something you decide to do, and the same person studies and wants to work: ために, "in order to". のに here would need a following word like {使|つか}う or いい, and ようになって / ようにして describe change or effort, not a goal.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank (can't any more): 「{目|め}が{悪|わる}くなって、{小|ちい}さい{字|じ}が{読|よ}め___なりました。」
questions.explanation: For "not any more", the ない form becomes なくなる: {読|よ}めない → {読|よ}めなくなりました. 〜ないようになる exists but isn't the everyday choice.

questions.stem: Choose: 「はさみは{紙|かみ}を{切|き}る＿＿＿{使|つか}います。」 (Scissors are used for cutting paper.)
questions.explanation: Dictionary form + のに + {使|つか}う: "used for doing". The の turns the verb phrase into a noun (a nominalizer), and に marks the purpose. ように would need a hoped-for result, and ので means "because".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "Please turn the TV down"?
choices: テレビの{音|おと}を{小|ちい}さくなってください。
テレビの{音|おと}を{小|ちい}さくしてください。
テレビの{音|おと}を{小|ちい}さいにしてください。
テレビの{音|おと}を{小|ちい}さいくしてください。
questions.explanation: い-adjective → 〜く + する: "make it small". 〜くなる is "become", which can't take を or be a request here, and い-adjectives never take に or keep their い before く.

questions.stem: Choose: 「すみません、しずか___してください。」 (Excuse me, please be quiet.)
questions.explanation: しずか is a な-adjective, so "make it quiet" is しずかにする. く is for い-adjectives ({小|ちい}さくする), and な goes only before a noun.

questions.stem: Choose: 「だんだん{寒|さむ}くなって___ね。」 (It's been getting colder, hasn't it.)
questions.explanation: 〜てくる is change up to now, so a change that has been happening is 〜てきました. 〜ていく looks forward from now, and 〜ておく / 〜てみる are "do in advance" and "try".

questions.stem: Choose: 「これからも{日本語|にほんご}の{勉強|べんきょう}をつづけて___たいです。」 (I want to keep on studying Japanese from now on.)
questions.explanation: これからも points forward in time, so it's 〜ていく: つづけていきたい. 〜てくる would look back from the present, and 〜ておく / 〜てしまう don't describe carrying on.

questions.topic: ように and ために
questions.stem: Listen. A student says this at a shrine before an exam. What does it mean?

audio.text: ごうかくできますように。

choices: I tried to pass the exam.
questions.explanation: 〜ますように on its own is a wish: "may it be that…". It says nothing about having passed, having to pass or having tried.

questions.stem: Read: 「{私|わたし}は{去年|きょねん}までタバコをすっていましたが、{今年|ことし}からすわなくなりました。けんこうのために、{毎朝|まいあさ}{走|はし}るようにしています。」 What is true?
choices: The speaker started smoking this year.
The speaker runs only to lose weight.
The speaker stopped smoking this year and makes a point of running every morning.
The speaker wants to stop smoking next year.
questions.explanation: すわなくなりました is "stopped smoking" (〜なくなる), and {走|はし}るようにしています is "I make a point of running", for the speaker's health (けんこうのために), not specifically to lose weight.

questions.stem: What does 「{毎日|まいにち}{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べるようにしています。」 mean?
choices: I've become able to eat vegetables.
I'm made to eat vegetables every day.
I make a point of eating vegetables every day.
questions.explanation: 〜ようにしている is an effort the speaker keeps up. "Become able" would be {食|た}べられるようになった, "stopped" would be {食|た}べなくなった, and "made to" would be the causative-passive {食|た}べさせられている.

questions.stem: How is 研究 read?
questions.explanation: 研 is ケン and 究 is キュウ: けんきゅう (research). けんきょう has the wrong vowel (きょ), a common slip.

questions.stem: How is 集 read in 「{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}に集まってください。」?
questions.explanation: {集|あつ}まる (to gather): 集まって is あつまって. シュウ is the on'yomi, used in compounds such as {集中|しゅうちゅう}.

questions.stem: How is 習 read in 「ピアノを習っています。」?
questions.explanation: {習|なら}う (to learn from someone): 習って is ならって. まな(ぶ) is written with 学, and シュウ is 習's on'yomi in {学習|がくしゅう}.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear, in hiragana: ___

audio.text: けんこう

questions.explanation: けんこう (health), with a long こう at the end. けんこうのために = for your health.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I make a point of not eating sweet things.
questions.explanation: あまい{物|もの}を{食|た}べないようにしています. The ない form + ようにしている is a habit of avoiding something. ために can't follow a ない form in this sense.

questions.topic: ように and ために
questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
tiles: {集中|しゅうちゅう}できるように、
distractors: {集中|しゅうちゅう}するために、
accept: {集中|しゅうちゅう}できるように、
questions.prompt: I put my phone in another room so that I can concentrate on studying.
questions.explanation: {勉強|べんきょう}に{集中|しゅうちゅう}できるように、スマホを{別|べつ}のへやにおきます. With a potential ({集中|しゅうちゅう}できる), "so that" is ように. The purpose clause normally comes first.

questions.stem: Listen. What has changed?

audio.text: かんじがよめるようになりました。

choices: The speaker has started writing kanji.
The speaker has stopped studying kanji.
The speaker is trying hard to read kanji.
The speaker can now read kanji.
questions.explanation: よめる (can read) + ようになりました: a new ability. "Trying" would be ようにしています, and "stopped" would be よまなくなりました.

questions.topic: やすい and にくい
questions.stem: How do you say "easy to use"?
questions.explanation: The ます stem + やすい: {使|つか}い + やすい. The dictionary form and the て form don't take やすい, and {使|つか}いにくい is the opposite, "hard to use".

questions.stem: How do you say "too expensive"?
questions.explanation: い-adjectives drop the い before すぎる: {高|たか} + すぎる. Keeping the い or using the く form are the usual mistakes.

questions.stem: What is いい (good) + すぎる?
questions.explanation: いい uses its よ- stem, as in よくない: よすぎる. いすぎる drops too much, and adding く is never right before すぎる.

questions.stem: Type the noun "weight" made from {重|おも}い + さ: ___
questions.explanation: Drop the い and add さ: {重|おも}さ. The same pattern gives {長|なが}さ, {高|たか}さ and {大|おお}きさ.

questions.stem: Choose the particle: 「この{漢字|かんじ}＿＿＿{読|よ}み{方|かた}を{教|おし}えてください。」
questions.explanation: {読|よ}み{方|かた} is a noun ("the way of reading"), so the word before it takes の: {漢字|かんじ}の{読|よ}み{方|かた}. を belongs to the verb {読|よ}む, not to the noun.

questions.stem: Which is the most natural way to say "My little brother wants the new game"?
choices: {弟|おとうと}は{新|あたら}しいゲームがほしいです。
{弟|おとうと}は{新|あたら}しいゲームをほしがっています。
{弟|おとうと}は{新|あたら}しいゲームをほしいです。
{私|わたし}は{新|あたら}しいゲームをほしがっています。
questions.explanation: For someone else's feelings, 〜がっている describes what you can see: ほしがっています, with を. ほしいです states the brother's inner feeling directly, which sounds odd, and 〜がる about yourself is unnatural.

questions.stem: How do you say "a bag of the same colour"?
choices: {同|おな}じな{色|いろ}のかばん
{同|おな}じの{色|いろ}のかばん
{同|おな}じい{色|いろ}のかばん
questions.explanation: {同|おな}じ goes straight before a noun, without な or の: {同|おな}じ{色|いろ}. It looks like a な-adjective, which is why {同|おな}じな is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Choose the particle: 「とどいた{品物|しなもの}は、{写真|しゃしん}___ちがいました。」 (The item that arrived was different from the photo.)
questions.explanation: "Different from N" is Nとちがう, as "the same as N" is Nと{同|おな}じ. を would make the photo an object, and が would make it the subject.

questions.stem: Listen to the announcement. What does it mean?

audio.text: のみすぎにちゅういしましょう。

choices: Take care not to drink too much.
Be careful when drinking hot drinks.
questions.explanation: {飲|の}みすぎ is the noun "drinking too much", and {注意|ちゅうい}する is "take care". It doesn't ban drinking; that would be something like おさけはだめです.

questions.topic: やすい and にくい
questions.stem: What does 「このコップはわれやすいです。」 mean? (われる = to break, of glass)
choices: This glass is hard to break.
questions.explanation: With a verb of something happening by itself, stem + やすい means "tends to, easily": breaks easily. やすい here is not {安|やす}い (cheap), and "hard to break" would be われにくい.

questions.stem: Read the review: 「このパソコンは{軽|かる}くて、{持|も}って{歩|ある}きやすいです。でも、キーボードが{小|ちい}さすぎて、{少|すこ}し{使|つか}いにくいです。」 What does the reviewer dislike?
questions.explanation: キーボードが{小|ちい}さすぎて…{使|つか}いにくい: the keyboard is too small, so it's a bit hard to use. The reviewer says the computer is light ({軽|かる}くて) and easy to carry around; price and breaking aren't mentioned.

questions.stem: Choose: 「このつくえの___はどのぐらいですか。」 (How high is this desk?)
questions.explanation: The noun "height" is {高|たか}さ, which can take の and は. {高|たか}い and {高|たか}く are adjective forms, and {高|たか}すぎ would mean "too high".

questions.stem: How is 品物 read?
questions.explanation: 品物 uses two kun'yomi: しな + もの. ヒン and ブツ are the on'yomi used in words like {食品|しょくひん} and {動物|どうぶつ}.

questions.stem: How is 軽い read?
questions.explanation: {軽|かる}い (light): the kun'yomi かる + い. おもい is {重|おも}い (heavy), the opposite, and けい is the on'yomi, used in compounds.

questions.stem: Which word is written 低い?
questions.explanation: 低い is ひくい (low). みじかい is {短|みじか}い, かるい is {軽|かる}い, and おもい is {重|おも}い.

questions.stem: How is 物 read in {動|どう}物 (animal)?
questions.explanation: In {動物|どうぶつ}, 物 has its on'yomi ブツ. もの is the kun'yomi ({物|もの}, {買|か}い{物|もの}), and モツ is the other on'yomi, as in にもつ (luggage).

questions.topic: やすい and にくい
questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: This bag is light and easy to use.
questions.explanation: このかばんは{軽|かる}くて{使|つか}いやすいです. {軽|かる}くて joins the two adjectives, and やすい follows the ます stem {使|つか}い, not the dictionary form {使|つか}う.

questions.stem: Build the request in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Please show me how to use this app.
questions.explanation: このアプリの{使|つか}い{方|かた}を{教|おし}えてください. {使|つか}い{方|かた} is a noun, so アプリ takes の; the whole {使|つか}い{方|かた} then takes を for {教|おし}える.

questions.stem: Listen. Why didn't the speaker buy it?

audio.text: ねだんがたかすぎて、かえませんでした。

questions.explanation: ねだんがたかすぎて: the price was too high, so the speaker couldn't buy it (かえませんでした, the potential of かう). Too heavy would be おもすぎて, too small ちいさすぎて.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear, in hiragana or kanji: ___

audio.text: つかいかた

questions.explanation: つかいかた ({使|つか}い{方|かた}): how to use. The ます stem + {方|かた} makes a noun, "the way of doing".

questions.stem: When does the Japanese school year start?
questions.explanation: The school year runs from April to March, with the entrance ceremony in early April. March is when it ends, with the graduation ceremony.

questions.stem: Which schools are compulsory in Japan?
choices: {小学校|しょうがっこう} only
{小学校|しょうがっこう}, {中学校|ちゅうがっこう} and {高校|こうこう}
{高校|こうこう} and {大学|だいがく}
{小学校|しょうがっこう} and {中学校|ちゅうがっこう}
questions.explanation: Nine years are compulsory: six of {小学校|しょうがっこう} and three of {中学校|ちゅうがっこう}. {高校|こうこう} isn't compulsory, although almost everyone goes.

questions.stem: What is ぶかつ?
questions.explanation: ぶかつ is club activities after school, sports or culture. Cram school is じゅく, an entrance exam is {入試|にゅうし}, and a uniform is せいふく.

questions.stem: Who is your せんぱい?
choices: Someone who started at the school or club before you
questions.explanation: A せんぱい started before you; a こうはい started after you. The relationship is about who joined first, and it carries on into working life.

questions.stem: At most Japanese schools, who cleans the classrooms every day?
choices: The students, in groups that take turns
questions.explanation: Students clean their own classrooms and corridors in a short daily cleaning time, taking turns in groups.

questions.stem: Read: 「せんぱいにボールを{集|あつ}めさせられました。」 What happened?
choices: The speaker made the seniors collect the balls.
The seniors collected the balls for the speaker.
The speaker let the seniors collect the balls.
The seniors made the speaker collect the balls.
questions.explanation: {集|あつ}めさせられました is the causative-passive: the speaker was made to collect, and せんぱいに marks who made them. "The speaker made the seniors" would be the causative せんぱいに{集|あつ}めさせました.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows that the speaker was happy about it?
choices: {先生|せんせい}が{好|す}きな{歌|うた}を{歌|うた}わせてくれました。
{先生|せんせい}に{歌|うた}を{歌|うた}わされました。
{先生|せんせい}に{歌|うた}を{歌|うた}われました。
{先生|せんせい}に{歌|うた}を{歌|うた}わせられました。
questions.explanation: The causative + くれる means the teacher kindly let the speaker sing. {歌|うた}わされました and {歌|うた}わせられました are the causative-passive (made to sing, unwillingly), and {歌|うた}われました is the plain passive.

questions.stem: Type the word for "sports day" (the school sports festival): ___
questions.explanation: {運動会|うんどうかい}: {運動|うんどう} (exercise, sport) + {会|かい} (meeting, event). The school festival is ぶんかさい.

questions.stem: Listen. Why did the speaker go to cram school?

audio.text: こうこうにゅうしのために、じゅくにかよいました。

choices: To prepare for the high school entrance exam
To practise for a club match
To get ready for the school festival
questions.explanation: こうこうにゅうしのために: for the high school entrance exam. じゅくにかよいました: went regularly to cram school.

questions.stem: What do students usually do at the entrance of a Japanese school building?
questions.explanation: Students change into indoor shoes (うわばき) at the entrance, as people take their shoes off at home. Uniforms are worn from home.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
tiles: {一年生|いちねんせい}のとき、
accept: {一年生|いちねんせい}のとき、
questions.prompt: In my first year, the seniors made me collect the balls.
questions.explanation: {一年生|いちねんせい}のとき、せんぱいにボールを{集|あつ}めさせられました. The speaker was made to act, so it's the causative-passive, with the seniors on に. {集|あつ}めさせました would mean the speaker made someone collect them.

questions.stem: Which describes a ぶんかさい?
choices: Students run races in red and white teams.
Students take exams to get into high school.
New students are welcomed in an April ceremony.
Classes and clubs run cafés, plays and exhibitions for visitors.
questions.explanation: The ぶんかさい (school festival) is when classes and clubs put on cafés, plays, concerts and exhibitions. Races in teams are the {運動会|うんどうかい}, exams are {入試|にゅうし}, and the April ceremony is the entrance ceremony.

questions.stem: In the office word ほうれんそう, what do the three parts stand for?
questions.explanation: ほう = ほうこく (report), れん = れんらく (contact, let know), そう = そうだん (consult). It sounds like the word for spinach, which makes it easy to remember.

questions.stem: Which is the polite way to ask your boss for paid leave?
choices: ゆうきゅうをとらせていただけませんか。
ゆうきゅうをとらされませんか。
ゆうきゅうをとってください。
ゆうきゅうをとられませんか。
questions.explanation: The causative て form + いただけませんか asks to be allowed, politely. とらされる is the causative-passive (be made to take), とってください tells the boss to take leave, and とられる is the passive.

questions.stem: You're leaving the office while your colleagues are still working. What do you say?
choices: お{先|さき}にしつれいします。
questions.explanation: お{先|さき}にしつれいします: "excuse me for leaving before you". いただきます is said before eating, and the other two greet someone coming home or leaving.

questions.stem: A colleague says 「お{先|さき}にしつれいします。」 as they leave. What is the usual reply?
questions.explanation: おつかれさまでした thanks them for their work. おじゃまします is said when entering someone's home, and the others don't fit a goodbye.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: めんせつ interview, ざんぎょう overtime, ゆうきゅう paid leave, きゅうりょう salary. A drinking party is {飲|の}み{会|かい}.

questions.stem: A friend says 「きのうも{夜|よる}{九時|くじ}までざんぎょうさせられたよ。」 What happened?
choices: They made their staff work overtime until nine.
They happily chose to work until nine.
Their boss worked overtime until nine.
They were made to work overtime until nine again.
questions.explanation: させられた is the causative-passive of する: they were made to do overtime and didn't like it. も in きのうも means it happened again. Making staff work would be the causative ざんぎょうさせた.

questions.stem: What has been required of companies since 2019, according to the lesson?
choices: Making sure most full-time workers take at least five days of paid leave a year
Giving every worker a month of paid leave
Holding a drinking party every month
questions.explanation: Since 2019 companies must make sure that most full-time workers take at least five days of their paid leave a year. Overtime is limited by law, not banned, and drinking parties are not a rule.

questions.stem: At a job interview, what do you say as you go into the room?
questions.explanation: しつれいします is the phrase for entering an office or interview room. おじゃまします is for entering someone's home, ただいま for coming home, and ごちそうさまでした for after a meal.

questions.stem: Type the する verb meaning "to consult, to ask for advice": ___
questions.explanation: そうだんする, the そう of ほうれんそう. Nにそうだんする: to ask N for advice.

questions.stem: Listen. How many days a week can the speaker work?

audio.text: しゅうに、みっかはたらけます。

questions.explanation: みっか is three days. Four would be よっか, two ふつか and five いつか.

questions.stem: According to the lesson, what is true of {飲|の}み{会|かい} today?
choices: Everyone must go and drink alcohol.
They were banned by law in 2019.
Only new employees go to them.
Many companies hold fewer than before, and saying no politely is normal.
questions.explanation: Drinking parties are still part of office life, but less common than before, and many younger workers prefer not to go or not to drink. すみません、{今日|きょう}はちょっと…… is an accepted way to decline.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker doing?

audio.text: おさきにしつれいします。

choices: Arriving at work in the morning
questions.explanation: おさきにしつれいします is said when you leave before your colleagues. Arriving is おはようございます, a meal starts with いただきます, and an apology to a customer is もうしわけありません.

questions.stem: {明日|あした}は{試験|しけん}___、{今夜|こんや}は{出|で}かけません。 Choose the words for the blank (I have an exam tomorrow, so I'm not going out tonight).
questions.explanation: A noun takes な before ので: {試験|しけん}なので. だ is used before から ({試験|しけん}だから), but never before ので. A bare noun can't take ので either, and なのに means "even though", which turns the sentence into a contradiction.

questions.stem: {毎日|まいにち}れんしゅうしている___、なかなか{上手|じょうず}になりません。 Choose the word for the blank.
questions.explanation: The result is the opposite of what the practice should bring, so the link is のに, "even though": "I practise every day, and yet I just don't get better." ので and から would say the practice is the reason for not improving, and し only lists reasons.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: {雨|あめ}なのに、{出|で}かけましょう。
{雨|あめ}のに、{試合|しあい}は{中止|ちゅうし}になりませんでした。
{雨|あめ}なのに、{試合|しあい}は{中止|ちゅうし}になりませんでした。
{雨|あめ}なのに、{家|いえ}にいてください。
questions.explanation: のに needs な after a noun ({雨|あめ}なのに), and the second half must be a fact that has turned out against expectation: "even though it rained, the match wasn't cancelled." のに can't be followed by an invitation (〜ましょう) or a request (〜てください); for those use けど: {雨|あめ}だけど、{出|で}かけましょう.

questions.stem: 「どうしてちこくしたんですか。」「バスがおくれた___。」 Choose the ending for the blank.
questions.explanation: To answer どうして with "it's because…", end with からです. ので can't be followed by です, so のでです is wrong even though ので also means "because". のに (even though) and し (and) don't give the answer to "why".

questions.stem: この{店|みせ}は{安|やす}い___、おいしい___、いつもこんでいます。 Choose the words for the two blanks (This place is cheap and tasty, so it's always crowded).
questions.explanation: 〜し〜し lists two reasons that lead to the result: cheap, tasty, so it's crowded. のに would mean "even though", which contradicts the result, ても means "even if", and か…か offers alternatives ("cheap or tasty").

questions.stem: {今日|きょう}は{日曜日|にちようび}___、{天気|てんき}もいいし、どこかへ{行|い}こうよ。 Choose the word for the blank.
questions.explanation: A noun or な-adjective takes だ before し: {日曜日|にちようび}だし. Unlike ので and のに, し never takes な, and a bare noun + し is wrong.

questions.stem: You are writing a formal report. Which is the best way to write "I visited places such as Kyoto and Hokkaido"?
choices: {京都|きょうと}とか{北海道|ほっかいどう}とかに{行|い}きました。
{京都|きょうと}し{北海道|ほっかいどう}しに{行|い}きました。
{京都|きょうと}や{北海道|ほっかいどう}などに{行|い}きました。
{京都|きょうと}のに{北海道|ほっかいどう}に{行|い}きました。
questions.explanation: や…など is the neutral, written way to give examples. とか…とか means the same but belongs to casual speech, so it's out of place in a formal report. し lists reasons, not examples (and a noun would need だ before it), and のに means "even though".

questions.stem: In the advice-column letter in lesson 26, the boyfriend says 「そんなにおこらなくてもいいのに」. Why does this upset the writer?
choices: He says he wants to break up with her.
He says he will be late again next time.
He refuses to tell her why he was late.
She hates waiting, and his remark treats her complaint as a fuss about nothing.
questions.explanation: She writes {待|ま}つのがきらいなので、そう{言|い}われると、いやな{気持|きも}ちになります: she hates waiting, so being told that makes her feel awful. The のに at the end turns "you don't need to get angry" into a complaint about her. He never talks of breaking up (she is the one who doesn't want to), and he does give reasons, the same excuses every time.

questions.stem: A message from a colleague: 「すみません、{電車|でんしゃ}が{止|と}まっているので、{十分|じゅっぷん}ぐらいおくれます。{先|さき}に{始|はじ}めていてください。」 What does she want you to do?
choices: Wait for her at the station.
Put the meeting off for a day.
Phone her when the train is moving.
questions.explanation: {先|さき}に{始|はじ}めていてください is "please start (and carry on) before I get there". The ので clause is her excuse: the trains have stopped, so she'll be about ten minutes late. She doesn't ask anyone to wait, cancel or call.

questions.stem: What does 「{言|い}ってくれればよかったのに。」 mean?
questions.explanation: 〜ばよかった is "it would have been good if…", and のに at the end adds the complaint: "if only you'd told me", "you could have told me". The speaker was not told, so it can't be a thank-you or "I'm glad you told me", and it is about the past, not next time.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: やくそくしたのに、かれはこなかった。

choices: He didn't come, so he made a promise.
He promised, and yet he didn't come.
He didn't promise, so he didn't come.
questions.explanation: やくそくしたのに、かれは{来|こ}なかった: のに links a promise with what shouldn't have followed it. The sentence is negative (こなかった, didn't come), so "he came" is wrong, and のに is "even though", not "so".

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: でんしゃがおくれたので、ちこくしました。

choices: Even though the train was late, I wasn't late.
I was late, so I took the train.
The train was on time, but I was late.
The train was late, so I was late.
questions.explanation: {電車|でんしゃ}がおくれたので、ちこくしました: ので gives the reason (the train was late) and the result follows (I was late). Listen for で at the end of ので; のに would have meant "even though".

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear, in kana or kanji. (It means "not particularly".)

audio.text: べつに

questions.explanation: {別|べつ}に, "not particularly", is used with a negative: {別|べつ}に{何|なに}もない (nothing in particular). It's flat in pitch: べつに.

questions.stem: {友|とも}だちを{駅|えき}まで見送りました。 How is 見送り read?
questions.explanation: 見送る (to see off) uses the kun'yomi of both kanji: み + おくる, so 見送り is みおくり. 送 is read ソウ in compounds like {送料|そうりょう}, but not here, and おくれ would be the verb おくれる (to be late).

questions.stem: {明日|あした}は都合が{悪|わる}いです。 How is 都合 read?
questions.explanation: 都合 is つごう: 都 is read ツ here (ト in {京都|きょうと}), and 合 is ゴウ. {都合|つごう}が{悪|わる}い means "the time doesn't suit me".

questions.stem: かれと別れました。 How is 別れました read?
questions.explanation: 別れる is わかれる (to part, to break up); the kun'yomi わか is followed by the okurigana れる. 別 alone is べつ ({別|べつ}の, another), but べつれる is not a word.

questions.stem: Match each kanji to its meaning.
questions.explanation: 好 as in {好|す}き, 悪 as in {悪|わる}い, 別 as in {別|わか}れる and {別|べつ}の, 合 as in {合|あ}う and {間|ま}に{合|あ}う, 送 as in {送|おく}る, and 不 as in {不安|ふあん}.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Even though it's Sunday, I have to go to work.
questions.explanation: {日曜日|にちようび}なのに、{仕事|しごと}に{行|い}かなければなりません。 A noun takes な before のに; the "must" pattern 〜なければなりません (lesson 15) ends the sentence. だので is never correct.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Sorry, I have a fever, so may I go home early?
questions.explanation: すみません、ねつがあるので、{早|はや}く{帰|かえ}ってもいいですか。 The excuse comes first with ので, then the request for permission (〜てもいいですか). のに would make the fever something that should have stopped you asking.

questions.stem: You are apologizing to your boss for being late. Which is the most appropriate?
choices: バスがおくれたのに、ちこくしました。もうしわけありません。
バスがおくれたし、ちこくしたし。
バスがおくれたとか、ちこくしました。
バスがおくれたので、ちこくしました。もうしわけありません。
questions.explanation: ので gives the reason as a fact, which is exactly what an apology needs, and もうしわけありません is the polite apology. のに would mean "even though the bus was late, I was late", which makes no sense; the し sentence is unfinished and casual, and とか lists examples.

questions.stem: {先生|せんせい}は{今|いま}、{研究室|けんきゅうしつ}に___。 Choose the respectful form (The professor is in her office now).
questions.explanation: いらっしゃる is the honorific of いる, and its ます form is いらっしゃいます, with い, not り. おります and まいります are humble: you use them about yourself, never about your teacher.

questions.stem: しゅうまつは{何|なに}を___か。 Choose the honorific form of する for the blank (asking a customer what they will do at the weekend).
questions.explanation: なさる is the honorific of する, and its ます form is なさいます. なさります is a common slip (the ます form has い, like いらっしゃいます). いたします is the humble する, for yourself, and まいります is the humble "come/go".

questions.stem: Match each honorific verb to the ordinary verb it replaces.
questions.explanation: おっしゃる = {言|い}う, めしあがる = {食|た}べる/{飲|の}む, ごらんになる = {見|み}る, なさる = する, ごぞんじだ = {知|し}っている, いらっしゃる = いる/{行|い}く/{来|く}る.

questions.topic: お〜になる and お〜ください
questions.stem: Which is the honorific form of {帰|かえ}る (to go home)?
questions.explanation: The pattern is お + ます stem + になる: {帰|かえ}ります → {帰|かえ}り → お{帰|かえ}りになる. The dictionary form can't go in the pattern, ご is for Sino-Japanese nouns, and お{帰|かえ}りする is the humble pattern, for your own actions.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct keigo for "The teacher saw it"?
choices: {先生|せんせい}がお{見|み}になりました。
{先生|せんせい}がごらんしました。
{先生|せんせい}がはいけんしました。
{先生|せんせい}がごらんになりました。
questions.explanation: {見|み}る has a special honorific form, ごらんになる, so the お〜になる pattern isn't used with it (お{見|み}になる is wrong). ごらんしました drops the になる, and はいけんする is the humble "see", for your own looking, never the teacher's.

questions.topic: お〜になる and お〜ください
questions.stem: A hotel receptionist asks a guest to write their name, using the respectful request pattern お〜ください: こちらにお{名前|なまえ}を___ください。 Which fills the blank?
questions.explanation: The pattern is お + ます stem + ください: お{書|か}きください. お{書|か}きに would need なる (お{書|か}きになる is a statement, not a request), the て form doesn't go inside the pattern, and ご is for Sino-Japanese nouns such as ご{注意|ちゅうい}.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: {私|わたし}は{明日|あした}、{京都|きょうと}へいらっしゃいます。
{社長|しゃちょう}は{明日|あした}、{京都|きょうと}へいらっしゃいます。
{社長|しゃちょう}は{明日|あした}、{京都|きょうと}へいらっしゃります。
{私|わたし}は{明日|あした}、{京都|きょうと}へお{行|い}きになります。
questions.explanation: Honorific verbs are for the other person's actions, so the president can いらっしゃる, but you can't: never use いらっしゃる or お〜になる about yourself. The ます form is いらっしゃいます, not いらっしゃります.

questions.stem: Which of these, with its お or ご, would be wrong to use about your own family or things?
questions.explanation: In ご{家族|かぞく} the ご shows respect for the other person's family, so you can't use it for your own (say {私|わたし}の{家族|かぞく}). お{茶|ちゃ}, ご{飯|はん} and お{水|みず} have beautifying お/ご, which only makes the word sound refined, so they are fine for your own things.

questions.stem: Which word takes ご rather than お?
questions.explanation: {家族|かぞく} is a Sino-Japanese word (two kanji read in on'yomi), so it takes ご: ご{家族|かぞく}. {名前|なまえ} and {手紙|てがみ} are native words and take お. {電話|でんわ} is Sino-Japanese but one of the common exceptions: お{電話|でんわ}.

questions.stem: Which is the polite word for だれ (who)?
questions.explanation: どなた is the polite "who". どちら is the polite "where" (or "which"), いかが is the polite "how", and こちら is "here, this way".

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: せんせいはなんとおっしゃいましたか。

questions.explanation: {先生|せんせい}は{何|なん}とおっしゃいましたか: おっしゃる is the honorific "say", and {何|なん}と is "what (quoted)". "Go" would be いらっしゃる, "eat" めしあがる and "see" ごらんになる.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: どうぞ、めしあがってください。

questions.explanation: めしあがる is the honorific "eat, drink", so どうぞめしあがってください invites a guest to eat. "Come in" is お{入|はい}りください, "have a look" ごらんください, "take a seat" おかけください.

questions.stem: Listen. A shop assistant says this at the till. What does it mean?

audio.text: ポイントカードはおもちですか。

choices: Would you like a points card?
Shall I hold your points card?
Have you lost your points card?
Do you have a points card?
questions.explanation: お{持|も}ちですか is the short honorific お + ます stem + です: "do you have?" about the customer. "Would you like one" would be いかがですか, and "shall I hold it" would be humble: お{持|も}ちしましょうか.

questions.stem: What does this sentence mean? {先生|せんせい}はこの{本|ほん}を{三年前|さんねんまえ}に{書|か}かれました。
choices: The teacher wrote this book three years ago.
This book was written about the teacher three years ago.
The teacher was able to write this book in three years.
The teacher had someone write this book three years ago.
questions.explanation: {書|か}かれる here is the light honorific 〜られる: the subject is the teacher, and the object この{本|ほん}を is still there, so no one is acting on the teacher. It can't be the potential ({書|か}ける), and "had someone write" would be the causative ({書|か}かせる).

questions.stem: {大学|だいがく}の食堂は{安|やす}くておいしいです。 How is 食堂 read?
questions.explanation: 食堂 is しょくどう: 食 ショク + 堂 ドウ, with a voiced ど and a long vowel. たべ is the kun'yomi of 食, used in {食|た}べる, not in this compound.

questions.stem: {新|あたら}しい洋服を{買|か}いました。 How is 洋服 read?
questions.explanation: 洋服 is ようふく: 洋 ヨウ + 服 フク, with no voicing. It meant "Western clothes" and is now often just "clothes".

questions.stem: お___をどうぞ。 (Please have some tea.) Which kanji goes in the blank?
questions.explanation: お{茶|ちゃ} is (green) tea. 菜 (as in {野菜|やさい}) looks similar, with the grass radical on top, but means vegetables; 洋 is "Western" and 服 is "clothes".

questions.topic: お〜になる and お〜ください
questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese, as a hotel receptionist would say it.
questions.prompt: Please write your name and address here.
questions.explanation: こちらにお{名前|なまえ}とご{住所|じゅうしょ}をお{書|か}きください。 お + ます stem + ください is the respectful request; こちらに can also come after the objects. お{名前|なまえ} takes お (a native word), ご{住所|じゅうしょ} takes ご.

questions.topic: お〜になる and お〜ください
questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese, as hotel staff would say it.
questions.prompt: Please wait a moment in the lobby.
questions.explanation: ロビーでしょうしょうお{待|ま}ちください。 (しょうしょう can also come first.) The request is お + ます stem + ください; the て form doesn't go inside the pattern.

questions.stem: You work in a restaurant. How do you ask a customer whether they'd like something to drink?
choices: お{飲|の}み{物|もの}はいかがですか。
{飲|の}み{物|もの}をいただきますか。
お{飲|の}み{物|もの}をいたしますか。
{何|なに}をお{飲|の}みしますか。
questions.explanation: いかがですか is the polite "how about…?", and お{飲|の}み{物|もの} is the usual polite word. いただく is humble, so it can't describe the customer's drinking; いたす is the humble する; and お{飲|の}みする is the humble pattern, for your own actions.

questions.stem: はじめまして。リンと___。 Choose the humble form for the blank (How do you do? My name is Lin).
questions.explanation: もうす is the humble {言|い}う, and 〜ともうします is the standard way to give your name formally. おっしゃる is honorific (for others, never yourself), いたす is the humble する, and まいる the humble "come, go".

questions.stem: {明日|あした}、{三時|さんじ}にそちらへ___。 Choose the humble form (I'll come to your office at three tomorrow).
questions.explanation: まいる is the humble {行|い}く/{来|く}る, right for your own coming. いらっしゃいます is honorific (for the other person), おります is the humble いる (to be, not to come), and なさいます is the honorific する.

questions.stem: You offer to carry a customer's bags. Which is correct?
choices: おにもつ、お{持|も}ちになりましょうか。
おにもつ、{持|も}たせましょうか。
おにもつ、お{持|も}ちしましょうか。
おにもつ、お{持|も}ちくださいましょうか。
questions.explanation: You carry the bags for the customer, so the humble pattern お + ます stem + する is right: お{持|も}ちします, お{持|も}ちしましょうか. お〜になる is honorific (for the customer's own action), {持|も}たせる is causative ("make someone carry"), and お〜ください is a request.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses humble language correctly?
choices: {私|わたし}は{毎朝|まいあさ}{七時|しちじ}にお{起|お}きします。
{先生|せんせい}がしりょうをお{送|おく}りしました。
{私|わたし}がしりょうをお{送|おく}りになります。
{私|わたし}がしりょうをお{送|おく}りします。
questions.explanation: Sending documents to someone is an action that involves them, so the humble お{送|おく}りする fits. Getting up involves nobody else, so お{起|お}きします makes no sense; the teacher's action needs honorific forms, not humble; and お〜になる is honorific, so you can't use it about yourself.

questions.stem: Match each humble verb to the ordinary verb it replaces.
questions.explanation: まいる = {行|い}く/{来|く}る, もうす = {言|い}う, いたす = する, はいけんする = {見|み}る, おる = いる, うかがう = {聞|き}く (ask, hear) and visiting someone.

questions.stem: On the phone, you want to ask politely whether the caller is Mr Tanaka: 「{田中|たなか}さまで___か。」 Which fits?
questions.explanation: でいらっしゃる is the honorific "be", for the other person: {田中|たなか}さまでいらっしゃいますか. でございます is very polite but used for things or yourself ({田中|たなか}でございます, "this is Tanaka"), and おります and まいります are humble.

questions.stem: A customer phones for your colleague Mr Tanaka, who is out. Which reply is correct?
choices: {田中|たなか}さんはただいま{出|で}かけていらっしゃいます。
{田中|たなか}はただいま{出|で}かけております。
{田中|たなか}さんはただいま{出|で}かけております。
{田中|たなか}はただいま{出|で}かけていらっしゃいます。
questions.explanation: To an outsider, your own colleague is on your side: no さん, and humble (or courteous) forms, so {田中|たなか}は…{出|で}かけております. Inside the company you'd say {田中|たなか}さん and いらっしゃる, but to a customer that would raise your own side above them.

questions.stem: A waiter asks what you would like to eat. Which is correct?
choices: {何|なに}をお{食|た}べしますか。
{何|なに}をめしあがりますか。
questions.explanation: The customer does the eating, so the waiter uses the honorific めしあがる. いただく is the humble "eat", for your own eating (いただきます), お{食|た}べする is the humble pattern, and いたします is the humble する.

questions.stem: On the phone, a receptionist says: おりかえしお{電話|でんわ}いたしましょうか。 What is she offering?
choices: To have someone call you back
questions.explanation: おりかえし is "in return, calling back", and お{電話|でんわ}いたしましょうか is the humble "shall we phone (you)?". Taking a message would be でんごん, and putting you through is おつなぎします.

questions.stem: Listen. A caller begins with this phrase. What does it mean?

audio.text: いつもおせわになっております。

choices: Thank you for your continued support.
questions.explanation: いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております ("you always look after us") is the standard opening of a business call or email. "Sorry to keep you waiting" is お{待|ま}たせいたしました, "I'm very sorry" もうしわけございません, and "who's calling?" どちらさまでしょうか.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: たなかはただいまかいぎちゅうでございます。

choices: Tanaka is on a business trip.
Tanaka is in a meeting at the moment.
Tanaka has gone home for the day.
Tanaka will join the meeting soon.
questions.explanation: かいぎ{中|ちゅう} is "in a meeting", ただいま "at the moment", and でございます the very polite です. A business trip would be しゅっちょう; gone home would be {帰|かえ}りました.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: はじめまして。キムともうします。

choices: How do you do? This is Mr Kim.
Nice to meet you, Mr Kim.
How do you do? My name is Kim.
Mr Kim will be with you shortly.
questions.explanation: 〜ともうします is the humble "I am called…", so the speaker is Kim, introducing himself. Introducing someone else as a guest would be こちらはキムさんです.

questions.stem: この工場では{車|くるま}を{作|つく}っています。 How is 工場 read?
questions.explanation: 工場 is こうじょう: 工 コウ + 場 ジョウ, with a voiced じょ. こうしょう misses the voicing, ク is the rarer reading of 工 (as in {大工|だいく}), and こうちょう is a different word (school principal).

questions.stem: {先生|せんせい}に質問があります。 How is 質問 read?
questions.explanation: 質問 is しつもん: 質 シツ + 問 モン. It's the N5 word しつもん, now written with kanji.

questions.stem: もう{一度|いちど}説明してください。 How is 説明 read?
questions.explanation: 説明 is せつめい: 説 セツ + 明 メイ. 明 can be ミョウ in a few words, but not here, and せいめい is a different word.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "place"?
questions.explanation: 場 is "place": {場所|ばしょ}, {会場|かいじょう}, {工場|こうじょう}. 工 is craft or construction, 質 quality, and 説 explain.

questions.stem: A memo on Mr Yamada's desk: 「{山田|やまだ}ぶちょう：{十時|じゅうじ}ごろ、サクラ{電気|でんき}のかとうさまからお{電話|でんわ}がありました。{来週|らいしゅう}の{工場|こうじょう}{見学|けんがく}の{時間|じかん}がかわったので、メールを{送|おく}ったそうです。メールを{見|み}てください。おりかえしのお{電話|でんわ}はいらないそうです。すずき」 What should Mr Yamada do?
choices: Change the time of the factory tour himself.
questions.explanation: メールを{見|み}てください is the request. The memo says a call back isn't needed (おりかえしのお{電話|でんわ}はいらない), the time has already been changed by Sakura Electric, and Suzuki only wrote the memo.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese, as you'd say it to a visitor.
questions.prompt: Well then, I'll explain it.
questions.explanation: では、{私|わたし}がご{説明|せつめい}いたします。 ご + noun + いたす is the humble pattern for a する noun. なさいます is honorific, so it can't describe your own explaining.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese, as a receptionist would say it to a caller.
questions.prompt: Tanaka is away from his desk at the moment.
questions.explanation: {田中|たなか}はただいませきを{外|はず}しております。 (ただいま can also come first.) To a caller, your own colleague gets no さん and the humble 〜ております; いらっしゃいます would raise him.

questions.stem: You are introducing yourself at the start of a job interview. Which is best?
choices: リンともうします。よろしくおねがいいたします。
リンとおっしゃいます。よろしくおねがいいたします。
リンさんです。よろしくおねがいします。
リンといたします。よろしくおねがいいたします。
questions.explanation: 〜ともうします (humble "I am called") and よろしくおねがいいたします are the standard formal self-introduction. おっしゃる is honorific, so it can't be used about yourself; you never add さん to your own name; and いたす means "do", not "be called".

questions.stem: In the summer festival notice (lesson 29, text 1), what happens if it rains on the 23rd?
choices: The festival moves to the next day, the 24th.
The festival is held in a hall instead.
questions.explanation: {雨天|うてん}の{場合|ばあい}は、つぎの{日|ひ}（{二十四日|にじゅうよっか}）にえんきします: if it rains, it is postponed to the next day. えんき is postponement, not cancellation ({中止|ちゅうし}), and the notice says nothing about a hall.

questions.stem: In the same notice, who is given a free juice?
choices: People who come wearing a yukata
Children who come with an adult
questions.explanation: ゆかたを{着|き}て{来|き}た{方|かた}には、ジュースを{一本|いっぽん}さしあげます: one juice for anyone who comes in a yukata. Volunteers are asked to contact the office, and cars aren't allowed at all.

questions.stem: In the same notice, what should people who want to volunteer do?
choices: Come to the park on the 23rd.
Phone the town office on the 24th.
Contact the town office by 10 August.
Write their names on a list in the park.
questions.explanation: {八月|はちがつ}{十日|とおか}までに、{町|ちょう}のじむしょにごれんらくください: get in touch with the town office by (までに) 10 August. The 23rd and 24th are the festival days.

questions.stem: In the teacher's email (lesson 29, text 2), why is Monday's class cancelled?
choices: The teacher has to attend a university meeting.
questions.explanation: {私|わたし}が{大学|だいがく}のかいぎに{出|で}なければならないので: the reason comes before ので. Nothing is said about repairs, holidays or illness.

questions.stem: In the same email, what must students who can't come on Thursday do?
choices: Hand in their homework on Thursday.
questions.explanation: {木曜日|もくようび}に{来|こ}られない{人|ひと}は、{金曜日|きんようび}までにメールでれんらくしてください: email by Friday, and the teacher will send the class materials. Room 205 is where Thursday's class is held.

questions.stem: In the same email, when is the homework due?
choices: It has been postponed by a week.
questions.explanation: しゅくだいのしめきりはかわりません。{月曜日|げつようび}の{夜|よる}までに{出|だ}してください: the deadline doesn't change, Monday night. Friday is the deadline for the email, not the homework.

questions.stem: According to the coin laundry instructions (lesson 29, text 3), which is true?
choices: You must add your own detergent.
The door can't be opened until the wash finishes.
The blanket course takes thirty minutes.
questions.explanation: ドアは{終|お}わるまで{開|あ}けられません: the door can't be opened until it finishes. Detergent goes in automatically (and you mustn't add your own), only 100-yen coins work, and the blanket course takes forty minutes.

questions.stem: In the blog post (lesson 29, text 4), why couldn't the writer climb the mountain?
choices: The old woman asked her to stay.
questions.explanation: つぎの{日|ひ}は{雨|あめ}だったので、{山|やま}にはのぼれなかった: it rained, so she couldn't climb. The のに that follows (she'd been looking forward to it) shows her disappointment.

questions.stem: In the same blog post, who does the writer plan to take next time?
questions.explanation: {今度|こんど}は{友|とも}だちとか{家族|かぞく}といっしょに{来|こ}ようと{思|おも}う: とか gives friends and family as examples. Her first trip was the solo one.

questions.stem: According to the line notice (lesson 29, text 5), how can you travel from Kitamachi to Minamimachi at 11 p.m. on 15 November?
choices: By replacement bus from the east exit
There is no way to travel that night.
questions.explanation: From 10 p.m. to the last train the trains stop between the two stations, and {代|か}わりのバスが{走|はし}ります: replacement buses run, from the east exit ({東口|ひがしぐち}) of each station. They take about thirty minutes longer.

questions.stem: A friend says: しゅくだい、やっとかなきゃ。 What is the full form?
choices: しゅくだいを、やってしまわなければ。
しゅくだいを、やっていかなければ。
しゅくだいを、やっておかなければ。
しゅくだいを、やっていなければ。
questions.explanation: とか is ておか (〜ておく, do in advance) and なきゃ is なければ: "I'd better get my homework done." 〜てしまう contracts to ちゃう, 〜ていく to てく and 〜ている to てる.

questions.stem: A friend asks: かさ、{持|も}ってく？ What does it mean?
choices: Shall I get the umbrella ready?
Are you bringing the umbrella back?
questions.explanation: 〜てく is 〜ていく with the い dropped: {持|も}っていく, "take (it) with you". "Do you have" would be {持|も}ってる (〜ている), "get ready" {持|も}っとく (〜ておく), and "bring back" {持|も}ってくる.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: ちょっとまってて。すぐいくから。

choices: Wait a moment. I'll be right there.
I waited for a long time.
questions.explanation: {待|ま}ってて is {待|ま}っていて (keep waiting), and すぐ{行|い}くから is "because I'll come straight away". It is a request, not a statement about the speaker's own waiting.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: しゅくだい、もうやっちゃった。

choices: I haven't done my homework yet.
I have to do my homework.
questions.explanation: やっちゃった is やってしまった, "done (completely)", and もう is "already". "Have to" would be やらなきゃ; "not yet" まだやっていない.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: ここでしゃしんをとっちゃだめだよ。

questions.explanation: とっちゃだめ is とってはだめ: 〜ちゃ is the casual 〜ては, and 〜てはだめ is "you mustn't". Don't confuse it with とっちゃった (〜てしまった), which would mean "I (ended up) taking".

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: あしたははやくおきなきゃ。

choices: I don't need to get up early tomorrow.
I got up early this morning.
I'll try to get up early tomorrow.
I have to get up early tomorrow.
questions.explanation: {起|お}きなきゃ is {起|お}きなければ (ならない), "I must get up". "Don't need to" would be {起|お}きなくてもいい, and "try to" would be {起|お}きるようにする.

questions.stem: Listen. How will they go?

audio.text: バスでいこうとおもったけど、あめだし、やっぱりタクシーにしよう。

questions.explanation: The first plan was the bus, but やっぱり ("after all") brings the change: タクシーにしよう, let's take a taxi. The reason is given with し: {雨|あめ}だし. Listen to the end before choosing.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: ゆうこもくるって。

questions.explanation: って at the end is the casual quotation (〜と{言|い}っていた): "Yuko says she's coming too." くる is non-past (coming), and there is no request in it.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in casual Japanese.
questions.prompt: I'll buy the tickets at the station in advance, OK?
questions.explanation: {先|さき}に{駅|えき}できっぷ{買|か}っとくね。 {買|か}っとく is {買|か}っておく, "buy in advance"; casual speech often drops を. {先|さき}に and {駅|えき}で can swap. {買|か}ってる (〜ている) would mean "I'm buying".

questions.stem: Build the sentence as it would appear on a notice.
questions.prompt: If it rains, it will be postponed to the next day.
questions.explanation: {雨天|うてん}の{場合|ばあい}は、つぎの{日|ひ}にえんきします。 〜の{場合|ばあい}は (in the case of) sets the condition. {中止|ちゅうし} is cancellation, which can't be "to the next day".

questions.stem: How long is the listening section of the JLPT N4?
questions.explanation: N4 listening is 35 minutes. 25 minutes is the vocabulary section and 55 the grammar and reading section; 30 minutes is N5's listening.

questions.stem: A candidate scores 100 points in all, but only 17 in listening. What is the result?
choices: Fail: the total must be at least 120.
questions.explanation: To pass N4 you need at least 90 of 180 and the sectional pass marks: 38 for language knowledge and reading, 19 for listening. 17 is below 19, so the candidate fails whatever the total. 80 is N5's overall pass mark.

questions.stem: Which vocabulary question type does lesson 30 describe as new at N4?
choices: Usage: choosing the sentence in which a word is used correctly
questions.explanation: The usage question gives one word and four sentences, and only one uses it correctly. Kanji readings, writing, words in context and paraphrase are already in N5.

questions.stem: What is the range of the total score on the JLPT N4?
questions.explanation: Two scoring sections, 0–120 (language knowledge and reading) and 0–60 (listening), make a total of 0–180.

questions.stem: What is the sectional pass mark for language knowledge and reading at N4?
questions.explanation: 38 of 120 for language knowledge (vocabulary and grammar) and reading. 19 of 60 is the listening minimum, and 90 of 180 the overall pass mark.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "When you arrive at the station, please call me"?
choices: {駅|えき}に{着|つ}くと、{電話|でんわ}してください。
{駅|えき}に{着|つ}いたら、{電話|でんわ}してください。
{駅|えき}に{着|つ}けば、{電話|でんわ}してください。
{駅|えき}に{着|つ}くなら、{電話|でんわ}してください。
questions.explanation: たら works for "when (after) A happens, do B", including requests. と can't be followed by a request, ば with an action verb and a request sounds unnatural, and {着|つ}くなら means "if you are going to arrive", so you'd call before arriving.

questions.stem: 「このケーキ、おいし___ですね。」 (This cake looks delicious.) Choose what goes in the blank.
questions.explanation: "Looks like" is the adjective stem + そう: おいし + そう. With the full い (おいしいそう) it becomes hearsay, "I hear it's delicious", which isn't the meaning given. さそう is only for いい and ない (よさそう, なさそう), and そうだ can't be followed by です.

questions.stem: {友|とも}だちが{私|わたし}に{本|ほん}を___。 Choose the verb for the blank (A friend gave me a book).
questions.explanation: A gift coming to you or your side takes くれる. あげる and さしあげる are for giving outward, and もらう needs the receiver as the subject ({私|わたし}は{友|とも}だちに{本|ほん}をもらいました).

questions.stem: What does {母|はは}に{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べさせられました mean?
choices: My mother made me eat vegetables.
I made my mother eat vegetables.
My mother cooked vegetables for me.
questions.explanation: {食|た}べさせられる is the causative-passive: I was made to eat, and the one who made me is marked with に ({母|はは}に). "I made my mother eat" would be the causative {母|はは}に{食|た}べさせた, and "ate my vegetables" would be the passive {母|はは}に{野菜|やさい}を{食|た}べられた.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "The window has been left open (by someone, on purpose)"?
choices: まどが{開|あ}いてあります。
まどが{開|あ}けてあります。
まどを{開|あ}いています。
まどが{開|あ}けています。
questions.explanation: 〜てある follows a transitive verb ({開|あ}ける) and describes a state someone left on purpose: まどが{開|あ}けてあります. {開|あ}く is intransitive, so it takes 〜ている, not 〜てある (まどが{開|あ}いています = the window is open), and it can't take を.

questions.stem: Listen. Who will show the way?

audio.text: わたしがごあんないいたします。

questions.explanation: ごあんないいたします is the humble pattern ご + noun + いたす, used for the speaker's own action, and {私|わたし}が says so too. Humble forms point to the speaker; honorific forms to the other person.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: どっかいはじかんがたりなかった。

choices: The reading section was too easy.
I finished the reading section early.
I didn't study reading at all.
I ran out of time on the reading section.
questions.explanation: どっかい is reading comprehension, and {時間|じかん}がたりなかった is "the time wasn't enough". The opposite would be {早|はや}く{終|お}わった (finished early).

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: けっかがでたら、おしえてね。

choices: Tell me when the results come out.
I'll tell you the results tomorrow.
questions.explanation: けっかが{出|で}たら is "when the results come out" (たら for a future event), and {教|おし}えてね is a casual request: "let me know".

questions.stem: What does もうしこみ mean?
questions.explanation: もうしこみ is an application or registration (the verb is もうしこむ). The result is けっか, the score てんすう, and reading comprehension どっかい.

questions.stem: {試験|しけん}の___は、いつ{分|わ}かりますか。 Choose the word for the blank (When will we know the exam results?).
questions.explanation: けっか is the result. もうしこみ (application), ごい (vocabulary) and ぶんしょう (text) aren't things that become known after an exam.

questions.stem: {雨|あめ}___、{試合|しあい}は{中止|ちゅうし}になりませんでした。 Choose the words for the blank.
questions.explanation: The match wasn't cancelled, against what the rain would lead you to expect, so the link is なのに (even though). なので and だから would give the rain as the reason the match went ahead, and だし lists a reason.

questions.stem: A notice at a language school: 「N4のもうしこみ：{八月|はちがつ}{一日|ついたち}〜{九月|くがつ}{十日|とおか}。{試験|しけん}の{日|ひ}：{十二月|じゅうにがつ}{七日|なのか}（{日|にち}）。ただし、{九月|くがつ}{十日|とおか}をすぎると、もうしこみはできません。」 Today is 12 September. Can you still apply?
choices: Yes, until the end of September.
questions.explanation: The application period ends on 10 September, and ただし introduces the condition that after that date you can't apply. 7 December is the test date, not a deadline.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I plan to sit N4 in December.
questions.explanation: {私|わたし}は{十二月|じゅうにがつ}にN4をじゅけんするつもりです。 つもり follows the dictionary form, so じゅけんする, not じゅけんした. The time can come before or after the topic.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Even though I studied every day, I couldn't pass.
questions.explanation: {毎日|まいにち}{勉強|べんきょう}したのに、ごうかくできませんでした。 のに links the effort to the disappointing result. ので would make studying the reason for failing.

questions.stem: Which statement about the JLPT is true?
choices: There is no speaking or writing section.
Each listening recording is played twice.
questions.explanation: The JLPT tests only reading and listening, all multiple choice. There is no interview, no penalty for a wrong answer (so never leave a question blank), and each recording is played once.

questions.stem: In the story, what did Mrs Yamaguchi always say when she handed Haruto his bread?
choices: ありがとうございました
questions.explanation: パンをわたしながら、いつも「いってらっしゃい」と{言|い}ってくれた: "off you go, have a good day", the phrase a family says to someone leaving home, which meant a lot to Haruto living alone. また{来|き}てね is from lesson 29's blog, not this story.

questions.stem: Why was the bakery closed in October?
choices: She had gone to stay with her son in Osaka.
Mrs Yamaguchi fell in the shop and was hurt.
questions.explanation: The florist says {店|みせ}で{転|ころ}んで、けがをしたそうだ: she fell over in the shop and was hurt, and is in hospital. Her son lives in Osaka, but she didn't go there, and retiring was the son's idea, not her decision.

questions.stem: How did Haruto find out what had happened?
choices: He read it on the notice on the door.
He asked the florist next door.
questions.explanation: となりの{花屋|はなや}の{主人|しゅじん}に{聞|き}いてみた: he asked the florist. The notice only said the shop would be closed for a while, and the florist's そうだ and らしい show he too is passing on what he has heard.

questions.stem: What did Mrs Yamaguchi's son want at first?
choices: For her to move to Osaka
For Haruto to run the shop
For her to open only on Saturdays
For her to give up the shop
questions.explanation: もう{店|みせ}をやめたほうがいいと{言|い}っているそうだ: he says she should give up the shop. Moving to Osaka is never mentioned, and opening on Saturdays is what he agrees to at the end, after seeing her with Haruto.

questions.stem: What does Mrs Yamaguchi say has been her joy?
choices: Children who bought her bread now bring their own children.
Getting up at four every morning.
Winning prizes for her melon bread.
questions.explanation: The children of the neighbourhood have come since they were small, and now come with their own children: それが{私|わたし}の{楽|たの}しみだったのに. The のに shows her sadness that this may end. Getting up at four is what has become too hard.

questions.stem: Haruto says 「{私|わたし}にてつだわせていただけませんか」. What does he mean?
choices: Would you let me help you?
Shall I get someone to help you?
I was made to help you.
questions.explanation: てつだわせる is the causative of てつだう (let someone help), and 〜ていただけませんか is the politest request: "would you allow me to help?" (lesson 22). It isn't a request for help, and "was made to" would be the causative-passive てつだわされた.

questions.stem: Mrs Yamaguchi answers 「{学生|がくせい}さんにそんなことはさせられないわ」. What does she mean?
choices: A student made me do something like that.
A student can't do something like that.
I can't ask a student to do something like that.
I won't let a student eat that.
questions.explanation: させられない is the potential of させる (to have someone do): "I can't have you do that". The context shows it: she is turning down Haruto's offer, and the student (marked with に) is the one who would do the work. The same shape can be a causative-passive, but "I can't be made to do it" makes no sense here.

questions.stem: What reason does Haruto give for helping?
choices: He needs the money from a part-time job.
He wants to become a baker.
He gets up early anyway, and his day doesn't start without the melon bread.
questions.explanation: {朝|あさ}はどうせ{早|はや}く{起|お}きますから。それに、こむぎのメロンパンが{食|た}べられないと、{一日|いちにち}が{始|はじ}まらないんです: どうせ (anyway) and それに (besides) give his two reasons. He mentions his old part-time job only to show he can do the work.

questions.stem: What had happened by the third Saturday?
choices: A queue formed outside the shop.
Mrs Yamaguchi had gone back into hospital.
questions.explanation: {店|みせ}の{前|まえ}にれつができるようになった: a queue began to form (〜ようになる, lesson 24). Nothing says his bread became perfect; his first loaves were a funny shape.

questions.stem: What does the son decide?
choices: She can carry on, if it is only on Saturdays.
He will move back and run the shop himself.
questions.explanation: {土曜日|どようび}だけなら、つづけてもいいと{思|おも}います: if it's only Saturdays (なら, lesson 14), she may carry on (〜てもいい). He bows to Haruto to thank him.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: みためはわるいけど、あじはいいわよ。

choices: It looks good, but it doesn't taste good.
It looks good and tastes good.
It doesn't look good, but it tastes good.
It's gone bad, so don't eat it.
questions.explanation: {見|み}た{目|め} is how something looks, and けど contrasts it with the taste: it looks bad, but tastes good. わよ is the gentle, slightly old-fashioned ending Mrs Yamaguchi uses.

questions.stem: At the end, Haruto says いってらっしゃい to the little girl. Why is this a fitting ending?
choices: He is telling the girl to leave the shop quickly.
He is copying what the son said.
It is the shop's new name.
He now says what Mrs Yamaguchi used to say to him.
questions.explanation: {山口|やまぐち}さんと{同|おな}じように{言|い}った: he says it just as Mrs Yamaguchi did. The story ends where it began, with Haruto now on the other side of the counter.

questions.stem: In a polite email, what usually comes right after the reader's name?
choices: A set greeting, such as いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております, and who you are
Your request with all the details
questions.explanation: After the reader's name comes the set opening (いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております) and your class or company and name, so the reader knows at once who is writing. The main point follows; けいぐ belongs to letters, at the end.

questions.stem: Which is the politest way to ask your teacher, in an email, to let you miss a class?
choices: {休|やす}ませていただけないでしょうか。
questions.explanation: 〜させていただけないでしょうか is the politest request in the course: the causative (let me rest), いただく (receive the favour) and the soft でしょうか. 〜させてください is polite but direct, and the last two are casual.

questions.stem: Which word always pairs with はいけい at the opening of a letter?
choices: よろしくおねがいいたします
questions.explanation: はいけい opens a formal letter and けいぐ closes it, like "Dear…" and "Yours sincerely". さて turns to the main point, and よろしくおねがいいたします closes an email or request.

questions.stem: What does さて do in a letter?
choices: It asks after the reader's health.
It turns to the main point.
questions.explanation: After the seasonal greeting and asking after the reader, さて ("now", "well then") introduces the real subject of the letter.

questions.stem: In polite writing, how does {日|ひ}にちをまちがえてしまって、{今朝|けさ}{気|き}がつきました usually begin?
choices: {日|ひ}にちをまちがえてしまい、
{日|ひ}にちをまちがえてしまうので、
{日|ひ}にちをまちがえてしまえば、
{日|ひ}にちをまちがえてしまったのに、
questions.explanation: In formal writing, a clause that would end in the て form often ends in the ます stem: 〜てしまって → 〜てしまい. The other choices change the meaning (because, if, even though).

questions.stem: Which seasonal greeting suits a letter written in August?
choices: さくらの{花|はな}がきれいなきせつになりました。
{暑|あつ}い{日|ひ}がつづいていますが、お{元気|げんき}ですか。
{寒|さむ}さがきびしくなってまいりました。
すずしくなってまいりました。
questions.explanation: August is the height of summer, so the greeting about hot days fits. Cherry blossoms belong to spring, severe cold to winter, and "it has turned cool" to autumn.

questions.stem: Sarah tells her host family that she has sent them some sweets. Which is correct?
choices: おかしを{少|すこ}しお{送|おく}りになりました。
おかしを{少|すこ}しお{送|おく}りくださいました。
おかしを{少|すこ}しお{送|おく}りしました。
おかしを{少|すこ}しお{送|おく}りなさいました。
questions.explanation: Sarah does the sending, for the family, so the humble お + ます stem + する is right. お〜になる and なさる are honorific (for the family's actions), and くださる would mean the family sent something to her.

questions.stem: What does お{口|くち}に{合|あ}うとうれしいです mean, after sending some food?
choices: I hope it suits your taste.
questions.explanation: {合|あ}う is "to fit, suit", and お{口|くち}に{合|あ}う is "to suit your mouth", the polite way to hope someone likes the food you've given them. 〜とうれしいです is "I'd be happy if…".

questions.stem: Lin's email has the subject しゅくだいがおくれたおわび. What does おわび tell the reader?
questions.explanation: おわび is the formal noun "apology", so the subject line says at once that Lin is apologizing for late homework. A thank-you would be おれい, and a reply へんしん.

questions.stem: What is へんしん?
choices: The opening word of a letter
A reply to an email or message
The subject line of an email
questions.explanation: へんしん is a reply to an email or message (also へんしんする). The opening word of a letter is はいけい, a business card めいし, and the subject line けんめい.

questions.stem: Listen. What did you hear?

audio.text: おいそがしいところ、もうしわけありません。

choices: Thank you for being so busy.
Sorry to trouble you when you're busy.
questions.explanation: おいそがしいところ is "at a time when you are busy" (お makes it about the reader), and もうしわけありません is "I'm sorry". It apologizes for taking the other person's time.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese, for the end of an apology email.
questions.prompt: I'm very sorry for the trouble I caused.
questions.explanation: ごめいわくをおかけして、もうしわけありませんでした。 おかけする is humble (you caused the trouble); おかけになる would be honorific, as if the reader had caused it.
